Perry opens five at a time 


Perry Drug Stores cut the ribbons on five new drug stores 
Oct. 23 in simultaneous grand-opening celebrations. 
Among the new units, all located in suburban Detroit com- 
munities, are the chain’s first two stores with drive- 
through pharmacies. The opening events drew a number 
of federal, state, county and city officials, in addition to 
chain chairman and chief executive Jack Robinson (sec- 
ond from left), district manager Gerry Druzinski (far left), 
president Andy Giancamilli and other company brass. The 
new units are located in the towns of Eastpointe, Allen 
Park, Shelby Township, Houghton Lake and Southgate. 


Rockbottom founder Otto 
dead at the age of 95

Rockbottom Stores founder Sam Otto, 
an off-price retail pioneer whose ener- 
gy, entrepreneurial zeal and sound 


business principles helped propel the 
chain into a 39-store, $250 million re- 
gional powerhouse, died Oct. 14 after 
a brief illness. He was 95. 

Otto maintained his boundless en- 
thusiasm for retailing throughout his 
long life, and was at work and still 
visiting stores until just two weeks 
before he died. His tireless work habits, 
coupled with a hands-on approach that never left him and 


the chain drug industry’s most influential and legendary 
figures and the oldest active executive. 

“He was a guy with a great deal of intestinal fortitude, 
strength and vigor who loved his work, and he instilled 
that strength and vigor in the company,” said Richard Otto, 
son of the founder and current chairman and chief execu- 
tive. “He also knew he couldn't retire, because he felt his

Pharmacists file antitrust suits 


to strike back at unfair pricing 


by Ken Rankin 


ATLANTA — Retail phar- 
macists in 15° states 
launched a new offensive in 
the battle against pharma- 
ceutical price discrimination 
with a fresh series of an- 
titrust lawsuits that strike 
at the pharmaceutical in- 
dustry’s jugular: drug man 
ufacturer patent rights. 

The new suits, filed late 
last month by 1,346 commu- 
nity pharmacists from New 
England to Texas, are being 
spearheaded by the Georgia 
Pharmaceutical Association 
(GPhA) as part of the grow- 
ing legal attack on multi- 
tier pricing by drug makers. 

Like dozens of similar 
suits filed during the past 
two years by drug chains 
and independent pharma- 
cists across the country, the 
new actions accuse major 
pharmaceutical manufac- 
turers of engaging in sys- 


tematic price discrimina- 
tion against retail pharma- 
cists in violation of the an- 
titrust laws. 

Unlike those previous 
suits, however, the new fil- 


“The success or 
failure of these 
suits may well 
determine whether 
independent 
pharmacies in 
this country 
survive or die.’ 
—GPhA 


ings raise the ante by ask- 
ing the courts to effectively 
reduce patent protection for 
brand name drugs sold by 
manufacturers who engage 


in discriminatory pricing ac- 
tivities. 

Specifically, the pharma- 
cists in the new series of 
suits “are seeking to gain 
mandatory licensing of the 
manufacturer’s patents at 
reasonable royalty rates to 
all bona fide applicants to 
open the market to compe- 
tition and to cure illegal 
price discrimination,” the 
GPhA said. 

“Drug patents are the 
glue that make this game of 
price fixing work for the 
manufacturers because they 
block competitors from en- 
tering the market and facili- 
tate the group boycott,” said 
Houston attorney Aubrey B. 
Calvin, a spokesman for the 
plaintiffs. 

“Our case clearly will 
show that drug makers are 
using patents as a group 
and in lockstep to block nor- 
mal market forces,” he said.

P&G suit stirs up trade dress debate 


by Mike Troy 
and James Frederick 


WASHINGTON — Proc- 
ter & Gamble’s recent pack- 
aging infringement suit 
against F&M Distributors 
was undertaken reluctantly 
but with the realization that 
a dramatic step was needed 
to draw attention to the is- 
sue, a top company attorney 
said here. 

“It is a delicate matter to 
sue your customers, but we 
felt the need to take a stand,” 
P&G's head trademark attor- 
ney Doug Cherry said. 

The chain drug industry 
took notice in September 
when the consumer prod- 
ucts giant broke tradition 
by filing a trade dress com- 
plaint in court against sev- 
eral private-label manufac- 
turers and F&M. Lawsuits 
alleging package design in- 
fringement are fairly com- 
mon among manufacturers, 
but the action by P&G 
against one of its own retail 
accounts was largely un- 
precedented. 

The well-publicized dis- 
pute centered on five store- 
brand products that the 


supplier charged were near- 
ly identical to the national 
brand. F&M quickly re- 
sponded by removing the of- 
fending products from its 
shelves, but it called P&G’s 
move “highly unusual,” and 
said it was “dismayed” at 
the action, which targeted 
only a small fraction of its 
roughly 500 store-brand 
items. The deep-discount re- 


‘It is a delicate 
matter to sue your 
customers, but we 
felt the need to 


take a stand.’ 
—Cherry, P&G 


tailer also complained that 
it was not contacted about 
the dispute before P&G took 
legal action. 

But the move reflected a 
growing frustration by na- 
tional-brand manufacturers 
with mirror-like packaging 
on store-brand products, and 
revealed the tip of what may 


be a very large iceberg. The 
president of one large pri- 
vate-label supplier acknowl- 
edged that the trade dress 
issue is a hot button in the 
industry, but refused to 
comment directly about the 
lawsuit. For its part, P&G 
said it appears close to set- 
tling the dispute with F&M 
and continues to review pri- 
vate-label package designs 
at other retail locations. 

According to Cherry, “fil- 
ing a complaint is more ef- 
fective than sending a cease 
and desist letter because a 
lawsuit gets immediate at- 
tention. The downside is it 
may not have been neces- 
sary if a letter would have 
sufficed.” 


New approach for some 


In any case, the move 
may have accelerated ef- 
forts already under way at 
some drug chains to shift 
beyond a simple compare-

FTC clears PCS-Lilly roadblock 


SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — Eli Lilly & Co. has agreed 
to antitrust conditions imposed on its planned acquisi- 
tion of McKesson Corp.’s PCS Health Systems by the 
Federal Trade Commission (FTC), clearing the way 
for the deal, which is likely to close this month. 

McKesson announced its intention in July to sell 
PCS, the largest prescription benefits management 
(PBM) firm, to Lilly. Since then, consumer and drug 
industry groups, including NACDS, have come out 
against the planned merger. Opponents have ex- 
pressed concern about the anti-competitive potential 
of a drug company owning a PBM, asserting it could 
allow Lilly to sell more of its own products through a 
restricted formulary and thereby damage competition 
and drive up prices. 

Under an agreement hammered out in late October 
with the FTC, Lilly said it would not restrict access by 
other drug makers to PCS’s drug formulary. The FTC 
agreement also prevents Lilly from seeing bids by 
competing drug manufacturers bidding for inclusion 
on PCS§’s list of preferred drugs. 

A spokesperson for the FTC had earlier declined 
comment on negotiations with Lilly. “We are fore- 
closed by law from confirming or denying that we are 
reviewing the Lilly situation,” said Claudia Bourne 
Farrell, senior press officer for the regulatory agency. 


Pharmacists again “most trusted” 


For the sixth straight year, consumers responding 
to a nationwide Gailup poll have named pharmacists 
as the most trusted professionals in the United 
States. Sixty-two percent of respondents rate the hon- 
esty and ethical standards of pharmacists as “very 
high” or “high,” according to Gallup. 

Clergy members, dentists, college teachers and en- 
gineers rounded out the top five in trustworthiness. 
Bringing up the rear were car salesmen, congressmen, 
insurance salesmen, senators and advertising practi- 
tioners. 

More than 1,000 adults were asked to rate the hon- 
esty and ethical standards of 26 different occupations. 
The survey was conducted Sept. 23-25, 1994. 


Promotions announced at Harco 


Harco Drug veterans John Campbell and Frank 
Gable were promoted to senior vice president posts. 

Campbell, a 14-year Harco veteran who last served 
as comptroller, has been named senior vice president 
of finance. Gable, who joined Harco in 1984 and last 
served as vice president of distribution, will continue 
to head up distribution as senior vice president. 

Other recently announced promotions include the 
appointment of Kie Harrison as director of internal 
auditing. Harrison will be responsible for collecting, 
assimilating and summarizing information to enhance 
the company’s loss-prevention efforts. Harrison has 
been with Harco for 16 years. 

Named director of purchasing is former seasonal and 
general merchandise category manager Gene Bailey. 
With Harco for two years, Bailey is a veteran of Osco, 
Super D and Revco. 


Revco expo benefits Cleveland 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Visitors and participating 
vendors donated over six tons of food for The Cleve- 
land Foodbank during the Revco 1994 Health & Beau- 
ty Expo last month. 

In addition to providing more than 10,000 meals for 
the city’s disadvantaged, the event Oct. 7 and 8 also 
generated plenty of good will and publicity for Revco 
in its home market. The chain estimates that 120,000 
consumers jammed the Cleveland Convention Center 
for the free two-day event. 

The expo featured exhibitors, product demonstra- 
tions and giveaways, beauty makeovers and celebrity 
appearances.

‘Knock off’ the low-price limbo dance 


To me, the Private Label Manufac- 
turers Association’s annual show, 
which takes place this month, is one of 
the most exciting single opportunities 
a retailer could have. But what’s being 
missed by the majority of drug chains 
doing “private label” is the unparal- 
leled opportunity to create a strong 
point of differentiation for a line of 
products that bears your own brand, 
your valued store name. 

I have been dismayed to discover 
that most drug chains approach pri- 
vate-label products with a one-dimen- 


Would I go to that drug chain next 
time to get the store brand that was 
advertised? No, because the ad didn’t 
tell me what made that particular 
store brand better than anyone else’s. 
The fact is, everyone’s got a low-price 
story, although few drug chains can 
compete in the Master’s league with 
the likes of Wal-mart, the warehouse 
clubs and certain deep discounters. 

The low-price game is a dishearten- 
ing limbo—forcing everyone to go low- 
er and lower at the expense of product 
innovation, retailing creativity, and, I 

believe, genuine 


The development of a 
distinctive storewide brand 
. | is not just an antidote to 

>, anemic product margins, it 
is essential to a drug 
chain’s long-term health.

faction.

ment of a distinc-

private brand—

low price—is not

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


sional view: The story is price; the 
message, “compare and save.” I recent- 
ly saw TV ads from one of the top five 
drug chains that was fairly typical. It 
showed a series of brand name prod- 
ucts, followed by store brand versions. 
The voiceover said that the only differ- 
ence between the two products was 
price—and the savings tally was dis- 
played on the screen. 

Guess what message I, the con- 
sumer, received? “Now I feel stupid 
about paying too much for the Advil, 
Scope and Sudafed I already bought.” 


margins. It’s es- 
sential to a drug 
chain’s long-term 
health. 

The idea of a 
store brand is not new. But, during 
the past 10 years, while so many 
chains were scrambling to figure out 
how to compete with Wal-mart and 
the warehouse clubs, a few other re- 
tailers were quietly proving that con- 
sumers will still pay a premium when 
the products appear to be unique and 
the environment in which they are 
sold is special. The Gap, Crate & Bar- 
rel, Victoria’s Secret and The Body 
Shop certainly don’t price and mer- 
chandise their blue jeans, glassware, 
underwear, and skin and bath prod- 


ucts like commodities. 

The technique also works in the 
mass market. One great example 
comes from Wegmans Food Markets, a 
48-store grocery chain based in 
Rochester, NY. 

Wegmans’ television spots promot- 
ing its “Food You Feel Good About” 
line present a stark contrast to the 
drug chain ads I mentioned earlier. 
Wegmans aggressively markets this 
brand—which encompasses some 200 
products—around product distinctions 
with genuine consumer appeal: high 
quality natural products, specially se- 
lected, that are “affordable.” 

One ad talks about how Wegmans 
journeys across the country to find 
products, so you see New England 
fishermen unloading fresh seafood 
from a boat. In another spot, an 
African American “dad” appears with 
his “son” and the voiceover talks about 
how food with “natural goodness” is 
good for “your children and you.” The 
ads show “real” people in varied set- 
tings; the song has the catchy refrain, 
“wonderful world, beautiful people.” 

After seeing any one of those ads, I 
would go out of my way to try some of 
Wegmans’ foods, which, by the way, 
are also beautifully and distinctively 
packaged. Because I know I can’t get 
this line anywhere else, I wouldn’t be 
worrying about the price. Drug chains 
may not be at the forefront of this 
trend, but you don’t have to wait to 
jump on it. While some of the old 
“knockoff” mentality remains, most 
private-label manufacturers today are 
ready, willing and able to work with 
you to create packaging, programs and 
even products that will help you tell a 
unique story to your customers. Take 
advantage of this opportunity. Now.

Suddenly, pharmacy ethics is a hot

from Food and Drug Commissioner 
David Kessler to the faceless gnomes 
in the federal Medicaid bureaucracy 
are wrestling with the propriety—in- 
deed, the legality—of managed care- 
style product movement “incentive 
programs.” 


cern in many quarters is that these in- 
centive programs create a real and 
very substantial conflict of interest for 
pharmacists. 

Sifting through such thorny ethical 
issues is the responsibility of the 
watchdog of pharmacy’s professional 
standards—the American Pharmaceu- 
tical Association (APhA). 

And just last 


interest.

| quarters is that incentive 
programs create a real and 
very substantial conflict of 


month APhA 
moved to address 
the ethics of in- 
centive programs 
by proposing new 
guidelines on the 
subject, along 
with a major 
overhaul of the 
association’s 13-

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


Pharmacists participating in these 
programs are compensated for con- 
vincing prescribers to “switch” pa- 
tients from drugs made by competing 
manufacturers to those sold by the 
sponsoring manufacturer. 

You got a problem with that? If so, 
you have a lot of company. The con- 


Declaring the 
current 1981 ver- 
sion of the Code 
too paternalistic, 
APhA staffers are pushing a political- 
ly-correct rewrite that requires phar- 
macists to respect “cultural differences 
among patients,” avoid “discriminato- 
ry practices” on the job and “seek jus- 
tice in the distribution of health re- 
sources.” 

Deleted from APhA’s proposed new 


4 Drug Store News, November 7, 1994 


PC version: the long-standing ethical 
proscription against kickback schemes, 
which admonishes pharmacists to “nev- 
er agree to, or participate in transac- 
tions” that cause financial “exploitation 
in connection with the rendering of pro- 
fessional services.” 

Meanwhile, the association’s pro- 
posed new interpretive guidelines for 
pharmacist incentive programs— 
which were released along with the 
proposed Ethics Code rewrite— would 
offer pharmacists an ethical green 
light to accept payment for participat- 
ing in almost any managed care or in- 
dustry-sponsored scheme to increase 
one drug manufacturer’s market share 
at the expense of another’s. 

Under APhA’s plan, it would even 
be acceptable for pharmacists to par- 
ticipate in incentive programs that 
push alternative drugs that offer no 
therapeutic or economic benefit to the 
patient at all! 

To be sure, APhA’s proposed guide- 
lines do discourage pharmacists from 
accepting payment for dispensing a 
less effective drug than the one pre- 
scribed, or for pushing drug therapy 
that would actually harm the patient. 

But is this ethical threshold high 
enough for the nation’s most trusted 
profession? APhA is waiting for your 
comments.

Improved products and packaging, 
strong marketing elevate’ private label 


by Jim Frederick 
tore brands, which have ex- 
ploded in popularity over the 
past decade, continue to chew 
mo up more of the nation’s gro- 
cery, drug and general merchandise 
business. And retailers are reaping 
the lion’s share of the profits in this 
high-margin category as private label 
manufacturers wage a pitched compet- 
itive battle with one another to deliver 
high-quality goods at low prices. 

Fueling the steady growth of store 
brands is a potent blend of internal 
and external factors. Among the 
biggest: 

@ A middle-class consumer base that 
seems to have become permanently 
cost-conscious, the economic recovery 
notwithstanding; 

e “The vast improvement in the 
quality of the products, packaging and 
labeling, to the point where store 
brands often match or exceed the na- 
tional brands,” as consumer products 
analyst Gabe Lowy of Oppenheimer & 
Co. put it; 

e A continuing price gap between 
store and national brands, despite 
everyday low price moves by some 
suppliers like Procter & Gamble. 

e An increasingly high-tech commu- 
nity of suppliers able to deliver consis- 
tently high-quality products and pack- 
aging on demand and to offer EDI 
capabilities and other value-added 
services; 

e A more sophisticated retail com- 
munity intent on maximizing gross 
margins and store-brand equity 
through more intensive marketing and 
quality-control efforts—efforts that 
nurture both their own brand and 
their store’s overall image. Mouth- 
wash, light bulbs and soft drinks are 
making strong gains. 

What’s more, private label manufac- 
turers have high hopes for explosive 
sales growth in OTC medicines, given 
the outlook for rapid Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) approval of pre- 
scription-to-OTC product switches in 
the next few years. “We believe the 
Rx-to-OTC switches approved by the 
FDA will be able to make significant 
product claims, and we think there’s 
clearly going to be some new opportu- 
nity for retailers and manufacturers,” 
said Michael Jandernoa, president and 
chief executive of Perrigo Co. 

Ken Gordon, president of the Retail 


Division of Shuster Inc., a firm which 
specializes in the development and en- 
hancement of store-brand programs, 
agrees that prescription-to-OTC 
switches could yield big store-brand 
benefits in coming years. He also sees 
major potential in what he dubs “nu- 
traceuticals” or herbal medications, di- 
etary supplements and homeopathic 
remedies. 


Growing marketing efforts 


Drug chains still enjoy a natural ad- 
vantage in marketing private-label 
versions of HBA and OTC products, 
noted Private Label Manufacturers As- 
sociation (PLMA) president 
Brian Sharoff. But the rapid 
gains made by mass mer- 
chants in recent years under- 
score the growing competition 
for store-brand loyalty by re- 
tailers who are injecting new 
marketing and merchandis- 
ing muscle into their private- 
label items.

Marketing elevates’ private label 


Continued from page 11 
Added David Biernbaum, 
a St. Louis-based marketing 
consultant and former presi- 
dent of Vi-Jon Laboratories, 
“Where private label will 
thrive in the future is in 
brand equity. More than 
ever, the store brand has to 
fit into and work with the 


overall marketing image of 
the store.” 

Store brands, Biernbaum 
said, “should help to define 
the store’s point of differ- 
ence from its competitors.” 
He cited mass merchants 
like Kmart, Wal-Mart and 
Target Stores for their abili- 
ty to create store brands 


with strong department 
identity and strong con- 
sumer loyalty within areas 
of the store like toiletries, 
OTC medicines, cosmetics 
and personal care items. 
Among them: Kmart’s Relief 
Plus line of OTC medica- 
tions and Little Ones brand 
of children’s products. 


Drug chains probably 
don’t need that kind of de- 
partmentalized approach, 
primarily because their store 
brands already do—or 
should—carry a_ strong 
health and beauty care con- 
notation. But like their high- 
er-volume counterparts, 
drug retailers are beefing up 


store-brand marketing ef- 
forts. Prompted by increas- 
ingly sophisticated store per- 
formance data that 
highlights the bottom-line 
contribution of store brands 
vs. weaker’ secondary 
brands, a growing number of 
drug chains are promoting 
their own brand in their reg- 


ular ad vehicles, including 
radio, television and circu- 
lars. 


Stores market their own 


Among the most aggres- 
sive are CVS—which has 
developed a series of TV 
spots for its own brand— 
and Phar-Mor, which 
launched its own line of soft 
drinks early this year with 
a major in-store and print 
promotional campaign. Oth- 
er aggressive private label 
advertisers include Revco 
D.S., Walgreens, Thrift 
Drug— which last year to- 
tally redesigned its line of 
850 store-brand items—and 
Genovese Drug Stores. 

Walgreens got a potent 
dose of free image-building 
publicity earlier this year, 
when a Boston newspaper

“The bottom line is that 
companies that just do the 
commodity business are go- 
ing to be out of business,” 
said Biernbaum. He de- 
scribed a shift in which re- 
tailer gross margins for pri- 
vate label have gone up 
while manufacturer margins 
have shrunk for many items 
“into the single digits.” 

Margins for the suppliers 
are “really thin” in products 
like mouthwash, admitted 
one manufacturer, who said 
“a number of [second-tier] 
companies are facing severe 
situations in what to do 
with their business.” 

Adding to the pressure is 
the fact that the major- 
brand suppliers are learning 
to adapt to private label— 
both by lowering their own

has been raised in terms of 


what private-label suppliers 
need to provide. We’re going 
to have to upgrade our-

manufacture [me-too prod- 
ucts] and deliver them at 
low cost.” 


Prices go down 


Added Gordon of Shuster, 
“The national-brand compa-

more and more are coming 
down in price. It puts a 
squeeze on private label 
manufacturers, and one re- 
sult is consolidation.” 

PLMA head _  Sharoff 
agreed, but added that new 
players continue to spring 
up to fill niches and new op- 
portunities. He referred to 
this year’s PLMA annual 
convention, which will fea- 
ture a record 1,300 ex- 
hibitors. “Every time there’s 
a merger, there’s two new 
guys on the block,” he said.

Pictured is part of the lineup of new Quality Choice (QC) brand 
private-label products available to members of Chain Drug Mar- 
keting Association (CDMA) beginning Jan. 1, 1995. The CDMA 
will initially launch a selection of more than 400 products devel- 
oped by private-label specialist Shur-Fine, including a broad se- 
lection of health and beauty care items. CDMA will handle all or- 
ders and billing, as well as delivery on a 10-day cycle. The

greater than anticipated among the 60 companies in the group.

Premier: The other name in foot care 


“We have made Dr. 
Scholl's stand up and 
take notice of us,” said 
Steven D. Corsun, 
President of Premier 
Brands of America, Inc. 
“Now we intend to make 
them run for their life.” 

The days of one 
national company 
controlling the market- 
place with foot health 
and shoe care products 
has come to a close. 
Premier offers consumers 
and drug store chains a 
cost-saving alternative, 
plus a way to increase 
bottom-line profits with the 
only line of independent 
laboratory-tested national 
brand equivalent products. 

A recent survey by Towne- 
Oller & Associates, Inc., a 
national market data company, 
supports Corsun’s views. For a 
12-month period through 
November 1993 vs. November 
1992, Dr. Scholl’s sales were 
down 9 percent, while private 


label sales increased 15 percent. 
Until this decade, most drug 
store chains had only one foot 
care supplier. That’s like 
saying, “I already stock one 
shampoo, so why do I need 
another?” Research shows that 
there is a significant increase in 
total category movement when 
consumers are given a choice. 


People in the foot 
care business estimate 
that the entire industry 

is growing. Currently 

the foot care market is 
in excess of one-half 
billion dollars at retail. 
By 1996, it’s expected to 
double to $1 billion at 
retail (drug, food and 
mass merchandisers). 
“Drug chains currently 
have $200 million of that 
business,” Corsun said. “Re- 
cent increased dollars have 
caused the chain drug 
industry to redress their line 
and advertise private label 
products.” 

According to Corsun, Dr. 
Scholl's allows drug chains to 
make just slightly over 40 
percent profit. “However, few 
chains get that because of the 
competitive marketplace. 
Instead, chains average between 
20 percent and 30 percent.” 

When a chain drug store adds 
Premier private label products, 
the retailer makes in excess of a 


Call Premier today at (718) 522-0520 


Premier Brands of America Inc., 127 Wallabout St., Brooklyn, NY 11206 


50 percent profit. Plus, at the 
same time the per-package 
retail is generally 30 percent to 
50 percent below Dr. Scholl's. 
This enables consumers to 
realize a substantial savings on 
a private label foot care 
product which is of equal 
quality to Dr. Scholl's. 

“By offering Premier 
products, drug store chains 
prevent their customers from 
switching to mass merchandis- 
ers or supermarkets to get a 
better deal,” Corsun explained. 

No other category in HBA is 
dominated by one company like 
the foot care category. Give 
yourself a choice of suppliers 
rather than depending on only 
one. Premier is the only full line 
of medicated and non- 
medicated foot care pads and 
remedies other than Dr. Scholl's. 

Premier knows that in the 
past foot care has not been 
thought of as a strong profit 
center. Now, buyers have an 
opportunity to make it their 
highest grossing section.

| NAIL CARE SPECIAL REPORT 


Nail care offers double-digit growth at chains 


Continued from page S1 

aggressive in expanding nail care at 
the beginning of the growth curve, 
that reacted by quickly adding 
many new lines to test their appeal 
to consumers and that kept expand- 
ing space as the category kept 
growing, now are reporting that 
growth is starting to moderate, 
ranging between the low to high 
teens on average. 

On the other hand, chains that 
initially took a conservative ap- 
proach to the category, but who 
have been more aggressive in the 
last two years in adding lines, ex- 
panding space or using POS scan- 
ning data to manage SKU prof- 
itability within individual lines, are 
reporting gains as high as 30 per- 
cent vs. a year ago. 

“The growth in nail care for us is 


not what it was on the front end of 


the launch of professional lines,’ 
said Steve Lubin, divisional mer- 
chandise manager of cosmetics for 
Deerfield, Ill.-based Walgreens. 

“But we were one of the first to 
expand manicure, adding lines like 
IBD’s Five Second Nail and Kiss 
long before anyone else did. Today 
almost everyone has a professional 
salon section in their planogram, 
and continued growth is much more 
of a challenge.” 

Lubin said the category remains a 
major contributor to the productivity 
of Walgreens stores, growing ata 
rate faster than the cosmetics cate- 
gory as a whole. “Manicure is still an 
excellent category overall. We’re still 
supporting it. In our last reset, we 
added more lines, and that’s to help 
us keep it viable and help maintain 
its momentum,” Lubin said. 


A view from a competitor 


Other channels of distribution are 
having similar experiences. 

“There’s been a tremendous 
growth in nail salons,” said Mary 
St. Ledger, who buys nail care for 
The Cosmetic Center, a 60-store 
specialty beauty chain based in Sav- 
age, Md., “and as a result, more and 
more women are using artificial 
nails. But a nail salon will charge 
$40, sometimes more to apply 
acrylic nails, and many women 
know they can save money by buy- 
ing their false nails in retail stores 
and applying them at home. 

“Nail color goes 
in cycles,” 


she pointed out. “It.can be up or 
down depending on fashion, but 
women always need nail treatments, 
and as long as they want their own 

natural nails to be healthy and 
beautiful, they will come to your 
stores to buy treatments.” 

Because she buys for a specialty 
beauty store chain, St. Ledger has 
been able to expand her professional 

nail care planogram to include some 
professional salon brands that 
aren't available to most mass mar- 
ket retailers. 

“A person who starts doing her 
nails at home has probably had 
them done before in a_ salon,” she 
said, “so when she comes to a store 
to buy kits to do her nails at home, 
she looks for the brand names she’s 
seen in the salons. 

“We do a very good business with 
professional nail salon brands,” St. 
Ledger said. In the franchised seg- 
ment, St. Ledger said her strongest 
growing brand is Cosmar with its 
LaJoie Press & Go and its new Pro 
10 line. 

Sally Hansen treatments are 
showing strong growth in Cosmetic 
Center stores. St. Ledger said Sally 
Hansen is one of the lines she regu- 
larly promotes be- 
cause it has 
such a 


strong 
brand 
following. 

“Their cuticle 
creams do particularly well as does 
Maximum Growth. And recently 
we've experienced a _mega-surge of 
their buffing creams.’ 

St. Ledger also thinks that Kristy 
Wells has done a good job reposi- 
tioning its nail care line. 

“The idea of packaging nails by 
size 1s great because it makes it eas- 
ier for women to find the size 
that’s right for their nails. 

“I also like their educational 
pamphlets because they ex- 
plain each process in an 
easy-to-understand, step-by- 
step fashion,” St. Ledger 


added.

Helps build traffic 


. “Right now, we’re seeing 
‘significant increases in every 
single line, including Cosmar, 
Jonel, Nailene, Kiss, Sally

In what is turning out to be 
very good news for mass market 
retailers, women can’t seem to 
get enough of a good thing when 
it comes to nail care products. 

According to Nails magazine, a 
leading trade magazine for the 
nail salon industry, women spent 
nearly $4.9 billion in beauty sa- 
lons last year, $200 million more 
than they spent the year before 
for salon services and profession- 
al salon brand nail care products. 

Sixty-four percent of their 
dollars ($3.1 billion) in fact, 
were spent on acrylic false nails, 
the long-wearing false nails that 
have to be bonded to and then 
sculptured over natural nails. 
That was a total increase of 
$181 million, or 6 percent over 
what they spent on false nails in 
1993. 

Acrylic nails are now the 
fastest growing service in beauty 
salons, but when women have to 
pay an average $41.83 for a full 
acrylic and $20.74 for a fill-in, 
which they need about every two

nail care sales boom 


weeks, and when they have to 
pay an average of $40.21 for full 
tips or $38.62 for a nail strength- 
ening silk wrap, it’s inevitable 
that opportunities will arise for 
do-it-yourself products like 
acrylic nails, French manicures, 
silk wraps and sculptured nails 
that women can buy at retail and 
apply at home. The service price

Wal-Mart expands planograms 


According to one knowledgeable 
source, Wal-Mart, one of the first 
mass merchandisers to test false 
nails and professional nail care 
products, plans to introduce three 
new expanded nail care plano- 
grams next year. Its biggest 
planogram will give 16 feet to the 
department. 

In its new planogram, Wal-Mart 
has carved out space for Cosmar, 
Nailene, Fing’rs, Jonel, Sally

treatment products. 

One cosmetician in a Florida-

finding that when we add new lines, 
they take off immediately and with-

NAIL CARE SPECIAL REPORT 


f you want to find out what 

women are doing to their nails, 

visit a nail salon. 
~ According to a survey done by the 
Beauty and Barber Supply Institute 
and published in Nails magazine, 
almost half of all American women, 
41 percent, have visited a nail sa- 
lon for some type of service at 
some time in their life, and 
half of these women say they 
feel pampered while they are 
getting their nails done pro- 
fessionally. 

Eight out of 10 salon vis- 
itors are current cus- 
tomers, according to the 
survey, having gone to a Sa- 
lon at least once in the past 
12 months. 

But while women certainly 

support the salon industry, 

they are not always happy 
about all aspects of the experi- 
ence. 

The study showed that while 
many women may like being pam- 
pered in a salon, many salon users 
(62 percent) feel that it costs too 
much to have a professional mani- 
cure done in a salon, and 67 percent 
said they don’t have a lot of time to 
spend on nail care, which is good 
news for retailers who sell “do-it- 
yourself” nail care products to con- 
venience- and value-minded Ameri- 
can women. 

Once a retailer knows what a sa- 
lon customer wants, it’s just a mat- 
ter of finding a manufacturer who 
can supply the appropriate item (or 
something very similar), adding it 
to the mix and then letting the word 
seep out through advertising or 
word of mouth. 

But what do women want in nail 
care? Yesterday, it was acrylic 
nails, glue-on nails, nail repair kits, 
glue that didn’t unglue, treatments 
that strengthened and fortified the 
nails, French manicures and sheer 
nails.

spent 90 percent of her time apply-

COLOR COSMETICS 


Color cosmetic outlook brighter for drug chains 


by Liz Parks 


lthough market research data 
showed that color cosmetic 
sales for the first half of 1994 
were soft in drug stores, some lead- 
ing chain drug stores are starting to 
report more robust sales, thanks in 
part to strong new launches from 


Revlon, the continuing strength of 


Maybelline’s Revitalizing and the 
marketing initiatives of Procter & 
Gamble and L’Oreal. 

In addition, a new analysis of 
drug store sales data, commissioned 
by P&G, one of the industry’s lead- 
ing cosmetic manufacturers, indi- 
cates a more rosy picture. 

The report, implemented by Chica- 
go-based Information Resources Inc. 
(IRI), a leading market research com- 
pany that tracks retail sales through 
drug, food and mass merchandise 
stores, indicates that the softness in 
drug store sales is primarily due to 
declining cosmetic sales in deep dis- 
count drug stores and in indepen- 
dently owned drug stores. 


John Devine, P&G’s director of 


business development for the chain 
drug store industry, reported that 
83 percent of the chain drug stores 
analyzed in this special report, 
done exclusively for P&G, showed 
incremental gains in cosmetic sales. 
The average traditional chain drug 
store was up 3 percent in units and 


4 percent in dollars for the first half 


of the year,

store data base, and 
their sales have 
been soft,” Devine

sales in several years, and one-on- 
one interviews with over a dozen 
traditional drug chains in the in- 
dustry’s top 50 rank, confirm that 
the numbers are looking positive 
and have been since April when 
many new launches debuted in 
chain drug stores. 

Forty percent of the drug chains 
interviewed for this report said 
their color cosmetic sales were ei- 
ther flat or up in low single-digit in- 
crements. Two chains said they 
were seeing above-average growth, 
and the rest said that while their 
basic business is still disappointing, 
some of the new product launches 
are doing very well and may be a 
sign of better days to come.

WHOLESALER REPORT 


Chain drug industry sees wholesale changes 


by Ken Rankin 


he chain drug industry is rely- 

ing more heavily than ever on 

wholesale druggists as a sup- 
ply source for prescription drugs, 
OTCs and health & beauty care 
products. 

According to the newly-published 
National Wholesale Druggists Asso- 
ciation 1994 Fact Book, NWDA 
member sales to chain drug stores 
jumped 15 percent last year to a 
record $8.8 billion—more than dou- 
ble total wholesale industry sales to 
drug chains in 1986. 

Gross sales to independent phar- 
macies also increased in 1993, ris- 
ing 4.7 percent to $14.2 billion, re- 
flecting a 79-percent increase in 
wholesale drug dollar sales to inde- 
pendents since 1986. 

But while wholesale druggists are 
selling more and more to drug 
chains and independents, the na- 
tion’s wholesalers are relying less 
on retail drug stores for their 
growth. 

Despite increased 


$47.5 billion. 

Estimates based on a nationwide 
survey by NWDA and Drug Store 
News’ sister publication, Drug Store 
News For The Pharmacist, suggest 
that gross sales by the nation’s 
wholesale druggists should top $53 
billion this year. 


Fewer wholesalers, more sales 


These increases have taken place 
despite a steady trend toward con- 
solidation throughout the wholesale 
drug industry. As a result of merg- 
ers and bankruptcies over the past 
15 years, the number of U.S. drug 
wholesalers has dropped by nearly 
50 percent from 139 in 1980 to 70 at 
the start of 1994. 

Similarly, the number of distribu- 
tion centers operated by wholesale 
druggists has also fallen sharply, 
from 347 in 1980 to 232 this year, 
according to NWDA. 

The result has been a significant 
increase in the volume of pharma- 
ceuticals and other products moved 
through wholesaler warehouses.

represented two-thirds of the total 
market for wholesalers. 

If this trend continues, within a 
decade the wholesale drug industry 
could be generating the majority of 
its sales volume from customers 
outside traditional retail drug store 
channels. 

Food store chains and mass mer- 
chandisers such as Kmart and Wal- 
Mart are becoming increasingly im- 
portant to the wholesale drug 
industry’s customer mix. 

Purchases by these chains from 
wholesale druggists climbed 37 per- 
cent last year to $2.3 billion—6 per- 
cent of total wholesaler sales, and a 
sixfold increase since 1986. 

Hospitals, nursing homes and 
clinics are also turning increasingly 
to drug wholesalers to supply them 
with pharmaceutical products. 

Hospitals alone purchased $11.2 
billion from wholesale druggists in 
1993—up 19 percent from the prior 
year, and more than triple the level 
of 1986. 

Sales to clinics and nursing 
homes are rising even faster—up 
336 percent since 1990 to $1.2 bil- 
lion last year. 

Total sales to all customers by the 
nation’s drug wholesalers—includ- 
ing “non-stock” sales of prescription 
products to chain drug warehous- 
es—rose by 12 percent last year to 


tion centers at 

many wholesale 
drug companies. But they also rep- 
resent a commitment to state-of- 
the-art technology that has pro- 
duced significant improvements in 
productivity by wholesalers. 

The bulk of sales generated by 
wholesale druggists has traditional- 
ly come from prescription pharma- 
ceuticals. If anything, legend drugs 
are an even more important strong- 
hold for the industry today. 

Last year more than $31 billion 
worth of prescription drug products 
were distributed by the nation’s 
drug wholesalers—a 10-percent in- 
crease over 1992 and double the in- 
dustry’s prescription volume in 
1987. 

While prescription drugs account 
for 80.7 percent of the average 
wholesale druggist’s gross stock 
sales, OTC products represent just 
under 10 percent of the total. 

During 1993 wholesaler sales of 
non-prescription drugs reached $3.7 
billion, an increase of 7 percent over

McKesson posts mixed 


second quarter results 


SAN FRANCISCO 
Paced by its McKesson 
Drug Co. division, 
McKesson Corp. reported 
an 8.9 percent increase in 
revenue to $3.26 billion for 
the second quarter ended 
Sept. 30, 1994. But one- 
time charges and the con- 
tinuing pressure of compe- 
tition on gross margins put 
a squeeze on earnings. 

McKesson’s operating 
profit declined 26.6 percent 
vs. the same period last 
year, to $30.6 million. In- 
cluding income of $8.4 mil- 
lion from discontinued oper- 
ations, principally PCS 
Health Systems, net income 
declined 14 percent to $25.5 
million for the quarter. (In 
July, McKesson announced 
it had entered into an 
agreement to sell PCS to Eli 
Lilly and Co. The transac- 
tion is awaiting clearance 
by regulatory agencies.) 

Before special items, prin- 


cipally a previously an- 
nounced credit reserve, 
earnings from continuing 
operations were $23.7 mil- 
lion, up 6 percent from the 
second quarter of last year. 

Special items included a 
charge of roughly $7 million 
due to a credit loss from a 
problem receivable involv- 
ing a drug store customer. 

For the six-month period, 
McKesson Corp. revenue 
rose 9.6 percent to $6.5 bil- 
lion, while operating profit 
declined 34.3 percent to 
$79.7 million and net in- 
come fell 4.1 percent to 
$61.5 million. 

McKesson’s Health Care 
Services unit, including 
McKesson Drug Co., com- 
prised $3.1 billion of total 
revenues for the fiscal 1995 
second quarter and showed 
operating profit of $33 mil- 
lion, down 21.8 percent 
compared with the same 
quarter last year. 


FoxlMeyer sees income gain 


DALLAS — FoxMeyer Health Corp. reported an increase 
in net income to $6.7 million on sales of $1.3 billion for the 
second quarter ended Sept. 30, 1994. 

Net sales declined slightly for the quarter and were flat 
for the first half. Net income was $11.9 million on sales of 
$2.5 billion for the six-month period, with operating income 
rising to $25.1 million, up 21.9 percent from last year. 

The company reported improved gross margins from roll- 
out of programs with higher-margin products and services. 
These include its Pharmasure generic pharmaceutical line, 
and expanding managed care business through Scrip Card 
Enterprises, a pharmacy benefits management company 


acquired in April.

Wal-Mart Canada cuts tobacco 


TORONTO — Bowing to growing regulatory pres- 
sure against the sale and use of tobacco in Canada, 
Wal-Mart Canada said it would voluntarily halt the 
sale of tobacco products in its-122 stores across the 
country. 

The company confirmed it has stopped ordering new 
tobacco products and is selling off existing stocks. The 
move was prompted by pending legislation in Ontario 
under Bill 119, which prohibits tobacco sales in all 
stores in the province that contain pharmacies, and by 
federal government efforts to discourage demand for 
tobacco products. 


Thrifty PayLess fine-tunes staff 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — Seven promotions were an- 
nounced recently by Thrifty PayLess as the merged 
chain continues to fine-tune its restructured staff. 

Andy Striefel has been named senior vice president 
of merchandise. Striefel, formerly vice president, has 
been with PayLess 27 years. 

Among other appointments, Jim Glime was named 
regional vice president of field merchandising for the 
northern stores and James Toney will hold the same 
position for the south. Glime was last with Kmart 
while Toney has worked for Thrifty since 1979. 

(In the Oct. 24 issue of DrSN, Roger Parisotto and 
Vince DiMaggio were inadvertently named as holding 
these positions. Parisotto is regional vice president for 
the northwest, DiMaggio is regional vice president for 
Northern California and Ron Payton is regional vice 
president for Southern California.) 

Other promotions announced after the company’s 
November board meeting include Don Davis to senior 
vice president of information systems; Jim Hamilton 
to senior vice president of human resources; Dennis 
Down to vice president of human resources, Sandie 
Schuler to vice president of benefits/payroll; Robert 
Sari to vice president of legal affairs; and Steven Self 
to group vice president of risk management. 


Rocheleau joins Vons 


ARCADIA, Calif. — Gary Rocheleau has joined The 
Vons Companies as vice president overseeing general 
merchandise. Rocheleau formerly was executive vice 
shar oni of merchandising and marketing for Thrifty 

ayLess Drug Stores. Prior to that, he was vice presi- 
dent in charge of grocery buying for Lucky Stores. 

Rocheleau is assuming a post last held by Bob 
Smith, who has been named vice president in charge 
of the meat division. 


Kmart launches home delivery 


TROY, Mich. — Joining a growing throng of drug 
and supermarket chains offering home delivery ser- 
vices, art Corp. began testing same-day delivery 
service in its Phoenix-area stores this month. The test 
makes Kmart the first mass merchandise chain to of- 
fer the service, according to the company. 

Consumers in the Phoenix market can consult a cata- 
logue to order a wide range of products, including pre- 
scription drugs, via toll-free S sacs number or fax 24 
hours a day, seven days a week. Orders are delivered 
twice daily, and include a charge of $2 for pharmacy or- 
ders and $5.95 for general merchandise delivery. 

The service is offered through Bethesda, Md.-based 
Shoppers Express, which now provides delivery ser- 
vice on a contract basis with retailers in 28 states.

Retailers plan for mild cough/cold season 


by Mike Troy 


A severe cough/cold sea- 
son during the holidays and 
into the new year exerts a 
strong influence on chain 
drug store sales. Last win- 
ter’s harsh season led to 
gains in cough/cold category 
sales and helped generate 
store traffic that gave retail- 
ers opportunities to move 
products in other categories. 

This year—with early in- 
dications forecasting a 
milder flu season—retailers 
may have to look for other 
traffic-building strategies. 

“Right now, we are signif- 
icantly below last year [in 
cough/cold sales],” said An- 
drew Kress, vice president 


of Surveillance Data, Inc. 
(SDI). “Our projection for 
the remainder of the calen- 
dar year is that we will con- 
tinue to be below last year.” 
With fewer people getting 
sick this year, Kress predicts 
cough/cold brands will wage 
a market share war that in- 
cludes more spending on ad- 
vertising and promotion. 
Manufacturers of many of 
the leading brands, as well 
as major retailers, rely on 
SDI’s Flu-Cold-Respiratory 
Illness Activity Notification 
Program to provide advance 
warning of cold and flu out- 
breaks. For 12 years, SDI 
has used a network of 1,700 
health professionals in 71 
markets nationwide to gath- 
er data on illness. Using a 


computer model and its ex- 
tensive data base, SDI is 
able to successfully forecast 
market by market when 
outbreaks are likely. 

The usefulness of such 
data can be seen by compar- 
ing cough/cold seasons from 
the previous two years. De- 
mand for products during 
the 1992-93 season remained 
steady throughout the win- 
ter months as there was no 
major cough/cold outbreak, 
Kress noted. However, last 
season saw strong demand 
from September through De- 
cember and then a sharp in- 
crease in January. 

Retailers alerted to the 
January outbreak were able 
to deepen inventories in an- 
ticipation of demand.

responsibilities and levels of control.

new people who came on board with 
HSI stores. How will they take to the 
“revved up” pace, the by-the-book con- 
trols, the strong reliance on technolo- 
gy, the relative lack of store-level deci- 
sion making? 

Dwayne Hoven acknowledges the 
culture shock, but he believes that the 
speed of the changes will actually 
make them easier to take, because, as 
he points out, the people will also see 
the results— presumably, extremely 
positive ones—in short order.

drives up the price of medicine to all

playing field and survive the competi-

pharmacy providers.

store industry to recognize that gain- 
ing equal access to fair prices from 
pharmaceutical manufacturers won't 
eliminate all the unfair pricing prac- 
tices that force them to charge artifi- 
cially high prices to their customers.

Triple A 
rduct St 


The hottest items driving select categories 


eeping the cash registers ringing 
steadily is the name of the game in re- 
tailing. But achieving that kind of mu- 
sic is a complicated process that retail- 
ers eternally struggle with. 

A large part of the solution is carrying the 
products consumers want to buy. 

The Triple A study sheds a lot of light on that 
subject. 

Culled from the database compiled by New 
York-based Towne-Oller & Associates, a divi- 
sion of Information Resources Inc., the Triple A 
study is a record of the best-selling items within 


a category, based on the year ending July 1994. 
In this study, seven product categories are pro- 
filed. Five are HBA categories: digestives, foot 
care, fragrances, hair care and vitamins. Two are 
GM categories: batteries and camera film. To- 
gether, these categories represent some 15 per- 
cent of chain drug sales. And the 25 top-selling 
items command up to 40 percent of their category. 
Some of the categories are more fragmented 
than others. In the foot care category, for exam- 
ple, the top 25 items account for nearly 40 per- 
cent of saies, and three manufacturers domi- 
nate the list. In the vitamins/nutritional 


category, the top 25 items account for more 
than a quarter (27.9 percent) of sales, and seven 
manufacturers are part of that honor roll. 

And growth rates also vary widely. Vita- 
mins/nutritionals, growing 17 percent as a cate- 
gory, also posted the most consistent growth 
within the top 25: a couple of new items explod- 
ed with four-digit increases; another 15 posted 
double-digit increases as high as 77 percent. 

Please note: Dollar volume, included in the 
majority of charts, is missing in some because of 
a lack of availability. But percent of market 
share is present.

PLMA spotlights 
store brand winners 


The Private Label Manufacturers Association honored 
some of the best and brightest in store-brand innovation 
at the conclusion of its 1994 Private Label Trade Show in 
Chicago last month. The show drew a record attendance 
from over 2,000 retailers and wholesalers and more than 


Presented with “Salute to Excellence” Awards were 
Walgreens, for best chain drug store brand program; CVS, 
for best television commercials; and Phar-Mor, for best 
private label advertising and promotion. 

Accepting the awards at a gala dinner concluding the 
trade show were (I-r, top row) Tom Sullivan, CVS; Scott 
Gorley and Bill Wolpe, Phar-Mor; Michael Smith, Wal- 
greens; (front row) Dan Maher, Phar-Mor; and Albert Tuhy 
and John Tuteur, both of Walgreens.

and chief ex-

21 units on

million in the six months 
ended in August. The result-

Rite Aid targets Manhattan 


with supermarket purchase 


by Lisa |. Fried 


NEW YORK — Despite its 
affluent, well-educated con- 
sumer base and dense popu- 
lation, Manhattan has been 
largely ignored by the lead- 
ing drug chains— until] now. 

In late November, Rite 
Aid Corp. became the third- 
largest chain operator in the 
city by purchasing up to 20 
stores from the Red Apple 
Group, which operates 
Sloan’s, Gristedes and Red 
Apple supermarkets. The 
majority of stores are locat- 
ed in Manhattan, with addi- 
tional stores based in Long 
Island and Westchester. 

The price of the sale was 
not disclosed. The stores 
range in size from 5,000 to 
10,000 square feet. 


Serious competition 


Rite Aid’s Manhattan 
push will give Duane Reade 
its first serious competition 
from a national chain. Du- 
ane Reade has built most of 
its 52-store base in New 
York’s central borough, 
where Love’s operates 24 
stores and Pathmark, and 


more recently, Genovese, 
have only dabbled. The mar- 


Despite the 
entrance of a 
heavy hitter, the 
city is large and 
diverse enough 
for chains and 
independents 
to flourish. 


ket could heat up even fur- 
ther next year, as Woolworth 
is considering opening 15 
more Drug Marts in the city. 
It currently operates eight. 
Most drug retailers have 
been put off by the city’s sky- 
high real estate costs. 
Despite the entrance of a 
heavy hitter into the mar- 
ket, the city is large and di- 
verse enough for both inde- 
penderts and chains to 
flourish, according to Len 
Genovese, chairman and

Stores, which opened its 
first store in Manhattan 
last year. 

Woolworth vp/general 
manager Joe Dickerson 
agrees. “The percentage of 
chain business done here 
compared to the rest of the 
country is quite small,” he 
said. “There are plenty of 
people to service.” 

Duane Reade executives 
did not return calls from 
Drug Store News. 

Although the sale was an- 
nounced last month, the 
transfer of ownership will 
occur in stages to give Red 
Apple time to shut down 
and empty the units. Rite 
Aid will actually buy 10 
stores by the end of Decem- 
ber and the rest by the end 
of March, according to John 
Catsimatidis, chairman of 
the Red Apple Group.

had hoped to conclude the

the deal on hold until No- 
vember. On Nov. 23, Red

Redefining convenience 


by Mike Troy 


onvenience has long 
been a key point of dif- 
ferentiation used by 
chain drug retailers to dis- 
tinguish themselves from 
large-format discount stores 


and supermarkets. 


Today the definition of 


convenience is taking on new 
meaning and added impor- 
tance, as some of the nation’s 
leading drug store operators 
pursue drive-through format 
stores to secure the percep- 
tion of convenience in the 
minds of consumers. 


No retailer is further along in this 
process than Walgreen Co. An estimated 
300 of the retailer’s 2,000 stores are 
equipped with drive-through pharmacy 
windows. Virtually all of the chain’s new 


stores have drive-throughs. 


‘Drive-throughs 
add to our 
convenience. That 
was the driving 
force behind 
developing 
drive-throughs’ 


—Polzin, Walgreens 


in Cleveland have drive-throughs. All 
were new construction. Because of that, 
Walgreen has been able to expand with 
the format more aggressively than com- 
petitors that are more reliant on acquisi- 


tions for growth. 


“Our niche is to be § 
competitive on price 
and be the most conve- 
nient drug store retail- 
er,” said Walgreen 
spokesman Mike Pol- 
zin. “Drive-throughs 
add to our conven- 
ience. That was the 
driving force behind 
developing  drive- 
throughs. The majority 
of our new stores will 
have drive-throughs 
where the site plan 
will allow us.”

green recently opened

look back at 1994, we see that the 
headlines were neither disastrous nor 
particularly positive, even though it 
had promised to be a pretty remark- 
able year. 

At the start, there were high hopes 
that President Clinton’s plan for 
health care reform would bring a fairly 
healthy boost to community retail 
pharmacy. Plus, the National Associa- 
tion of Chain Drug Stores (NACDS) 


Strategically, it was a very good year 


health care reform process—if it is 
ever to occur at the federal level — 
must essentially start all over again. 
In the early months of ‘94, it also 
looked as if this would be a banner 
year for consolidations. Two major ac- 
quisitions made headlines—with 
Thrifty Drug’s parent acquiring Pay- 
Less (subsequently combined as 
Thrifty PayLess) and Revco buying 
HSI—and with the close sales volumes 
of these new combined chains, it’s 
hard to tell who’s No. 2. 
Since then—

| been a strategically impor-

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


and NARD (the association for inde- 
pendent retail pharmacy) had posi- 
tioned themselves strongly in the pres- 
ident’s camp. As a result, the White 
House was very sensitive to the con- 
cerns of community retail pharmacy, 
and the Clintons were championing ef- 
forts to eliminate the descriminatory 
pricing policies of the pharmaceutical 
companies as well as building into 
their plan a pharmacy benefit for all 
Americans. 

It wasn’t big news when the Clinton 
plan expired, as it followed months of 
partisan politics and shifting agendas. 
Now, with a Republican-dominated 
legislature about to take office, the 


have been of few- 
er than 30 stores. 

And in today’s 
tumultuous re- 
tailing era, it is actually worth noting 
that all was quiet on the bankruptcy 
front (at least up until press time) in 
1994. 

This doesn’t mean, however, that 
nothing much happened this year. 

Beneath the surface of the head- 
lines, I think 1994 has been a strate- 
gically important year for the indus- 
try, as most of the drug chains 
concentrated on improving the way 
they did business. 

Most of the top chains have invested 
in new and improved technology, im- 
plemented some form of category man- 
agement, developed new prototypes or 
tested new formats, and added drive- 


through pharmacy windows, among 
other things. 

Meanwhile, although federal health 
care reform failed to materialize, re- 
tail pharmacy has made a significant 
proactive move to secure its future 
through the formation of the Pharma- 
cy Direct Network (PDN), which was 
formed out of an alliance with 
NACDS and NARD. With a strong 
staff now in place, PDN is approach- 
ing major third-party carriers and 
corporations to secure contracts that 
are guaranteed to be open to all 
30,000-plus PDN members. 

While the prospects for the chain 
drug industry in 1995 are not as bleak 
as they might have seemed a year or 
two ago, neither are they rosy. 

The competition gets more intense 
every day—forcing down profit mar- 
gins in all areas of the store. No mar- 
ket is sacred anymore. For example, 
Duane Reade, the small-size chain 
that did a mighty business because of 
its lock on New York’s Manhattan, 
will soon be competing with Rite-Aid’s 
new locations. (See story on page 1.) In 
Cleveland, Tulsa and Buffalo, Wal- 
green’s entry is raising the stakes for 
local chains. 

And the health care delivery system 
is still being transformed, even with- 
out federal intervention. That will con- 
tinue to have a huge impact on retail 
drug stores. 

At the end of this year, I'll make my 
big prediction for the coming one: 
Business will be tougher than ever to 
get, but it will be out there. Doing 
business profitably will continue to be 
a struggle, but it will be possible. 
Those chains that continue to do a ter- 
rific job will grow, but there will be lit- 
tle room for mistakes. 

In other words, 1995 will probably 
be a lot like 1994.

With the Republicans set to take 
control in Congress next month, many 
retail industry lobbyists suspect that 
the Clinton Administration will shift 
its emphasis to regulatory activities. 


pro-business bias on Capitol Hill.

Safety Commission, could find them- 

selves politically

well seek to achieve 
through regulations what it

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


Under this strategy, the White 
House might well seek to achieve 
through regulations what it can’t 
achieve legislatively. At the Labor De- 
partment, for example, both the Wage 
and Hour Division and the Occupa- 
tional Safety and Health Administra- 
tion could come under White House 
pressure to counteract the perceived 


process at the 
Food and Drug 
Administration 
(FDA). 

The FDA is one federal agency that 
has always maintained at least the ap- 
pearance of independence from political 
pressures. And for good reason. 

Food and drug regulators are re- 
sponsible for making difficult decisions 
on complex, often life-or-death issues. 
To do their job, FDA regulators need 
the trust of the public, 


4 Drug Store News, December 12, 1994 


the support of 


health care providers and the coopera- 
tion of drug manufacturers and other 
regulated industries. 

The perception that the FDA is 
making decisions based on raw politi- 
cal considerations rather than sound 
scientific judgment could critically un- 
dermine confidence in the agency. 

A strong, straight-shooting FDA 
commissioner, able to resist political 
intrigue and retain the trust of the 
health care system, would be a bul- 
wark against inappropriate politiciza- 
tion of the FDA. 

Unfortunately, the present FDA 
commissioner is not such a person. 
Since taking office during the Bush 
Administration, David Kessler has 
pursued an agenda that has been any- 
thing but straightforward. 

Among pharmacists, for example, 


Kessler’s track record on the issue of 


compounding is troublesome. After 
publicly assuring pharmacy leaders 


that the FDA would keep hands off 


the profession’s historic right to com- 
pound medicines, Kessler quietly or- 
chestrated a campaign to do just the 
opposite. 

Let’s keep a close eye on the FDA 
over the next six months.

by retailers to court price-conscious con- 

Sumers are just one more indicator of how 
powerful successful brands can be. 

Brands and the marketing ingenuity behind 
them have the power to convince people that a 
“better mousetrap” has been invented. 

A strong brand franchise, of course, is predicat- 
ed on product quality and, beyond that, on deliv- 
ering “value enhancements” to consumers. 

But consumers learn about brands, their quality 
and their value through advertising, and the most 
effective ad campaigns stress product benefits in a 
consistent, imaginative way. 


The value of advertising 


“Brand manufacturers are the ones who hit the 
mark with advertising,” said Allen Patrick, exec- 
utive vice president of Melville, N.Y.-based Gen- 
ovese Drug Stores. 

“P&G is right on this. It is the advertising for a 
brand that creates the demand that pulls con- 
sumers into our stores. Retailers don’t create the 
demand. 

“We fight for exposure in announcing that we car- 
ry the brand, and we try to court customers by 
stressing purchasing incentives like price. But 
were counting on the manu- 
facturers to educate con- 
sumers about the benefits of 
the brand and to create the 
demand that will make peo- 
ple want to come to our 
stores to buy it. 

“Without P&QG’s advertis- 
ing, consumers won’t know 
how Aleve is different from 
Advil or other pain killers 
on the market. Consumers 
won't understand the differ- 
ence overnight, that’s why 
it’s important that manufac- 
turers continue to advertise 
their brands.

In hair color, for example, Patrick said Clairol 
has also been a staunch supporter of its brands. 
using not just advertising but in-store merchan- 
dising aids to help consumers understand the dif- 
ferences between brands in what could otherwise 
be a very confusing category. 

“Clairol does an awful lot to help consumers un- 
derstand what each brand does, and to support its 
brands, just by the way it planogrammed the cate- 
gory. Because of Clairol, a woman who wants to 
buy just a 24-hour hair color is able to find what 
she wants relatively easily, and a woman who 
wants a more permanent hair color also knows how 
and where to find it.” 

In many cases, a manufacturer’s launch of one 
brand can actually create an entire category. 
L’Oréal did it with mousse. Straight Arrow did it 
with Mane & Tail. Neoteric did it with Alpha Hy- 
droxy. La Loren did it with Sarah Michaels, Coty 
did it with Vanilla Fields, and 3M did it with its 
Post-It™ notes. 


Without innovation, categories flatten 


All categories depend on innovation for growth, 
but the bigger and more mature the category, the 
more important it is to have innovation. 

Pat McCafferty, senior vice president of pur- 
chasing at Super D drug stores in Memphis, 
Tenn., pointed out that to 
the extent there is growth 
in high usage categories like 
shampoos and hair condi- 
tioners, it “is brand driven.” 

McCafferty also noted 
that the categories most in- 
fluenced by brands are cate- 
gories where brand manu- 
facturers have achieved 
technological differentia- 
tion—home diagnostics, 
and particularly blood glu- 
cose monitoring devices, for 
example.

“When a monitor comes 
out that is faster or easier to 
use, or more comfortable for 
the patient, then that is a 
meaningful technological 
difference in the consumer’s 
mind, and you get a lot of 
monitor and strip replace- 
ments,” he said. 

“Almost every category 
has its brand name leader 


that continues to bring in- 
novation and a quality im- 
age to the category—in 
lighting, it’s GE. In small 
appliances and personal ap- 
pliances, Black & Decker 
and, also in small appli- 
ances, Sunbeam,” comment- 
ed Andy Streifel, senior vice

Thrifty PayLess.

there are Revlon and Cover 
Girl, and some emerging 
names like Sarah Michaels 
in bath. In photo and elec- 
tronics, the Kodak brand 
continues to drive film and 
processing, and in electron- 
ics I think most of the tradi- 
tional names—AT&T, GE, 
Panasonic, Sony—continue 
to drive customers into those 


departments,” Streifel said. 
“And in batteries it’s Du- 

racell and Eveready. Who 

can miss their commercials?”

brands are important in all 
categories. 

“If the manufacturer is 
spending the money to pro- 
mote the brand, it then be- 
comes meaningful for the 
customer to find that brand 
on the shelf.” But, Gaddis 
pointed out, retailers can 
only take advantage ofa 
brand’s popularity by mak-

tently and reliably in stock. 

“When customers come 
into a store, they expect to 
purchase all of the products 
on their shopping list,” Gad-

Store brand/private label 
programs could not even ex- 
ist unless there were lead- 
ing brands_ successful 
enough to create a demand 
for imitations, he added.

there that would be success- 
ful without the brand sit- 
ting next to them. Without 
Tylenol on the shelf, a 
knock-off of Tylenol is 
meaningless,” Gaddis said. 


When brand = category 


In Detroit, Steve Lund, 
merchandise director of 
health & beauty care/cos- 
metics for F&M stores 
pointed out that “brands are 
where categories start in 
the consumer’s eye.” 

However, while brands 
create categories and brand 
advertising helps to drive 
consumers into retail stores, 
it is the retailers’ “utiliza- 
tion of brands, their product 
mix, their cross merchandis- 
ing of their stores, their de- 
partmental adjacencies and 
their promotional programs 
that determine how much 
growth the retailer ulti- 
mately derives form the 
brand’s presence on the 
playing field,” Lund added. 

In the past few years, 
Lund thinks, drug stores 
have benefited the most 
from the brands that 
emerged when popular pre- 
scription products went cff 
patent and were able to con- 
vert to over-the-counter 
health remedies. 

“Rx-to-OTC brands like 
Tavist-D and Monistat have 
had a very dramatic impact 
on drug stores,” Lund said. 

“The advertising for 
these brands hit hard when 
they launched, and it was 
consistent and very well 
done. As a result, they 
brought new customers into 
drug stores, and that’s a 


major contribution.”

The Top 25 adult cold remedies account 
for 87 percent of all dollar volume in both 
three-outlet stores (food, food/drug, drug 
and mass merchandise) and drug stores. 

Private label and store brands account for 
nearly 20 percent of dollar volume in the 
three-outlet trade class and in drug stores. 

Four brand families together account for 
a third of all the dollar sales generated by 
the Top 25 highest dollar volume brands: 
Vicks, Alka Seltzer, Tavist and Dimetapp. 

Sudafed and Benadryl, which do not have 
line extensions in the Top 25 highest dollar 
volume brands, are, nevertheless, very 
strong brands. 

Sudafed is the third highest dollar vol- 
ume brand in the three-outlet trade class 
and in drug, and Benadry] is the sixth in 
the three-outlet trade class and the fourth 
largest in drug.

<Adult cold remedy sales have been flat in 
drug stores for the 52 weeks ended Aug. 13, 
1994, but they were up nearly 6 percent in 
the three-outlet trade class (food, food/drug, 
drug and mass merchandise). 

The three-outlet trade class simply had 
stronger growth in a larger number of 
brands, and they did particularly well with 
some relatively new but very successful 
high volume brands like Tavist D. It's very 
likely that food stores and mass merchan- 
dise stores took quick note of the success 
the drug store trade class has had with 
Tavist D, a recent Rx-to-OTC conversion, 
and simply were very quick to work it into 
their distribution channels. The same thing 
seems to be happening now with Efidac/24, 
a new brand that is already ranked 18th in 
drug stores and 16th in the three-outlet 
trade class. 


Drug stores command a 42 percent > 
share of the total sales of the Top 25 dollar 
volume brands in adult cold remedies, and 
much of their strength comes from their excel- 
lent marketing of private label/store brands, 
where they have a 48 percent dollar share. 

They also do very well with Chlor-Trime- 
ton, which is the 10th highest dollar volume 
brand in drug stores. But on the highest 
volume brands like Vicks and Alka Seltzer, 
which are frequently promoted in food and 
mass merchandise stores, their shares hov- 
er around one third. Unless drug stores can 
develop marketing programs that pull more 
traffic into their OTC aisles, this situation 
is not likely to change.

store brands, drug stores enjoyed their high- 
est dollar sales share on the lower dollar vol- 
ume brands like Sinulin and Chlor-Trime- 
ton. On category leader Tylenol, their share 
dropped to 35 percent, under par, and on 
Tylenol Allergy Sinus, the No. 2 brand in the 
category, their share slipped to 33 percent. 

Once again, it's clear that consumers are 
buying most sinus remedies in high-traffic 
stores like food stores and mass merchan- 
dise stores where they can enjoy the conve- 
nience of one-stop shopping. Drug chains 
need to develop merchandising and market- 
ing programs that will help them reverse 
this trend.

Oral rinses and antiseptics is another one 
of those categories whose well-being really 
depends on the strength of a few dominant 
players. In this case, they’re Listerine with 
a 34 percent share of the Top 25 highest 
dollar volume brands through the three- 
outlet trade class (food, food/drug, drug and 
mass merchandise) in this category, and 
Scope with a 19 percent share of three-out- 
let dollars. In oral rinses and antiseptics, 
the Top 25 brands are the category, ac- 
counting for 99 percent of all sales in three 
outlets and 98 percent in drug. 

Private labels and store brands are pretty 
key in this category too, accounting for al- 
most 20 percent of total sales in both the 
three-outlet trade class and drug. 

The category's flat right now, and what 
buoyancy it does have is coming from pri- 
vate labels, store brands and Listerine's 
line extension, Cool Mint. Cool Mint not 
only successfully extended the Listerine 
brand franchise, but it also brought some 
excitement to drug stores, growing to where 
it is now the fourth ranked brand in the 
category. What the category seems to need, 
however, is a brand new introduction that 
will not cannibalize existing brands but will 
bring more new users into the category.

Oral rinses and antiseptics is a category 
in search of some excitement. Sales were 
down in drug for the 52 weeks ended Aug. 
13th and flat in the three-outlet trade 
class (food, food/drug, drug and mass mer- 
chandise). 

The growth was all in small volume 
brands and in low priced generics. Cool 
Mint and private label/store brands are the 
only players generating double-digit incre- 
ments where they really count among the 
high volume brand players. 

However, Oral B, which has been in na- 
tional distribution for less than a year, has 
already made it into the Top 25 highest vol- 
ume brand rankings in both drug and the 
three-outlet trade class. 


Drug stores only generate 28 percent » 
of all oral rinse/oral antiseptic sales. Their 
strongest shares come from low-volume spe- 
cialty or regional brands like Biotene, 
Amosan, Peroxyl, etc., and from their own 
store brands and private labels. 

There isn't much drug store retailers can 
do to change this situation either. It's really 
up to the manufacturers to introduce more 
innovative products or more exciting ways 
to expand usage of their existing brands.

ADrug stores enjoyed a 4.9 percent surge in tooth- 
paste sales for the 52 weeks ended Aug. 13, but they 
underperformed the mass market trade class as a 
whole. Toothpaste sales in the three-outlet trade class 
(food, food/drug, drug and mass merchandise) were up 
6.9 percent for the period. Dollar sales gains in such 
key brands as Mentadent, the No. 2 brand in both 
drug stores and the three-outlet trade class, were 
higher in the three-outlet trade class. So were the 
sales gains of Rembrandt, ranked 9th in three-outlet 
sales and 4th in drug store sales.

“It's true that the more a category becomes a commodity, 
the more likely people are to buy it in highly trafficked 
stores like food stores and mass merchandisers. That trend 
is clearly evident in the toothpaste brand share chart. 
Drug stores only have an average 21 percent dollar share of 
the Top 25 toothpaste brands, but their share of specialty 
brands like Rembrandt and Sensodyne is much higher, as 
is their share of private label/store brands.

Rite Aid buys a 
$132MM Xmas gift 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — With its 
$132 million acquisition of 
Perry Drug Stores, Rite Aid 
becomes a contender for the 
No. 2 spot in drug chain 
sales volume. The purchase 
added 224 stores to Rite 
Aid’s 2,617 stores. 

See page 5 


Smith, Barker lead 
Thrifty PayLess 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — As 
new chairman and chief ex- 
ecutive officer of Thrifty Pay- 
Less, Marty Smith brings 
three decades of “no frills” 
Bi-Mart discount retail expe- 
rience to the chain. With 
seasoned PayLess executive 
Gordon Barker as president 
and chief operating officer, 
the management team is ex- 
pected to keep the company 
on track in the wake of Tim 
McAlear’s ouster. 

See page 5 


Battie brews over 
tooth whiteners 


NEW YORK — CCA Indus- 
tries has sued the American 
Dental Association following 
the display of its products in 
a video about OTC tooth 
whiteners. While the video 
has generated harsh words 
from several manufacturers, 
it has also prompted the 
Food and Drug Administra- 
tion to study the safety of 
whiteners more closely.
