Drug Store News, January 9, 1995 


3 


ff DITORTAL 


Viewpoints 


Out with the old, 1/1 with the NeEWS 


equals opportunity. Now I, along with everyone here at 
Drug Store News, will test this principle firsthand. 

Starting with this issue, we are introducing many 
changes, all part of our effort to provide you with a “new and 
improved” Drug Store News. While Drug Store News served 
its readers well for 16 years in a traditional news tabloid for- 
mat, we felt that the industry and the world around us had 
changed so much that a new look and an updated editorial 
approach were warranted for 1995 and beyond. 

So, we took a good, hard look at Drug Store News in or- 
der to identify what we have been doing well—and also to 
see where we could be better. We personally spoke to 
many readers to elicit your input; we hired an outside 
firm, White Marketing Group, to conduct a readership 
study, and we tapped the creativity and experience of our 
editors, art director, pub- 
lishers and salespeople. 

The result of all these ef- 
forts is the new Drug Store 
News you see before you. 

We hope you notice, first 
of all, our dynamic redesign. 
It is a design with a purpose. 

In addition to late-break- 
ing headlines, our cover now 
highlights one big, impor- 
tant feature. “Market Dri- 
vers,” the cover feature of 
this issue, actually refers to 
a series of five stories in 
which our editors identify 
the categories, products and trends that we expect to drive 
sales in chain drug stores in this new year. 

Inside, we’ve changed our format to allow us to cover more 
news—about retailers, manufacturers and other factors that 
impact the chain drug industry—and we've changed the orga- 
nization of the publication to help you find what you need 
quickly. Each category has its own section, which starts with a 
“hot news” page and is easily identified by a colorful label: Re- 
tailing News, Pharmacy, Cosmetics & Fragrances, HBC/Toi- 
letries, HBC/OTCs, Consumables and General Merchandise. 

While our sister publication, Drug Store News For The 
Pharmacist, is written for retail pharmacists at all types of 
stores, we have added a pharmacy section to Drug Store 


ES often commented in this column that change 


We’ve changed our format 
to allow us to cover more 
news—and to help you find 
what you need quickly. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


News because executives throughout chain drug organiza- 
tions today need to know more about how developments in 
pharmacy and health care affect their businesses. 

Meanwhile, through our regular coverage of front-end 
product categories, we will keep buyers. merchandising 
personnel and top chain executives up to speed on the 
newest products, marketing strategies, supplier initiatives, 
and consumer purchasing trends. 

Like many chains, our editors will be taking a category 
management approach. Each expert will be responsible for 
gathering data, identifying trends, developing relationships 
with key retailers and manufacturers, and analyzing all this 
information for our readers. 

Liz Parks, who has certainly made a name for herself dur- 
ing her 12-year tenure at Drug Store News, continues as our 
cosmetics and fragrances category manager. Eight-year veter- 
an Jim Frederick is our cate- 
gory manager for consum- 
ables as well as our news 
editor. As our general mer- 
chandise category manager, 
Allene Symons focuses on the 
GM categories that are most 
important to drug chains. 
Mike Troy, our OTC category 
manager, will be making a 
greater contribution to Drug 
Store News this year as we 
expand coverage of this im- 
portant and growing health- 
care business. And Lisa 
Fried, the newest addition to 
our editorial staff, will handle our toiletries coverage while 
also making a large contribution to our retailing news section. 

The chain drug industry is entering the second half of 
the 90s in a strong position—due to the important changes 
and alterations chain drug retailers have made. And as you 
search for new ways to grow and prosper in a marketplace 
that is being transformed by technology, retail competition 
and consolidation, managed health care, demographics, 
and many other factors, the editorial team at Drug Store 
News is dedicated—as our new tag line says—to being “the 
information resource for the chain drug industry.” 

All in all, we’re really looking forward to 1995. It will be 
a year of tremendous opportunity. For all of us. 


Investors like chain drug’s prospects 


ho would have believed that one of the more dy- 
namic retailing concepts in 1994 would be the tra- 


GUEST COLUMN 


ditional drug store operator? Long written 


off by some retail industry observers as a dated 
format in the face of increasing competition and a 
radically changing health care delivery system, 
several of the nation’s leading chain drug store re- 
tailers reported impressive results all year in the 
form of higher same-store sales, better operating 
profit margins and rapid earnings growth. 

Moreover, Wall Street shook off apprehensions 
about the growth prospects of drug store retailers 
in 1994, and investors of certain publicly owned op- 
erators were rewarded with exceptional stock price 
performances. Examples include the stocks of Eck- 


erd Corp. (up 63 percent in the first 11 months of Bayi Peas 


ful drug store retailers will be gaining market share and 
keeping expenses low through: 

® Building and taking advantage of critical mass; 

@ The efficacious use of technology; and 

@ Leveraging customer convenience and phar- 
macist competency. 

Leading drug store retailers, such as Walgreen 
Co., benefit from increasing size and market share 
1 by leveraging costs. In addition, Walgreen can of- 
| fer third-party providers a density of customers 
within given markets, thus improving access. 
These advantages are just as well-evidenced at the 
smaller, well-run regional operators such as Arbor 
Drugs Inc. and Big B Inc. 

As a result, drug store operators blessed with 
sufficient financial capitalization will continue to 


iast year), Revco D.S. Inc. (up 58 percent), and Rit aggressively pursue consolidation through “file- 


Aid Corp. (up 37 percent), vs. a flat S&P 400 In- 
dustrials performance. In addition, there is further 
potential for share price appreciation in 1995 for 
well-positioned drug store retailers. 

What does it mean to be well positioned in the 
complex and rapidly changing drug store market- 
place? Well, successful drug store retailers are 
pursuing strategies built on the recognition that 
pharmacy volume will continue to drive overall 
drug store business, and third-party contractual 
business will drive the pharmacy area. 

Changing marketplace realities, such as increasing limi- 
tations on consumer choice and declining pharmacy gross 
margins, are manifestations of the proliferation of third- 
party participation levels. In this environment, the success-

Similarly, store-level technology will also be in- 
creasingly used in a myriad of ways to improve 
productivity and profitability, and ultimately im- 
prove market penetration through the generation 
and utilization of crucial product and customer 
data. The technology will also be able to provide 
such information to outside interested parties. 
Lastly, the traditional format will remain strong 
relative to deep drug discounters, mass merchants 
and food/drug combos, if the traditional strengths of conve- 
nience and pharmacist effectiveness are realized. Informal 
customer surveys suggest that a knowledgeable and friend- 
ly pharmacist force is a drug store retailer’s greatest asset.

ou’ve probably noticed that 
this issue of Drug Store 
News looks quite different 
from what you’ve been used 
to seeing. 

Basically, we’re changing our look 
because we want to make 
ourselves more accessible to 
our readers. We want you to 
be able to find what you 
need quickly and easily, and 
we want you to be enter- 
tained as well as informed 
as you browse through our # 
stories and charts. | 

If you look a little closer, 
you'll see that our content 
is changing too. In beauty 


ing to make our coverage of 
this very important department 
much broader and much deeper. 
Broader because we want to 
touch on all the issues that impact 
the success and the profitability of 
the cosmetic department, from sto- 
ries that focus on ways to enhance 
inventory management, to stories 
that explore changing consumer 
needs and consumer perceptions 
about beauty care shopping options.

against Polymer Technology.

has licensed undisclosed tech-

tions

test strips. Diagnostic Solu-

Carex wants new bathroom 
products to be simply safe 


ATLANTA — Rubbermaid’s 
acquisition of home health 
care manufacturer Carex last 
summer brought expectations 
of innovative new products. 

The company took the first 
step in that direction with the 
unveiling of 15 new and re- 
designed products at last fall’s 
15th annual Medtrade/ 
NHHCE show. 

Most of the new items on dis- 
play by Rubbermaid Health 
Products, the division of Rub- 
bermaid that will market the 
Carex line, were prototype bath 
safety items that will be avail- 
able to retailers in early 1995. 

A noticeable difference in 
the line is the elimination of 
the familiar tubular alu- 
minum, plastic and nuts and 
bolts design. The use of these 
materials in bath safety prod- 
ucts is so widespread that 
products from various manu- 
facturers are indistinguish- 
able. New products in the 


Carex line feature a sturdy, all 
plastic construction with close 
attention paid to user-friendly 
design features, an important 
consideration for incapacitated 
end-users of such products. 
“Consumers are really tired 
of products that come with a 
bag of nuts and bolts and an in- 
struction booklet,” said Wolf 
Schmitt, Rubbermaid’s chair- 
man and chief executive officer. 


Plenty of new products 


During 1995, Schmitt said, 
Rubbermaid plans to introduce 
about 400 new products with 
an unspecified number of those 
being home health care relat- 
ed. “Retailers can expect to see 
a very aggressive flow of new 
products because that’s what 
creates the momentum and the 
excitement,” he said. 

In addition to introducing 
new products, Schmitt wants 
to cultivate in the mind of the 
home health care consumer, 


the same perception of value 
that he believes is associated 
with Rubbermaid’s other prod- 
ucts. “We want to make sure 
the majority of our consumers 
will see our products as the 
most valuable, not necessarily 
the lowest priced because they 
probably won’t be,” he said. 

From the retailer’s perspec- 
tive, Rubbermaid’s involve- 
ment in the home health care 
arena should further invigo- 
rate the category by stimulat- 
ing competition. The home 
health care category is already 
poised to benefit from key de- 
mographic trends such as 
shorter hospital stays and an 
aging population that is enjoy- 
ing longer life expectancies. 
Meanwhile, chain drug retail- 
ers are increasingly expanding 
home health care product of- 
ferings to achieve the goal of 
giving consumers a one-stop 
shopping experience for all 
their health care needs.

cabbage and onions. 


During the subsequent 
six-hour period, partici- 
pants recorded the 
number of times they 
experienced flatulence.

Beano, which is avail-

form, was proven to be 
statistically significant 
when the participants 
were compared to the 
study group that re-

Worcestershire sauce 
and water. Alan 
Kligerman, Akphar- 
ma’s chief executive of- 
ficer and inventor of 
Beano, said the com- 
pany was not involved 
in funding the study 
and had no input in the 
methodology.

Drug Store News, January 9, 1995 


Has ADA tarnished 


25 


HBC 


Toiletries 


OTC tooth whiteners? 


FDA steps up investigation; Plus+White maker files suit 


By Lisa I. Fried 


NEW YORK — The Ameri- 
can Dental Association’s warn- 
ing about the perils of over-the- 
counter tooth whiteners has 
prompted a lawsuit from one 
manufacturer and harsh words 
from others. It has also 
breathed new life into the Food 
and Drug Administration’s 
two-year-long investigation of 
the category and left retailers 
wondering what might become 
of the most profitable segment 
of the oral care category. 

In mid-December, CCA, 
manufacturer of Plus+White 
products, filed a lawsuit 
against the ADA for false ad- 
vertising, commercial dispar- 
agement and unfair competi- 
tion. The suit centers on a 
video news release issued by 
the ADA in November as part 
of a major media campaign 
about OTC tooth whiteners. 

In late November, the ADA 
issued a full-blown media 
alert to 700 TV news stations, 
500 newspaper and magazine 
journalists and 10,000 small 
newspapers about the “dan- 
gers” of OTC tooth whiteners. 


The video news release im- 
plied that specific OTC whi- 
tening products may be dan- 
gerous. In the video, which 
resembles a news program, a 
voice-over warns that OTC 
tooth whiteners “may contain 
chemicals, which when used 
without the supervision of a 
dentist can actually damage 
healthy teeth and soft tissue in 
the mouth.” 

As the voice-over is heard, 
the camera focuses on Booster 
Toothpaste, White Step 
Whitening Toothpaste, Plus+ 
White Anti-Stain Fluoride Gel, 
Plus+White Desensitizing 
Toothpaste, Rembrandt Brush- 
ing Gel and Rembrandt Mouth 
Refreshing Rinse. 

The press materials sent to 
print media mentioned perox- 
ide as the potentially danger- 
ous chemical but did not cite 
the specific products by name. 

Although peroxide is not 
identified as the chemical in the 
video release, accompanying 
materials from the ADA make 
it clear that the association has 
some doubts about peroxide use 
in dental products. 

Saati. White Step tooth- 


paste, the two Plus+White 
products and Rembrandt’s 
mouth rinse do not contain 
peroxide. Rembrandt’s Brush- 
ing Gel does contain peroxide, 
but it is not a whitener. 

The video also shows a con- 
sumer reading the label of 
Plus+White Anti-Stain Oral 
Rinse while the voice-over is- 
sues this warning: “The Food 
and Drug Administration rec- 
ommends that consumers who 
are considering over-the- 
counter whitening products 
talk with their dentist first.” 

In fact, the ADA mischarac- 
terized the FDA’s position on 
tooth whiteners. “We don’t 
have the basis to agree or dis- 
agree with the ADA’s posi- 
tion,” said Brad Williams, di- 
rector of the FDA’s drug 
labeling compliance division, 
explaining that the FDA is 
still studying whether to clas- 
sify OTC whiteners as cosmet- 
ics or drugs. 

“What I [told the ADA] is a 
standard FDA statement,” 
said Williams. “Anyone who is 
concerned about medication 
they are using should consult

the people who work with her to use the word “opportu- 
nity” every time they find themselves about to utter the 
word “problem.” 

Managed care is certainly a situation that could be ap- 
proached as a “problem” by drug chains, which it was by 
many in the past. More recently, though, the industry has ac- 
cepted that managed care is here to stay, and, along with

As managed care evolves, the: focus of the third-party 
payors is broadening from one of simply driving down the 
cost of pharmaceutical products to a strategy of trimming 
costs through better patient management. As many drug 
chain executives are discovering, this new way of thinking 
takes managed care to a whole new level.

Good things still come to small chains 


erry Drug. Kerr Drug. Clark Drug. Standard Drug. 
As more and more venerable operators are ac- 
quired by the bigger players, it’s time to ask yourself 
this question: Are you getting ready to operate the chain 
drug store of the future or are you getting ready to sell out? 

Let me say that I firmly believe there is a positive future 
for small, mid-size and regional chains. However, the dy- 
namics of the marketplace demand that the chains of the 
future make the necessary moves today. 

Certainly we at the Chain Drug Marketing Asso- 
ciation are saddened to lose Kerr Drug—one of our 
largest members—through its pending acquisition 
by Thrift Drug. Like other small and regional 
chains, including Perry and Clark, Kerr Drug was 
an attractive target because of its strong market po- 
sition, good locations and seasoned store personnel. 
I think good small and regional drug chains will 
continue to be vulnerable because they do give the 
larger chains a relatively easy way to capture a new 
market or to strengthen their position in existing 
markets.

The smaller chains must pay attention to what their com-

Drug Store News, February 6, 1995 


DRUGSTRATEGESFOR 


By Allene Symons 


Continued from page 1 

The collapse of the Clinton Administration’s 
national health care reform initiative has not 
stopped the momentum of managed care: Over 
half of all Americans now participate in some 
kind of managed health care program. In phar- 
macy, the third-party share of prescriptions 
reached 45 percent for the month of November, 
up from less than 43 percent in June, according 
to the Source Prescription Audit (Scott-Levin As- 
sociates). 

Drug chains large and small are re-evaluating 
every element of their pharmacy operation in an 
effort to “manage” managed care. Despite the 
many unknowns in the constantly evolving world 
of government and private health care coverage, 
chains are creating new departments, divisions 
and positions in order to seize control of their 
own destinies. 

The costs—and the risks—are tremendous, 
and yet, say chain drug store executives, so are 
the opportunities. 

If the drug store as cost-and-outcomes facilita- 
tor lives up to its promise, then managed care 
and the entire “wellness” concept will help as- 
sure drug chain survival. 

As Rite Aid’s Joel Feldman, executive vice 
president of the chain’s Eagle Managed Care 

rogram, said: “The physician doesn’t necessarily 
ow whether a patient remains compliant with 
the therapy designated and prescribed to make 
the patient get well. We do. I think that’s a criti- 
cal component—if you want to define it as out- 
comes management, that is the ultimate in pa- 
tient care.” 

As for affording the strategies of survival in 
an era of managed care, Dave Fong, vice presi- 
dent of poems for Longs Drug Stores, point- 
ed out the importance of partnering and the in- 
ee ae role of the consumer in influencing 
choice of provider. 

“We are getting more into the relationship 
business than ever before,” said Fong. He said he 
expects this to “provide a higher level of cost-ef- 
fective poaetncy care and documented outcomes 
with the active involvement of the payors, 
providers and the patient.” 

A driver behind this, he added: “I think pa- 
tients are more actively involved in their own 
health care. We believe that will continue to 
grow.” 

So, too, will drug chains’ managed care efforts. 
On an almost daily basis, chains are announcing 
new initiatives, alliances and marketing pro- 
grams. 

Here’s a closer look at some of the managed 
care services and strategies currently being em- 
ployed by major drug chains:

CVS 


CVS has been in the managed care business 
for a decade, providing exclusive network man- 
agement services to HMOs. Last year it formal- 
ized the offering through PharmaCare/CVS, a 
full-service prescription-management company 
and a wholly owned subsidiary of Melville, CVS’ 
parent company. 

Besides its full-service menu, it is currently 
developing what senior vice president of pharma- 
cy Charles Conaway described as “sophisticated 
software applications to provide outcomes mea- 
surement.” PharmaCare’s goal is to position its 
stores as a leader in disease management and 
other value-added services. 

On working with HMOs, Conaway said CVS 
currently participates with a number of man- 
aged-care sites on a partner basis. “In the short 
term we are proceeding in a cautious and busi- 
nesslike manner to make sure we understand 
what we are getting into,” said Conaway. 

Conaway sees in the managed care market 
more and more integration of services and infor- 
mation between the payor, the physician, the 
pharmacist and the patient. PharmaCare is in- 
vesting “significantly” in information technolo- 
gies to support its focus on coordinated care. 


Genovese Drug Stores 


This chain has been marketing and managing 
patient prescription care for 18 years, according to 
director of managed care services Michael Caruso. 
Its program started with its long-term care 
provider, GeneRx, which provides services to 
nursing homes and other health care operators. 


Genovese also offers mail order and recently 
created a managed care department to oversee 
existing managed care services and further de- 
velop its market. In addition to the standard re- 
tail card and mail-service programs, Genovese is 
assembling additional value-added programs 
ranging from infusion to specific disease-state 
management as well as a number of other pre- 
scription-related services, all geared to quality 
patient care and customer service. 


Longs Drug Stores 


Longs has aggressively marketed its managed 
care business for over a decade and has operated 
a mail-order program since 1984. 

The chain also has network relationships with 
both independent and chain pharmacies and is 
doing a number of things to aggressively obtain 
managed care contracts, said vice president of 
pharmacy Dave Fong. 

Like many chains, Longs outsources a number 
of PBM-type services such as claims processing; 
the chain keeps some services in-house and out- 
sources others. It also takes different provider 
roles, depending on the situation. It is a primary 
provider in most cases, but in some situations it 
is the primary contact. 

Longs is partnering with a number of HMOs. 
In California, where consumers are regaled with 
competing HMO billboards, the consumer is 
gaining more clout in health care decisions. 
Fong thinks this will be a growing factor as 
wellness-conscious consumers put pressure on 
the market. “Not only does Longs have visible 
market share in most of the areas where we op- 
erate, Longs offers a quality drug store chain 
image,” noted Fong. 

Among its managed care strategies, Longs is 
pursuing value-added programs and is collabo- 
rating with a number of PBMs, drug manufac- 
turers and insurers in prototyping disease-state 
management and outcomes. 


Revco D:S. 


RxConnections, Revco’s managed care pro- 
gram, expanded its mail-order capability with 
the acquisition of HSI last year. HSI had a larger 
facility, and the two operations were combined. 
Gregory Raven, executive vice president and 
chief financial officer, said that since the expand- 
ed mail-order facility can handle more volume, 
its third-party marketing force is now focusing 
on being a full-service managed care operation. 

He noted that an advantage of having an ad- 
vanced mail-order service is that patient infor- 
mation for both chronic medication (mail) and 
acute medication (store) can be linked electroni- 
cally. This provides efficient drug interaction 
checking, more so than if chronic medication was 
served via mail by Medco and acute by Revco. 


Drug Store News, February 6, 1995 


Rite Aid Corp. 

After establishing a managed care program 
four years ago, Rite Aid launched its Eagle Man- 
aged Care Corp. program a year ago. The wholly 
owned subsidiary has a network of 30,000-plus 
pharmacies. Mail order is not a component in 
this chain’s managed care program, although it 
is provided through the Eagle’s affiliates if a con- 
tract requires it. 

Eagle is on the front edge of capitation among 
drug chains, noted Feldman. It has entered into 
programs whereby Eagle is paid on a per-mem- 
ber-per-month basis to provide pharmaceutical 
care for individuals covered under those pro- 
grams. “The onus shifts —we assume the risk to 
manage the program,” said Feldman. 

To beef up its program, a year ago Rite Aid 
purchased IntellRx, a clinical care coordinator/ 
utilization review company. The staff consists of 
PharmDs who have developed proprietary soft- 
ware and procedures designed to focus on physi- 
cian and patient behavior. Also a year ago Rite 
Aid purchased Pharmacy Card Inc. (PCI), a 
pharmacy benefit modeling and claims adminis- 
tering company. 


Snyder Drug Stores 


This chain’s individualized managed care pro- 
gram is around 5 years old. Snyder provides mail- 
order fulfillment if a customer requests it. “We fo- 
cus on small self-insured employer groups and 
unions of 30 people up to 1,000.” said Ed Pelant, 
director of professional services for Snyder. 

Among Snyder’s marketing points are its ser- 
vice level and its presence in smaller communi- 
ties and outlying areas in upper Michigan, Iowa, 


17 


RX 


Pharmacy 


Wisconsin and Minnesota. 

It also offers value to clients through pass- 
along savings. “I can provide DUR reports and 
all the reporting mechanisms that others can 
provide at a less expensive price,” including 
claims processing/eligibility standards for less 
per transaction, said Pelant. 


Thrift Drug 


Thrift has been an active marketer of its man- 
aged care program since 1983 with its mail-ser- 
vice Express Pharmacy Services, and has offered 
a full menu of managed care services since late 
1993, according to David Halpern, vice president 
of managed care. 

Thrift’s TDI Net is a national network of phar- 
macies; it includes around 40,000 pharmacies, 
including Thrift and Treasury stores, and has 
network members in many large chains as well 
as 10,000 independent drug stores. 

In conjunction with its DUR services, Thrift’s 
TDI has proprietary software that analyzes each 
member’s drug regimen. Clinical pharmacists 
monitor compliance and determine whether an 
intervention is appropriate. 


Thrifty PayLess 


Both divisions of this merged chain have been 
active in managed care for around four to five 
years, explained vice president of managed care 
Jerry Edwards. Marketing has accelerated dra- 
matically in the last two years, partly as a result 
of the doubling of locations from the merger. 

This chain’s dominance on the West Coast 
means it stresses geography-related issues, said 
Edwards. It also emphasizes the PayLess up- 


scale image as a quality issue, and said Ed- 
wards, “We believe the public has high quality 
expectations of Thrifty PayLess.” 

In response to requests for proposal by 
prospective third-party/managed care clients, 
Thrifty PayLess also includes other pharmacies 
(often independents) on a subcontracting basis in 
the Thrifty PayLess network when needed to 
provide additional doors. 


Walgreens 


Healthcare Plus, Walgreens’ full-service man- 
aged care subsidiary, is one of the six largest 
mail-service prescription providers, with fiscal 
1994 sales of $120 million. It is committed “to be- 
ing among the top three in the U.S. by the year 
2000,” according to the company. 

The chain doubled the size of its mail-service 
operation last year in a new Arizona facility, 
which opened a year ahead of original projec- 
tions because of accelerated sales growth for the 
Healthcare Plus division. Walgreens also report- 
ed this ratio: For every two mail prescriptions 
sold, Healthcare Plus marketing efforts also 
added three retail prescriptions to its stores. 


The mail-order dilemma 


Drug chains have a love-hate relationship with 
mail order, but in today’s managed care market 
they can’t do business without it. 

Thrift’s Halpern views it this way: Thrift is 
“beginning to eliminate the differentiation be- 
tween mail order and managed care. We’re say- 
ing it’s a managed care product, of which mail 
order is part.”

RETAILING 


Consolidation: 
Is it time to ‘buy or get out’: 


By Mike Troy 


Banners that tout weekly 
specials and promotions are 
commonplace in the front win- 
dows of the nation’s chain drug 
stores. So, too, apparently, are 
the “for sale” signs in the exec- 
utive offices of many a chain 
headquarters. 

Witness the significant accel- 
eration of acquisition activity 
that took place during 1994, 
and the prevailing feeling that 
there will be even more in 1995 
and beyond. Since the begin- 
ning of last year, 14 chains, 
which operated just over 2,500 
stores, have become the willing victims of the in- 
dustry’s march toward consolidation. 

In spite of good consumer recognition and—in 
most cases—healthy sales, such familiar names 
as Hook-SupeRx, Perry Drug, Mast, Treasury, 
Standard, Crown, Town & Country, Bill’s, Clark 
Drug and LaVerdiere’s may live on only in the 
resumes of former employees. 

Chain executives, suppliers and industry ana- 
lysts concur that mergers and acquisitions will 
continue to be a fact of life, for many reasons, 
most of which are interrelated. 

eLarger drug chains can more effectively offset 
declining pharmacy margins through increased 
volume, and they can compete on a more even 
playing field with big-volume competitors in 
mass market and supermarket channels. 

¢Consolidating themselves, industry suppliers 
have structured themselves to deal with large, 
technologically sophisticated retailers— making 
it difficult for the not-so-large chain. 

¢Third-party/managed-care payors—who con- 
trol more than half of all pharmacy customers— 
are looking not only for pharmacies that can pro- 
vide pharmaceuticals at low prices but also for 
broad coverage of their insured populations, or 
the number of doors. While there may be fewer 
“closed” networks, managed-care payors are said 
to be trying to limit their plans to the few leading 
pharmaceutical retailers in each given market. 

¢Due to managed care, as well as to the many 
cost efficiencies that accrue to the leadirg retail- 
ers in any geographic market, having dominant 
market share has become a key issue for most 
drug chains today. 


Here come the brides 


In today’s rapidly evelving marketplace, retail- 
ers’ motivations to sell and to buy are closely re- 
lated. And by all reports in the inZustry, acquisi- 
tion opportunities abound, providing willing 
“bait” for the big-chain feeding frenzy. 

Said one major chain drug chief executive offi- 
cer: “A lot of these buyouts make sense because 
of the availabili- 


ty of good small 
W” For extra profits, display & N or regional 


recommend with suncare products.|| chains. The way

take us years to catch up.” 

“Size really matters when it comes to drug 
stores,” said David Magee, an investment ana- 
lyst at Atlanta-based Robinson-Humphrey Co. 
“There are still a lot of acquisition opportunities 
because the drug store industry is still a pretty 
fragmented business. There are a lot of fairly siz- 
able chains in the $250-million to $1-billion 
range—all for sale for the right price.” 

For those on the selling side, the motivations 
are diverse and sometimes emotional. 

One big obstacle is the rapidly escalating capi- 
tal outlay that is necessary to stay in the game. 
POS equipment has become essential for chains to 
make informed decisions. Installing or upgrading 
pharmacy computers is necessary to enable a 
chain to compete for third-party business. Invest- 
ing in EAS equipment is often needed to effective- 
ly reduce shrink. And, with big chains like Wal- 
green building new stores, staying competitive 
often means expenditures in store remodeling. 

Meanwhile, pharmacy margins just get thin- 


ner and the mass merchandis- 
ers aren't going away. 

For many of those who 
founded chains or grew up in 
the business, the reasons for 
“selling out” are deeply person- 
al. As one small chain execu- 
tive put it, “chain drug retail- 
ing is not as much fun as it 
used to be.” 

Enticing the large chains is 
the fact that the small and re- 
gional chains that are for sale 
are often doing a very good 
business. 

Johnny Kerr, who served as 
president of Kerr Drug Stores 
prior to its recent acquisition 
by Thrift Drug, is the son of the chain’s founder, 
Banks Kerr. The junior Kerr explained that Kerr 
Drug was coming off its best year ever; his chain 
was leading Eckerd and Revco in the Raleigh/ 
Durham market where most of the chain’s 97 
stores are concentrated. 

However, for the long term, there were con- 
cerns about the impact of the growth of third- 
party, compressing pharmacy margins and a six- 
year degree requirement for pharmacists. 

“The compression of pharmacy margins is what 
is driving consolidation in the drug store indus- 
try,” said Kerr. “We didn’t want to sell. The deci- 
sion was purely a business decision a chain our 
size made in the best interest of its stockholders 
regarding the asset.” 

For other chains that have been sold recently, 
timing was an important issue. When Michael 
Simpson, chairman and president of the 13- 
store, east Texas Drug-Sav chain, announced the 
chain’s acquisition by Eckerd, he noted that sales 
for the past four years had been strong, adding 
that its final year—1993—was the best in the 
company’s history. 

Simpson reasoned it was best to sell while 
business was still good rather than waiting until 
things turned sour to make a hasty exit. “This 
really was an opportune time for them and for 
us,” Simpson commented. 


A place for small chains 


“It’s been said that probably within 10 or 15 
years, there will be three or four major chains 
left, and that may not be far off,” said Gerald 
Heller, president of 35-store May’s Drug of Tul- 
sa, Okla. “But I still think there is going to be a 
place for small chains in the future. 

“Small chains have an ability to move much 
faster and have closer ties to their employees 
and the local marketplace than the major 
chains,” Heller noted. “We get mail from cus- 
tomers every day telling us how much they ap- 
preciate the service we give them.” 

Managed care is a key concern for Rich 
Cognetti, president and chief executive officer of 
Kinney Drugs, which operates 43 stores in up- 
state New York. “Can we offer any type of net- 
work for managed care? That has to be a concern 
for any of the small regional chains,” he comment- 
ed. “If we can prove we can add something to this 
scenario, we should be okay. We have to be the 
patient advocate, the consumer advocate. If we 
get locked out [of a managed care plan], then the 


Drug Store News, February 20, 1995 


patient will scream.” 

“T think there are several small chains out 
there, like us, who are providing excellent patient 
therapies, taking responsibility for the outcomes 
of patient drug therapy and helping people deal 
with disease, face to face,” Cognetti added. “As 
smaller chains, we have an ex- 
cellent opportunity to do 
that...but we have to do a better 
job in terms of operating costs. 
We've got to become more effi- 
cient, and the smaller you are, 
the harder it is to be efficient.” 

On that same theme, Marvin 
Goldman, chairman of Miami- 
based wholesaler Gulf Distribu- 
tion, commented: “While some 
chains may be consolidating, 
new ones are emerging. They 
are lopping them off on the top, 
but they are springing up at 
the bottom.” Goldman was re- 
ferring to two of his small chain 
customers, Navarro and 
Sedano’s, both of which have opened new stores 
during the past year. “If you go out and hustle for 
it, there is always business to be had,” he said. 


Bigger gets better and better 


For most of the nation’s largest chains, acqui- 
sitions are the most efficient ways of achieving 
growth. A chain’s store base can be doubled 
(Revco/Hook-SupeRx [HSI], Thrifty/PayLess), 
new markets can be entered quickly 
(Thrift/Kerr) or market positions can be solidi- 
fied (Rite Aid/Perry). 

As one former executive at a recently acquired 
chain said, “It’s really Business 101.” By gaining 
new markets, profit opportunities are expanded 
and operating costs are spread over a larger 
store base. 

“We’re in a consolidating industry. That’s a 
fact,” said D. Dwayne Hoven, Revco’s president 
and chief executive officer. “And I believe that 
means you have to make a decision to grow—or 
leave the industry. You cannot stand still.” 

For Revco, which has kept more than 800 of 
the 1,200 HSI stores it purchased last July, this 
will not be the last acquisition, according to Hov- 
en. “It is our desire to be a player in the future 
and that means consolidation.” Since Revco came 
steamrolling out of bankruptcy in mid-1992, it 
has gobbled up chain after chain: Mast, Corn- 
well, Friendly, Fox, Begley and Rupert Heller’s 
are among its trophies. 

Virtually every major chain is involved in the 
acquisition game. The past few years have seen 
Eckerd, Rite Aid, CVS, Thrift, Fay’s, Big B, 
and—even prior to their own merger—Thrifty 
and PayLess expand their market share or fill in 
existing markets via acquisitions. 

Consolidation, of course, is not new to the chain 
drug store industry. Over the past five years, a

Managing managed care 


Acquisition isn’t the only way to grow, but it is 
the quickest strategy for chains struggling to 
catch up with large chains growing ever larger. 

Although many reasons are given for the race 
to increase volume, store count and market 
share, managed care is seen as the most critical 
factor driving the trend today. The two largest 
retailers of pharmaceuticals, Walgreen and Wal- 
Mart, are both capable of growing without acqui- 
sition—and they are doing so at a rapid pace. 

“Perhaps the biggest key to successful retail- 
ing in America today is market share,” Charles 
R. Walgreen III, chairman and chief executive of- 
ficer, told shareholders recently at the retailer’s 
annual meeting. “Any retailer that isn’t growing 
its market share is facing real trouble. That’s 
why expanding Walgreen’s share of the markets 
we serve is a key strategy for us.” 

Walgreen is achieving that result by sinking 
$300 million into a capital improvement program; 
it was able to open 196 new stores during 1994. 
With its enviable cash flow position and annual 
sales fast approaching $10 billion, Walgreen will 
continue to bankroll its $300 million annual 
growth fund without incurring long-term debt. 

Walgreen’s “3,000 by 2000” growth program 
dictates the opening of a daunting 200 stores a 
year through the end of the decade. At press 
time, Walgreen is on track to achieve its goal. 

“Walgreens now ranks first or second in 35 of our 
top 53 markets, all of which rank among the 
largest 100 drug store markets in the United 
States,” Walgreen stated. “At the same time, we 
better positioned ourselves as a full-service 


Acquisitions and mergers are a hot topic and 
source of constant speculation within the drug 
store industry. However, the industry’s level of 
consolidation apparently hasn’t yet reached a 

oint that it warrants extensive intervention 
y the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

tion and protecting consumers, the FTC has 
taken action in three recent i ha In 
each of the cases, however, the FTC merely re-

“Third party is playing a big role in our real

ecutive vice president and chief operating officer. 
“We are constantly talking to third-party people 
in terms of where we need better coverage. Good 
coverage allows you to give 
good service.” 

“With managed-care con- 
tracts come store traffic and 
the opportunity to sell prod- 
ucts,” commented Eckerd’s se-

years ago, third party at [Eck-

percent of our total business. 
Today it is more than 65 per-

our traffic counts and puts 
more consumers in direct inter-

As large chains get larger, they not only im- 
prove their ability to compete for third-party 
business, they also strengthen their negotiating 
position. 

“As the large chains grow larger, I think you 
are going to see them applying a lot more lever- 
age,” said one displaced chain executive. “If I 
were a third-party administrator, I would like to 
see a market with at least three or four chains to 
play one against another. If you have a market 
where there are two major chain players and one 
says, ‘I’m not taking your plan because your re- 
imbursement is too low,’ then the chains are in a 
situation where they have gained leverage.” 

That is a point not lost on Revco’s Bellini. “I 
don’t see much opportunity to change the erosion 
of margins, but I think we’ve got to stabilize 
them. And I think there are some places we may 
have to draw lines in the sand,” he said. 

For the chains that emerge larger than ever 
from the current consolidation environment, there 
are benefits beyond the issues of managed care. 
As their size increases, so does their ability to ex- 
tract more favorable sales terms from suppliers. 

But having that leverage is only one piece of 
the puzzle as more and more retailers form al- 
liances and partnerships with suppliers. 

This shift has been made possible by the fast 
and vast changes in technology over the past few 
years. Wal-Mart, because of its size and its con- 
scious effort to drive down costs through the use 
of technology, has encouraged/coerced its suppli- 
ers to move quickly in this respect. Retailers not 
using technology are at a huge disadvantage. 

Consolidation in itself does not help a chain 
compete in the technological arena. This was one 
hard lesson learned by HSI, which brought three 
viable chains together and was then unable to 
take advantage of its opportunities because of 
the lack of POS equipment and other systems. 

Today’s drug chain consolidations reflect — 
rather than cause—a rapidly changing environ- 
ment. And, like any single business strategy, 
they must be well executed in order to be effec- 
tive. Only time will tell whether or not today’s 
newly combined chains will go on to be the 
hunters or the prey in the next round. 

Conceding that consolidation in the industry 
will continue, Bob Hannan, president and chief 
executive officer of Thrift Drug, commented: 
“What the chains need to do [to avoid being taken 
over or becoming extinct] is determine what their 
strategy is and then do it. Do it. You have to de- 
cide what are your strengths and focus there. 

“To me, that means offering customers value with 
proper pricing, 
services and a 
good environ- 
ment to shop 
in,” he added. 
“And you have 
to invest signifi- 
cantly in people 
and technology.”

Consolidation ralSes the level of play for all 


at if consolidation is the best thing for the chain 
drug industry? Getting “really big” is a survival strat- 
egy that makes more sense today than ever before. 
Each retail trade channel is defined by its leaders; notice 
how Wal-Mart’s success 


tween the retailer and supplier is changing dramatically 
and quickly. As large manufacturers gear themselves—of-

Wal-Mart and other large retailers, they become less will-

gives a halo to all the other

As the companies at the

get bigger and stronger, the 
whole chain drug industry 
will gain clout with suppli- 
ers, consumers and the government. This will have a positive 
umbrella effect on those smaller chains that choose to stay in 
the game. Consolidation, as it always does, will also open up 
opportunities for the smaller, more nimble chains. 

Let’s face it, business isn’t going to get any easier. Man- 
aged care payors will increasingly favor market leaders with 
plenty of “doors,” big-volume retailers that can keep drug 
prices low and the companies that have the wherewithal to 
invest in technology in order to provide a full range of ser- 
vices. The cost of playing the game will also rise as more 
chains look to provide not only mail-order medications but 
also durable medical equipment, home infusion and more. 

But managed care isn’t the only dynamic at work, and it 
may not even be the most important one. 

Thanks to technology—and companies like Wal-Mart 
that really know how to maximize it—the relationship be-

to smaller chains. (And by

contracts, has the potential 
to block the smaller players 
from the playing field. Man-

After starting with lower prices, the big retailers then start 
to take advantage of their lower operating cost percentage. 

And, if all that’s not enough to discourage competition, 
the big chains can play hardball. With no holds barred, ap- 
parently. The recent court ruling in Arkansas seems to in- 
dicate that big retailers like Wal-Mart are free to price 
merchandise below cost—even if the objective is to drive lo- 
cal competitors out of business. 

It’s often said, “You can’t out-Wal-Mart Wal-Mart.” But, 
as they become larger through consolidation—or through 
an aggressive expansion plan like Walgreen’s—drug chains 
are closing the gap. They need to. 


Best is yet to come for regional chains 


ile a great deal of attention is centered on consoli- 
dations taking place in our industry, the case also 
can be made that this is an era of great opportunity 
for vibrant regional drug store chains. 

Our industry is exceptionally strong, advanced by an aging, 
health-conscious population, two-income families and the 
need for increased convenience. In a crowded and sometimes 
confusing marketplace, shoppers do not really need another 
warehouse club, superstore or deep discounter, but they will 
take to a highly disciplined drug store. Years from 
now, people will still shop at neighborhood drug 
stores, where they can talk with caring pharmacists. 

At the same time, we are “managing quite well” 
with managed care. Misunderstanding created by 
the drawn-out national debate on health care has 
cleared. Analysts and investors are now excited by 
the earnings potential of the conventional drug 
store format, one that has proven exceptionally re- 
silient to economic cycles. Additionally, the evolv- 
ing health care delivery system will provide sub- 
stantial fixed dollar dispensing fees—and 
income—for resourceful drug store chains that are 
adept in managing third-party payment plans.

Arbor store. We do this without highly promotion- 

al advertising or “13-hour sales,” instead we rely 
on proven messages delivered with clarity and confidence. 
Arbor customers identify with our health care orientation, 
that we are first and foremost a drug store with profession- 
al pharmacies that accept the wide range of third-party 
payment plans. 

Strong regionals like Arbor—with high volumes per store, 
valued relationships between pharmacist and customer and 
a shared culture—have much to teach. We are secure in our 
strategy for growth. From our vantage point, the best is yet 
to come for our industry and for our company.

COSMETICS 


Beauty care had 


happy holidays 


ith a few exceptions, the 
chain drug industry had 
an OK Christmas in 
beauty care. 

According to an informal Drug 
Store News survey of chains and 
manufacturers, cosmetics sales were 
stronger than fragrance sales. More 
than two-thirds of the chains inter- 
viewed reported that fragrance gift 
sets were disappointing, 
even though many buyers 
told us they tried to buy 
conservatively this year. 
Designer fragrances were 
also soft in many instances. 

In comparison, manufac- 
turer sources reported that 
mass volume discounters 
like Wal-Mart, Kmart and 
Target had much stronger 
sales gains and sell- 


cosmetics, and Sears, which 

is rapidly expanding cosmetics in its 
new prototype stores, had a great 
year. 

One reason why the mass volume 
retailers did so well is that some of 
the leading chains, particularly Tar- 
get, used some of the top fragrance 
brands as loss leaders. 

In the two weeks before Christ- 
mas, many retail chains were lower- 
ing prices to draw traffic. But while 
most drug chains were featuring pop- 
ular brands like Coty’s !exclamation 
and Lady Stetson at prices ranging 
from $11.95 to $14.95 for the cologne 

ift sets, Target had them on sale for 
§8.88, practically at cost. 

After Christmas, Target reduced 
its prices on all fragrance gift sets 
by 50 percent. 

Now there’s no arguing that drug 
chains can’t compete with those 
kinds of prices. But price isn’t the 
only weapon in a marketing arsenal, 
and there might be strategic changes 
that drug chains can make next year 
that will take at least some of the 
wind out of this kind of strategy. 

For one thing, chains like Target, 
Wal-Mart and Kmart are feeding 
their cosmetics/fragrance depart- 
ments with the traffic already in 
their stores. At Christmas, most 
fragrance sales are generated on 


LIZ PARKS 
throughs in fragrances 0. _U0a?—— motivator of a purchase. 


impulse by shoppers looking for gift 
items. With their expanded pres- 
ence in cosmetics and fragrances, 
chains like Wal-Mart, Kmart, Sears 
and Target are getting more and 
more of their existing shoppers, par- 
ticularly their apparel- and fashion- 
conscious shoppers, to notice cos- 
metics and fragrances and to come 
in and browse. 

Many drug chains did 
not have a lot of traffic in 
their cosmetics/fragrance 
departments at Christmas 
because they weren’t suc- 
cessful at converting the 
seasonal shoppers, the pre- 
scription shoppers, the 
card, candy and gift wrap 
shoppers into cosmetics/fra- 
grance shoppers. 

But price is not the only 


There’s convenience, being 
in stock, being pleasant to shop and 
being helpful to consumers. All these 
“hard-to-put-a-price-on-it” extra val- 
ue measures play strong roles in mo- 
tivating purchases. 

In Houston, one of Target’s most 
saturated markets, the average con- 
sumer has to drive 5 to 10 miles to 
get to one of its stores. When shop- 
pers finally arrive, they may not 
find the cosmetics department or 
they may not find the brands 
they’re looking for. At $8.88 for the 
Coty fragrance gift sets, many Tar- 
get stores quickly sold out, leaving 
them with out-of-stocks. 

Arbor Drug for years has been 
able to stand up to and triumph 
against stiff competitors, including 
Kmart. Its stores are always in 
stock. Prices are always fair. The 
merchandising presentations are 
clean, bright and attractive. 

The chain also actively cultivates 
the beauty care customer year- 
round and consequently has her in 
the habit of shopping Arbor stores 
for Christmas. 

And since many shoppers don’t 
comparison shop for fragrances and 
since they tend to buy on impulse as 
gifts, the Arbor stores have enough 
traffic going through to take advan- 
tage of these opportunities.

HOLIDAY NEWSBITES 


Here’s a look at how drug 
chains across the country fared 
during the 1994 holiday selling 
season. 


WINSBURG, Ohio — At 
| Mreveo 1994 Christmas sales 

were great, up significantly vs. 
last year and ahead of plan, cosmet- 
ics buyer Judy Wray reported. 
Wray started the season early with 
themed endcaps that went up in 
September and October. Among her 
best sellers were Coty’s Vanilla 
Fields, Quintessence’s Vanilla 
Musk, Tsumura’s bath sets for kids, 
Dana’s Canoe and Tabu, MEM’s 
British Sterling, Procter and Gam- 
ble’s Old Spice, Renaissance’s 
Chantilly, Revlon’s Fire and Ice For 
Women, Chesebrough-Pond’s Brut, 
Jean Philippe’s Jordache value- 
priced cosmetics sets and Parfums 
de Coeur’s Wind Song. 

According to Wray, sell-throughs 
for manufacturers who did not 
participate in Revco’s Christmas 
markdown program were disap- 
pointing. Percentages ranged from 
30 percent to 42 percent for most 
brands that did not participate in 
the program, and dipped as low as 
25 percent in some instances. 


ETROIT — Arbor Drug re- 
[)rxres an excellent Christ- 

mas with strong sales in cos- 
metics, mass fragrances and 
designer fragrances. Arbor spokes- 
man Fred Marx said that thanks 
to Arbor’s management informa- 
tion systems, “we got an early read 
on what was selling, and we re- 
ordered based on what was sell- 
ing.” He also said there was a di- 
rect correlation between what 
manufacturers advertised on TV 
and what was selling. Vanilla 
Fields, supported by Coty, and 
Fire and Ice, supported by Revlon, 
did particularly well in Arbor 
stores, he said. 

Next year, Marx said, Arbor will 
continue to do what it did this 
year: focus on the basics of its 
business. “Stock replenishment 
and store traffic are our two 
biggest strengths,” he said. “Our 
customers have a great familiarity 
with our stores because they shop 
us [year-round ].” 


INNEAPOLIS — Snyder 
W Be had a strong Christ- 
mas but not in beauty care, 
according to Phil Perkins, vice 
president of marketing. “Our sell- 
throughs on fragrance gift sets 
were disappointing. We thought we 
had bought conservatively this 
year, but apparently not conserva- 
tively ah" he said. Among the 
best sellers at Snyder were Wind 
Song (the No. 1 gift set item), Brut, 
Vanilla Fields, Yardley bath and 
body lotions, Stetson and Cachet. 
But Snyder’s cosmetics buyer, 
Peggy Williams, pointed out that 
even the best sellers were some- 
what disappointing, generating at 


best two pieces per store per season. 

Knowing from last year’s num- 
bers that gift set sales were trend- 
ing down, Williams did not buy 
multiples of gift sets this year. She 
bought the top set in the line and 
that was it. She said she will con- 
centrate on the top 10 gift sets, 
and “will use lower price points to 
move our entire selection.” 

“If you don’t sell more than two 
pieces per store, you don’t need 
multiples,” she said. “Next year, 
we'll repeat what we did this year. 
We'll only back the top 10 gift sets 
and we'll use lower price points to 
move the rest of our selection.” 


ILSONVILLE, Ore. — 
WW Thrifty PayLess had a 
mixed Christmas in fra- 
grances. Most fragrance gift sets 
did well, according to cosmetics 
buyer Sheri Ralston, but sales of 
basic stock and designer fra- 
grances were down vs. last year. 

Among the winners at the chain 
were the vanilla-scented fra- 
grances. Coty’s Vanilla Fields and 
Quintessence’s Vanilla Musk were 
“sreat,” said Ralston, while Del’s 
Naturally Vanilla and Men’s 
French Vanilla also did very well 
in Thrifty PayLess stores. 

Wind Song from Parfums de 
Coeur had exceptionally strong gift 
set sales, which Ralston thinks 
was partly due to its new packag- 
ing and advertising. Fragrance Im- 
pressions also turned in a strong 
performance in the alternative de- 
signer fragrance category. 

Revlon and L’Oréal cosmetics 
sold well both at Christmas and 
throughout the year. 

One of the strategic changes the 
chain will make next year, Ralston 
said, will be in advertising frequen- 
cy and the types of incentives of- 
fered to attract shoppers to the 
beauty care departments. 


OWELL, Ohio — On the ba- 
Ps of gains in comparable 

store sales, Bob Lyons, senior 
vice president for Drug Empori- 
um, reported the chain had a posi- 
tive Christmas overall. But sales 
of mass fragrances were soft while 
sales of designer fragrances and 
miniature designer fragrances 
were just fair. 

Color cosmetics, said Lyons, 
were fine while the pegged cosmet- 
ics, particularly Maybelline and 
Cover Girl, did great. 

In the mass fragrance categories, 
the vanilla scents, particularly 
Vanilla Fields and Vanilla Musk, 
were among the strongest brands. 

According to Lyons, there was a 
lot of discounting going on in Drug 
Emporium markets, especially at 
discount store chains. He also said 
the drug chain was “outspent” in 
advertising by mass market and de- 
partment store competitors. 

Next year, Doyle said, the chain 
will be “More specific and less gen- 
eral” in its beauty care advertising.

Hand and body lotions: A brand scorecard 


There was a time when drug stores knew some- 
thing about hand and body care that its competi- 
tors in the food and mass merchandise trade 
classes didn’t know: that many of the strongest 
growth brands were therapeutic brands like Lu- 
briderm, Curel, Eucerin and Jergens Extra Dry. 

But the secret seems to be out, and now sales 
of many of these brands are going up faster in 
three-outlet stores* than they are in drug stores. 


of their strongest category growth off smaller 
volume specialty brands like Aveeno and Lac- 
Hydrin Five, which didn’t even make it into the 
Top 25 highest volume brands for three outlet 
stores, and Curel. 

Drug stores also generated some nice growth 
on the higher volume brands like VIC and Jer-

A Hand and body lotions have a moderate- 
ly high household penetration level. Fifty- 
four percent of all households purchased a 
hand and body lotion in the past year, buy- 
ing an average 2.6 units and spending an 
average $8.99 a year. 

Some 28 percent of all households waited 
to buy their lotions on deal, and 15 percent 
of all unit purchases were accompanied 


with a coupon from either a store or manu- 


facturer. 


< How do you take a strong brand and > 
make it even stronger? You adopt the line- 


extension brand-family marketing philoso- 


phy, brilliantly illustrated here by Chese- 


brough Ponds, which makes Vaseline 


Intensive Care (VIC), and the Andrew Jer- 
gens Co., which makes Jergens products. 
Although the VIC regular formulation is 
second, as a brand, to Lubriderm in three- 
outlet* dollar volume sales and fourth in 
drug store dollar volume brand sales, the 
VIC brand family, with all its line exten- 


sions, dominates sales of the Top 25 highest 


dollar volume brands in the hand and body 


lotion category. 
The Jergens Top 25 brand-family line ex- 


tensions make it the third highest brand 


family within the drug store Top 25 highest 


dollar volume brands, with a 7.1 percent 
share. Lubriderm, without line extensions, is 


the No.1 hand and body lotion dollar volume 


brand in both drug and three outlet stores. 
It’s interesting that the leading brand in 


this category is a specialty brand targeted 


primarily to consumers who have especially 
dry skin. Lubriderm has been a steady 


growth brand in the hand and body category 
and that’s partly because it carved out a spe- 


cialty niche early and never let itself get di- 


verted or distracted from its core consumers.

Revco: Executing at a higher level 


Plan, then execute. Do it fast. Do it well. This is the 
Revco strategy in a nutshell. 

In every industry I have covered, I have found that the 
companies that are truly leaders, the ones that are most 
worth emulating, are the ones whose strategies sound like 
recitations of solid, basic business principles. Although 
Revco D.S. is one of those companies in many respects, 
don’t worry that this special issue on Revco will be boring. 

At Drug Store News, we rarely devote an issue to a single 
chain. But the value of doing an in-depth study of Revco be- 
came clear just hours after news editor Jim Frederick and I 
arrived at Revco’s headquarters for a three-day visit last 
November. 


do it fast.” It’s “Just do it fast and do it well.” 

I think the company’s dedication to technology is one of 
its key tactical weapons. 

Since purchasing the HSI stores, Revco has installed 
point-of-sale scanning and the PAL (Prescription Access 
Link) in more than 800 stores. In its new Indianapolis dis- 
tribution center, Revco installed a new central processing 
unit and its proprietary warehouse management software 
even before the HSI deal closed; otherwise, buyers in Twins- 
burg would have been unable to replenish merchandise for 
the newly acquired stores. 

Automation is also behind Revco’s firm insistence on cen- 

tralization—a stance that is 


We were fascinated by 
what Revco was doing to in- 
tegrate the more than 800 
stores it had acquired from 
Hook-SupeRx Inc. in July 
into the Revco organization, 
culture and systems. And 
we were just as interested 
in how Revco itself operates; 
even before the purchase of 
HSI, Revco was positioning 
itself at the forefront of 
chain drug retailing. 

But the thing that makes 
the Revco story so compelling 
today is the fact that this company emerged from a four-year- 
long bankruptcy less than three years ago. There’s nothing 
that touches the heart quite like a true comeback story. 

While a Chapter 11 bankruptcy does allow a company 
certain business advantages—like the ability to get out of 
unfavorable leases as well as the suspension of payments 
to creditors—the “psychic” effect of the bankruptcy seems 
to have been positive, too. 

The people of Revco came out of bankruptcy all “revved 
up.” And even though there is no longer a major threat 
overshadowing the company today, its management be- 
haves almost as if there is. 

Complacency is not well accepted at Revco. 

Having conquered bankruptcy, Revco’s executives got a 
chance to really test their mettle with the daunting task of 
bringing HSI on board. In fact, the plans instituted for the 
integration of HSI closely mirror the steps Revco took to re- 
make itself. 

With HSI, however, the time frames have been much, 
much quicker. 

Revco’s intolerance for inefficiency and sloppiness is just 
as intense as its aversion to complacency. Having spent 
time at Revco, I’ve found that the company’s motto is not 
the same as Nike’s. It’s not “Just do it.” It’s not even “Just 


What makes the Revco story 
so compelling is the fact that 
Revco emerged from bank- 
ruptcy less than three years 
ago. Nothing touches the heart 
like a true comeback story. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


in total contrast to HSI, 
which did almost nothing to 
integrate the three drug 
chains when they were un- 
der its ownership. 

My first impression of 
Revco, in fact, was that its 
insistence on centralization 
left no room for creativity, 
especially at store level, 
where managers cannot buy 
merchandise or decide how 
or where to display products. 
But D. Dwayne Hoven, 
Revco’s president and chief 
executive officer, explained that Revco’s intention is to cen- 
tralize and automate every possible store-level function in 
order to free the people to concentrate on customer service. 

I discovered the level to which Revco will go to minimalize 
“drudgery” for store employees when I was talking to David 
Lynn, Revco’s vice president of distribution. At the ware- 
house, totes are automatically loaded with only one depart- 
ment’s merchandise so that a store employee can just grab 
the pre-sorted tote and restock quickly and efficiently. 

At Drug Store News, we are very pleased that so many 
executives at Revco were willing to share their expertise 
with us and you, our readers. 

While some retailers shy away from publicity because 
they fear that competitors will learn their “secrets,” Hoven 
understands that, like sports, business has a few simple 
principles that work. Lots of people know how basketball 
should be played, for instance, but how many people actu- 
ally play ball like Shaquille O’Neal? 

What makes any person or company a “player” is perfor- 
mance, and performance is what makes Revco stand out. 
As Hoven so aptly explained it: “Success in our industry to- 
day is not about brilliant strategy, it’s about brilliant exe- 
cution. What makes Revco different from much of the in- 
dustry today, I think, is that we execute at a higher level.”

Drug Store News, March 13, 1995 


By Liz Parks 


OONSOCKET, R.I. 
— CVS, which has 
been looking for 


ways to transform some of 
its core front-end depart- 
ments into destination 
shops for consumers, is 
about to test a new mer- 
chandising presentation 
with a stronger focus on its 
beauty care department. 

Hank Mackor, vice presi- 
dent of store presentation 
and analysis for CVS, said 
that an “enhanced beauty 
care presentation” is in the 
early developmental stages 
of what he said will be an 
ongoing, fluid process of 
change and improvement. 

CVS, he said, will begin 
testing its ideas in some re- 
gional mall stores, as well 
as in some neighborhood 
pharmacy stores, by late 
spring or early summer. 

The objective with the 
modifications is to make 
CVS stores “a more relaxed 
and pleasant shopping expe- 
rience.” 

A key part of the concept is 
the linking together of CVS’ 
beauty care categories into 
one integrated presentation. 
According to Mackor, the 
word “boutique” is too much 
of a cliché to describe the 
modifications CVS is mak- 
ing, but he said the company 
is trying to “accentuate” the 
beauty and fashion care cate- 
gories more emphatically. 

“We’re trying to tie cos- 
metics in with toiletries in 
visual ways to create a focal 
point for our shoppers,” he 
said. “We want customers to 
view CVS as their beauty 
care store as well as their 
health care store.” 


As an early step in consol- 
idating cosmetics and fra- 
grances with toiletries, CVS 
recently promoted Cheryl 
Mahoney to vice presi- 
dent/merchandise manager 
for cosmetics and toiletries. 
Previously, Mahoney had 
only been responsible for 
cosmetics. 

One supplier, who has seen 
early sketches of the presen- 
tation, said it draws on many 
of the merchandising strate- 
gies of specialty beauty care 
chains like The Cosmetic 


“We want 
customers to view 
CVS as their 
beauty care store 
as well as their 
health care store.” 
—Mackor, CVS 


Center and Ulta3. This 
source said it was the most 
exciting and attractive pre- 
sentation he’s ever seen in ei- 
ther the drug store industry 
or the food store industry. 
Another supplier said 
that some elements in the 
presentation resemble re- 
cent merchandising strate- 
gies that Thrifty PayLess, 
Eckerd Drug and Walgreen 
have adopted. Like these 
chains, and like Rite Aid 
with its new “beauty focus” 
stores, CVS is trying to 
bring all its fashion and 
toiletry sections together 
as a central department 


CVS to test service in cosmetics 


Cash registers will be 
included in CVS’ new 
merchandising presenta- 
tion for cosmetics. One 
source said that in some 
test stores, they will be 
staffed by women trained 
to help customers make 
product choices. 

If CVS ultimately de- 
cides to put service cos- 
meticians into all its 
beauty accent stores, it 
would be a major depar- 
ture for the chain. 

Up until now, all CVS 
stores have been self-ser- 
vice in cosmetics, but the 
company has what a sup- 

lier called one of the 

st cosmetics coordina- 


tor programs in the in- 
dustry: a corp of people 
who each have responsi- 
bility for between 12 and 
25 stores and who rotate 
from store to store mak- 
ing sure the cosmetics de- 
partments are clean and 
in stock. 

The coordinators insure 
that the planned seasonal 
displays and promotional 
endcaps go up in time and 
are well maintained. 

“It would be relativel 
easy,” this source said, 
“to draw on this pool of 
talent to create a in- 
store service prorcram 
wherever sales justifies 
such an approach.”

& Fragrances 


CVS courts 


stronger fashion image 


within the store. 

One supplier said that the 
new presentation will bring 
CVS stores, particularly 
higher-volume cosmetic 
doors, into the second half 
of the decade with a whole 
new image. 

“The idea behind the pre- 
sentation,” said one suppli- 
er, is “to take advantage of 
the synergy between cos- 
metics and toiletries. 

“Management at CVS 
asked the question ‘What 
else is my cosmetic shopper 
likely to buy when she’s in 
the store,” said this source, 
“and the answer was skin 
care, shampoo, hair color, 
sun care and bath products. 

“So if their customers are 
likely to be buying these 
types of products under 
CVS’ roof, why shouldn’t 
CVS make it easy for them 
by giving them a cohesive 
merchandising presenta- 
tion,” the source said. “They 
should be able to generate a 
lot more impulse sales if 
they transform the mer- 
chandising presentation for 
toiletries into a boutique.” 


New department design 


In the past, CVS has tra- 
ditionally merchandised 
cosmetics and fragrances 
along the right wall to- 
ward the front of its stores. 
Toiletries have been mer- 
chandised in gondolas to 
the left of the cosmetics de- 
partment. 

In the new environment, 
cosmetics and toiletries will 
be merchandised together in 
a brightly lit department, 
possibly equipped with up- 
scale cabinetry and definite- 
ly accentuated with fixtures 
and graphics that create a 
more relaxed and pleasant 
shopping experience. 

One source said that CVS 
has not given either depart- 
ment more space, but by re- 
deploying the space they do 
have, the chain has succeed- 
ed in creating the effect of a 
more focused department. 

“When Eckerd boutiqued 
their skin care department 
and located it adjacent to 
cosmetics, they generated 
gains of 20 percent to 30 
percent in most stores,” said 
this source. “CVS is trying 
to do the same.” 

This source also pointed 
out that this concept could 
immediately make CVS’ re- 
gional mall stores “much 
more attractive to the 
women now shopping for 
cosmetics in the depart- 
ment stores the chain com- 
petes with.”

be watching the local weather

Raising awareness 


While Schering-Plough’s dis- 
tribution plan for its UV index 
is the most ambitious, all 
three UV indexes are designed 
to raise consumer awareness 
about the dangers of UV rays. 
And they ali have the potential 
to dramatically affect con- 
sumers’ shopping behavior. 

Indeed, Schering-Plough, 
which manufactures Copper- 
tone sun care products, 
Bausch and Lomb, manufac- 
turer of Ray-Ban sunglasses, 
and the Environmental Protec- 
tion Agency (EPA) have major 
promotional programs planned 
to publicize the need and value 
of a national UV index. 

That’s particularly good 
news for HBC buyers who 


manage the sun care category. 
“Anything that will educate 
the public about protecting 
their skin will impact the cate- 
gory, said Andy Striefel, vice 
president of merchandising at 
Thrifty PayLess. “While there 
are a lot of people who are 
aware of the need to protect 
their skin, there is a whole 
segment of the public that isn’t 
using [sun care] products.” 

Schering-Plough’s proposed 
joint venture with Orbital Sci- 
ences is expected to be formal- 
ized sometime this month, ac- 
cording to executives from both 
companies. The venture calls 
for Schering-Plough to fund the 
distribution of the SunCast UV 
Monitor, which was tested by 
the latter and WSI, a supplier 
of weather data, in limited mar- 
kets last summer. 

The two companies have 
signed a letter of agreement to 
roll cut the Sun Cast UV Mon- 
itor in April. 

By funding the release of 
free, non-branded UV informa- 
tion to meteorologists, Scher- 
ing-Plough hopes to encourage 
as many media outlets as pos- 
sible to disseminate its region- 
al daily UV readings and advi- 
sories about sun protection. 

Schering-Plough plans to 
unveil a $2 million marketing 
program promoting the value 
of a national UV index May 
21-28 to tie in with National 
Sun Protection Awareness 


Week, a new observance fo- 
cused on sun protection. It is 
the company’s largest mer- 
chandising program of its kind 
to date. In-store materials in- 
clude educationally oriented 
displays, pamphlets, “Ask Me 
About the UV Index” buttons 
for store personnel to wear, 
window banners, inflatable 
rafts and audio sun care mes- 
sages designed for in-store ra- 
dio systems. 

Company executives have 
high hopes for its impact on 
sales. Promoting a national UV 
index “is the best approach to 
grow the sun care category,” 
said Jay Joyce, director of trade 
marketing for Schering-Plough. 
“The sun care category has been 
focused on growing efficiencies. 
The UV index is about in- 
creased consumption and in- 
creased penetration for the cat- 
egory.” 

Indeed, when the Canadian 
government launched a UV in- 
dex in that country, sun care 
product sales grew in double 
digits, Joyce explained. When 
the National Weather Service 
and Environmental Protection 
Agency launched a UV Index in 
in the U.S. last summer, it af- 
fected consumer awareness and 
behavior, according to a Scher- 
ing-Plough study. Nearly seven 
in 10 consumers in the 58 test 
markets claimed awareness of 
the index. Half of those aware

Oil of Olay recall 
raises questions 


CINCINNATI —Has 
Procter & Gamble’s de- 
cision to pull the Oil of 
Olay Visible Recovery 
Series Renewal line off 
the shelves cast a dark 
cloud on the bright hy- 
droxy acid-based skin 
care category? 

It wasn’t entirely 
clear at press time. 
P&G’s move, announced 
last month, involves two 
products with hydroxy 
acids, not the popular 
alpha hydroxy acids. 
Neverthelesss, the inci- 
dent has raised aware- 
ness about skin irrita- 
tion that products in 
both categories can 
cause. 

Like many manufac- 
turers of alpha hydroxy 
acid-based products, 
P&G added a warning 
to the Oil of Olay Visi- 
ble Recovery Renewal 
Cream and Lotion in 
October, urging cus- 
tomers not to use the 
product on their eyelids 
or under their eyes. 
Nevertheless, to date, 
572 customers have re- 
ported burning, sting- 
ing, redness or blurred 
vision, said Carol Boyd, 
a P&G spokesman, 
prompting the company 
to suspend the sale of 
the products in Febru- 
ary. (Retailers have un- 
til May to return the 
products for a refund.) 
“It was an unacceptably 
high level of com- 
plaints,” said Boyd. 
“With a brand like Olay, 
we wouldn’t take the 
risk that people would 
distrust the brand.” 

One thing is certain, 
more consumers and re- 
tailers are asking safety 
questions of manufac- 
turers of alpha hydroxy- 
acid based products. 

P&G’s competitors, 
including Chesebrough- 
Ponds and Neoteric, as- 
sert that their products 


are “less irritating” 
than the suspended Oil 
of Olay products. They 
acknowledge that their 
products have been 
known to cause some ir- 
ritation as well. 

The Oil of Olay prod- 
ucts contained salicylic 
acid, an ingredient 
found in acne and wart 
preparations. Alpha hy- 
droxy acid-based prod- 
ucts are made from oth- 
er acids, such as sodium 
lactate, glycolic acid and 
lactic acid. “There is a 
big difference between 
salicylic acid and glycol- 
ic acid,” said Mark 
Goldstein, president, 
Neoteric, which makes 
the glycolic acid-based 
Alpha Hydrox line. “Sal- 
icylic acid dissolves pro- 
tein, and glycolic acid 
loosens dead skin.” 

P&G does not believe 
that just the ingredient 
caused the problems. 
“We don’t know what 
the problem is,” Boyd 
said. “It may be a com- 
bination of ingredients.” 

Interestingly enough, 
the label on Pond’s Age 
Defying products, which 
are made with glycolic 
acid, hydroxycaprylic 
acid and lactic acid, in- 
forms consumers that 
they may experience a 
brief tingling sensation. 

“It’s a normal part of 
what can be expected 
with initial use of the 
product as it exfoliates 
the skin,” said Eileen 
Sharkey, vice president 
of public affairs for 
Chesebrough-Ponds. 

While  Beiersdorf 
takes the Oil of Olay in- 
cident “very seriously,” 
it will not add a warn- 
ing label to its AHA- 
based Nivea Visage In- 
ner Beauty line, due to 
a marginal number of 
complaints about irrita- 
tion said irena Valles, 
director of marketing.

Drug Store News, March 13, 1995 


e& Generai Merchandise 


Multipacks charge battery sales 


Rechargeable niche is picking up 


By Leslie Gilbert Elman 


[Minton good news: According to 
Information Resources Inc., for 
the year ending Jan. 1, 1995, 
drug stores saw a 5 percent dollar 
volume gain. The channel account- 
ed for sales of $523 million in the 
$1.8 billion battery category, out- 
pacing food stores in total dollar 
volume, but falling short of mass 
merchandisers. Overall, the battery 
category saw a 9.4 percent dollar 
volume growth versus a year ago. 

Growth in unit volume was slow- 
er however: 5.2 percent for the total 
category and a mere 1.1 percent for 
the drug trade in particular. 


Beyond the numbers 


In drug stores, the higher in- 
crease in dollar volume coincidental 
with the virtually flat volume in 
unit sales, can largely be attributed 
to a sales increase in higher-priced 
multipacks.

Among battery product “over-

8-packs saw a phenomenal 436 per-

smaller round cell batteries are 
most commonly used to power re-

other electronic devices. 

Jim Barone, vice president of field 
sales for Duracell, believes that mul- 
tipacks offer drug stores the great- 
est opportunity to grow battery 
sales. “Right now about 65 percent 
of the business is done in standard 
[single and 2-] packs and maybe 30 
percent is done in ‘saver’ packs like 
AA 8-packs,” he said. “Drug stores 
should look to move toward 40 to 50 
percent in saver packs.” He added 
that multipacks typically represent 
55 percent of battery sales in mass 
merchandisers. 

Sales of multipacks continue to 
grow, in spite of generally cautious 
consumer spending, because cus- 
tomers perceive the larger packs as 
offering the greatest value for their 
money. In fact, batteries have 
proven to be virtually recession- 
proof. “The average household con- 
tains about 12 battery-operated 
items,” Barone noted. Demand from 
that customer base remains con- 
stant, whether or not consumers are 
purchasing new appliances.

Drug chains’ glory days still ahead 


ike the “ugly duckling” that grew naturally to become a 
beautiful swan, the drug chain is finally being appreciat- 
ed as the desirable, long-term retailing format it is. 

In recent weeks, I’ve attended two financial analyst con- 
claves, hosted by Raymond James & Associates in Florida 
and Merrill Lynch in New York. Both organizations made it a 
point to put the spotlight on four top public drug chains— 
Walgreen, Revco, Rite Aid and Eckerd—through individual 
presentations as well as panel discussions specifically dedi- 
cated to chain drug retailing. 

“Food and drug store stocks outperformed almost every- 
thing last year,” said Gary Vineberg, first vice 
president/Global Securities Research & Economics Group 
for Merrill Lynch, at Merrill 


supermarkets. (And this could hurt combo operators, at least 
some of them, at least in the short term.) On the outskirts of 
this battleground, though, drug chains have identified a gap- 
ing window of opportunity in the “convenience” area. 
Walgreen, Rite Aid, Revco and Eckerd are all concentrating 
on improving the convenience aspects of their stores: increas- 
ing store size so that aisies can be widened for easier shop- 
ping; stepping up convenience food assortments and adding 
more coolers for consumable basics like milk, ice cream and 
beer; installing drive-up pharmacy windows and one-hour 
photo processing; and building freestanding units at busy in- 
tersections with quick and easy in-and-out access to compete 
with congested malls and strip centers. 
Meanwhile, despite di-
