difficult but necessary internal restructuring. Drug chains 
did have a lot of catching up to do in the areas of point-of- 
sale technology, store renovations, competitive pricing and 
promotional strategies, and merchandising focus. 

It is interesting that now, when drug chains are begin- 
ning to reap the benefits of their hard work, some of the 
shiny veneer may be starting to chip off the “darling” mass 
merchants. Certainly, Joseph Antonini’s long-anticipated 
ouster at Kmart is a sign that a turnaround at the nation’s 
number-two retailer will not happen quickly or easily. 

Moreover, the dynamic duo’s latest strategy may create 
the biggest opportunity yet for chain drug operators. Wal- 
Mart and Kmart are racing to build bigger and bigger boxes, 
hoping to continue their growth rate at the expense of the 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


aging populace will increase 
naturally but incrementally. 

Because pharmacy is their 
primary business, drug 
chains have the motivation 
and wherewithal to dedicate both capital and manpower to 
the pharmacy business while mass merchants and super- 
markets inherently have different priorities. At the Merrill 
Lynch conference, one supermarket CEO told the story very 
succinctly as he responded to a question about his company’s 
efforts in managed care: “Our main goal is to get people to 
buy food in our stores,” he said. 

Where it might have looked a few years back as if the 
drug store format would go the way of the dodo, the “cli- 
mate” has already started to change because the consumer 
values her time every bit as much as her money. It makes 
me wonder: Don’t those omnivorous, fast-growing, ever-ex- 
panding retailers that have recently dominated the land- 
scape have something in common with the dinosaurs? 


Teamwork is the way to brighten future 


WDA’s 1994-95 chairman, Mel Whitmire, vice chair- 

man of Cardinal Health, stated in his acceptance re- 

marks at this year’s annual meeting that “for whole- 
salers, the bottom line is no longer measured by our ability 
to cut cost—but on the value we provide our customers 
and suppliers.” 

For more than 20 years, drug wholesalers 
have expanded their role in distributing phar- 
maceuticals and health and beauty care prod- 
ucts by cutting their operating expenses and dri- 
ving their gross margins lower to provide better, 
less expensive service to our customers. 

We watched the percentage of pharmaceutical 
product distributed through wholesalers grow 
from about 47 percent in 1970 to about 80 per- 
cent today as average gross margins in the in- 
dustry declined from more than 14 percent to 
under 6 percent. 

The economies of scale we were able to 
achieve, coupled with operating efficiencies and 
value added services to our customers, made us 
a vital link in the channel. 

Today with major structural changes in our 
customers’ industry as well as our suppliers’ and 
our own industries, it is clear that efficiency and 
our abilities to reduce cost are no longer enough. 
Wholesalers are inextricably tied to the indus- 
tries they service, and our ability to remain at- 
tractive partners lies in our ability to provide val- 
ue to help these industries not survive, but prosper in the 
future. 

Today, I am pleased to report that interindustry efforts 
NWDA championed this year have shown improvements in 


the perennial problem of year-end shipments. NWDA’s Pro- 


GUEST COLUMN 


ductivity, Retail Marketing and Institutional Marketing 
committees have all reported a much smoother and consis- 
tent inventory supply at year’s end. 

We had support from the pharmacy and manufacturing 
communities alike this year in urging responsible behavior by 
all parties to end the conditions that created serious and po- 
tentially life-threatening shortages of vital product 
during the holiday season in 1993 and prior years. 
Lots of people took the time to think the problem 
through, develop reasonable courses of action and 
urge others to do so as well. 

We want to thank all of you for your support in 
this area. If we all put the need of the patient first, 
we can come together to resolve this issue perma- 
nently. 

This is not the only area that teamwork and fo- 
cus on the consumer can make a positive differ- 
ence. Efficient consumer response is another ini- 
tiative in which wholesalers working together 


OV OMMSsa a) with their customers and suppliers can take 


mens §=transactions out of the system and leverage our

of the National

infrastructure to provide genuine value. 

As health and beauty care companies move to au- 
tomatic replenishment of inventory in retail out- 
lets, we are positioned with not only the distribu- 
tion system, but also the right relationships in 
technology to make efficient consumer response a 
reality. We now know that the information infra- 
structure we have amassed gives us tremendous 
ability to provide service that will allow us, our customers, 
and suppliers all to benefit greatly. 

These are just two of the many areas in which we can and 
must work together to meet the needs of the patient. In doing 
so, we can create a future with real possibilities for us all.

Soap marketing gets a fresh approach 


EMPHIS, Tenn.— Yara- 

ley of London has un- 

veiled a fresh, aggres- 
sive marketing program to 
broaden appeal of its 24-year 
old commodity soap line. 

In January, the company 
lowered prices for the soaps by 
5 percent hoping to sway re- 
tailers to drop retail prices be- 
low $1, according to John 
Nuechterlein, senior market- 
ing manager of The Yardley 
Limited Co. At the same time, 
it also began shipping the soap 
in new packages that show- 
case the Yardley name and 
tout its “natural moisturizers” 
(glycerin and petrolatum). 


Beginning next month, the 
company rolls out an aggressive 
direct mail program. The com- 
pany has teamed up with di- 
rect marketing company to dis- 
tribute 2.3 million coupons in 
39 markets to households with 
consumers 55 and over, the tra- 
ditional Yardley customers. The 
promotion offers three coupons 
totaling $1.10 off Yardley bar 
and liquid soap. 

But in an attempt to build 
awareness of the brand among a 
younger audience, Yardley 
plans to offer samples of its oat- 
meal and almond soap in college 
book stores later this year. This 
flavor of the soap generated 


strong response from young 
women in tests, Nuechterlein 
said. 

Traditional, mass-oriented 
direct mail efforts are also 
planned. In May, the company 
will distribute 4.7 million 
coupons through FSIs, worth 
40 cents off two bars of any 
Yardley of London soap or 
twinpack, and 30 cents off any 
16-ounce liquid. 

The company is also distribut- 
ing 500,000 coupons for its re- 
cently re-introduced Baby Soap 
in packs of Baby Ambesol. The 
coupons can be redeemed for 50 
cents off two single bars of Baby 
Soap or one twinpack.

Drug’s top 10 


Drug Store News, April 3, 1995 


G General Merchandise 


Retailers experimenting 
with home security centers 


ore drug chains are enticing consumers 

with vertical merchandising—the group- 

ing of unrelated products with a common 
merchandising theme, like cold centers, 
body/bath kiosks and party shops, for example. 
Now some drug chains, like Walgreens and 
Thrift, are thinking about another kind of prob- 
lem-solving merchandiser: a security 
center. 

Vertical merchandising can rein- 
force the impression of customer ser- 
vice, even though the display may be 
self-service. Busy consumers love to 
find solutions in one place. And, for 
the retailer, it’s a chance to trade up 
the customer to more than one item in 
a themed feeding frenzy. 

One security concept— The Security 
Center, promoted to retailers by The 
Club anti-auto theft device—is in- 
tended to be merchandised in-line but 
designed to stand out from the larger in-line 
section with self-serve signing and a product 
range selected to help mom and dad sleep bet- 
ter at night. 

The Club’s Security Center concept combines 
products from different manufacturers and can 
be as small as four feet (in Sears, it’s 24 feet). 
The suggested small version includes products 
ranging from First Alert fire extinguishers and 
smoke detectors, to night lights, pepper spray, 
locks and personal alarms. 


Security question 


For the retailer, the decision to create vertical 
merchandising may not be an easy one, because 
products have to be gathered from different 
planograms across the store. 

At Walgreens, spokesperson Michael Polzin 
reported, “We’re looking at how we can mer- 


ALLENE SYMONS 
ee 


chandise the items together. We have a num- 
ber of products in that area like pepper spray, 
personal alarms, door and window alarms, 
combination locks, smoke detectors and light 
timers.” 

Tom Kutosky, vice president of merchandising 
for Thrift Drug, said, “So far we carry pieces, and 
we may pursue a test [of a security 
center]. Currently we have smoke and 
carbon monoxide detectors and fire ex- 
tinguishers in the health care appli- 
ance area—with heating pads.” 

Kutosky acknowledged that this 
heating pad/fire extinguisher match 
is a “a kind of adjacency, but it isn’t— 
and yet it seems to fit from a physical 
presence perspective. These things 
are meant to protect your health.” 

Kutosky noted that The Club—the 
metal hook that clamps onto and 
locks a car’s steering wheel—doesn’t 
have a home, but Thrift end caps it on a power 
panel in appliances or in a high traffic area and 
also carries First Alert’s self-sell display unit. 
Pepper spray, which Thrift has carried for 
around six months, is found at the checkout. 
And when The Bike Club arrives this spring, it 
will be merchandised as a summer seasonal 
product rather than in a security section, re- 
ported Kutosky. 

Space is tight and inventory dollars can’t be 
spread too liberally around the store. But for a 
drug chain with the space and desire to market 
multiple opportunities—like Bike Club in both 
the Security Center and in summer seasonal, or 
Animal lover (an electronic security device that 
alerts animals to oncoming vehicles) in Security 
and in the pet section—then it’s an ideal world 
for manufacturer, retailer and consumer. So let 
the feeding frenzy begin.

Rite Aid breaks down wall between pharmacy, front-end 


By Lisa I. Fried 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Moving swift- 
ly to weave Rite Aid’s pharmacy and 
front-end operations closer together, 
new chairman and chief executive 
Martin Grass has flattened out his 
chain’s management team 
and restructured the field 
sales force. 

Rather than operate two 
separate reporting struc- 
tures for pharmacy and the 
front-end, Grass has elimi- 
nated regional front-end 
and pharmacy posts and 
empowered district man- 
agers with broader respon- 
sibilities for the entire oper- 
ation of their stores. District 
managers now report to one of sev- 
eral market managers who are ac- 
countable to Chuck Kibler’s new op- 
erations team. 

Kibler, formerly vice president of 
drug store operations, was recently 
promoted to senior vice president of 
drug store operations. Greg Webb, 


formerly a divisional pharmacy 
manager, and Mike Podgurski, for- 
merly director of customer service, 
are now assistant vice presidents of 
drug store operations. 

While the previous structure had 
served Rite Aid well, shrinking profit 
margins in pharmacy, a big- 
ger emphasis on larger, ser- 
vice-oriented stores and a 


arm to take advantage of the best of 
both [operations].” 

The goal: a team-oriented sales ap- 
proach and improved efficiency. 
Training began last month and will 
continue for several weeks. 

In other management news, Grass 
recently promoted senior vice presi- 
dent of finance Frank Bergonzi to ex- 
ecutive vice president and chief finan- 


cial officer. Ray McKeeby, formerly 
vice president of marketing research, 
is heading up a new team responsible 
for evaluating product pricing for the 
front end and pharmacy. His new ti- 
tle is vice president of pricing. Eric 
Elliot has been named vice president 
of third-party administration from as-

Shoppers adds Bi-Rite 
to its Canadian arsenal 


WILLOWDALE, Ont. — 
Shoppers Drug Mart, which 
already dominates drug re- 
tailing in Canada as the 
only national drug store 
chain, will soon pack more 
wallop in the central-west 
province of Saskatchewan. 

Shoppers has signed a 
pact to buy Saskatchewan's 
Bi-Rite Drug Stores chain 
effective June 30. The 
agreement includes all 26 
Bi-Rite locations. 

Based in the provincial 
capital of Regina, Bi-Rite 
has operated for more than 
30 years. Its addition to 
Snoppers’ arsenal will give 


the chain 717 drug stores 
nationwide, and 42 stores 
in Saskatchewan. 

“The Bi-Rite acquisitiion 
is an excellent one for 
Shoppers Drug Mart as 
well as for the Bi-Rite 
chain,” said Shoppers 
chairman and chief execu- 
tive David Bloom. “Their 
stores are located in many 
centers where we have no 
presence, and where there 
is an existing Shoppers 
Drug Mart, there is little 
overlap of trading activity.” 

Conversion of the stores 
will begin in August, Shop- 
pers said. 


Manufacturer coupons still spark sales if used correctly 


WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. 
— Coupon distribution re- 
sumed its growth curve dur- 
ing 1994 after a nominal in- 
crease in 1993 nearly 
stalled two decades of con- 
secutive growth. 

An industry-record 327 
billion coupons were distrib- 
uted during 1994, a 1 per- 
cent increase from 1993’s 
323 billion, according to 
CMS Inc., the nation’s 
largest manufacturer's 
agent in coupon redemption 
management. Freestanding 
inserts accounted for 88 per- 
cent of all coupons distrib- 
uted—clear proof that man- 
ufacturers continued to rely 
on FSIs even though re- 
demption rates have fallen 
to 1.9 percent in 1994 from 


2.3 percent in 1990. 

The reason for the re- 
demption decline, CMS sug- 
gests in its latest study of 
coupon usage, is that manu- 
facturers aren’t responding 
adequately to consumer de- 
mand. “It is not a question 
of the efficacy or value of 
FSIs, it is a matter of using 
them correctly and giving 
consumers what they say 
they want,” Joan Johnson, 
marketing manager of CMS, 
said. Manufacturers contin- 
ue to put expiration dates 
and low face values on 
coupons even though re- 
search suggests consumers 
are less likely to redeem 
them. Also hurting FSI re- 
demption rates are multiple 
coupons on an FSI page and 


coupons that require multi- 
ple purchases. 


Instant hit 


Instantly redeemable 
coupons were the biggest hit 
with consumers during 1994. 
They only accounted for 0.3 
percent of coupons distrib- 
uted, but they achieved the 
highest redemption rate as 
consumers took advantage of 
the immediate savings they 
offer. The redemption rate 
for this type of OTC product 
coupon increased to 38.4 per- 
cent in 1994 from 29.7 per- 
cent during 1993. Redemp- 
tion rates were also high for 
direct mail coupons, 14.1 
percent, and in-package 
coupons, 5.3 percent. 

Some of the year’s most 


interesting couponing devel- 
opments were in the OTC 
department, where FSI us- 
age in 1994 declined to 86.6 
percent of all OTC coupons 
distributed, down from 90.4 
percent in 1993. The re- 
demption rate of those 
coupons dropped from 1.2 
percent during 1993 to 1 
percent in 1994 as manufac- 
turers shortened expiration 
periods from an average of 
5.6 months in 1993 to 4.3 
months in 1994. Also con- 
tributing to the decline in 
FSI usage for OTCs is the 
availability of other distrib- 
ution methods. 

For more information or 
to obtain a copy of CMS’ 
“1994 Coupon Trends” re- 
port, call (910) 631-2500.

Viewpoints 


Chain drug’s ‘all-stars’ set new records 


en the all-star team is fielded in any sport, there are 

usually just a few names you can count on seeing 

year after year. These 

are the “legends,” the “big 


dustry. There’s a gap of some $4.5 billion in sales separating 
Walgreen from the latest No. 2, which, as of this writing, is 
actually Rite Aid. (With its acquisition of Perry Drug in Janu- 
ary 1995, Rite Aid overtook 


name” players who inspire 
and challenge all the others. 

If chain drug retailing 
had an all-star team, the 
same seven names would be 
represented today as they 
were four years ago: Wal- 
green, American Drug 
Stores, Rite Aid, Eckerd, 
Thrifty (now Thrifty Pay- 
Less), CVS and Revco. 

Aside from some shifts in 
the pecking order, the big 
difference between the all- 
star teams of ’90 and 794 is 
in the size and strength of the players. Combined revenues 
for those top seven drug chains in 1990 were $24.83 billion; 
the same group amassed $35.82 billion in sales in 1994. 

Walgreen, still reigning supreme, was 50 percent bigger 
in 1994 than it was in 1990, beefing up to $9.23 billion from 
$6.05 billion. 

In fact, Walgreen is expecting to hit the $10 billion 
benchmark right about the time you read this. For the 12- 
month period ended February 28, 1995, Walgreen’s sales 
totaled $9.83 billion. 

Over the past four years, Walgreen has significantly 
lengthened its lead without participating in the merger-ac- 
quisition trend that has gripped much of the chain drug in- 


Walgreen is expecting 
to hit the $10 billion 
benchmark right about 
the time you read this. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


American Drug with annual 
sales of $5.2 billion.) 

One of the most interest- 
ing aspects of Drug Store 
News’ ranking of the top 50 
drug chains is how close the 
race for second place contin- 
ues to be. On our 1994 list— 
which is not an exact 
barometer because different 
chains end their fiscal years 
months apart from one an- 
other—the margin between 
No. 2 and No. 7 is only $220 
million, or 5 percent. 

Twice last year, we crowned a new “No. 2” when the 
Thrifty-PayLess merger and the Revco-HSI (Hook-SupeRx 
Inc.) acquisition, respectively, were announced. Initially, 
spokespeople for both organizations were pegging their 
sales at $4.5 billion. As it turned out, American Drug, Rite 
Aid and Eckerd edged out both combined chains, while 
CVS and Revco ended in almost a dead heat. 

Like the sports “all-stars,” the top drug chains will con- 
tinue to jockey for position this year, no doubt. But the 
tough competition is also going to force every one of these 
players to stay in peak condition. Considering the strong 
performance we saw from these players in 1994, that bodes 
very well for a healthy, growing chain drug industry in ’95. 


Restrictions may not benefit Medicaid 


s you read this, members of Congress are re- BQUSSMeORU IER costs for the period 1983-93 as part of an analysis 


turning from Spring recess and are beginning 


of the 370 percent growth in the drug component 


to reshape the Medicare and Medicaid pro- 
grams. Their efforts are directed at reducing the 
costs of these programs as part of an effort to reduce 
the federal budget deficit. Their actions could have a 
significant impact on community retail pharmacy. 
Consider the fact that the elderly, who currently 
lack a prescription drug benefit in the Medicare pro- 
gram, consume 34 percent of all outpatient prescrip- 
tions, over 650 million annually. An additional 16 
percent, or 338 million prescriptions, are dispensed 


of the Medicaid program. The two primary fac- 
tors determined to be driving significant increas- 
es in Medicaid prescription drug program were a 
74 percent increase in recipients and an 88 per- 
cent increase in the manufacturers’ prices for 
drug products used to fill the prescription. 

These trends continued in 1994. Last year, the 
average Medicaid pharmacy payment was esti- 
mated to be $23.99 per prescription. Of this 
amount, about 82 percent continues to be reim- 


through the Medicaid program. Collectively, these Bitiriw4cdame bursement for the drug product purchased by the 
two groups represent half, or nearly 1 billion, of th oo! pharmacists from the manufacturer used to fill 


total outpatient prescription volume each year. 

Current Medicaid reform proposals would give 
the states enhanced freedom through “block grants” 
in operating their Medicaid programs. In return, 
the federal government’s annual contribution to 
Medicaid spending would be capped at a fixed rate 
of increase. Under this approach, states will likely 
place many of their Medicaid recipients into “man- 
aged care” programs. Eligibility, the scope of benefits, as 
well as the level of reimbursement to providers would also 
shift to state governments. 

Currently, all state Medicaid programs cover outpatient 
drugs. Drugs and pharmacy services constituted only about 
8 percent, or $9 billion, of Medicaid’s $140 billion in spend- 
ing last year. These pharmacy expenditures save money in 
other parts of the Medicaid health care budget. Medicaid 
recipients use, on average, about 15 prescriptions each 
year, while the rest of the population uses about four pre- 
scription drugs annually. 

Due to the high prescription drug use by Medicaid recipi- 
ents, it is important for them to have easy access to a phar- 
macist. The sooner that Medicaid recipients are able to 
have prescriptions filled (or refilled), the more likely that 
their health will improve or their medical condition will be 
brought under control, avoiding costly medical problems. 

Because the prescription drug program has been the 
fastest growing component of the Medicaid program, many 
budget cutters and policy makers believe shifting these re- 
cipients into restricted provider networks will reduce these 
expenditures. But such an approach will not achieve their 
goal of overall Medicaid program cost reduction. 

Recently, the PRIME Institute at the University of Min- 
nesota completed a study of Medicaid prescription drug 


Ronald Ziegler is 
president and chief 
executive officer of 
the National Asso- 
ciation of Chain 
Drug Stores. 


the prescription. Less than 18 percent represent- 
ed the dispensing fee payment to the pharma- 
cists. Using inflation adjusted dollars, this dis- 
pensing fee has actually declined by 6 percent. 

It is clear that Medicaid pharmacy reimburse- 
ment is not the cause of rising Medicaid prescrip- 
tion drug program expenditures. 

In the zeal to cut costs, Congress and state poli- 
cy makers should not lose sight of the cost-saving role of 
community retail pharmacy in our health care system. Out- 
patient prescription drug benefits can be effectively “man- 
aged” without requiring that Medicaid recipients and 
Medicare beneficiaries join restrictive “managed care plans.” 
Such “restrictive” approaches often make it more difficult for 
these individuals to have easy access to prescription drugs 
and pharmacist services. Adopting such an approach would 
defeat the purpose of the readily available primary preventa- 
tive care that community retail pharmacy can provide. 

Current law provides the Medicaid prescription drug pro- 
gram with mechanisms now used by managed care plans to 
effectively “manage” an outpatient prescription drug bene- 
fit. These mechanisms include drug formularies, drug man- 
ufacturer rebates, drug use review (DUR) programs and 
computerized patient medication record retrieval. 

To assure access, quality and effective cost management of 
their pharmacy benefit, state Medicaid programs should 
“carve out” their pharmacy benefits from Medicaid managed 
care programs. 

State Medicaid programs should continue to recognize the 
value of highly accessible cost-effective pharmacy services 
and include them as part of the package of Medicaid health 
benefits. The Community Medicare program would be wise to 
adopt the same position.

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


33 


» Homeopathic firm seeks 


aturaLife, Sunsource and homeopathy 
N reweomer Cabot Laboratories are part 

of a flurry of topical homeopathic prod- 
ucts hitting the market. All are seeking chain 
drug distribution for the recently introduced 
lines. 

NaturaLife Corp. has launched a line of 
homeopathic gels to treat burns, diaper rash, 
arthritis, injuries and backaches. Those prod- 
ucts are now part of the company’s Natural 
Pharmacy merchandising vehicle, according 
to group product manager Ken Ruick. 

Sunsource is launching a three-SKU line 
that includes an arthritis-relief formula, a 
sports-injury formula and an eczema and 
psoriasis formula. 

Cabot, already known for its skin care prod- 
ucts, will begin shipping in June a four-SKU 
line of sports-oriented homeopathy products. 
An antiseptic ointment, pain-relief gel and 
deep-heat muscle rub round out the topical of- 
ferings. An epsom salts mineral bath is also 
included in the line. 

Boericke & Tafel introduced a line of topi- 
cals back in 1988, including formulas for 
bruises, sprains and strains, sports injuries, 
arthritis, insect bites, stings and burns, and 
cuts and abrasions. The products have en- 
joyed success in the health food industry and 
were repackaged earlier this year. 

Boiron USA has also been involved in topi- 


outlet for new topical line 


cals as far back as 1985, although with very 
limited chain drug distribution. Boiron offers 
gel and ointment formulas for bruises and 
sore muscles, cuts and burns and a sensitive 
version of the cuts and burns product. 


Which merchandising strategy works? 


Meanwhile, a split continues to exist on 
whether it is more effective to merchandise 
products in-line with their respective cate- 
gories or group all homeopathics together as 
part of a natural products presentation. The 
jury is still out on which approach produces 
the highest turns, but for the time being 
the family approach appears to be most 
popular. 

“The challenge is going to be where do you 
go from here,” one chain drug buyer said. 
“Right now, the consumer looks for the prod- 
ucts in a natural products section. I don’t 
know when the time will come to break 
them out.” 

Sunsource president Steve Lefkowitz said, 
“Eventually, we feel like these products can 
compete with anybody, but we prefer at the 
present time to be merchandised as a family.” 

It is a question of evolution, according to 
Boericke and Tafel marketing manager Anne 
Hatfield. “Starting out, they need their own 
department, but eventually they will be able 
to stand on their own.” 


Pharmacists as advisers 
an untapped resource 


Chain drug stores have 
proven their staying pow- 
er over the years by evolv- 
ing to meet changing mar- 
ket conditions. In today’s 
market, for many drug re- 
tailers, an important part 
of being successful means 
being convenient and de- 
veloping a product mix for 
the convenience customer. 
Drug stores recognized 
the niche mass mer- 
chandisers and food stores created when 
they moved toward larger and larger 
stores. 

The increased shelf space and cold cases 
for consumables now found in many 
drug stores are enabling drug chains to 
intercept customers who want to avoid the 
hassle of visiting a 100,000-square-foot store. 
It has proven to be an effective strategy as 
evidenced by consumables’ strong sales 
growth. 

A similar opportunity, but not a fully ex- 
ploited one is ripening in the OTC depart- 
ment. Consumer confusion fueled by line ex- 
tensions and product reformulations has been 
a rule of thumb for many OTC categories. It’s 
the reason pharmacists are so often asked for 
product recommendations. 


MIKE TROY 


Now is the time 


Pharmacists recommend dozens of products 
every day, yet chains do little to directly pro- 
mote the valuable service these professionals 
provide. 


Consumer confusion in the OTC depart- 
ment is only going to get worse for a variety 
of reasons, not the least of which will be more 
Rx-to-OTC switches. Witness last summer’s 
launch of Aleve. The Procter & Gamble prod- 
uct declared, “All day long, all day strong.” 
Meanwhile, Whitehall-Robins said, “Nothing 
has been proven to last longer than Advil.” At 
about the same time, Johnson & Johnson’s 
McNeil subsidiary launched extended relief 
Tylenol. Tough to decide? You bet. 

The impending introduction of OTC ver- 
sions of Tagamet and Pepcid, the resulting 
advertising claims and competitors’ responses 
will soon throw the antacid category into tur- 
moil. Future switches in other categories will 
have the same effect. 

Retailers who move now to leverage the ac- 
cessibility of their pharmacists, and the abili- 
ty of these professionals to help consumers 
understand which products they should use, 
will benefit from increased OTC sales. Chains 
already employ image advertising to promote 
their pharmacy services. However, the OTC 
connection never seems to be clearly commu- 
nicated with a targeted campaign. 

Retailers can help to ensure customer 
loyalty and _ consistent, long-term 
sales growth by more aggressively pro- 
moting the accessibility of the pharm- 
acist to aid in the selection of OTC 
products. Of course, retailers will have 
to live up to the expectations created 
in the ad campaign and deliver the cus- 
tomer service that distinguishes the 
truly successful retailers from the marginal 
operators.

Will baseball cards strike out? 


By Leslie Gilbert Elman 


ith opening day just a 
few days ago, card 
makers and retailers 


are wondering how quickly 
they can recover trading card 
sales lost from the 234-day 
baseball strike. 

For drug stores, this year’s 
oddball season presents an in- 
teresting situation. Although 
sales of baseball cards are not 
booming the way they did in 
the late 1980s, drug stores 
have historically counted on a 
steady trade in baseball cards 
starting as early as February 
and continuing into October. 

Trading card manufacturers 
acknowledge a strong tie between 
action on the field and sales of 
sports cards. “The best example I 
can give is when the Toronto 
Blue Jays were in the World Se- 
ries {1992 and 1993]. We saw a 
huge change in distribution to 
Canada,” said Vince Nauss, di- 
rector of marketing for Donruss. 

However, baseball card 
manufacturers have let it be 
known that they are producing 
far fewer cards for the 1995 

eason. Topps, for example, 
has printed its smallest quan- 
tity in 30 years. This alone 
could make the 1995 cards 
more desirable to collectors. 

While orders for baseball 
cards have been down across 
all channels of trade, Nauss 
reported that one drug chain 
has actually doubled its card 
order for this year, banking on 
the desirability of cards from 
the oddball season. Most 
chains, however. are taking a 
more conservative view. 

“We’re buying some of all the 
major brands for all of our 
stores, but probably not more 
than one or two boxes per store,” 
said Rick Burns of Snyder Drug. 
“It’s a real dilemma. I expect 
we'll see interest from collectors, 


but not as much from the aver- 
age kid—and that is our prima- 
ry baseball card customer.” 
Added Gerry Hoeppner, 
spokesman for Eckerd Drug, 
“We’re tempering our buying. 
Kids are traditionally loyal con- 
sumers of baseball cards, but if 
they’re not collecting baseball 
cards because of the strike or a

BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — Big B is tying its 
major spring scratch-and-win sweepstakes 
promotion to NASCAR auto racing events in 
the Southeast. The 13-week promotion kicked 
off March 12. The grand prize is an all-ex- 
penses-paid trip for four to the 1996 Daytona 
500 in February. In addition, each of Big B’s 
370 stores will give away-one pair of tickets 
to the July 1995 Diehard 500 in Talladega, 
Ala. 

“The growth of NASCAR racing has been dy- 
namic in these markets [Alabama, Florida, 
Georgia, Mississippi, Tennessee], among both 
men and women. There is quite a bit of loyalty 
among race fans to drivers, racing teams and 
the products they promote,” said James Bruno, 
Big B vice president of marketing. 

Every sweepstakes ticket is a winner, Bruno 
noted. Some entitle customers to free products, 


and others are cents-off coupons that can be 
used at Big B stores. The chain has enlisted 75 
manufacturer sponsors for the promotion, in- 
cluding Pepsi-Cola and Fuji film. The promo- 
tion is supported by TV, radio, outdoor and FSI 
advertising. Products are featured in the ads 
based on manufacturers’ level of participation 
in the program. 

“The Big B promotion made sense for us, 
since we are the official soft drink of 
NASCAR,” said a Pepsi spokesman. “We saw it 
as a good fit.” Pepsi also sponsors the Pepsi 
400 in Daytona Beach, Fla., and the Mountain 
Dew Southern 500 at Darlington Raceway in 
South Carolina. 

Bruno explained, “It works out well for every- 
one. The vendors get to feature the products 
they want to feature and we get to run the type 
of promotion we prefer.”

Drug chains reach new heights 


Continued from page 45 
The chain drug industry’s No. 1 
position remains uncontested, with 
Walgreen maintaining its long lead 
over all the other drug chains. But 
the race for No. 2 is very, very close. 
Although by the middle of last 


year it looked as if one of the 


chains created out of 1994’s two 
big merger/acquisitions— Thrifty 
and PayLess or Revco with its ac- 
quired Hook-SupeRx (HSI) 
stores— would nab the No. 2 spot, 
that title remained where it was 
last year, with American Drug 
Stores, the division of American 
Stores that operates Osco and Sav- 
On drug stores. 

However, the difference in sales 
volume between American Drug at 
No. 2 and Revco at No. 7 was only 
$200 million. Clustered closely in 
between were Rite Aid, Eckerd, 
Thrifty PayLess and CVS. 

Due to consolidation, Thrifty 
and PayLess, formerly a division 
of Kmart, are now combined un- 
der the single ownership of Los 
Angeles-based TCH Corp. (headed 
by the investor group Leonard 
Green & Partners). Hooks-SupeRx 
Inc. (HSI) is no longer on the list 
due to its acquisition and subse- 
quent absorption by Revco D.S., 
which moved from ninth place to 
seventh place. . 

Thrift Drug, which moved into 
the top 10 rankings as those spaces 
opened up, was one of the first 


chains to jump on the consolidation 
bandwagon in 795, purchasing 97- 
store Kerr Drug in North Carolina. 

Industry insiders and outside an- 
alysts expect the consolidation 
trend to continue in 1995 and be- 
yond, fueled by several factors. One 
primary driver is managed care, 
which favors full coverage of mem- 
bership (read, “lots of retail loca- 
tions”), a high level of technological 
and service sophistication (read, 
“become your own pharmaceutical 
benefit manager”), and low pharma- 
ceutical prices (read, “High volume 
can improve your buying power 
with manufacturers and dominant 
market share can be used as lever- 
age against the pressures of third 
parties”). 

Another factor behind the acqui- 
sition binge is the availability of 
several small- and mid-size chains, 
say industry insiders and analysts. 
Three such chains recently came on 
the market: Perry Drug, which was 
scooped up by Rite Aid; Kerr Drug, 
which was acquired by Thrift, and 
Clark Drug, which is being ab- 
sorbed into American Drug Stores. 


Strong chain performance 


Despite the attention given to the 
major drug chain consolidations in 
1994, most top chains maintained 
their leading positions through in- 
ternal growth. As a whole, the chain 
drug store industry had a strong 
year in 1994, coming on top of a

In fact, Rite Aid’s newly elevated 
chairman and chief executive officer 
Martin Grass says he is determined 
to grow the chain internally as well 
as through acquisitions. Leading 
the industry in store count, Rite Aid 
plans to add some 300 stores a 
year—125 new units and the re- 
mainder split between enlarge- 
ments and relocations—for the next 
three years. 

Among the Top 10 chains, Revco 
reported the highest jump in 
same-store sales, 9 percent. This 
number, however, only applies to 
“core” Revco stores, the 1,200 units 
Revco was already operating prior 
to the acquisition of HSI; Revco 
kept 800 stores of HSI’s 1,100-unit 
store base. 

Meanwhile, Medicine Shoppe, 
the country’s largest pharmacy 
franchise operator, also reported 
a same-store sales increase of 9 
percent. 

Among the major chains that 
didn’t get involved in the consolida- 
tion business in 1994, Eckerd post- 
ed the highest same-store sales 
growth, 8.2 percent; as a whole, 
Eckerd reported a 9.4 percent in- 
crease in sales. 

CVS, the drug store division of 
Melville Corp., reported that its 
same-store sales increased 6.1 per- 
cent in 1994. The chain added 84 
stores for a net gain in units of 6.5 
percent, but saw its total sales jump 
9.6 percent, from $3.95 billion in 
1993 to $4.33 billion in 1994. 


Smaller chains enjoy big gains 


Among second-tier chains, Gen- 
ovese, the Melville, N.Y.-based 
chain of 110 stores, reported the 
strongest same-store-sales gain, 8.8 
percent. Genovese’s total revenues 
increased 16.5 percent from $489 
million last year to $570 million in 
the fiscal year ending Feb. 3, 1995. 

Big B, however, wasn’t far be- 
hind. The Alabama-based chain 
reported same-store gains of 8 
percent. Total sales for the compa- 
ny were up from $595 million to 
$670 million, for an increase of 
12.6 percent. 

Cisealy following Big B was Arbor 
Drug. The Troy, Mich.-based chain 
of 159 stores reported a same-store 
sales increase of 7.7 percent. Ar- 
bor’s total sales went from $535 mil- 
lion to $619 million, for an increase 
of almost 16 percent, and its store 
count popped up to 159 from 138. 

While traditional drug chains 
have been performing well for the 
past couple of years, the deep dis- 
count drug chains continued to 
struggle in 1994. 

In December, the third-largest 
deep discounter, F&M, filed for 
Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, 
joining the biggest deep discount 
chain, Phar-Mor, which has been in 
Chapter 11 since 1992.

Drug chains reach new heights 


Continued from page 54 

er, has weathered a tide of red ink, 
but it has begun to return to prof-

cused chain. 


Return to ‘tradition’ 


Midway through the decade of the 
1990s, the companies that are prov- 
ing most successful are those that 
have stuck to—or returned to—a 
fairly traditional drug store size, 
format and mix of products. 

In terms of size, for example, 
most chains seem to be aiming to- 
ward an optimum square footage in 
the range of 10,000 to 12,000 square 
feet. Interestingly, companies are 
aiming toward this moderate size 
from both sides. 

Chains that have traditionally 
had larger-size stores, like Pay- 
Less, have been trimming back 
their mix and focusing on some- 
what smaller, more productive 
spaces. On the other side, chains 
that have traditionally operated 
smaller units are moving to larger 
prototypes; Revco, Rite Aid and 
Brooks Pharmacy (a division of 
Maxi Drug) are among the chains 
that are expanding their square 
footage and merchandise mix. 

The latter group tends to follow 
this scenario: A traditional drug 
store chain with stores in the 
6,000- to 8,000-square-foot range 
is usually pharmacy-oriented, 


gaining 50 percent or more of its 
sales from prescription drugs. As 
price pressure from managed care 
organizations has driven down 
pharmaceutical margins, this type 
of chain has seen the need to in- 
crease the volume and perfor- 
mance of its front-end to compen- 
sate for the lower profits in the 
pharmacy. 

This trend really picked up steam 
in 1994 as more and more chains 
open freestanding stores. 

Walgreen is leading this trend; 
the majority of its new stores are 
freestanding 13,000- to 14,000- 
square-foot units, often with drive- 
through pharmacy windows. 

Revco, which unveiled its RCD 
(Revco Convenience Drug) prototype 
in late 1993, is now rolling out this 
12,500-square-foot format. Larger 
than the typical Revco store, RCDs 
feature an expanded convenience 
food section, a roomier waiting area 
around the pharmacy, broaded as- 
sortments in key categories, and 
such embellishments as skylit atri- 
ums and drive-through pharmacies. 
More than half the 75 to 100 new 
stores Revco will open in the current 
fiscal year will be RCDs. 

With its new prototypical stores, 
Rite Aid, too, is moving toward 
larger, freestanding units. A 
change for pharmacy-oriented Rite 
Aid, the newer stores will showcase 
health and beauty, putting an ex-

panded cosmetics department as a 
focal point near the store’s en-

Also moving toward more free- 
standing stores with drive-through 
pharmacies is Eckerd Corp., which 
recently announced an accelerated 
store-opening program. At least 90 
new units are planned for 95, with 
another 100 slated for ’96. 

While other chains might not be 
retooling prototypes, many seem to 
be focusing their efforts on the core 
drug store departments: upgrading 
the presentation of cosmetics, fra- 
grances and niches categories like 
bath; expanding the vitamin sec- 
tion with related nutritionals and 
homeopathic products; adding 
more one-hour photo labs, and ac- 


centuating or expanding greeting 
card sections. 

Overall, drug stores themselves 
are looking better because they are 
new or they have been recently 
renovated. Explained one chain 
drug chief executive officer: “In the 
80s, the rule of thumb was that a 
drug store needed to be renovated 
every seven years, and sometimes 
you could stretch that to 10. With 
competition today, we’ve found 
that the stores must be renovated 
much more frequently, every four 
years or so.” 

All in all, the results of Drug 
Store News’ Annual Report of the 
Industry indicate that business is 
better than ever for chain drug 
stores, too.

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


By James Frederick 


s he confidently trod the stage 
A« a packed Chicago Art Insti- 

tute auditorium in January, 
Walgreen Co. president and chief 
operating officer Dan Jorndt gave 
shareholders a glimpse into the 
brave new world of chain drug re- 
tailing. The occasion was Wal- 
greens’ annual meeting, and the 
demonstration came courtesy of the 
chain’s computerized, state-of-the- 
art store location and demographic 
imaging system. 

Jorndt wanted to demonstrate 
how Walgreens maps out its store- 
expansion strategy, using a huge 
database of U.S. Census and re- 
search information on individual 
households and neighborhoods from 
coast to coast, married to a comput- 
erized, on-screen mapping system 
that pinpoints the exact location 
and name of each drug, food and 
discount store operating within any 
of its existing or potential markets. 

While Jorndt gave instructions, 
an off-stage assistant entered com- 
mands on a keyboard. Behind him, 
a massive projection of the assis- 
tant’s computer screen allowed the 
president to focus with startling 
precision on a tightly defined neigh- 
borhood in San Francisco, drilling 
swiftly down from a computer map 
of the whole city to a micro-view of 
a single neighborhood within the 
city. Competitors and their loca- 
tions were clearly marked. Detailed 
information on the demographic 
makeup of the neighborhood around 
the prospective store location—in- 
cluding household income levels, ed- 
ucation levels, racial composition, 
etc.—was available with a key- 
stroke or two. 

It was an impressive show. And it 
underscored, once again, the deter- 
mination of the nation’s leading 
drug chain to stay ahead of the pack 
in the pace of its expansion and 
marketing efforts and in the scope, 
precision and sheer horsepower of 
its technology. 

Walgreens opened 196 new drug 
stores—an average of nearly four 
every week—in fiscal 1994, the 
biggest single-year growth spurt in 
its 93-year history. The chain also 
weighed into major new markets 
last year, including its long-awaited 
re-entry into Cleveland with 15 
stores last fall—the biggest market 
entry in its history—and its first 
units in the Buffalo, N.Y.; Tulsa, 
Okla., and Anaheim, Calif., mar- 
kets. At the same time, Walgreens 
accelerated its store rollouts in ex- 
isting markets across the country 
where it already holds the No. 1 or 
No. 2 spot in drug store market 
share. 

Another 200 new stores are 
planned for this year, including the 
first of as many as 100 stores in the 
huge Philadelphia market and the 
first units in Seattle/Tacoma and 
Oklahoma City. Also targeted for 
entry are Richmond, Va. (in the 
spring of 1996); Chattanooga,

Tenn.; Little Rock, Ark.; and 
Springfield, Mo. In addition, Jorndt 
said, Walgreens will announce 
plans later this year to enter anoth- 
er as-yet-unnamed city—and it will 
be “a whopper,” he predicted. 

At this pace, Walgreens will oper- 
ate 3,000 stores cross-country by 
the turn of the century, its leaders 
expect. And the chain continues to 
support that growth with added dis- 


Walgreens maintains competitive edge 


ing to negotiate their rates, rather 
than lose Walgreens’ business.” 

By its own reckoning, Walgreens 
already has the largest patient 
database in the U.S. via its Inter- 
com pharmacy computer system, 
which includes a base of 25 million 
prescription customers. Also adding 
to its leverage is Healthcare Plus, 
its fast-growing mail-order and 
managed care prescription busi- 


out its store-expansion strategy. 


tribution capacity: its eighth major 
distribution center is slated to open 
in late spring or early summer in 
Woodland, Calif., near Sacramento. 

Behind the dizzying growth pace 
is a determined quest for top mar- 
ket share. As chairman and chief 
executive Charles R. Walgreen III 
put it, market share is “perhaps the 
biggest key to successful retailing in 
America today,” adding, “Any retail- 
er that isn’t growing its market 
share is facing real trouble.” 

Market share is also a key factor 
in the chain’s drive to position itself 
for the rapid shift to managed care. 
The simple reasoning: when it 
comes to dealing with prescription 
benefits management firms, more is 
more. The more store outlets you 
have as a chain drug prescription 
provider, and the more powerful 
your pharmacy network, the more 
clout you have with the PBMs that 
are coming to dominate patient care 
and pharmacy. 

“Our market share is tremendous 
leverage, which allows us to estab- 
lish a. fair price for the service we 
provide,” Jorndt said. “Our success 
with some very major [managed 
care] plans clearly reflects that 
these plans need our coverage.” 

Indeed, Walgreens has informed 
the health care industry that, 
henceforth, it will walk away from a 
third-party plan “in which we lose 
money each time we fill a prescrip- 
tion,” Jorndt said. 

“We're drawing the line on pricing 
with our third-party partners, to the 
point of relinquishing unprofitable ac- 
counts, if necessary,” added Walgreen. 
“We're finding these accounts are will- 


Walgreens uses a sophisticated, computerized, on-screen mapping system to plot 


ness, and AdvanceCare, which 
serves more than 200 nursing home 
accounts in 11 major markets. 
Healthcare Plus hit $120 million in 
sales in fiscal 1994 and now ser- 
vices major corporate group pre- 
scription plans including those of 
Motorola, Sara Lee, Walt Disney, 
Nordstrom and First Chicago Bank. 

In November, the chain opened a 
second mail-order facility in Tempe, 
Ariz., nearly double the size of its 
original, two-year-old counterpart 
in Orlando, Fla. Said the chairman, 
“I'm more convinced than ever that 
the mail service concept is working 
for us. A key reason is that for every 
two mail prescriptions sold, Health- 
care Plus’ marketing efforts are 
adding three retail prescriptions to 
our stores.” 

Altogether, Walgreens’ pharmacy 
sales jumped 18.9 percent in the 


last fiscal year and now account for 
more than 40 percent of total sales. 
“That figure will probably be 50 per- 
cent by the end of the decade,” 
added Walgreen. The down side: 
pharmacy gross margins have 
shrunk from 28.5 percent in 1990 to 
26 percent in fiscal ’94. 

To deal with those trends, Wal- 
greens began in April its first test 
rollout of a massive, multimillion- 
dollar re-engineering project for its 
pharmacies “to make them more 
productive, cost-efficient and user- 
friendly,” in the words of the chair- 
man. The project, called Intercom 
Plus, will do nothing less than 
“change the way we fill prescrip- 
tions in this country,” predicted 
Jorndt. 

“This is no small change,” Jorndt 
said. “We’ve had 120 programmers 
working on this full time for two 
years. Intercom Plus will take our 
pharmacies from the 1980s well 
into the next century.” 

Few details of the project are yet 
available, but Jorndt promised the 
re-engineering project, which has 
been tackled jointly by Walgreens 
and Andersen Consulting Inc., 
would streamline the filling process, 
provide faster and more organized 
service, and allow a store filling 300 
scripts today to fill 500 in the future, 
with no increase in staffing. One 
component of the system: a touch- 
tone refill service designed to reduce 
busy signals for customers and cut 
down on pharmacists’ phone time. 

Altogether, Walgreens will spend 
roughly $300 million this year on 
Intercom Plus, new-store expan- 
sion, store renovation, its new Cali- 
fornia distribution center and con- 
tinued technological refinements. 

On the human front, Walgreens 
saw the retirement early this year 
of two of the key architects of its 
growth into industry leader and $10 
billion retail powerhouse. Chuck 
Hunter retired as vice chairman 
and chief financial officer, and was 
replaced by new senior vice presi- 
dent and chief financial officer 
Roger Polark. And Fred Canning, 
who served for 12 years as Wal- 
greens president, retired from the 
board of directors after nearly 50 
years with the chain.

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


By James Frederick 


iscal 1994 was a year of 

changes for American Drug 

Stores, with shifts in man- 
agement, the recent purchase of 
17-store Clark Drugs and the roll- 
out of a new store-brand line of 
consumables. What’s more, the 
structural changes under way at 
the company will continue for the 
next two years as parent company 
American Stores presses ahead 
with a companywide, top-to-bot- 
tom overhaul of its operating and 
management structure and its 
strategic focus. 

In line with that effort, Ameri- 
can Drug has overhauled its own 
top management team, unifying 
the reporting structure for its 
Osco and Sav-on chain divisions 
under Dick Davis at American 
Stores’ corporate headquarters in 
Salt Lake City. Davis, who until 
recently was executive vice presi- 
dent and chief operating officer for 
Anaheim, Calif.-based Sav-on, is 
now executive vice president and 
chief operating officer of all drug 
stores. 

Also moved to Salt Lake City 
was Stephen Mannschreck, former 
head of the Osco division based in 
Oak Brook, Ill. Mannschreck 
is now chief human resources 
officer. 

Other senior executives at the 
company remain in Oak Brook, Ill. 
Among them: executive vice presi- 
dent of marketing Arlyn White; 
vice president of pharmacy opera- 
tions and marketing Kevin Tripp; 
and vice president of advertising 
and sales Terry Maloy. 

The bulk of American Drug’s 
buying is still done in Oak Brook, 
Ill., but the buying process itself 
has undergone big changes in re- 
cent months. The full extent of 
those changes won’t be completed 
until mid-1997, according to 
American Stores president and 
chief executive Vic Lund. 

As part of its massive Delta pro- 
ject, American Stores is consoli- 
dating buying efforts for all 1,597 
of its food and drug stores—in- 
cluding the company’s 781 Osco 
and Sav-on stores and its 816 
Jewel, Lucky, Acme and Super 
Saver supermarkets. One big step, 
now nearing completion, is the 
shift of all general merchandise 
procurement to American Drug’s 
buying staff in Oak Brook, IIl. 
Other functions have already been 
centralized, including liquor, wine 
and tobacco procurement and 
much of the information technolo- 
gy driving the re-engineering 
process. 

Warehousing and distribution 
efforts for both food and drug 
stores throughout the country are 
also being coordinated in Salt 
Lake City. 

The overall aim of centralized 
buying is to eliminate redundant 
buying practices, take better ad- 
vantage of bulk-buying leverage 


65 


ANNUAL REPORT 


Chain profiles 


and aid in company streamlining 
and unification efforts. 

Indeed, Delta’s overall objec- 
tive, according to Lund, is to 
scrap the company’s costly old 
structure as a financial holding 
company with multiple operating 
and support redundancies, and 
replace it with a new organiza- 
tion that “provides for common 
backstage operations to fit all of 
our operations uniformly, while 
maintaining the separateness 
and individuality of our store 
formats, marketing and mer- 
chandising.” 

One key executive in Salt Lake 
City who is advancing those 
efforts is Richard Fredericksen, 
executive vice president of nation- 
al buying and logistics. His hiring 
in late 1993 signaled the begin- 
ning of a new era of coordinated 
business strategy at American 
Stores. 

“The Delta project, particularly 
the integration of the supply 
chain functions, is critical to the 
future success of the company,” 
Lund said. “The very visible and 
tangible benefits that will result 
from the Delta project convince us 
that we should accelerate this 
effort.” 


Fiscal 1994 marked a 
year of changes for 
American Drug, including 
shifts in management, 
acquisition of 17-store 
Clark Drugs and a new 
store-brand line of 
consumables. 


Even without the restructuring 
project, Osco and Sav-on continue 
to set the pace for American 
Stores. Operating earnings for the 
division rose almost 16 percent for 
the fiscal year, ended Jan. 28, to 
$228.5 million. Same-store sales 
continued to improve, rising a 
modest but respectable 4.2 per- 
cent. Total sales for the drug 
stores rose 5.1 percent to $4.54 
billion, making American Drug 
the nation’s second-highest-selling 
drug chain in 1994, behind only 
Walgreen Co. 

Driving the improving prof- 
itability of the chain is a base of 
largely mature stores—some 200 
of which have now been remodeled 
along the lines of the highly effec- 
tive “Vision” store prototype first 
unveiled in 1991. The format fea- 
tures numerous design innova- 
tions, including color-coded, easy- 
to-find perimeter departments, a 
striking mid-floor cosmetics/fra- 
grance boutique, a nutrition cen- 
ter, a more prominent and accessi- 


American reorganization on 


Osco continues to help set the pace for American Stores, along with Sav-on. 


ble pharmacy and a more open 
and appealing floor plan. 

The format reflects what Lund 
called “the future direction of the 
drug store: its transition into a 
health care center.” It was hon- 


ored last fall as Drug Store News’ 


REX Award winner for drug store 
design of the decade. 

Beginning last year, Osco also 
began rolling out a new var- 
iation of the prototype on the 
former sites of 16 older Jew- 
el food stores in Chicago. Dubbed 
Osco Food and Pharmacy, 
the stores include “all the food 
categories you'd find in a 
Jewel food store, with the ex- 
ception of meat,” according to 
a company spokesperson. Osco 
has since begun adding larger food 
departments to other stores. 

American Drug also continued 
to refine its marketing efforts 
via direct-mail ads to targeted 
demographic cluster groups and 
specific market areas. Among 
the early results: what one execu- 
tive described as “very successful” 
direct-mail campaigns aimed 
at Hispanic and other ethnic 
shoppers. 

The chain has also launched a 
new line of premium private-label 


soft drinks and cookies, called 
American Premier. The brand 
kicked off with three varieties of 
soft drinks and four SKUs of cook- 
ies. Eventually, the company 
plans to add a much wider array 
of products including juices, bot- 
tled water, alcoholic beverages, 
pet food and skin and hair care 
products. 

On the expansion front, Ameri- 
can Drug added 28 new or ac- 
quired stores and closed 34 under- 
performing units in fiscal 94. Just 
after the close of the fiscal year, 
the chain announced an agree- 
ment to buy the 17-store operation 
of Los Angeles-based Clark Drugs 
for a price ranging from $35 mil- 
lion to $39 million. 

The deal was a boon to Ameri- 
can’s Sav-on Drugs unit. Founded 
in 1959 and spread throughout 
the five-county Los Angeles metro 
area in high-traffic shopping cen- 
ter sites with little overlap with 
Sav-on, Clark’s 17 stores racked 
up more than $100 million in an- 
nual sales, or $6 million per 
store. They also provided a good 
fit with Sav-on, averaging rough- 
ly 18,000 square feet of selling 
space and featuring a similar 
product mix.

trategic acquisitions, sales 
Ss: non-drug operations and 
an aggressive renovation 
plan created a more tightly fo- 


cused, service-oriented Rite Aid in 
1994. 
For the year ended March 4 


1995, revenues rose 11.7 percent 
to $4.5 billion. Net income grew to 
$141.3 million from $9.3 million a 
year earlier. 

Interested in firming up its core 
drug store business and slashing 
operating costs, Rite Aid closed 
200 underperforming drug stores 
and sold three of its four non- 
drug-related operations—Sera 
Tech, Encore Book and Concord 
Cleaners—for $100 million. 

At presstime, the chain was 
close to signing a deal to sell its 
ADAP discount auto supply di- 
vision for an estimated $69 mil- 
lion to a leveraged buyout group, 
according to Frank Bergonzi, 


executive vice president and chief 


financial officer. 


Rite Aid closed 200 
underperforming drug 
stores and sold three of 
its four non-drug-related 
operations to firm up its” 
core drug store business 
and trim operating costs. 


Closing the underperforming 
stores was definitely not an at- 
tempt to downsize the chain. In 
fact, in an aggressive buying 
spree, the chain tapped funds 
from the sales of the non-drug 
units to acquire 300 drug stores 
during the fiscal year. 

In September, Rite Aid pur- 
chased 12 Hooks stores from 
Revco and 64 La Verdiere’s Super 
Drug Stores. The La Verdiere’s 
stores have already delivered im- 
pressive performance, which 
helped to push Rite Aid’s revenues 
up 26 percent in the fourth quar- 
ter ended March 4, 1995. 

In January 1995, Rite Aid sur- 
prised many by swallowing up 
224-store Perry Drug Stores. The 
chain has high hopes for the Perry 
stores, which are similar in mer- 
chandise and size to Rite Aid’s 
new 10,000-square-foot prototype. 
By Labor Day, the chain will add 
the Rite Aid name to the Perry 
stores and incorporate the service 
features of the prototype stores: 
one-hour photo departments, 
convenience food, large cos- 
metic/fragrance/bath departments, 
shipping/fax services and a wide 
assortment of seasonal merchan- 


dise and appliances. 

The acquisitions, combined with 
a sizable investment in store reno- 
vations, comprises newly installed 
chairman and ceo Martin Grass’ 
strategy to operate larger, service- 
oriented stores. To date, Rite Aid 
operates 300 prototype stores and 
plans to add another 300 each 
year by opening new stores and 
expanding or relocating existing 
ones. Rite Aid currently operates 
2,829 drug stores. 

Plans for more than 100 of the 
larger, full-service stores are al- 
ready underway in Philadelphia, 
Baltimore, Cleveland, Buffalo 
and New York City. Specifically, 
the plan projects: in Philadel- 
phia, 14 new stores, 16 expan- 
sions and three relocations; in 
Baltimore four new stores, eight 
expansions and seven reloca- 
tions; in Cleveland, one new 
store, three expansions and 11 
relocations; and in Buffalo, one 
new store, seven expansions and 
six relocations. 

The chain is making a major 
push into New York City, an area 
in which it only dabbled until late 
last year when it purchased up to 
44 stores (leases are still being ne- 
gotiated) from Red Apple Group. 
Recently, in a series of separate 
deals with other parties, Grass ob- 
tained leases for 36 more stores in 
Manhattan, the Bronx, Queens 
and Brooklyn. Most of the new 
stores in New York City are large 
enough to accommodate the full- 
service features of the prototype 
stores. 

Expanded services, a strategic 
use of POS data, increased use of 
circulars in select markets and the 
addition of several 24-hour stores, 
pushed same-store sales up 7.2 
percent last year, according to 
Grass. 

Rite Aid also focused on 
strengthening its prescription 
business. It acquired Intell Rx 
Inc., a drug-utilization review 
company and Pharmacy-Card Inc. 
(PCI), a full-scale pharmacy bene- 
fit manager. The two organiza- 
tions were combined with the 
chain’s third-party marketing 
group to form Eagle Managed 
Care. PCI currently administers 
prescriptions for more than 2.5 
million lives. 

Managed care “is a major thrust 
for us,” explained Grass, who as- 
sumed the top post at Rite Aid 
from his father Alex Grass, in 
March. “We continue to very ag- 
gressively market our programs 
and do deals with manufacturers 
that involve using telemarketing 


to contact patients in terms of 


compliance.” 

Grass recently began refining 
his management team as a pre- 
cursor to some larger shifts in 
the sales and buying operations. 
Timothy Noonan, formerly ex- 
ecutive vice president of drug 
store operations was named 
president and chief operating of-

Eckerd hits stride with record results 


By Mike Troy _ 
: Eckerd Corp. chairman and 


chief executive officer Stewart 
Turley, 1994 was a year of mo- 
mentum. 

Eckerd positioned itself for suc- 
cess in 1994 by making savvy busi- 
ness decisions during the early ’90s. 
Those decisions led to record-setting 
financial results during the fiscal 
year that ended Jan. 28, 1995. It 
was Eckerd’s first full fiscal year 
since returning to public ownership 
in July 1993. 

“If you had to characterize 1994, I 
would say it was a year where our 
momentum from actions in the past 
built nicely and we’ve benefited 
from that momentum which contin- 
ues on today,” Turley said. “Getting 
the momentum going was not the 
easiest task in the world because it 
involved so many details.” 

Cost savings from corporate and fi- 
nancial restructuring, new front end 
programs, pharmacy initiatives and 
technology upgrades have combined 
to put Eckerd on solid footing for fu- 
ture growth. 


Expansion 


Eckerd’s store base has hovered 
around 1,700 units through most of 
this decade. However, actions dur- 
ing 1994 positioned the chain to up- 
grade and expand its store base in 
1995 and beyond. 

One key event was the sale of the 
company’s Insta-Care Pharmacy 
Services subsidiary, which netted 
$49.5 million. The cash infusion en- 
abled Eckerd to accelerate the clo- 
sure of under-performing stores 
without negatively impacting its 
balance sheet. Slated for closure 
during 1995 will be 90 stores with 


“«_.-1 would say it was 
a year where our 
momentum from actions 
in the past built nicely 
and we’ve benefited 
from that momentum, 
which carries on today.” 
—Stewart Turley

sales of $114 million that accounted 
for an annual operating loss of $5 
million. The stores are located in 
geographically dispersed markets. 

In conjunction with the accelerat- 
ed closings, there will be more new 
stores. In addition to the 55 stores 
opened during 1994, another 90 
units are planned during 1995 with 
at least another 100 to be added 
during 1996. About 80 of the new 
stores will be freestanding with dri- 
ve-through pharmacy windows.

The past year has been one of momentum for Eckerd Corp. as smart business deci-

Eckerd currently has 27 stores in 
New Jersey and 11 in neighboring 
Delaware. Another new market 
Eckerd entered during 1994 was 
Amarillo, Texas, giving Eckerd 
nearly 500 stores in Texas. 

Even though 1995 and 1996 will 
see Eckerd be more ambitious with 
new store construction than at any 
time in the past, the chain continues 
its quest for acquisitions. 

“We will still be actively looking 
at acquisition opportunities that 
make sense to us. I don’t think we 
have to do any acquisitions, but we 
see them as a strategic opportunity 
to increase market share,” Turley 
said. “Our strategy would not call 
for us to become a national chain, 
but that doesn’t mean over a period 
of years through acquisitions we 
won't be in a lot of territories we're 
not in-now. We don’t believe it is 
necessary to be a national chain to 
be in effective in the marketplace; 
what is important is to be effective 
in the markets that you are in.” 


Pharmacy 


In keeping with overall industry 
trends, prescription drug sales ac- 
counted for a larger percentage of 
Eckerd’s total sales than in 1994 
and third-party increased its share 
of pharmacy sales. Eckerd’s phar- 
macy sales rose 15.2 percent to 
$2 .236 billion for the fiscal year 
ended Jan. 28, 1995, with third-par- 
ty representing about 65 percent of 
that number. 

“We formed what we think is a 
very effective managed care sales 
force with the right kind of products 
and services that could make us 
successful in that environment,” 
Turley said. 

One of the big accomplishments 
of 1994 was the chainwide installa- 
tion of new pharmacy computers. 
Rolling out in 1995 will be Comp-U- 
Care 2000, described by Turley as 
new generation software that will 


give Eckerd many new capabilities. 

“Our capabilities in managed care 
are significantly enhanced this year 
with some of the technology we have 
available to us and the data that we 
can provide third party administra- 
tors,” Turley said. “What we need to 
do is be in a position where the 
third-party or managed care plan ad- 
ministrator can look at us as a 
source of information through which 
he can control his cost and control 
his bottom line as opposed to just 
squeezing it out of us. 

“In addition to increased pharma- 
cist productivity and reduced wait- 
ing time for customers, technology 
enhancements will also give Eckerd 
the capability to print its Rx Advisor 
patient education leaflets in Span- 
ish, a important service considering 
the chain operates more than 1,000 
stores in Texas and Florida. 


The front end 


Eckerd achieved 4.2 percent 
same-store sales growth in non-pre- 
scription front end categories dur- 
ing 1994. “We think that is pretty 
good compared to where the indus- 
try has been,” Turley said. 

Food related categories, OTC 
drugs, health related products and 
photo were strong departments dur- 
ing 1994. 

Eckerd will continue to play up 
those strengths during 1995 by 
adding another 50 to 60 Express 
Photo one-hour labs to its existing 


484. More food marts, essentially a 
greatly expanded product mix of con- 
venience foods and dairy, are also on 
the way, according to Turley. 

In the health care area, Eckerd 
continues probing the Florida market 
with its Lifecare Centers. A test of 
the concept, which includes expanded 
home health care products, testing 
services and a registered nurse, has 
begun in the Tampa Bay area, and 
will be expanded statewide with 25 
units during 1995. 

Eckerd’s front-end merchandising 
and decision-making abilities im- 
proved during 1994 as more stores 
went on-line with scanning. That ca- 
pability will continue to be expanded 
during 1995 as another 590 stores 
will be outfitted with equipment. 

“I feel good about where we are 
from a scanning standpoint,” Turley 
said. “By the end of this year we will 
have 1,100 stores scanning and all 
our Florida stores will have scanning 
so we can be working on some of the 
automatic replenishment processes.” 

As for the pace at which the rollout 
is taking place, he added, “I think we 
are moving are moving as fast as we 
need to. I don’t think we gain any 
material advantage by moving faster 
other than being able to stand up 
and say, ‘We are 100 percent scan- 
ning.’ It is irrelevant to be 100 per- 
cent scanning if you don’t have the 
capability to use that data in ways 
that will improve your business.” 


Debt 


Eckerd has come a long way from 
1986 when a leveraged buyout left 
the chain with long-term debt of 
$1.5 billion. A corporate restructur- 
ing in the early 90s led to $70 mil- 
lion being removed from Eckerd’s 
overhead. A $950 million refinanc- 
ing and subsequent amendment to 
that credit agreement reduced Eck- 
erd’s outstanding debt and resulted 
in significant interest expense Sav- 
ings. An initial public stock offering 
in July 1993 and a secondary stock 
offering during April 1994 injected 
Eckerd with capital to further pay 
down debt. 

Today, Eckerd has newfound finan- 
cial freedom and flexibility. Its out- 
standing debt is $786 million vs. 
$1.123 billion two years ago. Its an- 
nual interest expense is now about 
$95 million compared to $148 million.

By James Frederick 


Sam Zell, Talton “Tally” 

Embry and David Schulte 
look like financial geniuses. 
It was they, after all, who 
saw the enormous money- 
making potential in Revco 
D.S. at a time when most of 
the financial community 
shunned the still-bankrupt 
drug chain like a debt-rid- 
den basket case with little 
hope of survival. 

Putting their money 
where their mouths were, 
the three of them—dZell, 
known as the “grave dancer” 
for his ability to spot and 
buy up equity in distressed 
companies with unseen po- 
tential; Schulte, his partner 
at Chicago-based Chilmark 
Fund L.P.; and Embry, a 
savvy bond investor who had 
snapped up much of Revco’s 
debt securities at bargain 
prices—ponied up millions of 
dollars to buy big stakes in 
the troubled company in the 
months prior to its emer- 
gence from Chapter 11. 


A big pay off 


Their gamble has paid off 
handsomely. Revco’s stock 
has more than tripled in the 
34 months since the compa- 
ny roared out of Chapter 11. 
More importantly, Revco 
has rewarded the hard work 
and persistence of its own 
managers, support teams 
and store operations people 
with one of the best growth 
records in the industry, 
with sharply rising sales 
and profits and a sharply 
defined health and beauty 
care image. 

Sales and net income 
have risen steadily since 
Revco emerged from bank- 
ruptcy in June 1992. Net in- 
come in fiscal 1994 ending 
last May jumped 172.5 per- 
cent vs. the previous year, 
to $38.7 million, and same- 
store sales grew 8.5 percent. 

More recently, Revco 
capped its third quarter 
with an 8.7 percent same- 
store sales gain in core 
Revco stores and a 41.6 per- 
cent jump in net income vs. 
the same period last year, to 
$17.7 million. Year-to-date, 
its sales are up 69.1 percent 
with the addition of the for- 
mer Hook-SupeRx stores ac- 
quired last year, and same- 
store sales continue their 
healthy climb, rising 9.2

the result. Utilizing an arse-

By Allene Symons 
t ongs Drug Stores filled in some 


of its promising markets during 

1994 to strengthen the chain’s

phasis on visual merchandising and

of older, traditional Longs stores did.

sleek, exciting angled displays in 
spacious cosmetics and photo/elec- 
tronics departments and a high-visi-

Thrift now offers ‘complete package’ 


By James Frederick 
Fis: with intensifying competi- 


tion at the front end and fun- 

damental changes in how 
pharmacy services are delivered 
and paid for, Thrift Drug has risen 
to the occasion. 

The company has ess¢.:itially 
overhauled its market strategy and 
corporate focus to position itself as 
a full-service, information-driven 
prescription benefits manager with 
increasing market clout. The Pitts- 
burgh-based chain has also at- 
tacked margin erosion at the phar- 
macy and front-end with new 
merchandising programs and in- 
creasingly sophisticated niche mar- 
keting efforts aimed at specific store 
locations. 

“You have to find your niche and 
deliver what consumers want in a 
particular area,” noted Thrift 
chairman and chief executive Bob 
Hannan in an April 17 interview. 

“It’s no longer a question of what 
works for a Thrift store in the 
Pittsburgh market—now it’s tar- 
geting what customers want in Fox 
Chapel (a suburb of Pittsburgh).”

d 


Longs made key changes to its replenishment process, along with its management, in 1994.

system for well over a year, Longs 
was able to develop and begin to im- 
plement weekly replenishment or- 
ders for high-turnover merchandise. 
These orders, placed by the POS 
system, will continue to be an im- 
portant area of development for 
Longs in 1995. 

In some areas, the system is 
starting to deliver benefits. In the 
fourth quarter, gross margins were 
up to 26 percent from 25.4 percent, 
an improvement Roath attributed 
to the benefits of new systems. 

A slight rise in gross sales reflected 
the addition of 15 new stores. Sales 
in some of Longs’ market areas, in- 
cluding Southern California, were 
impacted by a continuing economic 


Hannan acknowledged that 
there is “extreme pressure on phar- 
macy gross margins” as third-party 
contractors continue to squeeze 
prescription providers for cost sav- 
ings through lower reimburse- 
ments. To survive, he said, drug 
chains “have to focus on technology 
and improving efficiencies...and 
they have to find new ways to sell 
OTC products.” 

To compete in the era of man- 
aged care and tight-fisted third- 
party payment systems, Thrift has 
developed what Hannan calls “a 
complete package” of prescription 
services and programs. The compa- 
ny launched TDI Managed Care 
Services last summer, offering cor- 
ppg and government prescrip- 

tion benefits programs what he 

called “a complete managed care 
offering,” including a nationwide 
network of 42,000 retail pharmacy 
providers, drug utilization review 
and clinical analysis. 

Thrift also added significant 
business in its Express Pharmacy 
mail-order service, now the na- 
tion’s third largest. It also made 
big inroads into institutional phar- 


downturn and high unemployment 
as well as sharp competition from 
new mass merchants and food-drug 
combo stores. Net income for the year 
was down slightly and that has pro- 
vided ample motivation for change. 


Process of change 


Besides focusing on replenish- 
ment, Roath explained, modification 
of the management process would 
make it more “planful,” or as some 
would call it, more strategic. 

Category management is part of 
this planful approach. Longs’ in- 
tention in category management is 
to improve its performance in core 
categories and manage each one 


as a separate business, said 
Roath. 


In an era of micro-marketing, 
where flexibility for local opportunity 
provides a competitive edge, “you 
have to be flexible to react to the 
needs and demands of local cus- 
tomers, and we think our decentral- 
ized philosophy fits that very well— 
perhaps better than anyone else,” said 
Roath. 

The uniqueness of each store 
will be developed through comple- 
mentary and ancillary products, 
which add character and fun to 
the shopping environment and “in 
addition to price, differentiate one 
retailer from another,” said 
Roath. 


Pharmacy moves forward 


Longs will market its managed 
care business more aggressively 
than it did in 1994, when the 
chain’s efforts were directed to- 
ward regulatory compliance. 
Longs is now targeting pharmacy 
and its managed care programs to 
improve efficiency, maintain qual- 
ity “and tie managed care into a 
marketing strategy that we can 
use for years to come,” said 
Roath. That, too, is a part of the 
chain’s strategic management 
process. In 1995, Longs plans to 
develop more sales and growth 
opportunities that already exist in 
its markets. 

Nineteen-ninety-four was a 
plateau between acquisitions. 
First there was the acquisition of 
the 20-unit Bills Drugs in late 
1993 and, at the end of the year, 
Longs was poised to acquire six 
PayLess stores and add to its ex- 
isting 26 Hawaiian stores. 


macy last spring 
with the purchase 
of Greenwood Rx, 
the largest pro- 
vider of pharmacy 
services to nurs- 
ing homes in 
Pennsylvania. 

More recently, 
Thrift made a ma- 
jor addition to its 
marketing muscle 
early this year with 
the savvy purchase 
of Raleigh, N.C.- 
based Kerr Drug 
Stores. The pur- 
chase added 97 
stores to Thrift’s 
026-store network 
and gave it a powerful entree in the 
Carolinas. Prior to the purchase, 
Thrift operated just five stores in 
those states. 

Kerr had sales of $185 million in 
its last fiscal year, or roughly $2 
million per store. Thrift may be 
able to improve significantly on 
those numbers; its own sales per 
store approached $3 million in fis- 
cal 1994. Total sales for the chain

of honors this past January. The 
Anti-Defamation League named 
him its Man of Achievement for his 
efforts on behalf of both Thrift

To shore up its business 
in the western part of New 
York, Fay’s acquired 12 
stores from Paterson Drug 
Stores last year. 

The company also opened 
16 new stores, remodeled 12 
and added coolers, banking 
services and mail service to a 
select number of stores. The 
chain is now evaluating sales 
from these new services and is 
considering offering them at 
more of its stores. 

Pharmacy continues to 
drive Fay’s revenues. The 
company’s mail-order pre- 
scription business helped 
drive pharmacy sales up 
18.8 percent. However, 
gains were accompanied by 
lower margins as more sales 
were made through third- 
party prescription plans. 

Despite the limited growth 
in comparable sales last year, 
Panasci is not concerned. 
“The main thing we go after 
is bottom lie, and our profits 
were better than a year ago. 

..If the prescription sales 
were soft and regular comp 
sales looked strong, then I 
would be concerned,” he said. 

Going forward, Fay’s is in- 
vesting considerable dollars in 
new automation at the store 
level. The Zadall pharmacy 
system, which automates 
scheduling and inventory 
management and links stores 
with headquarters, was re- 
cently installed at two stores. 
It will be expanded chainwide 
by the end of the first quarter 
next year. In June the chain 
will begin installation of a 
POS system. Panasci hopes to 
develop marketing programs 
that incorporate scanner data 
in the future. 

Real estate activity for 
this year will focus on 
strengthening market share 
in existing markets. Panasci 
is eyeing opportunities in 
markets where population 
movement from urban to 
suburban areas has created 
new shopping patterns. 

In management news, the 
chain has had a strategic posi- 
tion open since January when 
John Kogut, a 26-year veter- 
an, unexpectedly resigned 
from his post as drug store di- 
vision president. At presstime, 
Panasci, who is temporarily 
handling those duties, was 
still searching for a successor.
