UAL REPORT 


Medicine Shoppe ties success to satisfied customers 


By Mike Troy 


edicine Shoppe In- 
ternational Inc., the 
nation’s’ leading 


pharmacy franchisor, is 
coming off its best year 
since being founded in 1970. 
Record sales and earn- 
ings, strong same-store 
sales growth, the opening of 
its 1,000th store and the 
formation of a pharmacy 
benefit management sub- 
sidiary were all significant 
goals achieved by Medicine 
Shoppe during the 1994 fis- 
cal year ended Sept. 30. 
Buoyed by same-store 
sales gains of 9 percent, re- 
tail sales increased to $851 
million from $764 million, 
and net earnings increased 
to $14.4 million from $12.9 
million when compared to 
the previous year. Profit 
margins remained strong at 
28.6 percent, even though 
that was a decline from 29 
percent the previous year. 
The St. Louis-based phar- 
macy-oriented chain is also 
off to a good start in fiscal 
1995, turning in a record- 
setting first quarter. Retail 
sales for the quarter ended 
Dec. 31, 1994 were $232 
million compared to $209 
million a year ago. Same- 
store sales for the quarter 
increased 7 percent and 
earnings per share grew to 
$0.52 from $0.45. 
President and chief execu- 
tive officer David Abraham- 


son said Medicine Shoppe’s 
success is due to efforts in 
the managed care, market- 
ing, advertising and pur- 
chasing areas. The recently 
created wholly owned sub- 
sidiary, Managed Pharmacy 
Benefits Inc. (MPB), allows 
Medicine Shoppe to offer 
new services beyond its ex- 
isting third-party marketing 
subsidiary, Medicine Shoppe 
InterNet Inc. 

“The function of InterNet 
is to really enable us to act 
as chain pharmacy to get 
us access into managed 
care plans for our store 
owners,” Abrahamson s-.id. 
“Virtually all of our store 
owners participate in the 
program, and it allows us 
to emulate a chain. The 
purpose of MPB is to actu- 
ally hold the contracts and 
manage them.” 

MPB will offer complete 
prescription benefit man- 
agement, including claims 
administration, benefit de- 
sign consultation, drug uti- 
lization review and formula- 
ry management. Abraham- 
son said the reception in the 
marketplace has been favor- 
able since its formation on 
Oct. 1, 1994. 

“We began processing 
claims effective in January, 
and there is a lot of interest. 
We are trying to position 
MPB a little different where 
we go beyond dispensing 
product into delivering more 
value,” Abrahamson said. 


Medicine Shoppe is seeing 
the dividends of its new ag- 
gressiveness in the man- 
aged care arena. Third par- 
ty as a percent of pharmacy 
sales increased to 41 per- 
cent last year, compared to 
27 percent in 1990. Even at 
41 percent, there is plenty 
of opportunity to grow third- 
party business as other 
comparable-size chains are 
in the 50 percent to 60 per- 
cent ramge. 

“WV ¢ are a little below the 
navional average, and part 
of that may be because of 
the demographics of the ar- 
eas we serve, which tend to 
be smaller markets and sub- 
urban areas of major mar- 
kets,” Abrahamson said. 

Medicine Shoppe’s small, 
intimate format and empha- 
Sis on specializing in phar- 
macy give it a unique story 
to tell when approaching 
value-oriented third parties. 

“You hear a lot about au- 
tomation, but the profes- 
sional knowledge and care 
that the pharmacist is able 
to provide will never be able 
to be automated, and that is 
what MPB is hoping to take 
advantage of,” Abrahamson 
said. “Unless pharmacy is 
willing to assume these 
broader responsibilities, it 
will remain a commodity 
business.” 

Medicine Shoppe retail 
sales are roughly 94 percent 
pharmacy, with refills as a 
percent of total prescriptions

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


How the industry fared 


hain drug retailing did well in 

1994. Sales through the chain 

rug retail channel outpaced 

the nation’s average retail 

growth rate of 7.8 percent in 1994, 

climbing 8.1 percent to $59.8 billion, 
up from 1993's $55 billion. 

Sales through all drug stores— 
chains and independents—reached 
a record-high $82.9 billion in 1994, 
up from 1993’s $78 billion. That 6.4 
percent far outperformed the indus- 
try’s meager 1 percent growth rate 
in 1993. 

Thanks to its robust growth, 
chain drug extended its already 
dominant share of drug store indus- 
try sales in 1994. Up two points 
from 1993, chain drug now controls 
72 percent of the drug store mar- 
ket—some $60 billion. 

That growth was not achieved by 
a massive increase in store count. 
Indeed, the chain drug industry op- 
erated only 1.4 percent more loca- 
tions in 1994 than in 1993. 

Much of the sales growth was fu- 
eled by pharmacy sales. For the 
quarter ending Nov. 30, 1994, for 
example, Walgreen Co. reported a 
13.6 percent increase in sales, 
boosted by a 19.4 percent in phar- 
macy sales. Thrifty PayLess report- 
ed its PayLess same-stores rose 5 
percent, thanks to a 15.6 percent 
boost in pharmacy sales. Revco 
recorded a similar trend: for the 
quarter ended Feb. 4, 1995 core 
Revco stores recorded same-store 
increases of 12.7 percent increase, 
fueled by an 18.3 percent in pre- 
scription sales. 

Much of the pharmacy growth 
came from growth in third-party 
contracts, as chain retailers aggres- 
sively built that business. 


Where the numbers 
came from 

For the second year, Drug 
Store News is pleased to have 
collaborated with Information 
Resources Inc. (IRI) to pre- 
sent a comprehensive picture 
of category sales through 
drug stores. 

The majority of the statistics 
in this section on dollar vol- 
ume, unit volume, and market 
share by trade class and cate- 
gory were supplied by IRI. For 
chains’ market share and 
those categories not tracked 
by IRI, additional figures were 
supplied by exclusive Drug 
Store News industry research. 

IRI is a Chicago-based mar- 
ket research and software 
company. Its retail sales fig- 
ures for the 52-week period 
ended Jan. 1, 1995, are based 
on scanning data collected 
from a nationally representa- 
tive sample of supermarkets, 
drug stores and mass mer- 
chandisers.

In addition to bringing in new 
pharmacy business, the increase in 
third-party contracts brought an- 
other benefit: an increase in foot 
traffic—giving the beleaguered 
front end a chance to capture incre- 
mental sales. 

In 1994, drug stores’ front ends 
were engaged in a pitched battle 
with food and mass merchants for 
consumers’ mass market purchas- 
es. Mass merchandisers, still the 
new kids on the block, continued 
along their growth curve, and food 
stores, looking desperately for any 
product that still retains a re- 
spectable margin, looked with fa- 
vor at traditional drug store front 
end categories. 

According to Information Re- 
sources Inc., in virtually all seg- 
ments, sales through the drug chan- 
nel—independents and chain drug 
combined—dropped in 1994: OTC 
sales dropped 0.5 percent; toiletries 
dropped 1.5 percent; cosmetics and 
fragrances, flat. Consumables, a cat- 
egory that many drug chains are 
pursuing, saw a slight lift, up 1.6 
percent. The biggest gains were in 
general merchandise, up 11 percent. 

Sales through mass merchants, 
on the other hand, were up in 
many categories. And, for the most 
part, food stores held their own. 
When they lost sales, they lost 
them to the mass merchants. 

Despite the dip in sales, howev- 
er, drug stores retained their domi- 
nant market share in OTC and cos- 
metics sales, and still held the lead 
in key HBA segments such as hair 
care and skin care 

And, within every category, 
there is good news. 


Cosmetics 


Cosmetics buyers for most of the 
higher-volume chains reported that 
their sales were up for 1994—typi- 
cally in low single-digit incre- 
ments. A tew chains reported high- 
single and low double-digit growth. 
The chains recording gains were 
those actively pursuing the catego- 
ry—improving presentation, ex- 
panding the department, testing 
new merchandising ideas and part- 
nering with manufacturers. 

But some chains and indepen- 
dents seem to have thrown in the 
towel, cutting back to a minimal 
cosmetics presence and leading to 
the sales decline recorded by IRI. 


Toiletries 


Drug stores are still the domi- 
nant channel for skin and hair care 
sales. Hair coloring, where drug 
stores especially shine, is a bright 
spot in the category, exhibiting 
strong growth.

ized the bath category with their 
splashy new launches—supported 
by plenty of manufacturer ad dol- 
lars. And skin care’s sexy new in- 
gredient—alpha hydroxy acid—is 
still perceived to be new and desir- 
able by consumers. Its popularity is 
leading to an intensification of prod- 
uct proliferation as manufacturers 
seek to capitalize on the trend. 


OTCs 


Thank goodness consumers don’t 
change: Americans want to be thin 
and healthy while eating a Big Mac 
every day. That dichotomy will con- 
tinue to fuel sales of products like 
diet aids (up 11.6 percent in drug 
stores last year) and vitamins. Also 
doing well: first aid, incontinence 
and foot care. And, while numbers 
appear disappointing for the cough/ 
cold/allergy/sinus segment, just wait 
until next year: a delayed onset of 
the flu season has skewed 1994, and 
drug chains are reporting healthy 
category sales, thanks to an un- 
healthy start to 1995. 


Consumables 


General merchandise edged con- 
sumables out in 1994 as drug stores’ 
second largest department in terms 
of percent of sales. But consumables 
continued to play a significant part of 
front end sales. The nation’s healthy 
bent (New Age beverages, fat-free 
cookies) combined with its self-indul- 
gent streak (peg packaging and sin- 
gle servings) to produce double-digit 
increases in cookies, ready-to-drink 
ice teas and shelf-stable juices. 


General merchandise 


The most diverse category —and 
the most difficult to track—is gener- 
al merchandise. The largest seg- 
ment— greeting cards—continued 
on its growth path, benefiting sig- 
nificantly from the micromarketing 
efforts of the major vendors in the 
category. Photo finishing and film 
also remained strong through drug 
chains, as customers continued to 
feel comfortable entrusting their 
film to the retail outlet that fills 
their prescriptions. 

Several drug chains helped fvel 
the growth of the photo finishing 
category by continuing to roll out 
one-hour photoprocessing. 


Private label 


Private label products grew a 
healthy 9.1 percent in U.S. drug 
store sales in 1994, to $2.37 billion. 

What’s driving much of the 
growth at the nation’s drug chains 
is the move into new product ar- 
eas, and a growing awareness of 
how to price store brands to pro- 
vide both consumer value and a 
solid profit margin. 

Many drug chains successfully 
extended their store-brand efforts 
in 1994. Some of the hottest store- 
brand activity in 1994 was in ar- 
eas like snack foods and bever- 
ages, vitamin-formula shampoos, 


children’s toiletries and upscale 
bath/body lines.

Pharmacy takes the spotlight in ’94 


By Jean Barilla 


in Washington as the Clinton Ad- 

ministration made a concerted ef- 
fort to include a universal pharma- 
cy benefit within its ambitious 
proposal for national health care re- 
form. But outside the rhetoric of 
Washington, pharmacy was getting 
plenty of attention from the retail 
drug store industry as well. 

And while the Clintons failed to 
see a national health care reform 
package passed, the chain drug 
store industry—in aggregate, at 
least—did see their efforts pay off in 
significant sales increases. In 1994, 
drug chain pharmacy sales rose a 
healthy 15.4 percent, from $20.1 bil- 
lion to $23.2 billion, triple the 5 per- 
cent growth rate seen in 1992 and

Independent pharmacies did not 
fare as well. Collectively, they post- 
ed a 1.7 percent increase in phar- 
macy sales, from $18.0 billion to 
$18.3 billion. 

The total drug store channel post- 
ed a pharmacy sales increase of 9 
Stee: rising from $38.0 billion to 
$41.5 billion. Pharmacy market 
share as compared to the front end 
increased to 50 percent from last

Despite the lack of federal health 
care reform, forces were at work im- 
pelling the sales increase in retail 
pharmacy: a larger volume of pre- 
scriptions due to an increase in 
managed-care contracts, competi- 
tive pressure for drug stores to in- 
crease market share in pharmacy to 
compensate for mass merchants’ as- 
sault on front-end sales, and chang- 
ing demographics, particularly the 
aging population. 


Pharmacy in the headlines 


The year started off with the 
promise of national health care re- 
form coming in like a lion and ended 
with the Clinton platform looking 
more like souvalaki (chipped-away 
lamb). 

After embracing the prospect of 
national health reform with open 
arms in 1998, the retail pharmacy 
community slowly became disillu- 
sioned. By early 1994, despite the 
joint support of the Administration 
and the Community Retail Pharma- 
cy Health Care Reform Coalition, 
formed by associations NARD and 
NACDS, the industry was becoming 
skeptical of the Clinton reform plan. 

By early May ‘94, congressional 
support for the Clinton proposal 
was insufficient to diffuse opposi- 
tion interest groups that were 
throwing support behind competing 
reform proposals. Later in May, the 
health care reform bill was whittled 
away by finance committee chair- 
man Daniel Patrick Moynihan (D- 
N.Y.) and Senate tax writers. 

In September, George Mitchell, 
Senate majority leader, acknowl- 
edged that health reform 
was a legislative dead let- 
ter in the 103rd Congress. 
But some positive by- 
products remained: the 
drug chain/independent 
alliance, the NACDS/ 
NARD coalition, remained

A group of several of 
the nation’s leading drug 


chains, led by Rite Aid, initiated the 
effort by filing suit against seven 
major pharmaceutical companies in 
1993. The charge was violation of 
the Robinson-Patman law. In June 
1994, the drug chains were joined 
by independents in California and 
leading supermarket chains in fil- 
ing antitrust suits against drug 
manufacturers. 

In August, Maine passed its own 
version of an anti-price discrimina- 
tion law, the “Improved Access to 
Pharmaceuticals Act.” It didn’t 
work as expected. Instead of ex- 
tending discounts to include all 
purchasers, a dozen or so major 
pharmaceutical manufacturers 
abruptly eliminated all discounts, 
including “earned discounts” across 
the board. 

October found retail pharmacists 
in 15 states filing antitrust suits to 
strike back at unfair pricing. Led by 
the Georgia Pharmacy Association, 
the new suits urged courts to reduce 
patent protection for branded drugs 
if manufacturers didn’t comply. 


“Vertical integration” continues 


Meanwhile, as two more manufac- 
turers purchased Pharmaceutical 
Benefit Managers (PBMs), NACDS 
and others were voicing concerns 
about “vertical integration.” 

In February, NACDS president 
Ron Ziegler urged Congress to re- 
ject the 1993 Merck/Medco acquisi- 
tion saying it would give managed- 
care mail-order companies an un- 
fair competitive advantage. 

In May 1994, SmithKline 
Beecham agreed to acquire a PBM, 
Diversified Pharmaceutical Ser- 
vices, with a network of more than 
30,000 U.S. drug stores. This was 
followed by Pfizer entering into a 
joint venture with Value Health 
Inc., giving the manufacturer access 
to the formulary of Value Health’s 
PBM, ValueRx. 

In July, Eli Lilly agreed to ac- 
quire PCS, the PBM giant, from 
McKesson Drug Corp. (McKesson 
then launched another third-party 
network of its own, McKesson Phar- 
macy Provider Network, in August.) 

At the NACDS pharmacy meet- 
ings in August, Ziegler again voiced 
alarm, citing the takeovers of PBMs 
by Merck, SmithKline Beecham and 
Lilly. 

November found Lilly agreeing to 
conditions imposed by the Federal 
Trade Commission that cleared the 
way for the deal to acquire PCS. 


Chains control destiny 


While various segments of the 
public sector were performing their 
health care reform swan dance, 
were the chains sitting on their 
hands waiting for the finale? No. 

According to one top 10 chain 
pharmacy vice president: “Health 
care reform started 10 years ago, re- 
gardless of what Washington was 
or is doing—and we saw it coming.” 

Another chain executive said: 
“Reform is going on, it’s not legisla- 
tive, but pushed by marketplace

paid by third-party payors is sub-

Most industry insiders agree that 
managed “cost”—as opposed to 
managed “care” —is not going away. 

The question, as one chief execu- 
tive officer put it, is: “How do we 
survive and thrive?” 

Before and during the demise of 
health care reform, the chains were 
quietly, but efficiently, implementing 
strategies to deal with shrinking 
margins, the managed-care environ-

own PBMs and marketing their own 
pharmacy services.

sales in pharmacy in an effort to in- 
crease market share as competition 
for the prescription shopper gets 
more intense.

In 1994, service features 
increased in importance in

Cosmetics & Fragrances 


Cosmetics show only mild growth 


Dollar volume has increased but unit sales are down 


By Liz Parks 


C 


osmetics dollar sales through 
food, drug and mass merchan- 
dise stores were up slightly in 
1994, but unit sales remained flat. 

According to Chicago-based Infor- 
mation Resources Inc. (IRI), a mar- 
ket research company that tracks 
sales through food, drug and mass 
merchandise stores, the total cos- 
metics category was up 3.6 percent 
to $2.6 billion in 1994, but unit 
sales were down 0.6 percent. That 
means after factoring in price in- 
creases, there was no real growth in 
cosmetics in 1994. 

However, there were certain trade 
classes and certain category seg- 
ments that did generate growth in 
1994. 

Dollar and unit sales for cosmet- 
ics in mass merchandise chains like 
Wal-Mart, Target and Kmart in- 
creased 12.4 percent and 7.7 per- 
cent, respectively. In food stores, 
cosmetics sales were up 4 percent in 
dollars and 1 percent in units. 
Many combination food/drug stores 
reported stronger sales, but the av- 
erage for food stores was lower be- 
cause many of the non-combination 
food stores do not emphasize cos- 
metics as part of their mix. 

A similar trend is occurring in 
drug stores. Many independents 
and lower volume chains have cut 
back to a minimal presence in cos- 
metics, which is one reason why 
cosmetics sales for the total drug 
store industry softened again in 
1994, declining 8 percent in dollars 
and 7 percent in units. However, 
cosmetic buyers for most of the 
higher volume chain drug stores 
said their sales were up for the 
yeer, typically in low single-digit in- 
crements. A few chains saw growth 
in the high-single and low double- 
digit increments. 

According to chain drug store cos- 
metics buyers, the successful launch 
of several Revlon and L’Oréal prod-

ANNUAL REPOR 


Cosmetics & fragrances 


Nail treatments shine brightly 


More consumers are choosing at-home remedies as opposed to salon services 


By Liz Parks 


ith some exceptions such 
as nail treatments and 
nail manicure, the nail 


color/nail care category, which in- 
cludes sales of nail polish as well 
as treatment products and false 
nails, had a tough year in 1994. 
According to Information Re- 
sources Inc. (IRI), mass market 
dollar sales of all nail color/nail 
care products were down 3.7 per- 
cent in dollar sales and down 4.1 
percent in unit sales. Mass mer- 
chandise chains like Wal-Mart and 
Kmart were able to eke out a 3.6 
percent dollar gain and a 4 percent 
unit gain, but drug stores saw 
their dollar sales of nail color/nail 
care drop 7 percent in dollars and 
9 percent in units. In food stores, 
the category declined 4 percent in 
dollars and 3 percent in units.

Nail polish, which accounts for 
76 percent of all nail color/nail 
care sales, was responsible for 
most of the decline. The $230 mil- 
lion mass market polish category 
was down 5.4 percent in dollar 
sales. The much smaller volume 
nail care/nail treatment category 
was up 2 percent to $73.4 million. 

The No. 1 nail polish brand, 
Revlon, was only up 1 percent in 
dollar sales, ending the year with 
a 22.5 percent share and $51.7 
million in sales. 

The No. 2 color brand, Sally 
Hansen, was down 5.7 percent to 
$34.7 million. Sally Hansen had a 
15 percent share of all 1994 nail 
color dollar sales. 

Five other leading nail color 
brands also showed declines, some 
of them quite sharp. Sales of 
L’Oréal nail color aoueee 3.3 per- 
cent to $31 million; P&G’s Cover 
Girl nail color sales were down 
12.1 percent to $21 million. Cutex 


sales were down 18.4 percent to 
$19.9 million, while Maybelline 
nail color sales were down 8.8 per- 
cent to $14.7 million. Sales of Fac- 
tor’s nail polish, like Revlon’s pol- 
ish, were flat at $7.2 million. 

The only growth brands in nail 
color in 1994, according to IRI, 
were Del Lab’s Flame Glow nail 
polish, whose sales were up 46.9 
percent to $4.4 million; Artmatic, 
whose sales were up 27.2 percent 
to $7.2 million; and Pavion’s Wet 
‘n’ Wild, with sales up 7.3 percent 
to $12.7 million. 

Flame Glow’s growth is partly 
due to expanded distribution as 
more retailers added Flame Glow 
nail color to their nail care 
planograms. Wet ‘n’ Wild’s growth 
may be partly due to the fact that 
Pavion increased the number of 
pre-pack promotions in 1995, giv- 
ing its nail color line enhanced 
visibility. 

Nail treatment was a different 
story. In 1994, the driver in this 
segment was the leading brand. 
Del Lab’s Sally Hansen generated 
an 8.6 percent gain to end 1994 
with a 26.5 percent share and 
sales of $19.5 million. 

The No. 2 brand, Revlon, with a 
21.3 percent share of nail treat- 
ment sales, had a 1.6 percent dol- 
lar gain in 1994 while L’Oréal, 
with a 7 percent share, saw sales 
climb by 8.7 percent. 

Based on its performance in 
1994, Cover Girl is in danger of 
losing its fourth place in the cate- 
gory to Jonel treatment products. 
Cover Girl’s nail treatment sales 
dropped 26.3 percent in 1994 to 
$3.1 million, while Jonel’s sales 
soared 26.8 percent to $2.9 million. 

Wet ‘n’ Wild picked up 9.5 per- 
cent more in dollar sales to end 
1994 with $2.7 million in nail 
treatment sales. 

Nail Magic was flat, however, 
with sales at $1.6 million while 
Cutex, Artmatic and Max Factor 
treatment sales were all down in 
either single- or double-digit in- 
crements. What seems to be hap- 
pening in nail care is that all the 
higher-volume brands, except Cov- 
er Girl, are gaining sales at 
the expense of smaller-volume 
competitors. 

Wet ‘n’ Wild, probably because 
it is a value line with aggressive 
promotional activity going on in 
1994, was the only lower-volume 
brand able to show dynamic 
growth. 

The top 10 brands in nail care 
accounted for 77 percent of the to- 
tal category’s dollar sales through 
drug, food and mass outlets. 

There seem to be several rea- 
sons why nail treatments, 
strengtheners, hardeners, cuticle 
treatments, etc., have been able to 
do well while the entire nail care 
category itself is soft.

Cosmetics & fragrances 


Cosmetics show mild growth 


Continued from page 93 

The strongest face makeup 
launch of 1994 was Revlon’s 
Age Defying Makeup. 
Women responded enthusi- 
astically both to the product 
and to the ad campaigns that 
featured actress Melanie 
Griffin. One chain drug store 
buyer said he bought extra 


heavy at Christmas and still 
ran out on the most popular 
shades. 

“Age Defying was phenom- 
enal,” said the buyer for a 
major West Coast chain. 
“Revlon did everything right.” 
According to IRI, Revlon, 
which is the No. 2 brand in 
the face makeup category 


with 1994 sales of $93.3 
million, generated a 17.7 per- 
cent increase in face makeup 
dollar sales in 1994. 

L’Oréal, the No. 4 brand, 
with 1994 sales of $88 mil- 
lion, generated a 10.9 per- 
cent increase in dollar sales. 

L’Oréal did not have a 
runaway winner like Age 


Defying, but its makeup 
lines Visuelle, Mattique, 
Hydra Perfecte and Dualite 
all received good reports for 
steady growth. Two cosmet- 
ics buyers reported double- 


digit gains in their sales of 


L’Oréal face makeups. 

In addition to its face 
makeups, L’Oréal also had a 
good year with its new Ex- 
cel—a skin moisturizer, 
which some chains merchan-

division, Quintessence, had 
five of the top 10 best selling

had four of the top 10 best-

ANNUAL REPORT 


Cosmetics and fragrances 


Makeup puts on its best face 


Marketing, distribution, competitive prices give drug chains the edge 


By Liz Parks 
Ts face makeup category, which 


includes blush, liquids and pow- 

ders, was up nearly 4 percent in 
dollar sales in food, drug and mass 
merchandise stores in 1994. 

Sales in the drug store industry 
were flat, down 2.7 percent vs. a year 
ago. But drug chains appeared to do 
better in the category than indepen- 
dent drug stores and smaller volume 
retailers, thanks to their more effi- 
cient distribution programs, more 
competitive prices and their sophisti- 
cated marketing of the category. 

The 10 leading brands in face 
makeups account for 95 percent of 
all dollar sales, according to Infor- 
mation Resources Inc., so to a large 
extent, the category’s fate is depen- 
dent on these brands and the com- 
panies that market them. 

In 1994, Cover Girl dominated 
the mass market face makeup cate- 
gory, with a 34 percent share of all 
dollar sales through food, drug and 
mass merchandise stores. Revlon 
and Maybelline wound up in a close 
tie for second place with shares of 
13 percent and 12.6 percent respec- 
tively in dollar sales. 

L’Oréal, with an 11 percent 
share, Max Factor with 9 percent 
and Almay with 7 percent are the 
other major leading players. 

According to IRI, Cover Girl,

which generates almost three times 
as much dollar sales in face make- 
ups as Revlon, had a 5.4 percent 
sales gain for the 52 weeks ended 
Jan. 1, 1995. 

One chain drug cosmetics buyer 
said she was very happy with her 
gains for high-volume Cover Girl, “up 
7 percent to 8 percent in real sales af- 
ter deducting price increases.” 

But other buyers expressed some 
disappointment with Cover Girl, re- 

orting that their growth in the 
Rca was essentially flat. 


“The problem is that P&G is not 
doing enough promotions for Cover 
Girl,” said one chain buyer. “They 
are relying on coupons to drive sales 
of Cover Girl and Max Factor, and 
although coupons work, there isn’t 
any specific tie-in to our stores so a 
consumer can go anywhere to re- 
deem that coupon. I need P&G to 
help create promotions that will 
bring consumers into my stores.” 

According to IRI, Revlon squeaked 
ahead of Maybelline in 1994 to be 
come the No. 2 player in face mak -- 
ups, picking up 1.4 share points 
while Maybelline dropped .02 points. 


New launch hurts old brand 


There was complete consensus 
among chain drug cosmetics buyers 
that the launch of Age Defying defi- 
nitely helped Revlon gain momentum 
in face makeups. Three buyers specu- 
lated that Maybelline’s recent launch 
of Revitalizing makeups may have 
distracted its marketing team away 
from supporting its classic face 
makeups and, in the process, inad- 
vertently hurt the momentum of the 
classic Maybelline brand. 


Half the buyers we talked to said 


that the Maybelline face makeups 
showed “steady growth” over last 
year; two said Maybelline’s Revital- 
izing makeup sold well for them. 

The IRI sales figures for May- 
belline in 1994 did not include sales 
for Revitalizing or Maybelline’s eth- 
nic makeup, Shades of You. Neither 
did they include sales of Revlon’s 
ethnic makeup line, Color Style or 
Almay’s ethnic shade collection, 
Darker Tones. 

One buyer, who said she waited 
“later than almost everyone else to 
buy Revitalizing,” said that worked 
to her advantage. “In their initial 
pre-packs shipments, they did a lot 
of stock-on stock, and that hurt 
their turns.” 

“But we don’t have any leftover 
from the pre-packs, so we’re doing 
very well with Revitalizing. It’s 
turning nicely.” 

Another buyer said Maybelline 
was his fastest growing brand in all 
segments of the color category in his 
chain except nail. “It’s because they 
have people in our stores making 
service calls,” he said. “They make 
sure the product’s up, that it’s in 
stock, that it’s priced correctly and 
when it’s time to take markdowns, 
they’re in the store putting out in- 
stant rebate coupons to minimize 
our returns.” 

Almost two-thirds of the buyers 
surveyed reported that sales of 
their Almay and Max Factor face 
makeups picked up in the second 
quarter. According to IRI, Almay’s 
sales of face makeups were up 3 
percent in 1994 while Factor’s sales 
were up 2 percent. 

Almay’ s “Take The Clinique Chal- 
lenge” promotion kicked in double- 
digit gains for one regional chain 
during the third and fourth quarters 
of last year. The cosmetics buyer for

a Northeast-based chain reported 
that his stores could have done even 
better with the promotion if he 
hadn’t lost his rep for the line. 

“We did endcaps and point-of-pur- 
chase aids, but if we’d had a rep, we 
could have supported it more,” he 
said. 

Out of the top 10 brands, Physi- 
cians Formula, with sales last year 
of $10.2 million, generated the 
strongest growth, up 43.6 percent, 
according to IRI. Some of the 
growth is clearly coming from ex- 
panded distribution for Physician’s. 
Three of the chains we talked to 
said they were either adding or ex- 
panding the Physician’s Formula 
face makeups in their planograms. 

One buyer who expanded Physi- 
cian’s Formula into chainwide distri- 
bution said most of her growth from 
the line is incremental, meaning it is 
succeeding without cannibalizing 
sales of her existing brands. 

“We're trying to drive our face and 
our skin care business,” said one buy- 
er. “We’re going to add Physician’s 
Formula because we think that line 
will give our customers a greater se- 
lection of the products they’re most 
interested in. We’re going to give it at 
least two feet, and as it builds, we'll 
think about adding their lip, eye and 
nail color products.” 

The strongest gains in the face 
makeup segment, averaging high- 
double-digit increments of 20 per- 
cent or better in some cases, came 
for chains who aggressively promot- 
ed the cosmetics department. 


Linedrives are a hit 


Line drives were a popular adver- 
tising vehicle. The buyer for one 
Northeastern regional chain said it 
had a tremendously successful line 
drive program last year. “Our 
L’Oréal face makeups were up 26 
percent for the year,” he said, “and 
that was partly because we offer our 
customers a real value when we pro- 
mote a brand family. Their 
linedrives for L’Oréal, for example, 
were not limited to discounts off just 


L’Oréal face or L’Oréal eye products, 
but were good for any L’Oréal brand 
in skin, fragrance or cosmetics.” 

This chain also had a 23 percent 
increase in Revlon face makeups 
and a 23 percent increase with clas- 
sic Maybelline. “The driving force 
behind classic Maybelline,” this 
source said, “was their advertising, 
their coupons and our line drives.” 

There is evidence that the Ameri- 
ca woman’s obsession with the “nat- 
ural” look has run its course and 
that a new fashion trend is washing 
over the country: a passion for a 
laid-back look that can be varied to 
look more sophisticated or more 
natural depending on the woman’s 
mood and/or the occasion. 

One buyer said she’s seeing evi- 
dence that her customers are “enjoy- 
ing” making up more today. “Women 
love the fact that makeup can make 
them look a little different depending 
on what they feel like doing,” said an- 
other buyer, a male. 

None of the chains we surveyed re- 
ported any strong gains in face 
makeups targeted specifically toward 
teens, and several buyers said their 
Bonne Bell facial products were soft. 

However, there was a broad con- 
sensus that Del’s Natural Glow, 
which is marketed toward teens but 
which uses relatively sophisticated 
packaging, is doing very well. 

Three chains reported that their 
sales of Del’s Natural Glow make- 
ups were going up steadily. 

“I think the packaging on Natural 
Glow makes teens feel more adult,” 
one buyer reasoned, “and there’s good 
advertising behind it and good sup- 
port. Plus we have a very good rep 
and the bottom line is often tie rep.” 

Cabot Labs face makeups and 
skin care products were also a 
steady seller in 1994, most buyers 


told us. “Nothing dramatic, but a 
xyood steady business,” one source 
said.

New launch catapults women’s fragrance sales 


Six of the category’s highest volume brands didn’t fare as well, however 


By Liz Parks 


ollar sales of women’s fra- 
PD irances through food, drug 

and mass merchandise stores 
rose nearly 5 percent in 1994 to 
$794 million, according to Chicago- 
based Information Resources Inc. 
(IRI). 

Most chain drug store fragrance 
buyers say that New York-based 
Coty was predominantly responsi- 
ble for the growth, thanks to the 
knockout launch of Vanilla Fields. 

One chain drug store fragrance 
buyer called Vanilla Fields “the best 
launch of the past five years.” Like 
many fragrance buyers, she de- 
scribed Coty as an “outstanding 
marketing company,” and she 
praised the vendor for the “consis- 
tent support they give all their 
brands.”

Sales of women’s fragrances through food, drug and mass 
merchandise outlets rose almost 5 percent in 1994. 


According to IRI, five of Coty’s 
women’s fragrances accounted for 
o7 percent of the sales of the top 10 
highest volume women’s fragrance 
brands. 

Coty’s newest women’s fragrance, 
Vanilla Fields, had a 167 percent 
sales gain in 1994, a feat made all 
the more remarkable when com- 
pared to the category’s average 4.7 
percent gain. 

Six of the category’s highest vol- 
ume brands suffered declines in 
1994, including Coty’s !ExClaMa- 


Tion, down 14.9 percent in three 
outlet dollar sales, and Lady Stet- 
son, down 0.6 percent. 

The category leader, Jovan For 
Women, which is made by Coty’s 
sister division, Quintessence, was 
up 9.6 percent which, one chain 
drug buyer said, was “wonderful for 
a brand that’s been around as long 
as this one has.” 

The buyers for three drug chains 
said they believed that the runaway 
success of Vanilla Fields hurt some 
of its sister brands by cannibalizing 
sales. 

“Vanilla Fields appeals to a 
young customer, and I[ think it took 
sales away from !ExClaMaTion, 
which appeals to a similar con- 
sumer,” said the buyer for a Mid- 
western chain. 

Another Coty brand, Sand & 
Sable, which is ninth in dollar 
ranking, regis- 
tered a 4.5 per- 
cent sales gain. 
Sand & Sable has 
been around a 
long time, but un- 
til recently its 
strongest sales 
were in_ the 
South. Coty has 
been expanding 
its distribution, 
to the dismay of 
one buyer for a 
southern drug 
chain, who said 
Sand & Sable 
used to be “one of 
my best sleeper 
brands.” 

Vanilla Fields 
may also have tak- 
en sales away 
from L’Oréal’s 
Vanderbilt, which 
was down 24.2 
percent in dollar 
sales for the year, 
from Revlon’s 
Charlie, down 12.2 
percent, and from 
Procter & Gam- 
ble’s (P&G) Navy, 
down 11.2 percent. 

But there are 
many cosmetics/ 
fragrance buyers 
who felt that 
Vanilla Fields 
brought new 
users into the 
category and that 
the soft performance of brands 
like Vanderbilt, V and Navy were 
not due to cannibalization but to 
the lack of aggressive marketing 
support. 

Said the buyer for one regional 
chain in the Northeast, “L’Oréal 
and P&G did very little to sup- 
port their fragrances last year. 
Their attention was elsewhere, 
and that was reflected in their 
sales.” 

Negative reports on Vanderbilt 
and its newest sister brand, V, were 


wide-ranging, coming 
from virtually every chain 
interviewed. Some buyers 
even speculated that be- 
fore the year is out, 
L’Oréal will discontinue V.

ANNUAL REPORT 


Toiletries 


Drug stores grab hold of toiletries sales 


Control the market in hair care, skin care despite intense competition 


Toteteries market share 


By Lisa I. Fried 


drug stores managed to hold on 

to the leading share of sales of 
the biggest categories in toiletries: 
hair care and skin care. 

Bath, a troublesome category for 
a while, has finally received support 
from big-name national advertisers 
and is growing at a nice clip. And a 
flurry of new shaving products 
pushed sales up 10 percent in drug, 
food and mass merchants. 

Deodorant and oral care weren't 
as bright. While deodorant and oral 
care sales rose 6 percent and 3.8 
percent, respectively, across the 
three mass channels of food, drug 
and mass merchants, drug store 
sales dropped 4.6 percent and 2.2 
percent, respectively. 


[: a fiercely competitive year, 


Drug stores faced two 
major challenges in 
1994: stiffer competition 
from mass merchants 
and a proliferation of 
skin, sun and hair care 
products that are 
crowding shelves and 


confusing consumers. 


In total, drug store sales of over- 
all beauty care in drug stores 
dipped 1.5 percent to $5.5 billion. 

Drug stores faced two major chal- 
lenges in 1994: stiffer competition 
from mass merchants and a prolif- 
eration of skin, sun and hair care 
products that are crowding shelves 
and confusing consumers. 

In skin care, a 5.5 percent in- 
crease in sales across all three mass 
channels was dominated by higher- 
priced alpha hydroxy acid (AHA)- 
based formulations. Consumers are 
buying up and now expect to see fa- 
cial moisturizers, cleansers and 
hand and body lotions with this 
“magical” ingredient. 

The number of product introduc- 
tions in 1994 was dizzying, and in 
many cases consumers are trading 
old moisturizers for new ones. 
Thus, despite the availability of 
many more products, the skin care 
category is not growing in leaps 
and bounds. Manufacturers that 
haven’t yet embraced AHAs are 
studying the pros and cons of 
adding such a product/line to their 
mix, but retailers are thinking 
carefully before adding another 
AHA-based line. 

In hair care, total sales grew 3.6 
percent to $4.7 million, but mass 
merchants made it more difficult for 
drug stores to keep this category 
profitable. As a result, drug stores 
are banking on niche, professional

A move towards softer, more nat-

Drug chains No. 1 in hair care sales 


Competition from food and mass merchants not far behind 


By Lisa I. Fried 


rug stores are still king of the 
hill in terms of hair care sales. 
While it was not a strong year 
for drug stores in hair care sales, 
they maintained the largest share — 
35 percent of sales. But biting at 
their heels were food and mass mer- 
chants, with 33 percent and 32 per- 
cent shares, respectively. 

As more and more consumers 
flocked to mass merchants, drug 
stores experienced sales declines in 
shampoos. And women’s interest in 
softer, more natural styles limited 
total retail sales of hair spray and 
styling aids. The only hair care cat- 
egories that grew in drug stores 
were conditioners and hair color. 

Product lines have proliferated to 
the point that consumers and retail- 
ers are getting confused. As a re- 
sult, some retailers and manufac- 
turers are eliminating slower 
moving items. Procter & Gamble, 
for example, slashed its Vidal Sas- 
son line from 47 to 25 SKUs in 
March. 

Looking to deliver more value to 
the customer, the company also in- 
creased the size of the bottles in its 
Vidal Sasson and Pantene Pro-V 
styling line without passing along a 
higher retail price. As a result, 
sales of both lines have since grown, 
according to the company. 

Others are redesigning packag- 


ing to more clearly communicate 
the benefits of a particular prod- 
uct. For example, Redmond Prod- 
ucts has added more product infor- 
mation to the front of its Aussie 
Hair Care bottles and replaced the 
text-heavy backs with graphics 
showing the effects of a product on 
the hair. “We are making the 
choice simpler and drawing more 
attention to the line,” said Muggs 
Lerberg, director of education for 
Redmond Products. 

For the 52 weeks ending Jan. 1, 
1995, total sales of shampoo grew 
3.8 percent to $1.6 billion. 

Retailers continue to struggle 
with profit margins in the category. 
“The very low-end [99 cents and $1] 
is not selling [well], and some re- 
tailers are shrinking the number of 
products that aren’t moving,” said 
Lerberg. 

Hair products with a professional 
cachet are increasingly popular 
with drug store buyers as they typi- 
cally deliver a 35 percent to 40 per- 
cent margin. 


Professional product margins 


“The squeeze is on for profits, and 
drug stores are looking for more 
professional products,” said James 
McMillan, vice president of sales for 
John Frieda Professional Hair Care. 
And, as professional products be- 
come more popular, their margins 
are shrinking at mass merchants,

care products 


said Jerry Zlotnick, buyer at Medic 
Discount, based in Cleveland. “We 
are finding that we have to be more 
sharply priced.” 

Higher-priced niche products, 
such as Advanced Research’s Thick- 
er Fuller Hair Line and John Frie- 
da’s Frizz Ease, allowed retailers to 
continue to make solid margins. 


Getting into condition 


In the conditioner category, sales 
in drug stores grew 0.1 percent to 
$275 million. Drug stores main- 
tained a 33.1 percent share of all re- 
tail sales, beating out mass mer- 
chants. Across all mass outlets— 
food, drug and mass merchants— 
sales of conditioner grew 6.4 per- 
cent to $829.2 million. Leave-in con- 
ditioners and other repair-oriented 
products performed particularly 
well as more women sought to treat 
the damage that blow drying, 
perms, hair color and the sun 
wreaked on their hair. 

“The conditioning treatment cate- 
gory is flying,” said Steve Estrin, 
sales manager, General Therapeu- 
tics, which markets the Queen He- 
lene line. 

“As a result of perms, coloring 
and bleaching, women are going 
back to basics.” General Therapeu- 
tics was so pleased with response to 
its one year-old Queen Helene Cho- 
lesterol Hot Oil Treatment, it re- 
cently launched Placenta Hot Oil 
Treatment. 

Two-year-old Neutrogena Heat 
Safe has also performed so well that 
the company added a version for 
fine/thin hair last spring. 

A shift toward softer, more natur- 
al hair took its toll on sales of hair 


spray, styling gel and mousse. Hair 

spray sales declined 12 percent in 

drug stores to $226 million and 6.5 
ercent across all classes of trade to 
722.3 million. 

“Overall, the styling category has 
been in a trough for the past several 
years,” said Carol Hamilton, senior 
vice president of marketing for 
L’Oreal’s Hair Care Division. 
“Aerosol sprays and spritzes have 
fallen as they have been associated 
with providing a harder hold. Con- 
sumers are looking for products 
that control the hair without sticki- 
ness or stiffness.” 

“Our natural gel has been grow- 
ing for some time because it’s a soft- 
er style product,” added Redmond 
Products’ Lerberg, who predicts a 
surge in sales of curl products this 
year. 

Inexpensive gels sold in large 
tubs continued to perform well. 
Sales of Queen Helene’s styling aids 
actually grew 30 percent last year, 
according to the company. “Trade 
promotions of larger, cheap gels 
have been attracting consumers 
away from advertised, higher price 
point brands,” said L’Oreal’s Hamil- 
ton. “This takes the consumer out of 
the market for a year due to the im- 
mense quantity and size of these 
products.” 

Hair color was the brightest spot 
in drug stores last year. The cate- 
gory grew 7.1 percent in drug 
stores, which continued to be the 
dominant distribution channel,

ANNUAL REPORT 


Smooth sailing in skin care 


When consumers think of clear skin, they think of drug stores first 


By Lisa I. Fried 


rug stores are the destination 
I): choice for consumers look- 

ing to soften, exfoliate and 
cleanse their skin. For the 52 weeks 
ended Jan. 1, 1995, drug stores 
maintained a 45 percent share of 
skin care sales, dominating mass 
merchants, which had a 29 percent 
share, and food stores, with a 26 
percent share. 

Sales of skin care products rose 
5.5 percent across the three mass 
channels of food, drug and mass, 
due largely to the continuing popu- 
larity of products with alpha-hy- 
droxy acid (AHA), an ingredient 
which can now be found in every- 
thing from facial cleansers to masks 
to hand and body lotion. Con- 
sumers’ fascination with this magi- 
cal ingredient kept sales of Neoteric 
Cosmetics’ Alpha Hydrox and other 
early entrants strong last year, and 
prompted a slew of new players to 
enter the fray. 


A¢ hin core & morket chore 


Wi Drug BR Mass Gj Food 


Face care sales for Chesebrough- 
Pond’s Pond’s line, for example, 
grew 41 percent last year, according 
to the company. The primary driver: 
AHA-based products. 

Sales of facial moisturizers and 
cleansers in drug stores increased 
1.6 percent to $655 million. The 
number of skin care SKUs has 
grown so fast—by one retailer’s 
count there were 164 new AHA- 
based products introduced in 
1994—it’s become increasingly con- 
fusing for both retailers and con- 
sumers to distinguish the differ- 
ences between products. 

“The first, second, third, fourth 
and fifth (AHA-based products) vere 
easier decisions to make than the 
30th one,” said Paul Carlson, a buy- 
er for Snyder Drug Stores. Retailers’ 
scrutiny of the category is making it 
more difficult for manufacturers 


without substantive advertising and 
promotional campaigns to support a 
launch to get shelf space. 

That’s not to say it’s a picnic for 
national manufacturers, either. 
Drug chains are monitoring sales of 
skin care products closely and elimi- 
nating lines that aren’t performing. 
CVS, for example, recently dropped 
the Maybelline Revitalizing line. 

“The number of product introduc- 
tions is out of control,” said Greg 
Bosco, category manager for skin 
care at CVS. “In a drug store, with 
a 40-foot department devoted to all 
aspects of skin care, we have to be 
selective. Neoteric, which has estab- 
lished itself in this class of trade, 
doesn’t have a lot of consumer (ad- 
vertising/promotional) support but 
is doing very well. Now, we measure 
other lines against it.” 

Despite the onslaught of AHA- 
based products, consumer aware- 
ness is still in its infancy, according 
to Del Laboratories, which reports 
that less than 20 percent of con- 
sumers know what alpha-hydroxy 
acid is. In fact, the No. 1 skin care 
line at CVS is the non-AHA-based 
Oil of Olay line. 

The market potential for AHA 
products is prompting more and 
more skin care manufacturers to try 
to capitalize on the craze. 

“Everyone has jumped on the 
bandwagon, and we are looking at it 
now,” said Gary Talarico, vice presi- 
dent of sales for Cabot Laboratories, 
which currently offers an AHA- 
based cover makeup. “However, the 
number of skin care SKUs that are 
out there is mind-boggling. If we 
come out with something with AHA, 
it would have to be unique.” 

Some are doing so now by rolling 
out less-expensive, high-performing 
AHA-based products. Del’s Sally 
Hansen Skin Recovery Line, which 
includes a purifying mask, moistur- 
izing facial capsules, moisturizing 
facial creme and oil-free lotion, just 
hit stores. 

While the prevalence of AHA- 
based products hasn’t hurt sales of 
Neutrogena products, the manufac- 
turer is thinking hard about its reluc- 
tance to embrace AHAs. “AHAs are 
not a trend. Customers are basically 
satisfied with what they are getting,” 
said Linda Kurtzman, director of 
marketing for Neutrogena. “Who’s to 
say we wouldn’t have had bigger 
sales last year if we had an AHA- 
based line?” While the company is 
considering such a move, it does not 
want to cannibalize sales of its tradi- 
tional skin care products, she said. 

That’s an important concern since 
consumers are, in many cases, re- 
placing traditional moisturizers with 
AHA-based ones. Yet, despite the ex- 
plosive number of new products out 
there, sales growth of facial cleansers 
was relatively modest last year. 

“A number of brands are coming 
out with nine to 10 AHA products

Bath category cleaned up in 1994 


ANNUAL REPORT 


Toiletries 


Splashy launches of body washes helped invigorate sales 


By Lisa I. Fried 


he bath category was revital- 

ized last year thanks to the 

splashy launches of several 
body washes and solid growth in 
bubble baths. For the period end- 
ing Dec. 31, 1994, sales for bath 
and shower products grew 10 per- 
cent to $106.4 million (see box be- 
low), according to Tewne-Oller, a 
subsidiary of Information Re- 
sources Inc. 


Ads launch new category 


The entrants of major national 
brands into the bath category creat- 
ed a new subcategory in bath and 
helped lift sales across the category. 
Powerful ad campaigns developed to 
launch Jergen’s Body Shampoo and 
body washes under the Oil of Olay, 
Dove and Caress names educated 
consumers about a new category of 
products—liquid-based shower 
cleansers—and the value of using 
nylon sponges. 

“[Body/shower washes] is the 
fastest growing subcategory,” said 
one bath buyer for a national chain. 
“There have been substantial con- 
sumer requests for it.” 

Indeed, sales of shower gels, wash- 
es and scrubs, which generate consid- 
erably higher profit margins than 
bar soap for drug stores, grew 23 per- 
cent in drug stores last year, accord- 
ing to Towne-Oller. The launches 
have been so successful that Beiers- 
dorf, Dial and most recently Coty, in- 
troduced their own versions as well.

in “bath products” and listed un-

Premium still has a place in oral care 


High-end brushes continue to dominate crowded oral care departments 


By Barbara White 


rug retailers are still trying 
to manage their overcrowded 
oral care departments at the 
same time they are fighting to 
keep their share of the market as 
the mass and food channels 
threaten their once-dominant po- 
sition. Both the food and mass 
channels showed increases in al- 
most every oral care segment in 
both unit and dollar sales while 
the drug channel showed decreas- 
es in all but oral hygiene. 

Premium brush introductions 
have continued to dominate the 
brush category. Oral B’s Advantage 
has been universally praised by 
drug retailers even though the 
brush’s retail price is steep, ranging 
from $2.47 to $3.47. The popularity 
of Advantage and other premium 
products proves that there is a large 
segment of consumers who are will- 
ing to pay $3 or more for a tooth- 
brush.

And retailers have gotten be- 
hind these products because they 
rep.esent a significant margin, be- 
tween 25 percent and 30 percent 
on premium, high-performance 
brushes. 

Brushes with multilevel bris- 
tles—a trend started by Crest’s 
Complete product a few years 
ago—have become a large part of 
the market. Eric Happell, market- 
ing manager at John O. Butler, es- 
timates that brushes with rippled 
rows of bristles generate 25 per- 
cent of category sales. New entries 
into the category boast bendable 
necks, such as the Aquafresh Flex 
Direct, or bendable heads for better 
cleaning. 

Composite handles have also 
been a significant trend in the cat- 
egory. These brushes, which have 
two-piece handles made of hard 


plastic and soft rubber for better 
gripping, comprise about 25 per- 
cent of the sales in the market as 
well, according to Happell. And 
these high-tech brushes command 
a higher retail. 

But retailers aren’t forgetting the 
sizable consumer population that is 
looking for value. And neither are 
manufacturers. Oral B introduced 
Contura, a value line priced at an 
average $1.98 retail to address the 
value segment and to cover both 
ends of the price spectrum with its 
brand. And Colgate has been ag- 
gressively promoting its premium 
brushes. Although they started 
from a small base, Butler’s two- 
pack commodity brushes have been 
the fastest-growing brand in the 
last year. 

The children’s brush segment, 
which represents about 17 percent 
of the market, has had its share of 
new introductions. Johnson & 
Johnson (J&J) introduced the 
Reach Wonder Grip, a brush with a 
handle that’s easier for little hands 
to hold. The product also comes in a 
glow-in-the-dark model, a trend, 
along with products that change 
color, that is popular with the 
young set. 

To better juggle the constant flow 
of new brush SKUs, retailers have 
been consolidating their vendors. 
Only four or five strong players are 
being represented on shelves. 

The toothpaste category, as a 
whole, grew more rapidly than any 
other health and beauty product 
segment. But the increased sales 
did not result from greater demand 
for toothpaste, but instead from 
purchases of higher-priced specialty 
toothpastes. 

As commodity products are used 
as loss leaders to draw traffic, re- 
tailers depend more heavily on 
specialty, niche brands to generate 
much-needed margins. These 
items typically retail for at least 
$1 more than commodity products 
and carry margins between 25 and 
30 percent. 

Sensitive pastes are one solid 
niche; Aquafresh, Oral B and Crest 
have all introduced SKUs in this 
segment. The segment will continue 
to grow as the population ages and 
consumers grow increasingly con- 
cerned about the health of their 
teeth and gums. 

Mentadent, which Chese- 
brough-Pond’s has positioned as 
an everyday product, has created 
a new peroxide segment that re- 
tailers support wholeheartedly 
because of the high margins the 
product generates. 

Peroxide products are now 
flooding the market; Procter & 
Gamble (P&G) is due to release a 
gum care product as a Crest line 
extension. Inevitably, the wave of 
peroxide products will probably 
echo the baking soda explosion—

OTCs defining chain drug’s image 
OTC market share 


By Mike Troy 
Te: OTC department continues 


to be a significant component 

of the chain drug industry’s ef- 
fort to position itself as the health 
care class of trade. 

Drug Store News research indicates 
many individual chain drug operators 
experienced healthy gains throughout 
their OTC department, even though 
the overall drug class of trade in 
many categories registered sales de- 
clines and market share losses. 

Chain drug merchandising execu- 
tives contend the numbers don’t 
truly represent what is taking 
place. Scaled back operations and 
sales declines among discount drug 
store operators Phar Mor, Drug 
Emporium and F&M have skewed 
sales volume numbers downward. 
In addition, the ongoing demise of 
independent drug stores as an effec- 
tive OTC product distribution chan- 
nel further suppress what would 
otherwise be overall drug store 
sales volume increases. 

These two factors and the result- 
ing market share losses combine to 
paint an inaccurate picture of the 
true viability of chain drug stores 
as an OTC distribution channel. 
So, while chain drug stores suc- 
cessfully grew their OTC business 
during 1994 and prospects look 
bright for 1995, the industry will 
continue to battle misperceptions 
drawn from sales figures that are 
accurate but don’t represent a big 
picture view of what is happening 
in the OTC marketplace. 

Having said that, it is hard to not 
be impressed or alarmed, depending 
on one’s point of view, by the numbers 
being posted by mass merchandisers. 

Also going after a larger slice of 
the OTC pie are supermarkets. 
However, the supermarket indus- 
try’s push toward stores with phar- 
macies is boosting OTC sales. And 
new attitudes among supermarket 
operators toward the bottom line 
value of high margin nonfoods such 
as OTCs promises to keep OTC 
merchandise managers on their toes 
in 1995.

Nutritional products show healthy sales gains 


Public insecurity about poor eating habits drives growth 


by Mike Troy 


V 


itamins and herbal products 
were two of chain drug stores’ 
fastest-turning categories 
during 1994, and 1995 promises to 
offer retailers equally strong gains. 

Widespread publicity about the 
health benefits of nutritional supple- 
mentation continues to be the driving 
factor behind sales growth. Another 
powerful force is a widespread mood 
of nutritional insecurity fueled by the 
nation’s generally poor dietary habits 
and failure to eat adequate amounts 
of fruits and vegetables. 

These factors led to 1993’s blister- 
ing sales growth of 12 percent. That 
made it tough to beat in 1994. How-

lished by the New England Journal 
of Medicine, showed no statistical 
benefit from vitamin E supplements 
in preventing lung cancer in 29,133 
heavy, long-term smokers in Finland. 

When these two studies were 
published, retailers noticed modest 
slowdowns in sales. However, long- 
term, vitamins and nutritional sup- 
plements are categories with a posi- 
tive outlook because consumer fears 
about whether adequate amounts of 
vitamins and minerals a 2 obtained 
from diet alone aren’t ‘:kely to di- 
minish. For chain drug stores it will 
be a matter of growing or at least 
maintaining market share in the 
face of other distribution channels 
eager to grab part of a large and 
growing market. 

Drug’s biggest competitors for the 
vitamin business are mass mer- 
chandisers, with 22 percent of the 
market, and food stores with 27 per- 
cent of the market. However, health 
food retailer GNC is growing rapid- 
ly and siphoning off vitamin sales 
as are other alternative channels 
such as shop-at-home programs and 
multi-level marketing programs. 

The past year saw chain drug re- 
tailers expand shelf space for vita- 
mins and herbal supplements as 
manufacturers debuted new prod- 
uct lines that attempt to target spe- 
cific demographic groups that have 
different nutritional needs. Chains 
such as Thrifty PayLess and Ameri- 
can Drug Stores are mentioned fre-

ever, drug store sales growth was 
still a respectable 6 percent, push- 
ing the category to the $930 million 
mark, according to Information Re- 
sources Inc. (IRI). 

Helping to dampen sales some- 
what this year was the release of 
two studies that showed vitamins 
produced minimal or no health ben- 
efits. One of the studies, conducted 
by the Dartmouth Medical School 
and published in the July 21 issue 
of the New England Journal of 
Medicine, looked at beta carotene 
and vitamins C and E. The study, 
the results of which were widely re- 
ported, concluded that supplemen- 
tal beta carotene and vitamins C 
and E were not effective in prevent-

and have made the department a 
destination by devoting consider-

Managing the mix 


The only segments of the vitamin 
category that didn’t experience 
strong growth were vitamin B, iron 
and children’s vitamins. Herbal 
supplements and vitamin packs 
geared toward specific user groups 
experienced the largest percentage 
gains at 32 percent and 25 percent, 
respectively. 

One of the most interesting devel- 
opments last year was the brands re- 
gaining market share from private 
label competitors. According to 
Towne-Oller drug store specific fig- 


ures, private label sales slipped to 
33.2 percent in 1994 from 37.6 per- 
cent during 1993. One of the big rea- 
sons was a move by branded manu- 
facturers to market singles vitamins. 

Brand loyalty tends to be weakest 
among single vitamins, but two ma- 
jor new product launches during 
1994 sought to change that. Miles 
Consumer Healthcare Products in- 
troduced its One-a-Day multivita- 
mins and One-A-Day Extras and 
Lederle Consumer Healthcare de- 
buted Centrum Singles. 

Initially, some chain diug buyers 
were skeptical of the line exten- 
sions’ viability considering the pop- 
ularity of private label in the sin- 
gles area. However, ad support and 
marketing for the two brands was 
effective, and overall Centrum 
sales, including Centrum multivita- 
mins, were up 13 percent and One- 
A-Day sales were up 80 percent, ac- 
cording to Towne-Oller. 


Herbs are hot 


In the herbal area, the good news 
is that the segment is growing less 
reliant on the strength of ginseng 
and garlic. These two products still 
dominate the herbal segment and 
represent 77 percent of sales. How- 
ever, that is a decrease from last 
year when the two items combined 
for 82 percent of drug’s herbal sales. 
Other herbs, such as lecithin, bee 
pollen, acidophilus, brewer’s yeast, 
alfalfa, cranberry, echinacea, golden 
seal, ginko biloba and bilberry are 
starting to grow in popularity. 

As sales of these other herbs in- 
crease, even though sales of garlic 
and ginseng continue to grow, the 
herbal segment will become more 
well-rounded. This was certainly 
true last year. Even though ginseng 
sales were up 28 percent and garlic 
was up 20 percent last year, their 
share of the herbal market declined 
as consumers made drug store pur- 
chases of other herbs more often. 

Another interesting development 
with garlic and ginseng is the prolif- 
eration of brands and the inroads 
private label is making. Sales of 
herbal private labels are up 37 per- 
cent as many retailers have debuted 
store brand garlics and ginsengs. 
After building the mass market for 
ginseng, Sunsource saw store brand 
knock-offs take away some of its 
business. According to Towne-Oller, 
drug store sales of Sunsource’s Gin- 
sana declined 10 percent last year. 

The biggest gain in the herb de- 
partment was made by Nature’s 
Bounty, which grew to a 8.1 percent 
share of the fragmented drug store 
market, up from 3.6 percent in 1993. 
The introduction of new nutritional 
supplements and herbs gained 
broad distribution in chain drug 
stores, and Nature’s Bounty’s sales 
surged 92 percent in the overall vit- 
amins and tonics category, as 
tracked by Towne-Oller. Leading the 
way in sales, according to Towne- 
Oller, are private labels and brands 


by Pharmavite, Leiner and Lederle, 
followed by Nature’s Bounty. 


Still ahead of the curve 


First it was homeopathy and now 
phyto-chemicals. Both appear to be 
promising growth categories which 
will require patience and nurturing 
by chain drug stores. Homeopathy’s 
popularity worldwide has not yet 
translated to chain drug store sales. 
However manufacturers and retail- 
ers believe two keys that will help 
the category turn the corner this 
year are consumer education and 
merchandising. 

Homeopathy has already received 
some free press, and that has 
helped create awareness. Manufac- 
turers’ willingness to grant retailers 
product on a guaranteed sale basis 
assured homeopathy wider distribu- 
tion during 1994. Now, with addi- 
tional publicity, pharmacists should 
start to see products move. Once 
pharmacists get behind the prod- 
ucts, manufacturers expect to see 
stronger sales growth. 

The other key factor that helps 
these products move is retailers 
merchandising products in line with 
their respective category rather 
than as a family of products in a 
dedicated homeopathy department. 

As a category with margins in the 
40 percent range and a worldwide 
popularity just waiting to catch on 
in the United States, homeopathy is 
a opportunity on which chain drug 
stores can’t afford to be caught flat- 
footed. According to one major chain 
OTC buyer, there is already scat- 
tered interest in private label home- 
opathy products, and one branded 
homeopathy manufacturer reports 
at least one major private label sup- 
plier is very interested in develop- 
ing homeopathy. 

Another opportunity area within 
the vitamin and natural product 
arena involves phyto-chemicals. 
These vitamin-like products contain 
the beneficial chemicals contained 
in vegetables such as broccoli and 
spinach. Although brand new to the 
market, with Leiner as the first en- 
trant with its Phyto-Nutrient 
brand, such products have a power- 
ful marketing advantage with con- 
sumers. They play directly to con- 
sumer fears supported by 
well-documented statistics that 
most people don’t eat enough fruits 
and vegetables even though they 
know it is essential to a healthy 
diet. 

Retailers such as Walgreens, Eck- 
erd, American Stores and Revco were 
quick to put Leiner’s three-SKU Phy- 
to-Nutrient line in when the product 
was launched in late March. There 
will be more activity on the phyto- 
chemical front in 1995 as other maior 
vitamin manufacturers bring their 
offerings to market.

Cough/cold sets a record 


The 1994-95 cough/cold season 
ended almost before it got started. 
However, when the season’s final 
sales figures are available, manu- 
facturers and retailers may be look- 
ing at double-digit growth. Informa- 
tion Resources Inc. (IRI) numbers 
used in this annual report are on a 
calendar-year basis and reflect the 
end of the 1993-94 season and the 
beginning of the 1994-95 season. 

Sales figures for calendar 1994 
show the category in decline. The 
category’s performance on a calen- 
dar-year basis reflects the weakness 
of the 1993-94 season and a slow 
start to the 1994-95 season. Sales 
spiked sharply upward in January 
1994, creating a run on cough/cold 
products. The virus faded quickly as 
did sales during February and 
March 1994. Sales during November

Switches on the way 


The gastrointestinal cate- 
gory, specifically the antacids 
segment, also had its share 
of major development during 
1994. The impending arrival 
of Rx-to-OTC switches of 
SmithKline Beecham’s Taga- 
met (cimet.dine) and John- 
son & Johnson/Merck’s Pep- 
cid (famotodine) kept chain 
drug buyers in a holding pat- 
tern throughout 1994. 

Both products were the 
subject of hearings before 
FDA’s Gastrointestinal Drugs 
and Nonprescription Drugs 
advisory committees. The two 
groups had concerns about 
both products that were not 
resolved during 1994. 

Earlier this year, however, 
SmithKline Beecham ob- 
tained a favorable advisory 
committee recommendation 
and at presstime was await- 
ing a formal approval letter 
from the FDA. J&J/Merck 
did not obtain a favorable 
recommendation from the 
advisory committee, but the 
joint venture is reportedly 
tying up loose ends with the 
FDA, and approval of Pepcid 
may also be forthcoming. 

The OTC availability of 
Tagamet and Pepcid in the 
same year will set off rapid

OTC departments’ diversity enhances health image 


By Mike Troy 


he drug store’s OTC depart- 

ment is the embodiment of the 

expression “the whole is 
greater than the sum of its parts.” 

The blending of many interrelat- 
ed, non-core OTC categories rounds 
out the department and provides 
the breadth and depth that give 
chain drug retailers their OTC 
edge. 

When it comes to first aid prod- 
ucts, drug stores are clearly con- 
sumers’ first choice. Information 
Resources Inc.’s definition of first 
aid accessories is broad and in- 
cludes items such as bandages, heat 
and cold packs, first aid kits, ther- 
mometers, diabetes test kits and 
muscle and body support devices. 

Each segment of the category has 
unique factors impacting its growth, 
but it is safe to say overall sales 
were influenced by shorter hospital 
stays, technologically improved new 
products and a greater emphasis on 
self-care among consumers. 

The category of first aid treat- 
ments, defined by IRI as insect-relat- 
ed first aid products, smelling salts, 
anti-itch products and ointments, 
was also a strong category for drug 
stores during 1994.

ANNUAL REPORT 


General merchandise 


GM offered pizzazz and profit in 1994 


Drug chains see across-the-board gains, but competition is intensifying 
__By Allene Symons 


very year, core general mer- 
chandise (GM) categories like 
greeting cards and photo prod- 
ucts/services, along with sta- 
tionery, batteries and audio/video, 
are growing in importance to help 
differentiate drug chains from 
their competitors. 

In 1994, all of these core categories 
grew in drug chains, either in dollars 
or units or both, with dollar increases 
averaging around 5 percent or better 
for core GM in drug chains. 

That’s the good news. The bad 
news is that in most of these cate- 
gories, more aggressive channels 
like warehouse clubs and supermar- 
ket combos got an even bigger bite 
of the GM pie, taking most of the 
forkfuls from specialty retailers like 
card shops and photo dealers. 

GM’s healthy margins also helped 
drug chains offset margin points 
lost in pharmacy to growing third- 
party business in 1994. And against 
mass merchant competitors, GM of- 
fered a draw for neighborhood con- 
venience shopping ranging from 
pantyhose to pencils. 

The synergy continued between 
GM and other drug store depart- 
ments: Photo processing built on 
pharmacy’s image of trust, while 
greeting cards conveyed the “well- 
ness” image of caring. 

On the consumer-pleasing fron- 
tier, an enhanced shopping environ- 
ment compensates for not having 
the best prices in town. More drug 
chains are using GM—and especial- 
ly its seasonal opportunities—to set 
a tone, so the consumer has an en- 
joyable shopping experience. 

For all these reasons, well-mer- 
chandised GM categories again made 
a statement for drug chains in 1994. 


Photo products and processing 
continued to be a top GM driver. In 
1994, one-time-use cameras re- 
mained a star performer with more 
households trying trial-size 15-ex- 
posure versions and Kodak’s Wed- 
dings five-pack. 

Photo processing was a profitable 
traffic builder, since consumers 
make two trips to drop off and pick 
up prints, reprints or enlargements. 
When a consumer opted for one- 
hour processing (and there were 
more drug chain units than ever of- 
fering this opportunity in 1994), it 
often meant extra impulse sales, 
both in and outside the photo de- 
partment. 

For the drug chains that added 
more one-hour photo labs, the re- 
sult was more prominent photo cen- 
ters that conveyed a service image 
and provided added security for ad- 
jacencies like electronics, video and 
batteries. 


Expanded giving 


In social expression product, drug 
chains benefited from new lines in- 
troduced by major greeting card 
manufacturers in 1994. These in- 
cluded more alternative cards for 
non-occasions, which add incremen- 
tal sales on top of planned holiday 
or social occasion purchases. 

Greeting card movement provided 
a powerful tool for pinpointing a 
store’s specific market segments in 
1994. Major card manufacturers, 
who service their own installations, 
leveraged this information to re- 
spond to consumer preferences by 
working with retailers to change the 
mix. Greeting cards stand alone as a 
unique example of efficient con- 
sumer response, a goal these days of 
all drug chain product categories. 

Stationery, batteries and pre- 


recorded video all showed overall 
growth. Drug chains are getting a 
piece of the action, even if it’s a 
small piece compared to mass mer- 
chants and category killers. 

Drug chains are filling the sta- 
tionery convenience gap created 
when specialty discounters like Sta- 
ples and Office Club knocked out 
many small stationery stores. 

Back-to-school sales were re- 
portedly strong in 1994, as drug 
chains have learned to adjust 
their mix against the offerings of 
mass merchants. It’s the same 
with home office—the specialty 
discounters go for certain bulk 
products, so more drug chains are 
adjusting to offer smaller packs, 
mail center items and more value- 
added products along with select- 
ed commodities. 

Batteries, a convenience item 
with high impulse value, appeared 
on more clip strips and in secondary 
locations as well as in more multi- 
packs in drug chains last year. The 
increasing number of portable de- 
vices requiring batteries is certain 
to keep this category growing. Drug 
chains are getting more aggressive 
about offering batteries where con- 
sumers will be reminded to buy 
them—from check out to pharmacy, 
from photo to clip strips in the toy 
department. 


Tapes gain ground 


On the audio/video front, blank 
videotape held steady in 1994, with 
the lion’s share by far in T-120 (at 
hotly competitive prices) for every- 
day video recording. Camcorders 
are gradually pushing up sales in 
this sector, and this growth is ex- 
pected to continue. 

Audiotape got a boost in dollar 
sales from consumers trading up to

higher quality. What’s more, prices 
weren't as competitive as in blank 
video. Look for higher dollar sales in 
audio/video in 1995 due to price in- 
creases pushed up by materials costs, 
as will be the case in stationery. 

On the entertainment frontier, 
pre-recorded video (along with a 
gradually growing presence for CDs), 
are appearing in more drug chains. 
Home video is a convenience item for 
busy parents, since children’s video 
(or kidvid), which is dominated by 
Disney, rules the category. 

Home video in 1994 exceeded pre- 
vious years, report many drug 
chains, with fourth quarter hits 
“Snow White” and “Jurassic Park” 
pulling big volume but small mar- 
gins—still, it’s part of the evolving 
drug chain shopping environment 
with general merchandise offered 
for convenience, problem solving 
and pleasure, often with service and 
apparently at reasonable prices. 


Back to school, home/office lead the pack in stationery gains 


The right mix of basic and upgraded 
nproducts is the key to boosting sta- 
tionery dollars at chains. 


tationery remained a stable 

growth category in 1994 for 

drug chains, with an estimat- 
ed 4 percent in dollar growth for the 
channel compared with 1993, ac- 
cording to Drug Store News re- 
search. In 1995, that figure is ex- 
pected to climb, up to perhaps a 10 
percent increase in dollars (if not in 
units) because of the rise in materi- 
als costs. 

Strong stationery segments in 1994 
included school supplies, home/office 
products and mail supplies. 

Drug chains are primarily conve- 
nience stationery retailers. For 
most, price isn’t the main attrac- 
tion, although stationery promo- 
tions for back to school (BTS) and 
tax time are good traffic builders. 
Instead, drug chains are adding 
products to increase sales per 
square foot, and many are cutting 
back on the number of facings in 
commodity stationery items like 
tablets and filler paper. 

School supplies continue to grow 
in all channels as the crop of baby- 


boomer offspring swells the class- 
rooms. The challenge is to get the 
right mix of basics and upgraded— 
fashion and licensed— product, a 
process aided by store-specific mar- 
keting and scan data. 

Longs was among the chains that 
Saw increases in school related 
items—especially binders, note- 
books, pencils and writing instru- 
ments. All of these were very 
strong, reported buyer Mike Deim- 
ling, who noted that the chain is 
just undertaking category manage- 
ment in stationery. 

In 1994, major manufacturers 
added excitement to back-to-school 
shopping with value-added BTS 
items like Mead’s Nike line of nylon 
school supplies, and Stuart Hall’s 
Tek line of upgraded school prod- 
ucts. Organizers for students were 
another growth area in 1994—a seg- 
ment unknown two years ago. Then 
personal organizers were very hot in 
the adult personal/business category, 
and sales remain strong today.

selling pattern. Parents often stock 
up at a mass merchant, but drug

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995

Photo stays focused on growth in drug chains 


Enhanced photo departments develop image as the processing source 


By Allene Symons 


he photo category thrives on 

photo processing. Nineteen- 

ninety-four was a healthy year 
for drug chains with a 2.1 percent 
increase in rolls processed, accord- 
ing to preliminary results of the 
Photo Marketing Association’s 
(PMA) 1994 Consumer Survey. 

That 2-plus percent means more 
than rolls—it means repeat traffic 
when consumers drop off and pick 
up prints. It’s also likely they'll pur- 
chase film, a one-time-use camera, 
batteries or items in other drug 
store departments. 

Many drug chains reported that 
their photo category overall—includ- 
ing film, cameras, photo finishing, 
frames, albums and other photo 
products—was up in 1994. Enhanced 
photo departments in many drug 
chains helped to fuel the increase. 

Major chains are continuing to fo- 
cus on the photo customer by offering 
highly visible, well-merchandised 
photo departments with more trained 
staff. As many buyers noted, the ex- 
pectation of photo prints and shared 
memories contributes to an upbeat 
and inviting shopping environment. 

For all channels, fast or “one- 
hour” processing totalled 19.5 per- 


cent of rolls processed, with 80.5 
percent in overnight or regular pro- 
cessing. Regular processing in- 
creased by 5.3 percent in rolls for all 
channels in 1994, while fast pro- 
cessing slipped 5.1 percent. 

Industry experts note that the 
fast-processing slippage came large- 
ly from other channels, including 
stand-alone labs and, to some ex- 
tent, supermarkets. Some regions, 
like Southern California and Flori- 
da, experienced a downturn in 
tourism, which also impacted fast 
processing for all channels. 

Many drug chains added one-hour 
labs in 1994, however. In-store labs 
are still on a growth curve in this 
channel as shoppers consider the 
fast-print option now available in 
more drug chain locations each year. 

Drug chains still command the 
largest photo processing market 
share in rolls with 26 percent (22 per- 
cent for traditional drug chains, plus 
4 percent for discount drug chains). 

In all regions, drug chains rein- 
forced their quality photo processing 
image in 1994. Retailers from Eck- 
erd in the Southeast to Genovese in 
the Northeast to Bartell in the Pacif- 
ic Northwest appealed to customers 
with value-added offers like a second 
set of prints free or a mini-photo al- 


bum, rather than compete on price 
against mass merchants and whole- 
sale clubs. Genovese, for example, of- 
fers value-added protection on prints 
and negatives with 3M’s Scotchgard 
Photo Protector as a way to differen- 
tiate its premium photo service from 
discount photo processing. 


One-time use soars 


The robust sales growth of one- 
time-use cameras equals thousands 
of exposures that otherwise 
wouldn’t have been taken. For all 
channels, one-time-use purchases 
increased 34.8 percent over the pre- 
vious year for a total of around 40 
million cameras sold. Drug retailers 
surveyed by Drug Store News all re- 
ported one-time-use camera sales 
were up significantly in 1994. 

With only around 20 percent house- 
hold penetration, there is plenty of 
room for category growth in the com- 
ing years. More good news for drug 
retailers: The one-time-use segment 
skews high to female purchasers. 

In a time when the younger gen- 
eration is preoccupied with videos, 
the photo industry is urging con- 
sumers to participate in more still- 
picture taking. 

Sales of one-time-use cameras 
contributed to the overall increase
