A segment driver in 1994 was the 
Kodak FunSaver Wedding five-pack, 
which spread in popularity and con- 
verted new users to one-time-use cam- 
eras as consumers discovered them at 
weddings and bridal showers. 

The low-risk portability, especial- 
ly outdoors and on vacations, is a 
primary reason for the one-time-use 
segment’s growth. Another con- 
sumer incentive is a chance to try 
new lens types like underwater, 
telephoto and panoramic. 

Kodak and Fuji introduced trial 
size, 15-exposures in their Fun- 
Saver and QuickSnap one-time-use 
cameras in 1994, winning over more 
customers and leading manufactur- 
ers to turn the trial size into a year- 
round offering like Fuji’s new 
QuickSnap15. Retailers like 
Thrifty-PayLess, Snyder, Longs and 
other chains report that the 15-ex- 
posure was a segment driver. 

In conventional cameras, drug 
chains report continuing steady sales 
of cameras in the under-$50 range, 
with action in Polaroid’s Captiva (es- 
pecially when the ad campaigns are 
running, say some buyers) and in 
more expensive cameras with zoom- 
lens feature. Polaroid’s new camera 
entry is the OneStep Talking Cam- 
era, utilizing voice-chip technology so 
the operator can record funny “say- 
cheese” type messages to make pic- 
ture-taking more fun. 


Film upgrades 


For all trade channels, 35mm print 
film grew 2.2 percent in rolls pur- 
chased in 1994. Some drug chains re- 
ported that although film units were 
up, dollars were flat against 1993 
due to sharp pricing necessary to 
compete with mass merchants. 

Eastman Kodak marketed two 
types of new film product in 1994. 
One was its premium 35mm film, 
Royal Gold, targeted as a consumer 
film for special memories with en- 
hancements like greater sharpness 
and color saturation. Last year it 
was offered in 100 and 400 speeds, 
and this year is also available in 
200 speed. 

Kodak also introduced its Fun 
Time value-priced film, a limited- 
time release intended to compete 
with low-cost private-label and 
third brands like Konica during the 
big film seasons, spring/summer 
and fourth quarter. New from Fuji 
is its enhanced film, SuperGPlus. 

Technology is delivering new ser- 
vices to drug chains, where retailers 
with a photo-department presence 
are testing in-store processes like 
Fuji’s Pictrostat and Kodak’s Copy- 
Print Station. 

Drug chains will never be at the 
electronic forefront, but staying in 
the game with services like these 
shows consumers—in markets 
where it’s expected—that a drug 
chain is technically savvy with com- 
puters in the pharmacy and digital 
imaging in the photo department.

college students. 

More drug chains and 
food/drug combos are pro-

photocopying and fax to 
shipping. This is also push- 
ing up the mail segment. 
Another driver is the boom 
in catalog ordering, includ- 
ing mail supplies for return- 
ing unwanted items. 
Another segment showing 


steady sales is the chil- 
dren’s art/crafts segment, 
which is growing in all 
trade channels along with 
the demographic bulge of 
school supplies. In many 
drug chains, however, these 
are merchandised in the toy 
department.

Greeting cards deliver the right message 


Stores, manufacturers fine-tune selection to meet specific needs 


By Allene Symons 


n a year where more attention 

was placed on efficient consumer 

response, greeting cards was ar- 
guably the leading customer-focused 
category in 1994. That’s because 
major card manufacturers like 
American Greetings (AG), Hall- 
mark, Ambassador and Gibson 
helped drug retailers fine-tune their 
inventory to match each store’s cus- 
tomer base. 

They also pumped up seasonal ex- 
citement in drug chains with promo- 
tional concepts ranging from Ameri- 
can Greeting’s Frankie’s Castle for 
Halloween to Hallmark’s Valentine’s 
Day Love Bandit plush raccoon. 

There were new card lines, too— 
more popular alternative or non- 
traditional. 

The result of new product com- 
bined with demographic analysis, 
many retailers reported: a remix of 
the real estate dedicated to cards, 
gift wrap and party. 


Drug channel rises 


An estimated 7.4 billion greeting 
cards were purchased through all 
U.S. trade channels, for around 
$5.9 billion in retail sales, accord- 
ing to the Greeting Card Associa- 
tion. Of these cards, around half 
were seasonal and half were every- 
day cards. 

Cards remained a strong core de- 
partment for drug chains in 1994, 
despite expansion of mass mer- 
chants and especially food/drug re- 
tailers into this category. 

For all trade channels, drug 
picked up 1 point of market share 
for a 24 percent share (up from 23 
percent in 1993). The figures reflect 
all drug retail, but naturally chain 
drug outpaced independents, hav- 
ing the ability to dedicate more 
space to the category. 

Some drug chains reported catego- 
ry dollar increases of 3 percent to 10 
percent or more, often due to fine- 
tuning card offerings to fit specific 
store demographics and, in some cas- 
es, expanding departments. 

One regional chain buyer report- 
ed a 10 percent increase in its Hall- 
mark business. Frank Gable of Har- 
co said of his American Greetings 
departments: “We had a good year.”

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


Lack of rain dampens umbrella sales 
Innovative merchandising offsets fallen consumer demand 


By Wendy Friesen 


hen it rains, it pours: 
For manufacturers 
and retailers in the 


weather protection category, 
it’s a time-honored fact that 
sales go hand in hand with 
precipitation. 

Unfortunately, 1994 was 
an arid year both for average 
national precipitation, which 
fell 6 percent below the 30- 
year U.S. average, and for 
sales of umbrellas, rain bon- 
nets, ponchos and related 
items, with many manufac- 
turers and drug-chain buyers 
reporting sales that were flat 
or down about 5 percent. 

Regionally there were 
bright spots, so to speak, 
such as the perennially 
rainy Southeast, in which 
sales gains were noted, as 
well as the East, which 
managed to hold its own, 
precipitation-wise. The last 
quarter of the year, with its 
stepped-up holiday sales na- 
tionwide, as well as increas- 
es in precipitation on the 
West Coast, was met with 
great enthusiasm by retail- 
ers and vendors alike. 

Still, 1994 has gone down 
in weather protection histo- 
ry largely as a lackluster 
year, especially when in- 
dexed against the spectacu- 
lar ’93, which featured 
flooding and extraordinary 


rainfall in many regions of 
the country. 

All in all, 1994 brought lit- 
tle to speak of in the way of 
growth or increased market 
share in this mature catego- 
ry, which for years has seen 
total retail sales in the $250 
million to $300 million mark. 

However, some retailers 
managed to record big gains 
despite the odds. At Eckerd, 
the region’s strong rainfall 
helped spur sales that ran 
some 31 percent above those 
of the previous year. 


Strategy boosts sales 


CVS nearly doubled its 
93 sales figures for the cat- 
egory, a gain of proportions 
that can’t be explained only 
by the reasonably rainy con- 
ditions in the Northeast. 
What made the difference 
was a significant switch in 
merchandising strategies: 
In 1994 the chain moved 
from in-line displays of um- 
brellas and related items to 
well-stocked rolling carts 
that store personnel were 
encouraged to position at 
prominent spots as the rain- 
drops started to fall. 

Other chains, particularly 
those with strong represen- 
tation in the relatively 
parched Midwest, showed 
flat sales or downturns for 
94. Said one buyer, “As long 
as they were small, auto- 


Despite a drop in precipitation, weather protection sales were up at 
some chains last year because of innovative merchandising. 


matic and well under $10, 
our umbrellas sold at a slow 
but fairly steady pace, par- 
ticularly in black. But any- 
thing more innovative, espe- 
cially rain hats and scarves, 
just didn’t move.” 

Vendors tried to offset the 
discouraging weather pic- 
ture with innovations in 
products, merchandising, 
price point and service, often 
with positive results. Cincin- 
nati-based J Jay Products 
reported success with prod- 
ucts at extreme ends of the 
size scale: Both ultra-mini 
folding umbrellas and over- 
sized stick golf umbrellas 


fared well. The company also 
introduced new merchandis- 
ers in ‘94 and created special 
packaging sleeves for the 
holiday season to drive home 
the gift theme. Said Barry 
Brinker, J Jay’s vice presi- 
dent of marketing and prod- 
uct development, “Since 
rainfall increased pretty 
much nationwide at the end 
of the year, it’s difficult to 
separate holiday sales from 
weather-driven ones, but we 
saw a 20-percent increase in 
our end-of-the-year business 
over the same period in 93.”

a company-wide product 
price reduction courtesy of 
the GATT agreement and its 
elimination of long-standing 
trade tariffs. 

Boca Raton-based Raines 
has also devoted much atten- 
tion to providing pertinent re- 
search to retailers. Said com-

“We put a lot of effort last 
year into focusing our ap- 
proach to the demographics 
of each chain, such as includ- 
ing trade-ups in certain 
stores but not others, or offer- 
ing combinations of merchan- 
dise ranging from lower to 
higher ends that are tailored 
specifically to the needs of 
each store.” 


Fashion is affordable 


Portland Oregon-based 
Shedrain, which markets its 
Rainbow line of umbrellas 
and related products at the 
drug store level, continued 
its strategy of providing the 
look and fashion of depart-

drug chain prices. In one no- 
table case last year, a chain 
took the strategy a major 
step further. Said Jeff 
Blauer, the company’s vice- 
president for sales and mar- 
keting, “Thrifty Drug came to 
us and requested our 
Shedrain line, which usually 
sells in department stores 
like Bloomingdale’s and 
Nordstrom’s. They wanted 
our best for a specialty bou- 
tique, and we were happy to 
oblige.”

Growth predicted in small appliance category 


By Wendy Friesen 


gains at the drug store level for 

small appliances, with retailers 
and manufacturers alike optimistic 
at year’s end about prospects for fu- 
ture growth in the category. 

The portable humidifier and va- 
porizer segment, coming off double- 
digit gains in ’93 with the year’s sig- 
nificant cough-and-cold season, had 
to settle for more modest growth in 
94. Industry statistics show that 
wholesale figures were up some 3 to 
4 percent overall in this $100-mil- 
lion category, of which about one- 
quarter of sales were at the drug 
store level. 

“Last year didn’t follow the typi- 
cal cough-cold pattern,” said Marty 
Cohen, vice president for marketing 
at New York City, N.Y.-based Kaz. 
“At the beginning of the calendar 
year, we were still into the big ’93- 
94 flu season, but the 94-95 season 
began very late, well past the usual 
start in September or October.” 

Retailers reported the same phe- 
nomenon. “Nothing beats a good flu 
season,” said a buyer for a major 


: ast year brought single-digit 


Northeastern drug chain. “In Janu- 
ary and February we kept a selec- 
tion of humidifiers and vaporizers 
on an endcap in the cough-and-cold 
section. Customers would come in, 
select their over-the-counter med- 
ication, then choose a humidifier as 
part of the purchase. But we got off 
to a slow start in the fall because 
the next flu season rally didn’t hit 
until much later in the year, near 
Christmas.” 

“While sales overall are up slightly, 
there’s lots of segmentation going on 
within the category and a lot of it is 
driven by price point,” said Janey Tal- 
ley, director of marketing for West 
Palm Beach, Fla.-based Bionaire. 

Of the various technologies avail- 
able at the drug store level, the 
biggest growth continued to be 
recorded in cool-mist or impeller hu- 
midifiers, which mechanically break 
up water into small particles that are 
sprayed up into the air. The price 

oint—which ranges from just over 
$20 for basic models to a high end of 
$60 with a wide range of features— 
was seen as a major factor in sales 
increases of 10 to 12 percent in ’94. 
Second in growth at the drug store 


level were evaporative cool-mist hu- 
midifiers, which work by pulling dry 
air continually through a wicking fil- 


.ter, allowing the air to absorb mois- 


ture. With price points starting at 
$35, this product segment saw retail 
sales gains that approached 10 per- 
cent in some markets. 

Steam-producing vaporizers con- 
tinue to hold their own in the cate- 
gory, accounting for about half of all 
retail sales, while warm-mist units 
showed a small drop in some mar- 
kets. Ultrasonic humidifiers, which 
have a major perceived drawback of 
leaving a white-dust residue, saw 
drops in retail sales. 

In addition to price point, manu- 
facturers and retailers have been 
quick to play up another advan- 
tage of cool-mist humidifiers: As 
opposed to their vapor-producing 


cousins, cool-mist units can be 
used year-round to add moisture 
to the air. 

“You'd never want to run a vapor- 
izer when no one was sick” said a 
Midwestern buyer. “They make the 
air in the room very humid and 
swampy—perfect for a sickroom but 
pretty unappealing any other time. 
That’s why we play them way down 
once the flu season is over. But 
portable humidifiers have the po- 
tential of selling consistently 
throughout much of the year, and 
that’s a strong advantage. We just

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


Batteries gain force in 1994 


ANNUAL REPOR 


General merchandise 


151 


I 


Alkaline still accounts for the lion’s share of sales 


By Allene Symons 


atteries showed year-to-year 
Biv: growth in all trade 

channels, thanks to an ever- 
increasing number of battery-pow- 
ered devices. But drug chains en- 
joyed a small slice of the pie. 

Battery sales in the drug channel 
grew around 5 percent in dollar 
sales last year and around 1.1 per- 
cent in units, according to Informa- 
tion Resources Inc (IRI). 

Dollars outpaced units as con- 
sumers continued to trade up from 
zinc to alkaline batteries, even to 
lithium, resulting in higher rings. 

Alkaline drivers in 1994 were the 
eye-catching TV campaigns of bat- 
tery giants Eveready, with its 
celebrity Energizer Bunny, and Du- 
racell’s “Putterman Family.” 

Natural disasters in California 
and the Midwest also drove extra 
battery sales in 1994. But national- 
ly, the category’s vigorous growth 
showed that American consumers 
can’t get enough of battery-powered 
devices and gadgets. 

At Genovese in New York, buyer 
Arnold Portnoy saw a good battery 
year in 1994 and reported that the 
chain is adding a private-label bat- 
tery line next month. “Our battery 
sales are fantastic because of urban 
locations,” said Portnoy. 

But in many markets, mass mer- 


chants and discount electronics re- 
tailers are gobbling shares of the 
expanding battery business, and 
drug chains are competing with 
neighborhood convenience against 
aggressive battery merchandising. 

The battle is being waged over 
popular battery sizes like AA, C, D 
and 9-volt. Consumers are buying 
more of the smaller batteries—AA, 
and increasingly AAA—for minia- 
turized portable devices. With so 
many devices, like multiple remote 
controls, around the household, it’s 
no surprise that consumers are 
thinking more in terms of multi- 
pack purchases. 

Retailers reported they are sell- 
ing more “saver-packs” of 4’s and 8’s 
(mass merchants sell larger packs). 
Cross-merchandising in depart- 
ments like toys and small appli- 
ances, as well as at checkout, 
matches these smaller multi-packs 
with selling opportunities, said 
manufacturers. 


Drug chain edge 


Two growing battery segments for 
drug chains in 1994 were photo and 
hearing-aid batteries. Watch and 
other specialty batteries rounded out 
this profitable specialty segment. 
Many chains are now merchandising 
these in serviced departments. 

A driver is the drug chain trend 
toward high visibility, serviced pho- 


to departments, where a growing 
photo battery segment is high-pow- 
ered lithium batteries offering quick 
recharges for photo flash. 

Lithium is gradually catching on. 
Said one buyer: “I think the public 
is becoming more aware of the bene- 
fits, once they get over the sticker 
shock” of an $8 battery. 

Drug chains are also selling more 
hearing-aid batteries (zinc air), and 
pharmacy is a strong disp!ay outpost. 
Lithium is displayed more frequently 
there too, for diagnostic equipment 
like blood glucometer testing kits. 

Drug chains reportedly have a 
solid share of this specialty battery 
segment (many are sold through 
hearing-aid dealers or audiologists). 
Hearing-aid batteries remain a 
small but profitable percentage of 
the total category. 


Rechargeables drag 


Rechargeables got mixed reviews 
in drug chains. Round-cell recharge- 
ables showed modest growth for all 
channels in 1994. 

One drawback is that the recharg- 
ing unit, which retails for $15 to $30, 
is on the high end for a drug chain. 
Shoppers are also used to the conve- 
nience of consuming fresh batteries. 

Alkaline still captures the lion’s 
share of battery sales, and as the 
overall battery business continues 
to grow—reaching around $3.5 bil-

move them from cough-and-cold to 
housewares in the spring and sell 
some units that way.” 

Manufacturers have been ven- 
turing into accessories to increase 
sales and bring customers back 
into the store, and the results 
have been encouraging. Most ven- 
dors now offer a line of replace- 
able filter cartridges, and some 
are marketing their own inhalants 
for use in vaporizers. 

“Accessories helped a lot toward 
making 1994 a good year for us,” 
said Cohen “We stressed products 
like our Kaz-brand inhalant, 
which came in second in ’94 sales 
to Vicks Vap-O-Steam, as well as 
our air-cleaning cool-mist humidi- 
fiers, which brought customers 
back to purchase replacement 
filters.” 

Accessories figured into the 
steady 94 sales reported by Fort 
Lauderdale, Fla.-based Sun- 
beam-Oster, as did innovations 
like the clean-start tab for va- 
porizers, which cleans the unit's 
electrodes to enhance its start- 
up time. “We also put a lot of ef- 
fort into retailer support, such 
as with co-op ad programs and 
endcap promotions,” said a com- 
pany spokesman. 

In the hair-care segment, man- 


ufacturers and retailers reported 
modest gains of 5 percent or so 
in their ’94 retail sales. The 
$600-million-retail category last 
year saw some 16 percent to 17 
percent of its sales at the drug- 
store level, with about $55 mil- 
lion in sales of hair dryers, $22 
to $23 million in curling irons 
and another $22 million or so in 
sales of electric hairsetters and 
other appliances. 

The industry was able to ride an 
increasing trend toward more vol- 
ume in hair styles by featuring 
volume-enhancing attachments 
and curling irons with barrels up 
to 1'/: inches in diameter. “When 
models on the covers of Fille and 
Vogue have big curls and volume 
in their hair, it’s great for us,” 
said a small appliances buyer for 
an eastern drug chain. “It means 
we’re going to sell higher-wattage 
dryers with attachments, curling 
irons and hairsetters that can de- 
liver lots of big curls.” 

Retailers reported success in ’94 
with product mixes that included 
compact, no-frills dryers at a 
$9.99 price point, stepped-up 
models with variable speed and 
heat settings at price points rang- 
ing from $11 to $15 or so, all the 
way up to professional, high- 
wattage attachments, at price 


points above $20. 

As to curling irons, “The $4 ba- 
sic unit did a lot of business, as 
did the similarly priced travel 
models,” said a representative for 
a West Coast drug chain. “For a 
few dollars more, you get into the 
salon models and they did steady 
business, too. But customers 
were, and continue to be, quite 
enthusiastic about the bigger- 
barrel models, even though the 
price points start above the $10 
mark. 

“A big advantage in this cate- 
gory,” she continued, “is that 
prices have remained pretty 
much unchanged in the last four 
or five years, at least. That 
means our customers see the 
lower-end price points as being 
quite reasonable and even inex- 
pensive, and don’t consider it to 
be too much of an extravagance 
to trade up a step or two to get 
some extra features.” 

Retailers also reported success 
with electric hair setters that 
ran the gamut from travel mod- 
els with flexible rollers that re- 
tailed at about $10 to profession- 
al steam-set units featuring 
multiple-sized rollers in foam or 
standard hard plastic that re- 
tailed in the $20 to $30 range 
and above.

growth by offering more supplemen-

tunistic clip strips and power wings.

year-round promotions.

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


By Leslie Gilbert Elman 


down year for consumables. The 
brightest spot for the drug channel 
was single-serving, non-carbonated 
beverages. Dollar volume growth in 
drug store sales of single-serving juices 
was 13.8 percent, almost double that 
of the total market (7 percent), and 
more than double the growth in food 
stores (5.4 percent). Similarly, drug 
stores saw a 51 percent dollar volume 
increase in sales of ready-to-drink tea. 
However, the gains come at a cost. 
Drug stores lost 4.7 percent dollar vol- 
ume and 9.1 percent unit volume in car- 
bonated beverage sales, even as the mar- 
ket gained 6.7 percent in dollars and lost 
just 0.1 percent in units. Some of this 
loss is due to juices and iced teas canni- 
balizing soda sales. It is also influenced 
by the fact that food stores and mass 
merchants—both of which saw gains in 
carbonated beverages—sell more large 
bottles of soda than drug stores. 
Despite a lackluster year, drug 
stores have demonstrated their com- 
mitment to the consumables catego- 
ry. At least three major chains— 
American Drug Stores, Eckerd and 
CVS—introduced private-label bev- 
erages in the past year. 
Consumables continue to be highly 
promotable traffic builders. Most drug 
stores, chains and independents have 
worked staples, such as 2-liter sodas, 
snack nuts and microwave popcorn into 
weekly advertising plans. Many have 
embarked on aggressive programs to 
add cooler space, and facings in the can- 
dy and snack aisle continue to increase. 
With this growth has come an in- 
creased interest in category manage- 
ment programs from manufacturers 
such as Pepsi-Cola, Nabisco and Frito- 
Lay. “Scanning helps a lot,” said Gregg 
Heller, consumables buyer for May’s 
Drug. “We generate monthly reports 
that help us to do planograms and de- 
cide which items to discontinue.” 
Manufacturers also report that 
drug stores have increased requests 
for flexible-display merchandisers.

Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


Non-fat candies a sweet spot in chains 


Ox to other consumables 
categories, candy sales were 
relatively flat in 1994. 

“Consumers are getting more in- 
volved in what they’re eating, and 
concerns about fat in products like 
chocolate may be the issue influenc- 
ing sales,” said one southern drug 
store buyer. 

On the other hand, fat conscious- 
ness has opened the door for growth 
in non-chocolate candy. “Jelly beans 
are doing really well because of the 
[zero] fat content,” said another 
southern candy buyer. 

Indeed, many non-chocolate can- 
dies, such as jelly beans, gummies 
and hard candy, have no fat at all. 
This is a fact that Leaf has tried to 
use to its advantage with new pack- 


ages, which highlight fat-free candies. 

“Consumers are looking for per- 
mission to buy candy,” said Randy 
Lund, Leaf’s trade development 
manager. He added that the more 
stringent FDA nutritional labeling 
requirements, which took effect this 
year, will actually help sales of non- 
chocolate candy by pointing out its 
comparative benefits to chocolate. 

The most notable change in the 
candy aisle has been the prolifera- 
tion of peg packaging. This year 
M&M/Mars introduced a line of peg 
packs, joining Hershey’s, Leaf, 
Brach’s and LifeSavers. 

“Pegs are where the action is. 
They’ve been very big for drug 
stores,” said Jay Price, director of 
trade marketing for LifeSavers. “In

added. To capture these impulse 
buyers, drug stores are using cus- 
tomized displays placed strategical- 
ly in the store—including cooler 
door merchandisers. 


Chips, nuts suffer 


The remaining snack categories— 
chips, crackers and snack nuts— 
were flat in the total market and 
down significantly in drug stores. 

All have suffered from consumers’ 
increasing nutritional consciousness. 

Chips and snacks gained 5.6 per- 
cent dollar volume in the total mar- 
ket, but lost 1 percent in drug 
stores. Crackers lost 0.6 percent dol- 
lar volume overall and 13.6 percent 
in drug. Snack nuts lost 4.4 percent 
in. total and 6.6 percent in drug. 

“The drug stores that are per- 
forming the best are the ones that 
have made snacks a destination 
and are devoting at least 4 feet, top 
to bottom, to a good distribution of 
SKUs,” said a spokeswoman for 
Procter & Gamble’s Pringles brand 
snacks. 


Chips & snacks 


rE 14% 26% 


EXE 15% 25% 


WB brug fe Mass ta Food 


Cans and jars of snack nuts con- 
tinue to be used as traffic builders 
by many chains. “The core users of 
these products generally are older 
people, which ties in well with the 
drug store customer base,” said 
Gary Olive, trade marketing man- 
ager for Planter’s. 

With continued emphasis on re- 
duced-fat products, the addition of 
more flavored chips and crackers, 
and advertising targeted to teen 
consumers, manufacturers hope to 
recapture some of the sales momen- 
tum they lost during 1994. 


Tobacco continues its slow burn 


Tics sales continued their 
slow decline last year, as 
adults cut down consumption 
or stopped smoking completely. 
Full-priced brands, however, after 
losing some share to discount and 
generic-brand cigarettes in the past 
two years, regained their position 
and stabilized. 

Most drug stores consider ciga- 
rettes an important component to 
competition with convenience 
stores, the largest retail channel 
for cigarette sales. “Smokers have 

atterns. There is a lot of repeat 
eben to be gained by making it 
convenient for customers to buy 
cigarettes,” said a chain drug 
store spokesman. It’s interesting 


to note, however, that drug stores 
attract slightly older, more female 
buyers. Convenience store ciga- 
rette buyers tend to be younger 
men. 

The most notable trend in drug 
store sales is the virtual elimination 
of self-serve racks and displays. 
Most stores now stock cigarettes be- 
hind the register, where they’re safe 
from pilferage, but also less visible 
to casual consumers. 

“The elimination of self-service 
has led to a decline in sales,” said 
Karen Daragan, a Philip Morris 
spokeswoman. 

Bill Whitlatch, an R.J. Rey- 
nolds spokesman, agreed. “When 
customers don’t see cigarettes 


where they expect to see them, 
they tend to assume you’ve 
stopped carrying them altogeth- 
er,” he said. 

Though the primary reason for 
placing cigarettes behind the 
counter may be to deter theft, the 
underlying thought is to de-empha- 
size the presence of cigarettes in the 
drug store. Similarly, most chains 
and independents use little point-of- 
sale promotional material to sup- 
port cigarettes. 

“There’s also not as much high- 
value couponing,” noted one south- 
ern retailer. “There’s not much 
point to it if the products are no 
longer self-serve.” 

Chains and independents con- 


tinue to agonize over the contra- 
diction of selling cigarettes and 
nicotine patches under the same 
roof. Discount drug stores, on the 
other hand, seem to be enjoying 
strong sales of off-priced ciga- 
rettes. “A typical chain might sell 
93 cartons in a week,” said Whit- 
latch, “but a typical discount 
drug store sells 260 cartons a 
week.” 

He speculates that many dis- 
count drug customers buy more 
than one carton per store visit. 
“Your normal drug store cus- 
tomer is typically a fill-in pur- 
chaser, but the discount drug 


store shopper may be stocking 
up,” he added. 


Drug Store News, May 1, 1995 


Iced drinks beverages’ cup of tea 


ith a constant stream of new 
Wi ereicee: and heavy adver-

manufacturers managed to keep the 
category at the top of consumers’ 
minds. Juices and iced teas saw 
double-digit growth, according to 
Information Resources Inc. (IRI), 
and although the reports show a 
slight downward trend in carbonat- 
ed beverages and bottled waters, 
both chains and manufacturers 
claim there has not been a decline. 
“We’ve seen explosive growth in 
the past year, and we see the cate- 
gory growing faster in the next 18 
months,” said Kerry Brooks, direc- 
tor of marketing for Coca-Cola 
Foods, marketers of Hi-C and 
Minute Maid beverages. “Drug

stores are actually slightly behind 
the curve, but with chains like CVS 
going heavily into cold vaults, 
growth will definitely continue.” 

Said a spokesman for a southern 
chain, “We have gone into more pro- 
motion efforts for juice and soda, we 
promote them every week in our 
ads, and we’re adding more coolers 
in our stores. The result has been 
very strong sales.” 

Sales of ready-to-drink teas, while 
not showing the explosive triple-digit 
growth of the past two years, contin- 
ued to be strong, showing a 51 per- 
cent dollar sales increase in 1994. To- 
tal category sales across all classes of 
trade were $409 million, and drug 
stores accounted for $48 million, or 
11.8 percent of the total—about dou- 
ble that of mass merchandisers, but 
far less than grocery stores. 

Although percentage growth con- 
tinues to be strong, the ready-to- 
drink tea category remains relative- 
ly small in comparison to 


shelf-stable juices and sodas. 

New flavors of iced teas have 
flooded the market as manufactur- 
ers jockey for position in the cooler 


Consumables 


case. Among the newest are Snap- 
ple’s Passion Fruit Iced Tea and a 
reintroduction of decaffeinated iced 
tea. Coca-Cola’s Fruitopia brand 
has added four new fruit-flavored 
iced teas. The Pepsi Lipton Tea 
partnership just introduced 
Caribbean Cooler. 

While retailers have added cooler 
space to accommodate single-serve 
non-carbonated drinks, a shakeout 
is likely to occur soon. “Retailers are 
looking at new products with a fine- 
tooth comb,” said David Bilisic, 
manager of customer development 
for Tropicana Products. “It’s a ques- 
tion of adding variety vs. duplica- 
tion. With the continuing move to- 
ward category management, they’re 
telling manufacturers, ‘I already 
have a product like this and I don’t 
need another one.” 

- Category management has be- 
come especially important in shelf- 
stable juices where new products 
come fast and furious. The next 
wave is decidedly tropical. Ocean 
Spray debuted Caribbean Colada, 
Mango Mango, Mandarin Magic and 
Kiwi Strawberry. Fruitopia intro- 
duced Tangerine Wavelength, and 
Snapple added Mango Melon Berry, 
Cantaloupe Cocktail and Bali Blast. 

Taking a value-oriented approach, 
Tropicana has repackaged its blend- 
ed bottled juices in 20-ounce sizes for 
the same price as its 16-ounce size. 

Further segmenting the shelf-sta- 
ble juice category are new reduced- 
calorie products, such as Snapple’s 
Diet Pink Lemonade, Mango and 
Kiwi Strawberry, and Fruitopia’s 
Apple Raspberry Embrace and 
Tropical Consideration light juices. 

Drug stores continue to enjoy 
healthy increases in shelf stable 
juices, with dollar volume gains of 
13.8 percent and unit sales gains of 
15.2 percent during 1994, according 
to IRI. Chain sales, according to 
manufacturer and chain estimates, 
are significantly higher. 

“Our growth is actually closer to 35 
percent,” said Xavier Bagala, nation- 
al chain sales manager for Snapple 
Beverages, now part of Quaker Oats. 
“The main reason is that we’ve final- 
ly secured national distribution.” 

Ocean Spray, now in the third 
year of its distribution alliance with 
Pepsi-Cola, reported similar results, 
and the southern drug chain also 
noted gains of about 35 percent in 
shelf-stable juices. 

The gain can also be attributed to 
growing acceptance of juice as an 
all-day beverage. As such, juices 
have clearly cut into carbonated 
beverage sales. IRI reported a 4.7 
percent decline in soda sales. How- 
ever, chains and manufacturers, 
while agreeing that sales are flat, 
did not show a loss. 

Said Skip Colcord, an Ocean 
Spray spokesman, “We used to com- 
pete against other shelf-stable bev- 
erages, but now our competition is 
cola, orange soda, water, tea...any- 
thing that quenches your thirst. 
We’re all competing for the same 
share of stomach.”

Consumers show great interest

the minimum age group, and they 
are buying premium beer.”

Co. spokesman, agreed. “Trends 
are similar in drug stores and con- 
venience stores,” he said. “Con- 
sumers are trading up to premium 
brands.” In 1994, Miller introduced 
Red Dog premium lager, with 
“more bite” than traditional beers.

introduced about two years ago, 
now accounts for 6 percent to 8 
percent of the beer market. Miller

The flood of specialty brews

of better-quality wines. “We're do-

products, and there has been a 
shift from 750-milliliter to 1.5-liter 
bottles,” he said. In response to 
the trend, Banfi now offers a 1.5- 
liter bottle of Placido Pinot Grigio. 

He has also seen drug store 
liquor departments moving to- 
ward a cleaner look, using fewer 
point-of-sale materials and 
striving for a consistent appear- 
ance chain-wide. “What they do 
use is customized to their 
stores,” he added.

Cosmetics and fragrances 


Lipsticks show rosy growth with new launches 


By Liz Parks 


ipsticks were a hot category in 
1994, up 11 percent in dollar 


sales in mass market stores and 
4 percent in unit sales, according to 
Information Resources Inc. 

Most chain drug cosmetics buyers 
say Revlon drove the category in 
1994, with its “sensational” launch of 
Colorstay. L’Oréal also gets some 
credit for coming out with some great 
seasonal color collections and strong 
advertising support for its Colour 
Supreme and Colour Riche lines. 

“Colorstay was phenomenal,” said 
the buyer for one large Northeast-

based chain. “It seemed to be all in-

think women didn’t stop buying

Both the L’Oréal Colour Supreme

sell-throughs on all their pre-packs.” 

Maybelline and Cover Girl held 
their own in 1994, but neither gen- 
erated strong growth surges in 
chain drug stores. One buyer said 
her sales with both the Cover Girl 
and Maybelline lipsticks were just 
okay. “I do much better with their 
face makeups and with the May- 
belline mascaras,” she said. 

Max Factor lipsticks, however, did 
surprisingly well in 1994. IRI report- 
ed that Factor, which has a 5.4 per- 
cent share of lipstick sales through 
the mass channel (drug, food and 
mass merchants combined), was up 
24.5 percent for the year.

units continues. One goal,

Many changes 


But Revco’s accomplish- 
ments over the past year 
haven’t been limited to the 
HSI conversion. The chain 
also bought 10-store Mast

new drug stores exclusive of

prototype store.

was first unveiled in No-

assortment of convenience 
foods, larger core depart-

square feet. The intent, said

president of operations, is 
“to backfill in all our mar-

possible,” but the wide range 
in store sizes also gives the 
chain added expansion flexi- 
bility.

tinue at an aggressive and 
determined pace, both 
through internal growth and 
via acquisitions, say Revco’s 
managers. The intent: to po- 
sition the company as a drug 
store force to be reckoned 
with in the era of managed 
care—both in the number of 
pharmacy outlets it offers 
and in its own managed care 
marketing efforts.

American Stores 
bids to buy PDN 


ALEXANDRIA, Va.— 
American Stores’ has 
reached a tentative agree- 
ment to acquire the Phar- 
macy Direct Network 
(PDN), the PBM formed last 
year by drug store industry 
leaders. 

The proposed acquisition 
must be approved by PDN 
chain and independent 
members. Details of the pro- 
posal will be mailed out by 
the end of this month. 

American Stores hopes “to 
help PDN achieve its origi- 
nal vision of success,” said

Never underestimate the power of change 


ost everyone knows the story of Charles Dickens’ 
Christmas Carol, where Ebenezer Scrooge is taken 
on a nightmare jour- 
ney with the gkosts of 


of marketing Kevin Mann explained, Rite Aid is purpose- 
ly “softening the shopping experience” to appeal more to 


women. 
Much of what Rite Aid is 


Christmas Past, Christmas 
Present and Christmas-Yet- 
To-Come. As the reader/lis- 
tener/viewer who journeys 
with Scrooge, you’re not too 
surprised when the old coot 
runs out on Christmas 
morning to shower people 
with gifts and ready to help 
save the life of the sickly 
Tiny Tim. 

But what if you were 
Scrooge’s faithful lackey, 
Bob Cratchit? I’m sure you’d 
be caught off guard, to say 
the least, by the overnight transformation of your miserly 
boss after decades of contrary experience. 

Well, most outsiders don’t know what was going on in the 
minds of the people from Rite Aid for the past few years, 
but, like Dickens’ Cratchit, we do know now that things are 
really changing. 

I hope Rite Aid can forgive my analogy to the notorious 
Mr. Scrooge, but my point is that even the most predictable 
people and organizations can transform themselves sud- 
denly and dramatically. 

It’s a mistake to assume that your competitor isn’t going 
to change—and I believe there are some people in the in- 
dustry who have underestimated Rite Aid. 

After years of following its successful and consistent for- 
mula, Rite Aid was looking very predictable. The company 
knew how to make money by operating a huge number of 
small-volume, pharmacy-oriented units and applying strin- 
gent cost controls. The tradeoff was that not much effort 
went into fancy merchandising, television advertising or a 
tremendous in-stock position. 

The “magic” of Rite Aid was invisible: extremely efficient 
operations, an ongoing dedication to technology, a very lean 
organization and a focus on the pharmacy. 

Few people were expecting much in the way of change 
when Martin Grass, son of Rite Aid founder Alex Grass, 
succeeded his father as chairman and chief executive. 
But now we're finding out that Martin has been quietly 
planting the seeds for a genuinely new Rite Aid for a cou- 
ple of years. 

You can see some of the changes in the new stores. 
They’re bright, clean, spacious and well-stocked, featur- 
ing a full-fledged cosmetics department, beverage coolers, 
and Rite Express and one-hour photo desks. The new pro- 
totype is much more attractive because, as vice president 


It’s a mistake to assume 
that your competitor isn’t 
going to change—and I be- 
lieve there are some people 
in the industry who have 
underestimated Rite Aid. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


doing in the stores is what 
I would call “mainstream,” 
not too different from the 
new and renovated units of 
Eckerd or CVS or Revco. 
Rite Aid is remerchandis- 
ing and upgrading the cos- 
metics section, expanding 
the food section to capture 
customers from conve- 
nience stores, adding drive- 
up pharmacy windows and 
building larger freestand- 
ing stores. We’re not used 
to seeing Rite Aid among 
the leaders in so many key trends. 

Even Michel Coutu, scion of the Canadian chain 
drug family Coutu, remarked that he was very im- 
pressed by the new Rite Aid stores he saw while look- 
ing for ideas for Coutu’s recently acquired Brooks 
chain. 

What’s most interesting is that, like before, the most sig- 
nificant changes at Rite Aid aren’t apparent in the stores 
per se. Beyond changing the size and format of the stores— 
and aggressively rolling out the prototype at a pace of more 
than 300 stores a year—Rite Aid is transforming itself in- 
ternally as well. 

A revamped field structure, which undoes a decades- 
old separation of the pharmacy and front-end command 
chains, went on line last month. Category management 
will transform the buying organization in a similar way 
in the near future. Advertising agencies are currently 
making their bids to lead a major media campaign (an- 
other Rite Aid first). The real estate department is busy 
lining up locations for new stores and relocations, and 
attention is also being given to sizing up acquisition 
opportunities. 

Given the fact that Rite Aid is the No. 1 chain in store 
count and No. 2 in dollar volume, we think these develop- 
ments deserve significant coverage in Drug Store News. 
That’s why we’re planning a two-part series on Rite Aid; 
part one starts on the cover of this issue and you can look 
for the next installment on June 26. 

On a personal note, Martin Grass has one more thing 
to be happy about beyond his new role at Rite Aid and 
the positive reception the industry seems to be giving his 
new approach. He’s also the proud father of a third child, 
his first son. Noah Stanleigh Grass made his debut on 
April 25. 


Pharmaceutical sales driving chains 


GUEST COLUMN 


he chain drug industry continues to derive 
an increasing percentage of its sales from 
health-related products, particularly phar- 
maceuticals. This magazine’s most recent annual 
report indicated that health-related products ac- 
count for about 49 percent of sales for the chains 
as a group. This number is much higher for the 
large chains. 
Yet even more important, when viewed from a 
health care perspective, the solid position of the 
industry becomes more apparent. The combina- 


tion of lower pharmaceutical price inflation and ATR Hultgren 


pressures associated with managed care appears 
to be a net benefit for the chains. 

The outlook for the chain drug industry is as 
ood as it has been for decades. The industry 
aces an incredible opportunity as a result of the 
inability of small chains and independent opera- 
tors to be efficient competitors. This may sound 
like an old theme. In fact, however, it is a fairly 
recent development brought about by two factors 
that cause casual observers concern. 

The first is pharmaceutical price inflation. 
While at a high rate, inflation allowed many inef- 
ficient operators to stay in business. The inflation 
rate has declined in recent years, and instead of 


Revco. 


Donald W. Hult- 
gren, CFA., is direc- 
tor of health care re- 
search at Raymond 
James & Associ- 
ates which issues 
investment opinions 
on Walgreen, Rite 
Aid, Eckerd and 


being the death knell for the large chains, it has 
triggered a consolidation that is working in their 
favor. 

The second is the increasing role of third party 
payors. The consolidation is further stimulated by 
the economic demands of the third party payors 
such as insurance companies and health mainte- 
nance organizations that represent about 60 per- 
cent of pharmacy sales for the large chains. As the 
health care system strives to control costs, the in- 
herent efficiencies of the large drug chains will po- 
sition them as the providers of choice. 

The large drug chains appear to be the best po- 
sitioned of all the retail formats to capitalize on 
consolidation and on changes brought about by 
the increasing role of third-party payors. This flies 
in the face of the conventional wisdom among in- 
vestors in the retail sector, many of whom mistak- 
enly believe the mass merchandisers or other for- 
mats are capable of driving the large «hains from 
the business. 

Chains are achieving efficiency as a result of 
their focus on the retail distribution of pharmaceu- 
ticals. This fact, coupled with their superior conve- 
nience, will make chain drug stores the choice of 
payers and customers alike.

ONSUMABLES 


Penalties stiffen, stings increase 
to prevent tobacco sales to minors 


By Leslie Gilbert Elman 
ast December, a 15-year-old boy 


in Philadelphia walked into a 

store to buy a pack of cigarettes. 
He didn’t lie about his age when the 
clerk asked. He didn’t say he was 
buying the cigarettes for a parent or 
adult. And even though in Pennsylva- 
nia it’s a criminal offense to sell ciga- 
rettes to anyone under age 18, the 
clerk rang up the sale. 

What the clerk didn’t know was 
that the boy was part of a Tobacco- 
Free Education & Action Coalition 
for Health Youth Council “sting” in- 
tended to root out retailers who vio- 
late the law by selling tobacco to 
minors. 

Such programs are run nationwide, 
by local municipalities and watchdog 
groups. Most retailers are familiar 
with them. But what some might not 
know is that the stings have become 
more frequent, and penalties more se- 
vere, with the enactment of the Synar 
Amendment limiting youth access to 
tobacco. 

The Synar Amendment, which took 
effect in all 50 states and the District 
of Columbia in October 1994, makes 
it illegal to sell or distribute tobacco 
products to anyone under age 18 (19 
in some states). Violators may be sub- 
ject to criminal or civil penalties, as 
the state determines. States also de- 
cide which parties are liakle for viola- 
tions—the store owner, the employee 
or both. 

The Amendment also directs states 
to conduct “random, unannounced in- 
spections” of tobacco retailers, 
adding: “The sample must reflect 
that, because of location (i.e. near 
schools), or other factors, some out- 
lets are more likely to be used by mi- 
nors. States are to ensure...inspec- 
tions occur at times when minors are 
likely to purchase tobacco.” 

The results of these inspections will 
be submitted yearly to the federal De- 


Beer maker wins labeling war 


partment of Health & Human Ser- 
vices (DHHS). By October 1995, the 
first submission date, every state 
must demonstrate 50 percent compli- 
ance with the law. 

The Philadelphia sting shows 
there’s much work to be done. It hit 
102 Philadelphia stores and 63 in 
Delaware County, Pa., including 19 
drug stores. Eighty-five percent of 
stores in Philadelphi :, and 58 percent 
in Delaware County violated the law. 
Of the drug stores, only two of nine 
complied in Philadelphia and six of 
10 in Delaware County. 

In a similar sting in Massachu- 
setts, one store that broke the law 
was a pharmacy owned by a member 
of the local board of health—the 
group that conducted the sting. “It’s 
ironic, but pharmacies sell cigarettes 
to minors at the same or higher rates 
as other stores,” said Laura Mullen of 
Massachusetts Stop Teenage Addic- 
tion to Tobacco (STAT). 

Results of the stings are generally 
passed to the state agency responsi- 
ble for tobacco sales. They also may 
be published in local newspapers to 
call attention to stores that violate 
the laws. “The first time they violate, 
it's a warning,” said Mullen. “The sec- 
ond time, they’re fined.” 


Soothing the sting 


Drug stores are already acutely 
aware of the apparent conflict in sell- 
ing tobacco while promoting healthy 
behavior. Most have cut back drasti- 
cally on tobacco promotion and point 
of sale. Partly to deter theft and part- 
ly to make them less accessible to un- 
derage customers, many now stock 
cigarettes behind the checkout 
counter. 

Stores have also begun addressing to- 
bacco sales in employee training. At 
Medic Discount Drug, Cleveland, access 
regulations are covered in detail. “In 
Ohio, the store and the employee who 
sells cigarettes to an underage customer 


can be held liable,” noted Tom 
McWilliams, director of store operations. 

Medic clearly posts signs informing 
shoppers that cashiers will ask for 
identification before ringing up tobac- 
co or alcohol. As the Synar Amend- 
ment takes hold, it’s likely that more 
states will require such signage. “It’s 
a caution, and hopefully a deterrent, 
to underage customers,” said 
McWilliams. 

Taylor Drug Stores, Louisville, Ky., 
reviews tobacco laws in initial train- 
ing and reinforces them in periodic 
employee bulletins. But even more ef- 
fective are the chain’s own secret 
shoppers, who make frequent visits to 
the stores to assess customer service, 
loss prevention and compliance with 
local laws. 

Chains that use cash register scan- 
ners to remind employees to check ID 
for alcohol purchases are now doing 
the same for tobacco. “When a tobacco 
product is scanned, the register tells 
you exactly the day and year that a 
person has to be born by to be 18,” ex- 
plained Brian Borzone, associate train- 
ing and development supervisor for 
Thrifty PayLess. 

Medic has a similar program. “It’s ef- 
fective because you don’t have to rely 
on the employee to calculate the cus- 
tomer’s age,” McWilliams noted. 

Tobacco manufacturers offer help, 
too. Both R.J. Reynolds and Philip 
Morris will provide employee training 
kits (including videos), and in-store 
signage and training materials. 

If merchants are effectively pre- 
venting the sale of tobacco to m!- 
nors, they might never be aware 
that a sting operation has hit their 
stores. Said McWilliams, “We’re 
aware that the department of liquor 
control can and does do stings at 
any time, but the only way I know if 
they’ve done it is to see it in the pa- 
per or on TV. If you’re doing every- 
thing right, you don’t even know 
they’ve been there.”

Happy holidays 


Holiday candy sales took a great leap forward in 1994 


GOLDEN, Colo. — Coors Brewing Co. 
emerged victorious after the U.S. Supreme Court 
voted unanimously to strike down a ban on 
brewers listing alcoho! content of beer products. 
While makers of wine and distilled spirits are re- 
quired by federal law to list alcohol content by 
volume, a 1935 federal law prohibited beer man- 
ufacturers from stating alcohol content. 

The U.S. Justice Department, which had ap- 
pealed the decision all the way to the Supreme 
Court, contended that displaying alcohol con- 
tent on beer packaging would lead to “strength 
wars” among brewers. The Court called this 
thinking unique and puzzling. 

“We view this as a very consumer-friendly issue 
and were surprised that it was contested this far,” 
said Coors spokesman Willis Lyford. He added 
that Coors’ consumer telephone hotline receives 
some 100,000 calls per year. About half are asking 
about alcohol content. “People are aware of and in- 
terested in what they eat and drink,” Lyford noted. 

At present, most regular beer contains between 
4.5 percent and 5 percent alcohol by volume; light 


beer contains slightly less. The new “ice” beers may 
contain as much as 5.5 percent. Malt liquors gener- 
ally contain over 7 percent alcohol by volume. 

Michael Brophy, a Miller Brewing Co. 
spokesman, said his company was pleased with 
the ruling, “We think it makes good common 
sense as well as good legal sense. This is infor- 
mation that consumers deserve to know.” At 
present, Miller states alcohol content on its 
Molson Ice, Icehouse and Lite Ice products. 

In September 1993, after the Coors decision 
had been upheld by the U.S. Circuit Court, the 
federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco & Firearms 
initiated interim rules allowing labeling. Now 
that the decision is final, firmer guidelines are 
expected. They do not make labeling mandato- 
ry; they simply make it allowable in all states. 

Coors hopes to enlist other brewers and the 
brewing industry to develop a labeling prototype. 
Said Lyford, “Right now, alcohol content may be ex- 
pressed by weight or by volume depending on the 
state regulations. The next step is to work with the 
states to develop a uniform standard for labeling.”

COSMETICS 


& Fragrances 


Scaling the ‘wall to new 


One of the biggest 
challenges for chain 
drug store operators is 
to get customers al- 
ready in the store to 
shop the cosmetic wall. 

Buyers tell Drug 
Store News that as 
much as they appreci- 
ate the business that 
promotional pre-packs 
can generate, their cos- 
metic departments 
would become much more profitable if their 
regular shoppers would just spend more 
time browsing the wall. 

Well, Maybelline is trying to help retailers 
solve that problem with a new wall system 
now being rolled out and with a new promotion 
called “Urge To Splurge,” specifically designed 
to support the wall and to attract customers. 

Christine Riese, senior marketing manag- 
er of Maybelline mascaras, and Carolvn 
Wise, marketing manager of Maybelline eye- 
liners, said this is the first time Maybelline 
has created a promotion that supports the 
whole wall. “We’ve always done promotions 
to support secondary locations, our pre-pack 
collections,” said Wise. “But we wanted to do 
something to introduce our new wall system, 
and our retailer customers kept asking us to 
do more to support the wall as a way to in- 
crease turns and improve inventories, so we 
created ‘Urge to Splurge.’ ” 

The “Urge to Splurge” campaign broke 
just before Easter, and it will remain in ef- 


LIZ PARKS 


heights in cosmetics sales 


fect at least through the Fourth of July. 
There will be ads in major consumer maga- 
zines to support the promotion as well as 
shelf-talkers and in-store brochures. 

Consumers benefit because if they buy 
two Maybelline products, they can get a $3 
refund. If they buy three Maybelline prod- 
ucts, they qualify for a $5 refund. Retailers 
benefit because consumers have to come to 
the store and go to the Maybelline wall to 
get their redeemable coupons. 

Retailers benefit because the promotion is 
designed to increase turns and move invento- 
ry through the store faster. One Maybelline 
source said the company is hoping the promo- 
tion will turn Maybelline products at least 
four times on an annual basis. 

Maybelline will also help drive more traffic 
into the store by distributing instant re- 
deemable coupons (IRC) in major beauty care 
magazines. The IRC coupons are good for $1 
off any Maybelline face, eye, lip or nail product. 

To help make its cosmetic wall easier to 
shop, Maybelline is also rolling out a new 
wall unit, designed to make selection sim- 
pler. For the first time, Maybelline will mer- 
chandise its face makeups and lipsticks in 
modular units rather than on blister cards. 

All Maybelline color cosmetics have 
been organized by shade selections. 

In the new unit, Maybelline’s bread-and- 
butter products, its top-selling mascaras 
and eyeliners, are in the center of the pre- 
sentation, flanked on the left by the face 
makeups and on the right by the color cos- 
metics, lip, nail and eye shadows. 


Cosmetics leader puts a 90s 


twist on a ’70s fragrance 


Drug Store News, May 22, 1995 


evion, which had two of 
the best launches in 
cosmetics last year, 
Age Defying and Color Stay, 
is about to initiate another 
major fragrance revita!iza- 
tion, this time with its 22- 
year-old Ciara fragrance. 
Revlon execs are launching 
the company’s first line ex- 
tension to Ciara, called Ciara 
Femme Fatale, and targeting 
it toward young and sophisti- 
cated women who still pur- 
chase most of their fra- 
grances in department stores. 
They are hoping that 
Femme Fatale will turn out, 
like Age Defying and Color 
Stay, to be another “bridge 
brand” capable of luring de- 
partment store shoppers into 
the mass environment for 
their beauty care purchases. 
Revlon also hopes that 
the presence of Femme Fa- 
tale on the market will re- 
vive interest in the original 
Ciara just as the launch last 
year of Charlie Red rejuve- 
nated Revlon’s original 
Charlie fragrance. 


In researching the Ciara 
brand, Revlon found that 
women still perceive it as a 
very “female” fragrance. 
Revlon also discovered 
that in stores where Ciara 
and the Sunflowers depart- 
ment store brand are both 
available, Ciara outsells 
Sunflowers. 

The performance is rather 
unusual when you consider 
that Revion hasn’t put any 
major advertising support. be- 
hind Ciara since at least 1990.

the same kind of support it 
gave last year’s launch of

are being given away, and

in all the major magazines 
and will run continuously 
throughout the year.

brand” marketing tradition 
established with Color Stay 


and Age Defying.

[highest] spending adver- 
tised fragrance brands in 
1995” and that will probably

the Ciara combined brands.

thing unusual during the 
launch of Femme Fatale: It is 
co-launching a single shade 
of nail color, Vixen, and tying 
it in with Femme Fatale in 
its ads and promotions. 

This is the first time that 
Revlon has launched a single 
shade, but it has done single- 
shade pre-packs of some of 
the most popular sellers. 

Vixen, in its advertising, 
is being positioned as the 
perfect shade for the woman 
who would be attracted to 
Femme Fatale, the woman 
that Revlon’s ad copy de- 
scribes as “alive, seductive, 
confident and much more 
dangerous than the male of 
the species.” 


LEARWATER, Fla. 

— Eckerd Drug

more for environmentally-friendly products; 
61 percent have changed their lifestyles for environmental 


871 percent say there are no fur coats in their future; 

53 percent say a company’s environmental reputation is 
important in whether or not they buy their products; 

65 percent say, when asked, that fragrance manufacturers 
should use more natural oils and botanical extracts in 


Source: MEMCO, The Timberline ONLINE poll

personal grooming products, but marketers are still busy trying to 


figure out what this generation, commonly referred to as Genera- 


tion X, really wants out of life. MEMCO, which makes Timberline, 
Love’s, Heaven Scent and other fragrances, has gone on-line with 
Xers to find out more about them. Its latest cyberspace poll reveals 
that 80 percent of Xers are optimistic about the future. Eight out of 
10 said they believe that their lives will improve in 1995 and their 


incomes will rise.

Viewpoints 


Managed care can ‘choke’ golden goose 


can’t help wondering why the great minds of the chain 

drug industry are putting so much effort into managed 

care, a concept that by its very nature is all about lower- 
ing costs and diminishing profits, without making an equal 
or stronger effort to shore up the drug store’s biggest asset— 
the dollar value of the pharmacist’s professional services. 

Every time I look towara the horizon of a world con- 
trolled by managed care, I picture a ship setting sail across 
the ocean with a small but steady leak. You know from the 
start that you’re going to have to do a lot of bailing to get 
where you want to go. 

Drug chains must develop effective ways to cope with man- 
aged care, but they must also recognize the threat managed 
care poses. By aggressively seeking t to lower the profit margin 
made by the drug store, caanagen care is an outright attack 
on the “value” of the pharmacist (who was traditionally paid 
via that profit margin). 

Re-establishing the value 


hard for the opportunity to provide “the most” for “the least.” 

The independent pharmacists have been left pretty much 
on their own to try to demand that the pharmacist’s ser- 
vices are given the dollar value they rightly deserve. It 
seems that drug chain executives think that being bigger 
and more technologically sophisticated will enable them to 
compete with the “big boys’—mass merchants, supermar- 
kets, mail-order pharmacies, HMOs, and so forth. 

What’s missing in that str ategy is recognition of the fact that 
drug stores of all types still need to preserve their unique iden- 
tity. And, more than any other distribution channel, the drug 
store’s identity is dependent upon the pharmacist. 

I’ve heard lots of “excuses,” mainly ¢ along the line of “No 


one will pay for the professional knowledge and expertise of 


a pharmacist.” Frankly, I don’t believe it. 

I say no one will pay for the professional services of the 
pharmacist until a unified drug store industry—all of com- 
munity pharmacy in al- 


of the pharmacist’ s profes- 
sional expertise is a rock- 
solid beach head from which 
the industry could launch a 
counter-attack. However, I 
just don’t see the drug store 
industry (drug chains and 
independents together) ) ad- 
dressing this critical issue. 
The pharmacist is the 
drug store’s unique competi- 
tive advantage. In study af- 
ter study, consumers associ- 
ate pharmacists—who they 
view as the most accessible 
and trusted health care professional—more closely with 
drug stores than with supermarkets and mass merchants, 
or mail-order companies or HMOs, for that matter. 
Managed care is rapidly “leveling the playing field,” forcing 
pricing and margins about as low as they can go, and generic 
and therapeutic substitution rates about as high as they can 
go. Meanwhile, technology is leveling the field in its own way, 
making it harder and harder for drug chains to differentiate 
themselves through the other services they provide managed 
care customers _ The result is that everyone is fighting very 


More than any other 
distribution channel, the drug 
store’s identity is dependent 
upon the pharmacist. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


liance with the professional 
and educational sectors—re- 
establish that value. 

Insurance plans may not 
pay for this service initially, 
but I just see this as an oppor- 
tunity for the industry to de- 
velop a new cash-paying cus- 
tomer. After all, look how 
much out-of-pocket money 
consumers are “saving” on the 
cost of the drugs themselves. 
Once consumers recognize the 
value of a consultation session 
with a pharmacist (along the 
lines of a consultation with an attorney or an optometrist), they 
will demand that their health-care plans cover that service. 

Getting consumers to pay a fee for pharmaceutical ser- 
vices (again) won't be an easy process, but it certainly won't 
begin until the drug store industry sees itself as a single in- 
dustry that is (in the customer’s mind) defined by its link 
with the professional pharmacist. 

This link is the industry’s “golden goose.” Don’t let this 
golden goose starve while you're w restling with the new chal- 
lenges of managed care. 


Chains find ‘brand’ new key to success 


he latest numbers from Information Resources Inc. 

show that drug chains have re-asserted themselves as 

leaders of store brand marketing in the United States. 
Private label sales were up more than 11 percent to a new 
high of $2.2 billion, while market share in units increased a 
full percentage point to 9.6 percent. By contrast, brands 
were down in dollar volume, unit volume, dollar 
share and unit share. 

Behind these statistics is an important lesson for 
retailers of all types. Consumers will support retail- 
ers with their purchases and with store loyalty if 
they are given store brand products of quality, vari- 
ety and value. This was certainly the case from 1986 
to 1993 in the supermarket industry, as private la- 
bel jumped from less than 14 percent unit market 
share to nearly 20 percent. One major food chain af- 
ter the other replaced tired packaging and unimagi- 
native assortment with a competitive image and 
more innovative products, including the introduc- 
tion of premium private label pastas, sauces, cookies 
and so on. For mass merchandisers, it has been 
more tip-toeing than marching perhaps, but they, 
too, have signaled consumers that the retailer's 
brand will be more than a no-frills generic, and will 
meet or exceed national brands in many cases. 

Drug chains realized years ago the importance of 
private label, and they were among the earliest, 
most aggressive developers of their owns brands in 
core OTC categories. But price—or, more precisely, 
maintaining a hase price gap between private label and na- 
tional brands—seemed to be an all-consuming strategy. 
While the advantages of such a price spread are not insignifi- 
cant in attracting consumers, many drug chains now seem to 
recognize that price alone is not sufficient to expand sales. In 
some cases, low price connotes poor quality, and may do more 
harm than good to store image and customer loyalty. 


GUEST COLUMN 


BRIAN SHAROFF 


y 


Brian Sharoff is 
President of the Pri- 
vate Label Manu- 
facturers Associa- 
tion (PLMA). 


Recent experience makes it clear that variety and greater 
assortment have taken over as the engines of private label 
erowth. It is gratifying to see the change. U.S. drug chains 
are a unique channel. ‘Indeed, few countries offer consumers 
a place to buy prescription medicine, over-the-counter drugs, 
health and beauty items, sundries, household necessities and 
even snacks or greeting cards under one roof. The 
drug store plays a role that is quite different from 
and more definable than supermarkets, where im- 
ages of produce and canned goods come readily to 
mind, or a mass merchandiser, where clothing, elec- 
tronic appliances and even beach chairs may domi- 
nate. The core business of drug chains is personal 
and family health. 

Projecting that image to the consumer requires 
a strong statement by the retailer, and that’s 
where store brand assortment, attractively pack- 
aged and closely identified with the retailer by sig- 
nage and experience, is crucial. The more products 
that carry the retailer's name and logo, the more 
locations in the store or in the parking lot that 
promote that name and logo, the better the projec- 
tion will be of what that retailer stands for and 
what consumers can expect. 

The implications for drug chains as they battle 
with other retail formats are enormous. Store 
brands are a readily available weapon, where suc- 
cess depends on the courage to innovate and mar- 
ket them aggressively. It separates one drug chain 
from another, and a chain drug store from a supermarket 
or mass merchandiser. Moreover, store brands play on the 
channel's strength—the diversity of the core products cur- 
rently on the shelves as brands—and unifies them under 
the retailer’s own image and label. It is no wonder that 
drug chains have re-asserted themselves in the world of 
private label. It is a key to their survival and success.

Among the most aggressive: 

e American Stores has set a goal 
to grow its private label share of to- 
tal sales to 25 percent in the next 
five years, from a current level of 16 
to 18 percent. To that end, the com- 
pany recently debuted a new, up- 
scale store brand for its Osco and 
Sav-on drug stores, called American 
Premier, as a premium-quality ad- 
dition to its Osco line of equivalent- 
quality products. The brand first 
appeared on a line of cookies and 
soft drinks, and will soon expand to 
other beverage categories like 
ready-to-drink iced teas, fruit juices 
and even a premium line of wine 
and liquor. 

Also planned: use of the American 
Premier brand on upscale skin care, 
hair care and bath products. 

® Genovese Drug Stores is pushing 
hard to grow its store-brand segment 
with additional product and deter- 
mined marketing efforts. “We’re pro- 
moting our own brand much, much 
more heavily than we used to” with 
floor stands, POP signage and circu- 
lar advertising, said Irwin Livon, 
vice president and director of mer- 
chandising for Genovese.

“will probably have more than 750 
[store brand] items by year-end,” 
Livon told Drug Store News. In the 
last fiscal year, sales of Genovese 
brand products jumped 39 percent.

image-builder, he added.

Besides increased

what’s driving much of

how to price store 
brands to provide both

“With many items, a 10

[below a national brand]

Drug chains have 
also realized that low

in a store brand; the

a distinct appeal to the

quality and value. Said

a cheap, no-label prod-

quality alternative.”

readily acknowledge that pricing 
their store brand alternatives is a 
delicate balancing act. Said CDMA’s 
Logsdon, “What we try to get across 
to our members...is that they don’t 
have to give the product away, but 
that they should shop their competi- 
tion constantly. If they price their 
private label brand too low, the per- 
ceived value won't be there.”

National brands respond 


National brand manufac- 
turers—caught off guard a 
few years ago by the contin- 
uing and rapid growth of 
store brands even as the 
economy regained momen- 
tum—have found new ways 
to respond effectively to pri- 
vate label competition. 

They've shifted market- 
ing priorities ‘in favor of re- 
tail partnering programs 
and a more targeted ap- 
proach. They’ve gotten 
more heavily into the pri- 
vate label manufacturing 
game themselves. They’ve 
unilaterally cut prices on a 
broad array of the biggest- 
selling consumer staples. 
They’ve gone back and re- 
formulated some of the 
most heavily knocked-off 
products, like mouthwash, 
thus making it harder and 
more expensive for store 
brand manufacturers to 
play on the same field. 

And some—most notably 
Procter & Gamble (P&G)— 
have taken the gloves off in 
their determination to pro-

Viewpoints 


Know your most important customers 


’m a chain drug store shopper; I have been since I was 

about 12 years old and a Genovese drug store opened in 

my favorite shopping district in Queens, New York. I 
still shop at Genovese when I’m in Queens or Long Island, 
and I’ve added several stores to my list of favorites, includ- 
ing the new Rite Aid on Lexington Avenue in Manhattan 
that Lisa Fried writes about in this issue (page 18). 

I shop drug stores about twice a week on average—not 
counting visits related to my job—and I rarely leave a store 
without making an impulse purchase. Take last night, for 
instance. The two items I went in to get would have cost 
about $5. At the checkout, I found myself with a $19 receipt 
and a hair conditioner, a styling mousse, a packet of hair 
accessories and a facial masque I hadn’t planned to buy. 

Not only am I the type of customer drug chains should 
concentrate on keeping, but I’m also a consumer who could 
be swayed to spend a greater

market. 

Next, in an exclusive study commissioned by Drug Store 
News, we present the findings of America’s Research 
Group’s survey of 1,000 drug store shoppers across the 
country. Focusing only on peopie who shop in drug stores, 
we set out to find out why these consumers go to drug 
stores, what they buy there, and what they like and don't 
like about the experience. (The report starts on page 101.) 

For the purposes of this survey, America’s Research 
Group only talked to consumers who said they had shopped 
in a chain drug store within the previous three months. Al- 
though we didn’t screen for drug store shopping frequency, 
almost 80 percent of the re-

drug stores. And I firmly be-

merchants—that there are 
plenty of people like me who 
still prefer to shop drug 
stores for certain products 
and certain reasons. 

Consumers who shop 
drug stores regularly are 
your best and most valuable 
customers, and your biggest 
opportunity to increase your 
sales is to build upon your existing franchise with them. 

To help you identify more of those opportunities, Drug 
Store News is putting “the spotlight” on the highly valued 
drug store shopper via three separate studies in this issue, 
which is timed for the NACDS Marketplace Conference in 
San Francisco. 

First, in seven major metropolitan markets, we identify

drug stores. “Who’s Shopping Where?” (page 31) utilizes

Looking at consumers from these different angles reveals

tunities for drug chains tu capture more sales from the cus- 
tomers shopping in your stores every day. 

I’m not only a drug store shopper; I’m an optimist about 
the chain drug industry. I see the leading chains making 
strategic moves to gear their stores to their customers in 
better and more effective ways than ever before. Without a 
doubt, that is the most direct and cost-effective ticket to a 
profitable future. 


Regaining confidence in a Wal-Mart world 


‘ve been covering the chain drug industry now MAGUS MRNEU Ie view. The drug chains that have survived the ram- 


for nearly 13 years—a fact which surprises no 

one more than me. That takes my close-up ex- 
perience with this industry back to 1982: back far 
enough to remember when POS scanning was 
strictly for supermarkets, home health care was 
one of the hottest buzzes around, Walgreens still 
owned restaurants and a travel agency, and Per- 
ry was selling outboard motors. 

I don’t kid myself. There’s still a lot about chain 
drug retailing I don’t know—TI still can’t discuss 
with any degree of comfort the relative advantages 
of LIFO vs. FIFO accounting, for instance—but I’ve 
learned enough and seen enough in 13 years of 
walking stores and pestering the industry’s best 
practitioners to have developed some perspective 
about this business. And my perspective tells me 
that chain drug retailing is in fundamentally better 
shape than it was at any time since the early ’80s. 

I know that sounds like the kind of self-serving, “let’s pat 
each other on the back” boosterism you hear from at least one 
of the speakers at any trade conference, but I mean it. Over 
the past two or three years, I’ve seen the outlines of real evo- 
lution taking shape. The industry is firming up. 

It’s leaner, to be sure. There are fewer players, and the 
players that have survived, and in most cases prospered, are 
leaner too, with fewer headquarters employees and more em- 
powered decision-makers throughout the organization. That 
slimming-down process has been painful for those whose jobs 
evaporated, and it’s meant longer hours for the people who 
remain. But given the competitive dogfight chain drug retail- 
ers are now waging, was there really any alternative? 

Restructuring certainly isn’t unique to the chain drug in- 
dustry; it’s been a global reality. The evolution I’m talking 
about is subtler, but no less apparent if you take the long 


JIM FREDERICK 


Jim Frederick is 
the news editor for 
Drug Store News. 


pant consolidation of the past few years—and that 
consolidation is by no means over—are in better 
shape because they have learned how to play for 
keeps in a retail world re-defined by Wal-Mart. 

They have learned how to adapt. Merchants have 
learned they can sell convenience foods and baby 
products and other front-end goods they once ceded 
to the discounters and the combo stores. POS-based 
information systems have taken much of the guess 
work out of store-level demand and replenishment. 
In terms of marketing, the drug chains seem to have 
regained their sense of what they are, and where 
their strengths lie. 

Chain drug leaders like Dan Jorndt of Walgreens, 
Bob Hannan of Thrift and Dwayne Hoven of Revco 
are quick to credit Wal-Mart for its super-efficient dis- 
tribution practices, vendor clout, unique corporate 
culture and enormous drawing power—all of which have led 
the giant discounter to reset America’s retail table. But it’s 
also readily apparent by now that drug stores aren’t going 
away. Consumers still want to shop smaller, conveniently lo- 
cated, service-oriented neighborhood drug stores where they 
know the pharmacist and the kid behind the checkstand. 

It isn’t rocket science, but for the chains that have come 
closest to orchestrating the myriad details perfectly, day after 
day, it has paid big dividends. The lesson has been hammered 
home by same-store sales gains that are ringing up at 7, 8, 
even 9 percent or better at many of the best chains. 

And given the demographic outlook—an aging population 
and an explosion of dual-income, time-strapped families will- 
ing to pay for convenience if it saves them time on the way 
home—there’s every reason to think the industry will contin- 
ue to adapt to whatever changes managed care or new com- 
petition will throw its way.

position yourself to win is to identify and de- 

velop your strengths. From market to market 
across the country, chain drug stores have vary- 
ing strengths and different areas of opportunity. 

This Drug Store News study of top drug store 
markets looks beyond mere demographics and 
involves lifestyle—upscale vs. downscale, urban 
vs. suburban, etc.—and lifestage—absence or 
presence of children as well as age—paraineters. 
Using a 54-cell grid developed by Spectra Mar- 
keting Systems Inc. (Chicago, Ill.), we can shaw 
which lifestyles and lifestages have the greatest 
propensity toward shopping in drug chains, and 
which have the least within each Designated 
Market Area (DMA). 

Further, by using consumer panel data collect- 
ed by Scarborough Research Corp., we identify 
lifestyle/lifestage areas where specific chains 
outperform the norm in a given market. 

In this year’s study, we’re taking a look at sev- 
en major metropolitan markets. (See chart for 
the markets’ 1994 drug store sales.) 


What the charts reveal 


For each metropolitan market, there are three 
charts. 

The chart labeled “Incidence of chain drug 
store shopping” shows how drug stores in gener- 
al perform within each lifestyle/lifestage cell in a 
particular market. The tables are based on con- 
sumer panel data collected by Scarborough Re- 
search Corp. The cells in which there is a high

age) are the ones where consumers are most like- 
ly to shop in drug stores. 

“Drug chains shopped most often” identifies 
the particular chains that have an above-aver- 
age number of mentions by consumers when 


they were asked which drug stores they 


“shopped last month.”

About the sources 


Spectra Marketing Systems Inc., the Chica- 
go-based firm that provided the 54-cell grids, 
is an integrated micromarketing firm. It mar- 


Power 


kets a software system, Spectra Advantage, 
that integrates demographic data with 
lifestyle information designed to identify 
where the greatest consumer opportunities lie 
for both retailer and manufacturer. 

Demographic data is derived from U.S. cen- 
sus reports; the lifestyle clusters represent ab- 
breviated versions of PRIZM’s 42 lifestyles. 

All information on shopping—consumer 
penetration, shopping frequency and prescrip-

panel studies.

TOP DRUG STORE MARKETS 


Drug chains shopped most often” 


Market basics 


Philadelphia’s expected popu- 
lation increase of 2 percent over 
the next five years trails that of 
the total U.S. by 3 percent. 
Over the same span, household 
growth may be as much as 53 
percent below the projected 
norm. 

The City of Brotherly Love is 
home to a fair number of afflu- 
ent households. Indeed, 8 per- 
cent earn in excess of $100,000 


(32 percent above the U.S. aver- 
age). There is a relatively high 
number of households without 
kids. Some 34 percent of house- 
holds have children, 4 percent 
below the U.S. mean. 

African Americans account for 
17 percent of the market’s popu- 
lation, 38 percent above the 
country as whole. Relatively few 
Asians and Hispanics make their 
home in this area.

Drug Store News, June 26, 1995 


TOP DRUG STORE MARKETS 


Detroit 


Drug chains shopped most often* 


Market basics 


Growth of Detroit’s population 
(4,749,552) is expected to lag the 
nation’s by 3 percent over the 
next five years. Estimated house- 
hold growth is 50 percent of the 
U.S. norm. 

Detroit is solidly middle-class. 
Some 19 percent of households 
earn $50,000-$74,999, while 18 
percent make $35,000-$49,999. 
Median home value at $72,151 
is 3 percent below the national 
average of $74,479. 


At 33.6, the mean market age 
is close to the national average, 
but Detroit has fewer 18-to-24- 
year-olds than the U.S. norm 
and 8 percent fewer seniors. 

While Black consumers consti- 
tute 21 percent of the Detroit 
population, Hispanics and Asians 
comprise roughly 2 percent each, 
only 20 percent and 50 percent, 
respectively, of the United States 
market average.
