Market basics 


The Washington, D.C., popula- 


tion (5,101,464) is expected to 
grow | percent faster than the

years. 

This is a very affluent market. 
The median household income 
of $48,173 is 59 percent higher 
than the U.S. average. Some 12.6 
percent of households earn 
$100,000 or more. 

Washingtonians are also 


highly educated. Some 34 per- 
cent of the population has com- 
pleted four or more years of 
college, 65 percent above the 
U.S. norm. 

African American consumers 
represent 22.9 percent of the 
population. Asian consumers 
comprise 5.1 percent of the pop- 
ulation. Both percentages are 
significantly higher than the 
U.S. average.

ORONTO — Barbara 

Brocklebank, vp of 

cosmetics for Shop- 
pers Drug Mart, has re- 
signed. Brocklebank, who 
started with Shoppers in 
1969 as a cosmetic coordi- 
nator, will be relocating to 
New York City where she 
will live with her new hus- 
band, actor Michael Scott. 
Brocklebank, who will 
keep her maiden name for 
business purposes, is in- 
vestigating new business 
opportunities including the 
possibility of consulting. 
Shoppers has not yet 
named a replacement for 
her. 


ANCOUVER, B.C. 

— Cosmetic buyers 

looking for some- 
thing new and different 
might want to check out a 
line of budget cosmetics 
targeted to teens called 
Colours of Australis. It’s 
made by a company called 
Australis, which has a di- 
vision based in Vancouver, 
Canada. 

One western Canadian 
chain is averaging over 
$450 per square foot with 
the line. American chains 
testing the line include 
Osco, Drug Emporium and 
Ulta3. A space-efficient, 11- 
square-inch display is avail- 
able as well as GWPs. Sug- 
gested retail price is $2.99.

Chains intensify marketing programs 


Continued from page 66 

Potts said the company will also 
continue to aggressively advertise cos- 
metics as well as continue to promote 
the cosmeticians who give the chain a 
valuable “point of difference” vs. the 
competition. 

Walgreens, always a strong play- 
er in cosmetics, is striving to be- 
come a much more sophisticated 
marketer as well as an effective 
merchandiser. 

Steve Lubin, the divisional mer- 
chandise manager for cosmetics and 
fragrances, said the company is col- 
lecting a good deal of useful strate- 
gic marketing information from its 
sophisticated computer systems. 

“Down the line, we will have the 
ability to capture sales for individ- 
ual lines on a per-store basis which, 
in, turn, will help us fine-tune our 
mix to be demographically correct 
on a store-by-store basis,” he said. 

Lubin added that while Wal- 
greens can make a big difference by 
enhancing its marketing of beauty 
care products, “marketing must 
have strong, new product launches 
to be able to continually drive the 
business.” 

“Drug chains, as an industry,” he 
said, “do a very good job with new 
product launches. They seem to have 
the ability to capture a large market 
share at the front end of a launch. 
This is where the industry excels.” 

The vice president of marketing 


Department ty percent chare 


and advertising for a major regional 
chain said the most effective market- 
ing campaigns enable a chain to offer 
its customers “value-added benefits 
that the competition doesn’t have.” 

“We can never compete with the 
Wal-Marts, Kmarts and Targets on 
price,” he said. “We have to offer 
customers something more, some- 
thing they can’t get in the mass 
merchandisers, things like service, 
product selection, in-store events, 
convenience, and with marketing 
we're learning which benefits our 
customers want and how best to 
communicate that we have those 
benefits.” 

Even though 1995 is turning out 
to be a much stronger year for chain 
drug stores in the cosmetics catego- 
ry, the threat from the mass mer- 
chandisers has not gone away, and 
it will never completely go away. 


Discounters competition tough 


In some markets, head-to-head 
competition from price discounters 
like Wal-Mart, Target and Kmart is 
still making it tough for drug stores to 
grow the cosmetic/fragrance business. 

Sources for two West Coast chains 
reported that their sales in cosmetics 
are good “except in markets where 
we now compete with Wal-Mart.” 

Having the right technology in 
place, however, can make a difference.

Lip outshines all categories 


The category that’s con- 
tributed the most to drug stores 
this year is lip. Lip cosmetic 
products account for 23 percent 
of all color cosmetic sales and 26 
percent of all drug store cosmet- 
ic sales. Lip care is outperform- 
ing all other segments of cos- 
metics, according to IRI. 

In drug stores, sales of all lip 
cosmetic products were up 12 
percent for the 52 weeks ended 
April 30. In all mass outlets 
combined (food, drug and 
mass), they went up 13 percent 
Mass merchandisers registered 
a gain of 17 percent on all lip 


chandise stores, 16 percent. 

Lip pencils, a $54.4 million 
category that accounts for 2.4 
percent of all cosmetic sales, 
were up an incredible 37.5 per- 
cent over a year ago. Lip gloss, 
a $49 million category, was up 
5.9 percent. 

So far, the bulk of the credit 
for driving lip cosmetic sales 
belongs to Revlon, primarily 
because of its outstanding 
launch of Color Stay. 

Thanks to the remarkable 
non-transfer formulation of Col- 
or Stay, Revlon’s lip color sales 
were up 45.9 percent to $156 
million for the period through 
April 30th. Revlon now has 
three times the share of second 
place Cover Girl whose sales 
were down 5.9 percent for the 52 
weeks ende d April 30th. 

But Revlon is not the only 
growth brand in lip care.

74 


f you talk to most chain drug fra- 

grance buyers, you'll hear that 

the category has been soft for the 
past few years and is basically still 
flat in most chain drug stores. 

But, outside drug stores, the cate- 
gory is growing. Women’s fra- 
grances were up 4.6 percent in dol- 
lar sales—growth that is ahead of 
the inflation rate—for the 52 weeks 
ended April 30, according to Chica- 
go-based Information Resources Inc. 
(IRI), and men’s fragrances were 
up 9.8 percent for the period. 

But in the drug store industry, 
there was no growth in women’s 
fragrances. In fact the category was 
down 3.4 percent to $392 million for 
the period. Men’s was up, but only 
by 2.9 percent to $213 million. 

Food stores don't normally give a 
lot of space to men’s fragrances, but 
they still managed to register a 3.7 
percent gain in men’s fragrances 
sales to reach sales of $63 million. 
They were up even more dramatical- 
ly in women’s fragrances, surging 10 
percent to sales of $46 million. 

But the category was really hot in 
mass merchandise stores, up 18 per- 
cent in men’s to $2! 50 million; up 14 
percent in women’s to $362 million. 

Some of the growth in mass is 
due to gains in distribution as more 
and more Kmarts, Wal-Marts, Cal- 
dors and Bradlees flesh out their 
cosmetics and fragrance depart- 
ments to turn themselves into 
“fashion” merchants. 


Diskys vs. drug chains 


Some growth is also coming from 
the fact that discount stores often 
undercut chain drug stores on 
prices, running sales at margins of- 
ten less than 20 percent and some- 
times virtually at cost. 

However, drug chains are fighting 
back. Some are finding innovative 
new ways to promote fragrances. 

One buyer said he has worked out 
an allowance system based on his 
sell-throughs that allows his stores to 
pass enormous savings along to con- 
sumers without sacrificing margins. 

In the last year and a half, sever- 
al drug chains have been experi- 
menting with such allowances. In- 
stead of giving a traditional volume 
discount when a buyer orders x 
amount of fragrances, which may 
translate into a 20-cent price reduc- 
tion per item purchased, the vendor 
gives the buyer a much larger al- 
lowance for each item the chain 
sells through the front end. 

The chain keeps track of its sell- 
throughs via its point of sale scan- 
ners. Because the program rewards 
sell-throughs rather than buy-ins 
and because it gives retailers a 
raat higher per-item discount than 

aditional allowances, it is becom- 
a a popular promotional strategy 
with both retailers and vendors.

Fragrance forecast: 
Drug chains find new ways to Orive sales 


Chains like Payless have been 1nding innovative ways to drive sales of cosmetics in 
the wake of stiff competition from deep discounters. 


One manufacturer said the “scan- 
ner allowances,” as he called them, 
are a particularly effective way to 
promote fragrances. “You can give 
the chain a higher allowance,” he 
said, “because you're only compen- 
sating them for what they sell. In 
turn, that means they can give their 
customers a higher discount with- 
out lowering margins, and that 
helps them be more competitive 
against the mass merchandisers.” 

Many chains are also trying to 
grow fragrance sales by promoting 
different “fragrances of the month,” 
doing more gifts with purchases and 
spending more time encouraging cos- 
meticians to suggestively sell fra- 
grances. 

Because there are so 
many new launches in 
fragrances this year, 


many new launches coming out be- 
cause manufacturers have reached 
the conclusion that if they put 
enough new products out on the 
market in any given year, it will 
turn the category around. 

Another buyer for a mid-size 
chain in the southwest put it this 
way: “It’s been soft so long, I think 
people have just decided there’s an 
opportunity here.” 

It may also be that Coty has had 
so much marketing success and 
done such a good job supporting its 
brands with in-store events that 
other vendors have decided to copy 
their formula.

Launches don’t hurt sales 


Coty has also proven that it can 
launch new brands without canni- 
balizing sales of existing brands. 
One buyer commented that other 
manufacturers now are starting to 
copy that approach. 

“I think Revlon’s launch of Ciara 
Femme Fatale could be very good,” 
said Taylor. “Ciara has been such a 
strong brand, and now they have a 
chance to revitalize it and, at the 
same time, maybe attract a new 
market of younger users with 
Femme Fatale. 

“Revlon is talking about a master 
brand marketing strategy, and capi- 
talizing on the strengths of its exist- 
ing brands. Coty has done this very 
successfully, and so has L’Oréal.” 

Revlon is also betting that it can 
use technology to drive fragrance 
sales just as it used it to drive sales 
of lipsticks and face makeups. 

This fall, the company is intro- 
ducing a major new fragrance 
brana, Lasting. Just as Color Stay 
is formulated to last all day and not 
transfer off the lips, Lasting is for- 
mulated to smell the same at the 
end of the day as when it was first 
applied. 

According to a buyer who has 
seen and liked Lasting a lot, Revlon 
used a new way of layering oils to 
minimize the phases that a fra- 
grance normally goes through. “It 
smells the same when it dries down 
as when you first put it on,” said the 
buyer. 

However Lasting is expensive: 
$17.50 for a 5-ounce cologne and 
$40 for a quarter-ounce perfume. 

Revlon, of course, believes the 
brand’s packaging, advertising and 
innovative formula justifies the 
price, but some buyers are ske »pti- 
cal. “It may work if they support it, 
said the buyer for a major regional 
chain in the Midwest, “but at that 
price point, it’s going to have to be 
perceived as more than just another 
mass fragrance. It’s going to have to 
compete with Sunflowers and CK 
One and all the rest of the designer 
brands we carry.” 

Out on the West Coast, Joe Potts, 
beauty and fashion merchandise 
manager for Thrifty PayLess, is bet- 
ting that fragrance sales will get 
better this year, particularly for 
Christmas. 

Potts said he’s seen some exciting 
gift sets and is particularly im-

NEWARK, Del. — Interested in strengthening consumers’ awareness of bath 
brands, Happy Harry’s Discount 7 S‘ures created an extensive upscale bath 
wail in its largest store at Branmar Plaza here a year ago. Located adjacent to 
the Photo Shop, the bath department is booming, with the strongest sales com- 
ing from Sarah Michaels and Freeman Cosmetic Corp., according to Valerie 
Cheney, cosmetic buyer for the chain. 

The shelved aqua wall unit features a full line of bath accessories, bath 
salts, gift sets, glycerine soap, body lotion, bath beads, bath gel and other re- 
lated shige eee Other brands featured include Bodycology, Sherwood of Eng- 
land, San Francisco Soap Co., Nature’s Essence and Crebel. 

Among the trends Cheney sees: strong interest in vanilla and raspberry 
scents and dwindling interest in tropical fruit scents.

Label viewers gaining popularity 


ORLANDO, Fla. — To in- 
crease private label OTC 
sales while providing a cus- 
tomer convenience, chain 
crug retailers are eyeing the 
use of label magnifiers affixed 
to OTC department shelves. 

Such devices give retailers 
an on-shelf promotional vehi- 
cle to promote their own 
brands and a service to those 
who have difficulty reading 
OTC labels 

One such product on the 
market, manufactured by 
Orlando, Fla.-based MDI 
Products, mounts perpen- 
dicular to the shelf and ex- 
tends about 5 inches from 
the shelf. In addition to a 
rugged magnifier, a main 


vides retailers room for ad- 
vertising messages that are 
easily interchangeable de- 
pending on promotions. 


Numerous benefits 


MDI president Barry 
Marciniak said label magni- 
fiers give retailers the dual 
benefit of offering a needed 
and appreciated customer 
service while also serving as 
a valuable point-of-purchase 
promotional vehicle. The con- 
cept of label magnifiers is 
not new, according to 
Marciniak, but past prob- 
lems with product durability, 
functionality and lens quali- 
ty prevented their wide- 
spread use. 

One retailer that plans to 
use the devices is American 


Drug Stores’ Osco and Sav- 
on divisions. Each of the 
chain’s 781 stores will have 
four of the devices affixed to 
OTC department shelves. 

American Drug Stores’ pri- 
vate brands manager Bill 
Bergin said the decision to 
install the devices made 
sense. 

“With a high percentage of 
elderly customer and as an 
enhancement to overall cus- 
tomer service, we felt this 
program would provide us 
with a real benefit for cus- 
tomers that have difficulty 
reading the small print that 
appears on some product,” 
Bergin said. 

Kmart will also reportedly 
be installing the devices on 
OTC department shelves.

Eckerd’s Food Mart format 
targets convenience shopper 


LEARWATER, Fla. — 
In its continuing at- 


tempt to capture the 
convenience customer, Eckerd 
plans to add 400 new Food 
Mart sections to existing 
stores this year, according to 
company chairman Stewart 
Turley, who addressed the 
Eckerd shareholders’ meeting 
in May. 

The Food Mart conversions 
are part of an extensive 
chainwide remodeling and re- 
location program, which be- 
gan close to two years ago. 
When the conversions are 
complete, 880 of the chain’s 


1,735 stores will contain Food 
Marts. 

Situated at the store’s 
front end, the Food Mart sec- 
tion includes three aisles 
and 34 linear feet of coolers. 
In addition to the usual drug 
store array of snacks, soft 
drinks and sundries, Food 
Marts feature household food 
staples such as milk and 
eggs as well as microwave- 
able meals and other shelf- 
stable foods. 

“Today’s convenience shop- 
per could buy dinner at Eck- 
erd,” said chain spokesman 
Gerry Hoeppner, who was 


quoted in the St. Petersburg 
Times. 

Convenience stores tradi- 
tionally appeal to young, 
male customers. While wo- 
men and older shoppers 
might have the same desire 
for convenience purchases, 
they generally prefer to fre- 
quent other channels such as 
supermarkets and drug 
stores. Eckerd is confident 
that its Food Mart formats 
will serve the convenience 
food needs of these shoppers 
in a retail environment that 
they'll feel more comfortable 
with.

Leinenkugel’s Red Lager, distributed by Miller; 
and Elk Mountain, Red Hook, Elephant Red 
and Red Wolf Lager, all distributed by the spe- 
cialty brewing group of Anheuser-Busch.

THE DRUG STORE SHOPPER 


How well do you know 
vour customer? 


An exclusive Drug Store News survey shines 
the spotlight on today’s drug store shopper. 


By Nancy Maline 


acing fierce competition from mass merchants, supermarket 
combos and specialty stores, not to mention mail-order and other 
threats to the pharmacy business, chain drug stores can’t afford 
to lose an existing customer. And even as the financial picture 
for most major drug chains improves, management is well aware 
that the easiest and most cost-effective way to drive sales is to 

get the customer you already have to spend more in your stores. 
So, in an effort to learn more about your current customers, Drug Store 
News set out to profile today’s drug store shopper to uncover motivations 
and shopping habits and to identify the strengths and weaknesses of 


drug stores in the minds of consumers.

In an exclusive survey conducted 
for Drug Store News, America’s Re- 
search Group interviewed 1,000 
consumers who had shopped in a 
chain drug store within the previ- 
ous three months. Once identified, 
drug store shoppers were asked 
what factors are important to them 
in terms of in-store service, conve- 
nience and pricing, and we asked 
them what they bought. 

The majority of drug store shop- 
pers interviewed (65 percent) tend 


Statistics provided by America’s 
Research Group 


to be in a drug store between one 
and three times per month (See 
chart, below). Thirteen percent 
shopped drug stores at least 
once a week, while more than 
one-third (34 percent) shopped 
drug stores between two and 
three times during the month. 
Of the total sample, more than 
three quarters (78 percent) shop 
drug stores once a month or 
more often. 

Our sample included both men 
and women and spanned the en- 
tire country. (See sidebar on “Re- 
spondent Demographics,” page 
108). 

What did we discover about 
these drug store shoppers? Basi- 
cally, we were told by consumers 
that they want their shopping 
experience to be uncomplicated. 
With so many priorities to deal 
with, the public neither expects 
nor wants shopping in a store to 
be a life-altering experience. 
Consumers value the simple 
things: A store should be easy to 
get to. Merchandise should be 
easy to find and fairly priced. 
Paying for purchases and getting 
out of the store should not be a 
hassle. 

In fact, consumers mentioned 
location most often as being an im- 
portant factor when it comes to 
choosing a store (see chart, page 101). 
Finding a store that is close to home 
or work is the deciding factor for two- 
thirds (67 percent) of shoppers.

However, while the conve- 
nience of the store’s location 
may be outside your control, 
don’t underestimate the power 
of a well-trained staff. After 
convenient location, almost as 
many drug store shoppers (65 
percent) cited the presence of a 
knowledgeable staff as an im- 
portant factor in the decision to 
choose a store. 

Knowledgeable staff, in fact, 
is considered to be important to 
more of our respondents than 
price. Shoppers certainly do 
have certain expectations with 
regard to price: They expect a 
store’s pricing to be in line with 
other stores in the market. Six- 
ty-three percent say “competi- 
tive pricing” is an important 
reason for choosing a store. 

Almost equally important to 
shoppers is the knowledge they 
won't get stuck on a long check- 
out line, which was mentioned 
by 62 percent. And while they 
are walking the aisles, shoppers 
like to be able to locate what 
they need quickly and easily. 
Fifty-eight percent appreciate a 
store that has good signage. 

Over half of the shoppers we 
surveyed want to be able to find 
a parking space easily (56 percent). 
Slightly less than half the group say 
they like the idea of a store that is 
not too crowded (45 percent) and 
many appreciate stores that are not 
too large (30 percent)—factors that 
give most drug stores an edge over 
major mass marketers. 

Again, in the interest of simplici- 
ty, a store that allows the customer 
the luxury of one-stop shopping is 
attractive (44 percent). Twenty-two 
percent of respondents choose a 
store that has both drug and food 
items.

Again, price is a secondary issue. 
Only 25 percent of the respondents 
say they like to see what’s on sale. 
A group of comparison shoppers (24 
percent) say they like to see what’s 
on sale at several stores before de- 
ciding where to buy. 

Then, there are the browsers. 
These are the shoppers who spend 
more time in the store, providing 
plenty of opportunity for incre- 
mental sales. Approximately two 
of every 10 drug store shoppers (19 
percent) admit they like to browse. 
For 11 percent, trying the testers 
is fun. 

The destination categories 


We asked shoppers who made a 
purchase at a drug store within the 
past three months to tell us what 
they bought on their most recent 
trip (see chart, page 102). 

The majority (69 percent) went to 
the drug store to fill a prescription. 
The second most popular category 
was closely related, non-prescrip- 
tion medicine (52 percent). Three 
out of 10 drug store shoppers (30 
percent) bought a toiletry item or 
personal care product on their last 
visit to a drug store. And the greet-

When we asked our sample of 
drug store shoppers to tell us 
which retail outlet they frequent 
most for various products (see 
chart, page 102) chain drug stores 
were overwhelmingly dominant in 
prescription medicine, with 77 per- 
cent reporting they most often 
have their prescriptions filled in 
drug stores. In contrast, only 7 per-

likely to fill a prescription in a 
mass merchant and just 4 percent 
in a supermarket. 

When it comes to prescriptions, 
it’s not surprising to find that pa- 
tients are loyal to the store where 
they know the pharmacist and their 
pharmacy records are on file, but it 
also seems that drug store shoppers 
have an affinity for buying other 
health-related products in a drug 
store. Six in 10 respondents said 
they frequent drug stores when 
they need to buy over-the-counter 
medicine. Less than 20 percent of 
the sample (19 percent) buy OTCs 
most often in a mass merchant and 
16 percent frequent supermarkets 
for OTCs.

Are you on their list? 


In general, shoppers mentally 
plan their purchases in advance. 
When they head for the store, it is 
most often with a specific purchase 
in mind. 

On their last trip to a drug store, 
nearly all shoppers (92 percent) say 
they bought everything they 
planned to buy (see chart, page 104). 
Filling prescriptions and buying 
non-prescription remedies proved to 
be planned purchases. Ninety-two 
percent of consumers say they 
planned to buy an OTC product 
when they went to the store. The 
photo department is, not surprising- 
ly, a planned stop (93 percent of 
purchases are planned). For 88 per- 
cent of the sample, a stop in the 
greeting card section was planned. 

And, despite the fact that sham- 
poo and other personal care items 
are often discounted to bring cus- 
tomers into the store, more than 
eight in 10 toiletries consumers (82 
percent) report planning in advance 
to replenish these items. 

The good news, however, is that 
there were several categories where 
purchases were less likely to have 
been planned. These categories rep- 
resent the greatest opportunities for 
drug stores in terms of in-store mer- 
chandising. 

Seventeen percent of the purchas- 
es made by our panel of respon- 
dents were unplanned. Products 
that promise instant gratification 
are the ones that are most likely to 
drive impulse sales. For example, 
snack foods and beverages that are 
bought in a drug store are more 
likely to be bought on impulse than 
they are to be a planned purchase 
(56 percent impulse vs. 44 percent 
planned). Fragrances have similar 
appeal. Nearly half the respondents 
who purchased a scent (46 percent ) 
did so on the spur of the moment. In 
addition, three in 10 cosmetic pur- 
chasers bought something that they 
didn’t think they needed before en- 
tering the drug store. 


The prescription shopper 


The prescription customer’s value 
to a store cannot be overstated. 
Luckily, as mentioned earlier, the 
most important reason people like 
shopping in drug stores is their 
knowledgeable staff. This certainly 
indicates that the seamaction of a 
drug store with the pharmacy pro- 
fessional is a major asset. 

Prescription purchasers estimat- 
ed spending an average of $22.00 
on each prescription purchased at a 
drug store. Over three-fourths (77 
percent) said their health insur- 
ance policy would cover at least a 
portion of the cost of the prescrip- 
tion medicine. 

People on prescription medicine 
consider location to be the most im-

About the survey 


America’s Research 
Group, based in 
Charleston, S.C., was 
selected for this research 
project because of its 
extensive background in 
interviewing consumers 
on retail, financial and 
service issues. 

The survey consisted of 
111 questions, including 
those dealing with 
demographic 
characteristics. 
Consumers from all 
regions of the country 
were contacted, but only 
people who had shopped 
at a chain drug store 
within the past three 
months were polled. The 
telephone interviews were 
made from America’s 
Research Group’ s offices 
in Charleston, S.C., from 
March 16 to 21, 1995. The 
margin of error for the 
survey is +/-4.3 percent. 

America’s Research 
Group is a 16-year-old 
consumer survey research 
organization that conducts 
more than 100 national 
studies each year to 
determine consumer 
opinions and attitudes on 
a wide variety of issues.

he Nielsen Consumer 
Panel, source of statis- 
tics for this section, 
provides retailers with com- 
prehensive insights into the 
key strategic issues that af- 
fect brand performance. 
The panel consists of 
40,000 households, each 


equipped with a hand-held 
scanner. When each of these 
households purchases an 
item with a Universal Prod- 
uct Code, the household 
uses this scanner to record 
the transaction. At the same 
time, the household is 
prompted to supply other

data, such as the location of 
the sale, which member of 
the household actually 
made the purchase or 
whether a coupon or other 
promotional item was used. 
Then, this information is 
transmitted by phone to 
Nielsen for compilation.

Making sense out of the numbers 


Most of the data in this 
report is compiled from the 
period between June 1993 
and June 1994. 

The sample is constructed 
in such a way to be geo- 
graphically and demograph- 
ically representative of the 
U.S. household population. 


The sample’s strong suit is 
that every type of sales out- 
let is included, not just drug 
or grocery stores or mass 
merchandisers. This infor- 
mation can be combined 
with the demographic infor- 
mation pertaining to each 
household, allowing a clear 
profile of who’s buying what 
and where they are buying it 
to emerge. By being so large, 
detailed population segmen-

A.C. Nielsen Report 


Antacids 


155 


he gastrointestinal category is 
presenting chain drug retailers with a 

major opportunity. With Johnson & 
Johnson/Merck’s Pepcid® AC now on the 
market and SmithKline Beecham’s Tagamet 
HB expected to be here soon, chain drug 
stores can look to gain some market share in 
a core OTC category. 

Unlike categories such as cough/cold and 
analgesics, where consumers indicate a 
preference for chain drug stores, in the 
antacids category drug stores follow food 
stores and mass merchandisers as the 
preferred outlet. 

Nielsen Household Panel data indicates 
food stores dominate with a nearly 39 percent 
market share. Mass merchandisers account 
for close to 28 percent while drug stores lag at 
27 percent. 

With a new class of products entering the 
market, drug stores have the opportunity to 
be more promotional with the category. 
According to projections from Nielsen data, 50 
percent of the United States population 
purchased an antacid during the past 12 
months, and the majority, almost 70 percent, 
were female. Of those purchasing an antacid 
during the past 12 months, about 20 percent 
said the product they bought was on sale or 
was part of some other kind of promotional 
activity, such as a coupon offer. 


Antacids work differently than the family of 


drugs know as H? blockers. Antacids 
neutralize stomach acids, whereas H? 
products such as Pepcid AC and Tagamet HB 
inhibit the production of stomach acids.

A.C. Nielsen Report 


Nutritional 
supplemen Ue 


pportunities to increase sales in the 

nutritional supplements category will 

come from capturing more male 
customers and gaining market share from 
alternative distribution channels. 

According to data from Nielsen’s household 
panel, a full 32 percent of nutritional 
supplement consumers rely on sources other 
than drug stores, supermarkets and mass 
merchandisers for their vitamins. Slightly 
more than 26 percent of consumers purchased 
vitamins at drug stores, according to Nielsen. 
That compares to 22.5 percent at 
supermarkets and 17.2 percent at mass 
merchandisers. 

Another opportunity for chain drug stems 
from the fact that even though nutritional 
supplement sales have grown considerably in 
recent years, there still exists a large 
untapped consumer base. Nielsen data show 
that many consumers still do not purchase 
nutritional supplements. Only 21 percent of 
Nielsen’s household panel bought nutritional 
supplements

A.C. Nielsen Report 


Conditioners 


nit growth in conditioners was 

practically flat for the 12 months 

ending June 1994, according to Nielsen 
Household Panel data. Drug stores, which 
should be able to woo shoppers with the 
largest selection, lagged far behind both food 
stores and mass merchants in unit and dollar 
sales. 

Leave-in conditioner were a bright spot, 
according to retailers, as more women looked 
to soften their hair from the effects of hair 
color, the sun, blow drying and perms. 
Women’s interest in softer, natural styles is 
influencing product introductions this year. 
Color-enhancing conditioners are also 
popping up as manufacturers try to woo the 
growing group of semi-permanent hair-color 
users.

MARKETPLACK 


A.C. Nielsen Report 


Hare coloring 


WOMEK § 


early one-quarter of all women colored 
their hair last year, with each 


individual spending a total of $16.99 on 
approximately three products. 

The growing popularity of semi-permanent 
hair color has helped to fuel the growth, as 
women responded to the opportunity to color 
their hair without commitment: L’Oréal’s 
Castings, Clairol’s Natural Instincts and 
Glints, and Revlon’s new Rev Up 
Conditioning Color Enhance all wash out in 
six to eight shampoos. Revlon is the latest 
entrant in this subcategory, and some 
retailers have been merchandising the 
product near cosmetics to rev up sales. 

Now that women are buying hair color more 
often, many chains are offering promotions on 
hair color once a week or once a month. In the 
12-month period ending June 1994, 
promotions were offered on 26.4 percent of all 
units sold.

ARKETPLACR 


A.C. Nielsen Report 


Ethnic hai 


prepara L/OKE 


n ethnic households, it is usually a woman 
[ss is primarily in charge of buying hair 

styling and other hair preparation 
products. 

According to Nielsen Househc'd Panel data, 
85 percent of all primary purch: sers are 
women, and they tend to buy c uite a lot of 
hair prep products. 

Nielsen North America found that the 
typical buyer shops for ethnic hair preps 3.9 
times a year, acquiring in the process an 
average of 5.4 units a year. 

Drug stores, however, are not capturing a 
very high share of those purchases. Just 21 
percent of all buyers make their purchase in a 
drug store. Most shoppers prefer to buy in 
stores with lower prices and greater variety. 

A third of all buyers, for example, buy their 
hair preps in a discount department store like 
Wal-Mart or Kmart, while 30.3 percent shop 
other non-food stores such as beauty and 
barber supply stores or buy their styling aids 
in the salons where they get their hair done. 

Most households don’t pay a lot for their 
hair preparations. The average purchase 
price, according to A.C. Nielsen, is just $3.46, 
which is 16 cents cheaper than the average a 
year ago. 

The low price partly explains why most 
households don’t wait to buy ethnic hair preps 
until it goes on deal. Just 11.9 percent of all 
households bought ethnic preps on deal last 
year, according to A.C. Nielsen.

Drug Store News, June 26, 1995 


air gel, mousse and other styling aids 
He: be found in 41 percent of

ttand/ body lation 


ore than half of all consumers bought 
hand and body lotions last year, 


according to the Nielsen Household 
Panel. The popularity of alpha-hydroxy acid- 
based creams and lotions fueled much of the 
crowth, and that trend will continue to 
dominate the category this year. Despite the 
plethora of AHA-based products already out 
there, new formulations are being cooked up 
in research and development departments of 
skin care manufacturers all the time. Drug 
store buyers continue to face tough decisions 
about how many AHA-based lotions to carry 
and where to put them.

purchases, a sizeable group of men—20 
percent—also purchased products to improve 
the look and feel of their skin. Overall, 
consumers spent a total of $8.89 on these 
products last year.

Drug Store News, June 26, 1995 


atteries are a necessity for most 
B shoppers, as is seen in the 87.9 percent 

penetration of this category. In a 
12-month period, 3.8 shopping occasions per 
buyer added up to a total of $17.44 per buyer 
or 5.61 units, with an average price of $3.11 
per unit, reflecting the dominant segment of 
alkaline batteries, especially in convenient 
smaller multipacks. 

Almost a quarter of purchases (23.1 
percent) were made on deal and 10 percent 
with a coupon. Discount/department stores 
led the retail channel race with 42.4 percent 
of units purchased and slightly less for dollars 
(41.3 percent). Drug lagged behind the food 
channel with 16.7 percent of units purchased 
in drug (14.5 percent in dollars) compared 
with 24.8 percent in food (22.6 percent in 
dollars). The primary female shopper 
percentage, at 68 percent (with 32 percent 
male), was the lowest for primary female 
purchaser among the general merchandise 
categories in this Nielsen study.

MARKETPLACK 


A.C. Nielsen Report 


F bow 


ore than half of all consumers (60.4 
percent) purchase film in a year, 
typically on two or three occasions. 


According to the study, on at least one 
occasion they bought more than one roll in 
that time (3.8 units total), probably due to 
attractively priced multipack film offers. 

The average price per unit is $5.84, adding 
up to $20.29 per buyer. 

The primary shopper for film is still female 
(72.7 percent). Most of her film shopping is 
done in discount/department stores, which 
racked up 42.8 percent of units purchased 
(43.9 percent of dollars). Drug garnered 22.3 
percent of units purchased (19.6 percent of 
dollars), and the food channel pulled in 23.7 
percent of units (18.4 percent in dollars). 

Since food and drug pull lower dollars in 
relation to units than do discount/department 
stores, one possible explanation is that the 
latter, which often has large electronics 
departments, consistently gets higher rings 
due to selling a higher percentage of product 
like advanced amateur film or more 36 vs, 24 
exposure rolls. 

Almost a third of rolls purchased (27.8 
percent) were bought on deal, with only 11.3 
percent purchased with a coupon. Film is a 
high-impulse item, and that is apparent in 
the fact that whether purchased on deal or 
with a coupon, film shows the highest 
percentage of units purchased at promotional 
prices among the general merchandise 
categories in this study.

MARKETPLACE 


A.C. Nielsen Report 


ree Ling corde 


Imost every consumer buys greeting 
Ai (89.6 percent) in a 12-month 

period. With eight shopping occasions 
per buyer, this is the kind of repeat purchase 
trips retailers want. It is also the most 
occasions per buyer of the general 
merchandise categories tracked in this study. 

As expected, women are primary card 
shoppers (78 percent), exceeded only by party 
goods as a higher primary female shopper 
percentage in the four general merchandise 
categories in the study. 

There is a good chance that the consumer 
will shop for cards in a drug store (23.9 
percent of units purchased), and although 
discount/department stores capture more card 
shoppers, it’s not by a wide gap (31.8 percent 
in units, 31.6 percent in dollars). Food is 
slightly behind the drug channel in units, but 
is neck in neck with drug in dollars (23.4 
percent for food, 23.7 percent for drug). In 
this category, dollars per unit was $1.66 per 
unit, but units per buyer (17.5) added up to 
$28.99. 

Around one-fifth of consumers reported 
that they bought cards on deal (21.4 percent), 
which reflects in-store promotions, but only 
3.2 percent bought with store or 
manufacturer coupons from ads. This activity 
reflects the everyday low price edge that 
discount department stores have in this 
category. The fact that price doesn’t capture 
more card business from drug suggests that 
the drug store is a retail environment where 
consumers are comfortable shopping for 
greeting cards.

A.C. Nielsen Report 


MARKETPLACR’ 


Nal, polish 


h J ail polish is one of the strongest 
impulse generators in chain drug 
stores. Nail polish users tend to buy at 

least two units a year, with most of the 

purchases motivated by price or color. 

According to Nielsen North An »rica 
household data, drug stores gene ate about 36 
percent of all nail polish dollar ¢aies. Discount 
department stores like Kmart and Wal-Mart 
and department stores like Macy’s and 
Penney’s generate about 43 percent of all 
dollar sales. 

Drug stores have tried in recent years to 
increase their share of polish sales by 
expanding space for nail care, bringing in a 
greater variety of nail treatment and nail 
manicure items. 

The strategy has given nail polish more 
visibility in drug stores, but sales have not 
kept pace with expectations. The polish 
category seems to need a jolt of product 
innovation like the bolt that hit lipsticks 
when Revlon launched Color Stay and the 
excitement that Factor created several years 
ago with its launch of No Color Mascara. 

But until then, the best thing that drug 
chains can do is to promote nail polish and tie 
it in as often as possible to sales in the nail 
treatment, nail manicure and lip color 
category. Lipstick, of course, is the most 
popular color cosmetic product and a natural 
companion to nail polish.

Eyehrouf 


eye bner 


ot every woman uses an eyebrow pencil 
| \ or an eyeliner as often as she uses 
lipstick or face makeup, but women 
who do use liners and pencils are very loyal to 
them, and there seems to be a great 
opportunity for drug stores to do more to 
court this shopper. 

According to Nielsen household pane! data, 
almost 43 percent of all dollar sales for 
eyeliners and eyebrow pencils are occurring 
in discount department stores like Wal-Mart 
or in more upscale department stores like 
Macy’s, Sears, J.C. Penney, etc. 

Food stores only get 19 percent of all dollar 
purchases, but drug stores, which have been 
expanding their assortment of liners and 
pencils in recent vears, get a respectable 35.4 
percent of al! dollars spent in this category. 

Drug stores can easily beat discount 
department stores on selection and variety in 
this category, and they can certainly beat 
department stores on price. In the past two 
years, women are shown a growing 
willingness to migrate from department 
stores into drug stores as they realize that 
many mass brands are just as high in quality 
as the much more expensive brands that 
department stores feature. 

On average, women spend about $2.66 for 
liners and brow pencils, and they don’t tend 
to wait for deals to make a purchase. Just 
about 15 percent of all units are bought with 
a coupon, rebate or other deal offer behind 
them.

MARKETPLACE 


A.C. Nielsen eee i 


lye shadow 


he natural look has made it tough for 

eye shadows of late. Fewer women use 

shadows, and many who do use them do 
so infrequently. 

According to A.C. Nielsen, the ty pical eye 
shadow shopper buys about one unit once a 
year. She spends, on average, about $5.07 for 
a shadow, and about 18 percent of all 
purchases are made on deal, meaning that a 
woman buys because she has a coupon or is 
offered a rebate or she spotted the shadow on 
sale. 

Grocery stores only capture about 15 
percent of all eye shadow dollar sales, and 
most of those sales are stimulated bs t 
convenience of doing one-stop s shop 
Discount department stores, regular 
department stores and drug stores gene! 
the bulk of eye shadow dollar sales 

Still, drug stores are only capturing 
percent of all dollars, which suggests that 
there is an opportunity for drug stores to lure 
women away from competing outlets. 

Drug stores might be able to get more 
women to buy shadows if they could find a 
way to make the product stand out more. 
Many women really seem to like the little 
pots of shadows sold in specialty and 
department stores, and brands that have 
brought that kind of packaging to the mass 
market have done well with shadows.

efinitely, the most popular cosmetic on a 
[ )rcomen' dressing table is lipstick. Just 

about every woman wears lipstick, and 
women on average buy lipstick nearly twice a 
year, averaging 2.4 units per buyer per year. 

The average price paid for a lipstick is $2.81, 
but many women have $9 lipsticks from 
Revlon and L’Oréal in their pocketbooks, co- 
existing quite naturally with Wet ‘n’ Wild and 
Artmatic lipsticks that cost substantially less 
than $2. 

Discount department stores, department 
stores and drug stores generate the bulk of all 
lipstick dollar sales. Food stores, which 
usually lack variety and don’t have the color 
impact of drug stores, only generate 14.5 
percent of all lipstick dollar sales.

women respond very positively when they have 
a coupon or rebate or sale to take advantage of. 
According to Nielsen household panel data, 
21.3 percent of all units are bought on deal.

starting to desert department store lipstick 
brands for mass market brands like Revlon’s 
Color Stay and L’Oréal’s Colour Supreme. At 
a time when shoppers demand value for their 
money, it is hard to justify spending $15 to 
$19 on a lipstick. And although Revlon and 
L’Oréal have a suggested retail price of about 
$9 for their lipsticks, they are often 
discounted in drug stores, and women who 
check the ads can find some very good buys 
these days.

Viewpoints 


Service helps more than just business 


bout 25 years ago, Jay signed up to tutor a 12-year- 

old boy from New York’s East Harlem. Of Puerto Ri- 

can heritage, Stanley was being raised by his grand- 
mother and an older brother in a “tough,” poor 
neighborhood. 

The initial idea was to help the boy improve his reading 
through basic tutoring sessions. Gradually, it evolved into 
much more. Jay and Stanley attended sports events together, 
played ball, watched movies and picked out books together. “I 
wanted to keep encouraging his reading,” Jay said. 

Soon, Jay was giving Stanley “lifestyle” lessons. For ex- 
ample, “I'd take him to furniture stores and show him the 
differences in quality between really cheap furniture—stuff 
that wouldn’t even outlast the payment scheme—and good 
quality products,” he said. And Jay didn’t hesitate to bring 
the boy to his home, to give him an example of a more tra- 
ditional nuclear family and 


We editors at Drug Store News wanted to recognize the 
chains we cover on a regular basis—in terms of news 
events, financial results, merchandising ideas, executive 
changes, etc.—for the ways in which they have made a pos- 
itive contribution to their communities. 

Becoming involved with local projects and charities often 
proves to be good for business, but community service also 
offers benefits that can’t be quantified on P&L statements. 
They’re measured in smiling faces, proud employees, 
stronger customer loyalty and happier, healthier, longer 
lives for people in the community. 

The Walgreen Co., winner in our largest chain category and 
the 1995 Community Service Award Grand Prize Winner, ex- 
emplifies the ongoing commitment and active involvement that 
characterizes a winning program. And Thomas Mammoser, 
Walgreen’s director of corporate communications, said it suc- 
cinctly: “We challenged our- 


let him see how more afflu- 
ent people lived. 

Stanley, 37 now, lives in 
Buffalo and works for the 
state of New York. Having 
attended three and a haif 
years of college when he 
was younger, Stanley is cur- 
rently going back to get his 
degree. But Jay is most 
proud that Stanley, married 
with two children, is “a good 
husband and father.” 

Developing this relation- 
ship with Stanley was “one of 
the most rewarding things I’ve ever done,” said Jay Forbes, 
who also happens to be publisher of Drug Store News. 

Jay’s experience with Stanley is just one example of how 
personal commitment coupled with active involvement can 
make a real difference in the lives of people who need the 
help. And the drug chains that have won Drug Store News’ 
Community Service Awards bring those qualities to life on 
an even bigger scale. 

The Community Service Awards winners you will read 
about in this issue have really “gone the extra mile,” not 
simply writing checks, but taking active leadership roles in 
charitable causes.

that genuinely benefit their communities.

munity Service Award winners, but we plan to make this

tions for our 1996 programs. If you think your chain quali-

Do what’s right and you'll be successful 


Ithough far from being a giant in the gro- 

cery industry, not even a giant in our home- 

town of Memphis, Tenn., our 11-store chain 
has developed guerilla marketing techniques and 
strategies designed to leverage market segments 
that the “big boys” overlook. 

One of our immediate interests is in developing | 
the African-American population in Memphis into 
a loyal customer base. One of our strategies is to f 
support positive issues that directly affect this 
market segment. 

Through several partnerships, we had achieved 
some level of market awareness, but we lacked hav- 
ing an event that tied “directly into” grocery sales. 

But in 1993, because of a close working relation- 
ship with our direct mail partner, we were given 
an opportunity to promote the Kwanza celebra- 
‘ion, and with it came the opportunity to actually 
bring customers into our stores. 

Graphically, our partner developed, and we ap- 
proved, a stand-alone four-page, four-color circular 
themed to the celebration of Kwanza. We chose art that sug- 
gested the closeness of the African-American family. 

We reserved space in the circular for valuable coupons, and 
we featured in that space products that were related to tradi- 
tional recipes such as Charleston crab spread with benne, 
sweet potage pudding, baked ham with a secret glaze, grand- 
ma’s creamed cornbread, etc. 

We sent the circular to the mailboxes of 119,000 African- 
American households. The response was overwhelming. We 
had a 6 percent coupon redemption for the nine coupons. A 
normal redemption for a piece that is not focused on a selected 
market-is about 1.3 percent. 


GUEST COLUMN 


22a GEST go 
— — 


BILL BUTLER 
| RRR 
Bill Butler is the 
advertising manag- 
er for Piggly-Wig- 
ly, a Memphis, 
enn.-based gro- 
cery store chain. 


In 1994, we chose to participate again with Kraft 
Foods as our only partner. And once again, we de- 
cided to tie our coupon offers to traditional recipes. 
Again, we decided to use restrained but tasteful 
graphics and copy points. We are still receiving acco- 
lades from the public. 

Our African-American consumers now feel that 
we are supportive of their efforts because we 
helped bring an important family concept and cel- 
ebration to the forefront in Memphis. 

Kraft was overjoyed with the results: 4.3 percent 
redemption. Other local firms have now expressed 
interest in being part of our 1995 mailing. 

Our cost each year has totaled no more than 
$10,100 for the complete turnkey effort. And for that 
investment, we’ve been able to maneuver a market 
segment pointedly, delicately, yet aggressively into 
our stores. Through other partnerships, we've also 
come to appreciate “cause marketing” as an effective 
way to create total market impact. Such programs are 
often developed with vendor partners and community 
leaders in the police, civic leaders and educators. We want the 
consumer to listen and hear, or watch and hear when we 
speak. 

Piggly Wiggly may be a food chain, and the readers of Drug 
Store News may be drug store operators, but our marketing 
needs are still the same. So to sum up, I would say this: 

Find your voice in the community. 

Pick your promotions and promotional partners. 

Look beyond the obvious. Listen to your heart. 

Read what others are doing in your market. 

Stay current with trends. 

Retain control of your advertising message and media,

COSMETICS 


& Fragrances 


Gleaning fragrance ideas 
from north of the border 


It’s July. The summer’s 
in full gear. It’s sizzling 
outside. So naturally, 
it’s time to talk about 
Christmas. 

Actually, it’s a little 
late to talk about 
Christmas. Most fra- 
grance buyers already 
have their Christmas 


LIZ PARKS programs in place. 
Ee or ee And it could be a good 
Christmas. There’s a lot 
happening in the mass market. Revlon has a 
major launch with Lasting. Coty/Quintes- 
sence has two major launches, Ghost Mysts 
and ICI. Renaissance has White Chantilly, 
plus a restage of Tabu and Alyssa Ashley. 

French Fragrances is repositioning Grey 
Flannel and Bowling Green; Perfumer’s 
Workshop is rolling out Les Girls and Water 
Colors; Jean Philippe has Romantic Illu- 
sions; Shiara has Sunset Café, Richard Bar- 
rie has Baryshnikov and Melrose Place; and 
Tsumura has Pierre Cardin Insatiable. This 
will be Pavion’s first year with a Wet ’n Wild 
fragrance. Plus, just about every alternative 
designer manufacturer, including Lady in 
Red, Parfums de Coeur, Fragrance Impres- 
sions and DQI has a version of CK One, ei- 
ther on the market or about to hit the mar- 
ket, and early reports are that sales of CK 
One knockoffs have been phenomenal. 

So what is there to worry about? 

Well, let’s forget for a moment about Wal- 
Mart, Kmart, Target and the other mass 
merchandisers who are honing in on the 
fragrance market and let’s look, for a sec- 
ond, at the department stores. 

Not too long ago, it looked like depart- 
ment store chains had lost their grip on the 
fragrance market. But, that wasn’t the case 
last year. Saks reported an 18 percent gain 
in fragrance sales post-Christmas. Bloom- 
ingdale’s said sales for the week of Christ- 
mas were up 27 percent. J.C. Penney’s 
Christmas fragrance sales were up 8 per- 
cent. And so on. 

Very few drug chains did as well. 

That could happen again because depart- 
ment stores seem to have figured out what fra- 
grance shoppers want. Not just low prices, but 
brands that promise something new, exciting, 
romantic and seductive. And, because it’s not 
always easy to know when a brand is the right 
brand, many women also want someone 
friendly and knowledgeable in the store. 

In the U:S., it’s very hard for the average 
chain drug store to offer any of that. For 
most drug stores, their strength is conve- 


nience and low prices. 

But is that enough to pull the fragrance 
shoppers away from the department store 
fragrance counters? 

In Canada, some of the chains with the 
strongest fragrance franchises don’t think 
so. Vancouver-based London Drugs, for ex- 
ample, has spent the last decade developing 
a cachet for its fragrance departments that 
lets the chain compete with department 
stores on an equal level, and it’s paid off. 

This year, London Drugs will be the only 
drug chain participating in the launch of 
several brand new department store fra- 
grances, including the launches of brands 
not normally available to the chain drug. 

Last Christmas, London was the only 
drug chain to have an exclusive on the 
launch of some Calvin Klein fragrances. 

Shirley Northorp, merchandise manager 
for cosmetics and fragrances, said that the 
chain is able to score such marketing coups 
because its customers and the upscale fra- 
grance manufacturers perceive London 
Drug as the equal of department stores in 
ambiance and product presentations. 

“We don’t deep discount the prestige fra- 
grances, she said. “We don’t have to. And 
we work with the manufacturers as part- 
ners, collaborating with them on promo- 
tions and GWPs just as the department 
stores do.” 

Now, it’s not realistic to think that the 
average American drug chain, at this stage 
in its development, could partner with de- 
signer fragrance manufacturers. The mer- 
chandising and servicing differences be- 
tween American drug stores and 
department stores are just too great. 

But, American drug chains could emulate 
department stores and Canadian chains 
like London Drug, Shoppers and Big V in 
other ways. They could alternate between 
price-off promotions and value-added pro- 
motions, and measure the effectiveness of 
the more sexy GWPs and catalog mailings. 

Just as they do now with lipsticks, nail pol- 
ish and other cosmetic and fashion acces- 
sories, they could look for niche items or niche 
brands that would give them some “exclusivi- 
ty” in fragrances, at least for a little while. 

Northorp points out that her customers 
certainly shop London Drug for conve- 
nience. But, it’s convenience plus that gives 
the chain its greatest appeal. 

American drug chains offer plenty of con- 
venience, but most are a little short on pro- 
viding “the plus”. Just a few little tweaks in 
that direction could make all the difference 
for the fragrance category this Christmas.

consolidation and retail focus.”

rapid expansion has

contributed to an 8 percent

for the fiscal year just ended.

corporate sales, including 
franchised stores, were up

Digestives market is all shook up 


Pepcid AC, Tagamet HB and Zantac switches present new opportunities 


By Mike Troy 


he arrival of Pepcid AC 

from Johnson & John- 

son/Merck in early June 
was the single biggest new 
product launch the OTC mar- 
ketplace has seen to date. 

With military precision, the 
joint venture engineered na- 
tionwide distribution just five 
weeks after getting Food and 
Drug Administration (FDA) 
approval on April 28. Product 
and merchandising materials 
were drop-shipped to retailers 
as ads were breaking; some 
chains even ran ads before 
the product was in stock to let 
customers know it would be 
available on June 8. 

The Pepcid AC launch has 
proven to be a case study of 
how to get an Rx-to-OTC 
switch to market quickly. And 
remarkable as the launch and 
the outlook for the product 
may be, the tip of the iceberg 
in the antacids category is 
only beginning to emerge. 

Joining Pepcid AC on 
store shelves later this year 
will be Tagamet HB from 
SmithKline Beecham. Final 
FDA marketing clearance 
was given to Tagamet HB 
on June 19. Early fall has 
been pinpointed as the 
launch date for the product. 

Another likely entry to the 
category will be an OTC ver- 
sion of Zantac. The Glaxo 
Wellcome joint venture will 
make its case before the 
FDA’s Nonprescription Drugs 
and Gastrointestinal Drugs 
advisory committees at an 
all-day hearing scheduled for 
July 13. The likelihood of a 
favorable recommendation 
appears to be strong. 

All three prescription prod- 
ucts—Pepcid, Tagamet and 
Zantac—belong to a class of 
drugs commonly referred to 
as H2s. It would seem un- 
likely then that FDA would 
balk at approving an OTC 
Zantac after clearing Taga- 
met HB and Pepcid AC. 

Although OTC versions of 
these drugs will compete 
against antacids, it is some- 
what of a misnomer to refer to 
them as such, since H2s pre- 
vent the production of stom- 
ach acids. Antacids neutralize 
stomach acid by absorbing it. 


Growth on the way 


Antacid sales grew 5 per- 
cent during 1994 to reach to- 
tal sales of roughly $866 mil- 
lion, according to Information 
Resources Inc. Of that, drug 
stores had about a 41 percent 
market share. 

Chain drug buyers and 
manufacturers agree the 
category is about to explode. 


“There has been an over- 
whelming response from the 
trade on the sell-in of Pep- 
cid AC,” said Louis Reyes, 
Pepcid AC professional 
product director with 
J&J/Merck. “I would have to 
agree with all 
of the analysts 
that say the 
category is go- 
ing to do noth- 
ing but grow. 
We feel there 
are a large 
number of 
new users 
who will be 
entering the 
market that in 
the past have 
not sought 
treatment.” 

Supporting 
that premise 
was a land- 
mark con- 
sumer study 
conducted in 
1992 by the 
Nonprescrip- 
tion Drug 
Manufactur- 
ers Associa- 
tion. Accord- 
ing to the 
study of self- 
medication 
trends, diges- 
tive problems due _ to 
overindulgence of food were 
encountered by more than 
half of the survey respon- 
dents. It was also a condi- 
tion most (60 percent) chose 
to tough out. 

Tagamet HB has been ap- 
proved for the treatment of 
heartburn. Pepcid

practically household names.

J&J/Merck is re-

ally going to be impacted by 
the arrival of Pepcid AC

because they were already 
losing market share before 
the product was switched,”

has such a strong following, 
I’m not sure they are going to 
get hit much, and J&J has 
done an excellent job growing 
Mylanta’s share. Mylanta 
will take a hit, but I don’t 
think it will be that severe.” 

Other buyers expressed 
similar opinions that liquid 
products will be hardest hit. 
One school of thought holds 
that liquid users tend to 
view their condition as se- 
vere and are more likely to 
use recently switched prod- 
ucts that are perceived as 
stronger and more effective. 

One certainty during the 
last half of 1995 and during 
1996 is that the antacids cat- 
egory will demand close 
scrutiny. Chain drug retail- 
ers have for years anticipat- 
ed the OTC availability of 
H2s. Some even expanded 
their planograms as far back 
as a year ago and overfaced 
existing brands pending the 
H2s’ arrival. The coming 
months will determine which 
antacids are culled from the 
product mix, and those that 
are able to survive in an 
emerging marketplace that 
seems certain to be dominat- 
ed by the H2 products.

batteries grew 22.3 percent. 


Image power

ness has developed rapidly 
thanks to point-and-shoot 
cameras with auto-every- 
thing features that eat up 
battery power.

Kodak are all launching 
new 3-volt photo lithium 
batteries this summer. 
These are smaller than the 
typical 6-volt photo lithium 
battery and are used in 
new, smaller cameras. 

Panasonic is introducing 
its new CR-2 photo lithium 
battery, and Duracell is 
launching its DLCR2. East- 
man Kodak’s new 3-volt 
lithium battery KCR-2 joins 
the Kodak Photolife line of 
photo/electronic batteries. 

Eveready is the only bat- 
tery manufacturer with a 
lithium AA battery, a high 
flash performer (since flash 
is high drain) for cameras 
that take the AA type. 

For the lithium AA, 
“flash is where it really 
shines and outlasts alkaline 
by three or four times,” said

years ago there is a vast im- 
provement—and I think the 
drug chains are probably do- 
ing better than most classes of 
trade in specialty batteries.”

Have a healthy respect for ‘side effects’ 


Whether you have pharmacy training or not, you know 
that most effective remedies also have side effects. The 


same rule applies in retailing. 


There are drawbacks to even the most successful strate- 
gies, as our cover story on the male consumer brings to 


mind. 
The good news is that drug chains, recogniz 


women are a significant majority of drug store shoppers, 
have been “softening” the decor of their stores, moving cos- 
metics and beauty care to more prominent positions, and 
adding signage, fixturing and displays that are more entic- 


ing to women. 


Even in these so-called enlightened times, however, it is 
also possible that making the drug store more attractive for 


women—with pastel colors, floral scents wafting 1 


and prominent beauty displays at the entry—could make a 


store seem too “feminine” 


Rather than ignoring or minimizing the downside that 
comes with every new strategy, drug chains should ac- 
tively look for these “side effects,” for therein lie the op- 
portunities. 

Getting back to that somewhat neglected male cus- 
tomer, drug chains should reach out to men now rather 
than later. Even if males represent only 20 percent of 
drug store shoppers (the low end of the various estimates 
available), that “minority” is worth billions of dollars of 
drug store sales. 

To balance their new attentiveness to women, chains 
should also make new overtures toward men thr ough ad- 
vertising, marketing and merchandising. As senior editor 
Lisa Fried points out in the cover story in this issue, ag- 
ing baby boomer males are more willing than their fa- 
thers to use products that mask the effects of aging. Male 
hair color is already show- 


ing that 


n the air 


for the men. 

Similarly, while develop- 
ing alliances with certain 
key manufacturers can be 
very positive and productive 
for retailer and manufactur- 
er alike, this is also a two- 
sided coin. 

For one thing, I wonder 
if the partner suppliers, 
who by nature have an 
edge with the retailer, may 
become complacent as com- 
petitive pressures ease. For 
another, I think it could 
become too difficult for new and innovative smal

Another good strategy with a “dark side” 


vertising to people with certain conditions—such 
nancy and diabetes—is an excellent way to get the 
formation to the right customer in a very cost- 


manner, it also has the potential to alienate a loyal cus- 
tomer who feels his or her privacy has been breached. 


is the use of

To balance out the possi- 
ble biases that can crop up 
when a chain forms special 
alliances with manufactur- 
ers, the retailer can set up a 
system of checks and bal- 
ances beforehand. Your 
chain can develop a series of 
reviews that will help keep 
manufacturers from becom- 
ing complacent and also 
build in avenues to give small and new suppliers direct ac- 
cess to the category manager at your chain. 

When it comes to direct mail programs targeted at pre- 
scription customers, chains can take a proactive stance by, 
for example, polling recipients of the mailing on a regular 
basis to make sure the chain’s integrity and good will is in- 
tact ?n the eyes of its customer. 

New methods, new programs and new ideas are essential 
to the continued health of the chain drug industry, but they 
won't be a long-terni cure if they cause you to sacrifice your 
core strengths of old. It’s up to you to keep that balance. 


Rather than ignoring or 
minimizing the downside of a 
new strategy, drug chains 
should actively look for these 
“side effects,” for therein lie 
the opportunities.

Drug Store News, July 24, 1995 


COSMETICS 


& Fragrances 


Marketplace its forum for what’s hot 


There was a lot going on at 
last month’s NACDS Market- 
place show in San Francisco. 
Buyers looking for trendy 
new items or smart new mer- 
chandising presentations had 
easy access to plenty of excit- 
ing opportunities. 

Drug Store News can’t do 
justice to all that was hap- 
pening in cosmetics and fra- 
grances in one short column. 
The tremendous variety of 
items made it difficult to see everything, but we 
did keep an eye out for interesting niche items. 
Here’s a sample of some of the programs and 
products that caught our eye. 

Victoria Vogue, which makes powder puffs 
and other cosmetic applicators, cleansers and 
accessories, is starting to build a brand fran- 
chise in what has been considered just a 
commodity category. The Bethlehem, 
Pa.-based company has a new header 
panel, which invites customers to 
“see and feel” the difference in its 
products. 

The company is extending its 
brand franchise to include a line 
of “professional” sponges, mitts, 
wedges and puffs, as well as a 
new “safer” cotton swab for babies 
available in blue or pink stems. 

Marlyn Nutritionals, based in 
Scottsdale, Ariz., is getting some posi- 
tive feedback from buyers who tested its 
oral and topical products meant to be used to- 
gether for healthier skin, hair and nails. 
Marlyn’s 4 Hair, 4 Skin and 4 Nails have been 
doing very well in what seems to be an emerging 
market segment. 

This year, Los Angeles-based An-Kar Prod- 
ucts is entering the “dual defense” category with 
a system called the Dermanova Dual Defense 
Anti-Wrinkle System, which includes a nutri- 
tional supplement for the skin. The oral supple- 
ment is meant to be used in combination with a 
topical anti-wrinkle cream. An-Kar is already a 
player in the niche category of thigh creams with 
its ATC Thigh Cream. 

Ever since Sassaby’s Jane proved that the 
MAC packaging concept combined with value- 
oriented price points could work fabulously in a 
mass environment, there’s been a lot of buyer in- 
terest in finding other products that could have a 
similar positive impact on customer impulse 
spending habits. 


Marketplace had a number of them on display 
including a new modular unit from Deerfield 
Beach, Fla.-based Prestige Cosmetics. The 
presentation, the packaging and the product for- 
mulations all came across as innovative and af- 
fordable. The company’s waterproof lipstick and 
eyeliner pencils, self-sharpening eye and lip au- 
tomatic liners and jumbo crayons for eyes and 
lips looked particularly interesting. 

Buyers found a similarly striking presentation 
at the Nat Robbins booth. Made by Port Wash- 
ington, N.Y.-based Great American Cosmetics, 
Nat Robbins also has a new, striking in-line fix- 
ture. The company is also introducing a jumbo 
mechanical eye shadow pencil and a jumbo matte 
lipstick crayon, perhaps the first such products to 
reach the mass market. 


Some leading 
drug chains are currently generating over a mil- 
lion dollars a year chainwide off the Nat Robbins 
counter unit, which is only 9 inches high by 12 
inches wide. 


Lip service 


Another sleeper with similar potential is the 
Designer Lipstick Collection from Zalon Profes- 
sional, out of Ontario, Calif. One leading drug 
chain is doing a million-dollar-plus business just 
from its 72-piece counter displays. There are 12 
moisturizing shade formulas housed in distinc- 
tively colorful designer lipstick cases. 

The company is also producing a controlled la- 
bel lipstick collection for another leading drug 
chain. For Christmas, there is a collection of gold 
cosmetic gift sets. 


Coty’s done it again. 

Vanilla Musk, which launched last 
year, has won the Fragrance Founda- 
tion’s prestigious FIFI award as the best 


Fragrance innovators recognized 


aging in both the men’s and the women’s 
broad distribution categories. 

Sears, Roebuck and 
Fragrance Foundation’s “Retailer of the 


Oo. was named the 


Some buyers think there is an undeveloped op- 
portunity to sell natural cosmetics in chain drug 
stores, and they are probably right. Ulta3, a 
chain of Chicago-based beauty specialty stores, 
has been generating some exceptional turns with 
a selection of natural ingredient lipsticks made 
by Kiss My Face, based in Gardiner, N.Y. 

Kiss My Face is positioned to appeal to environ- 
mentally sensitive consumers who tend +o be the 
younger shoppers that drug stores are trying to 
court. The products use no animal ingredients, no 
preservatives, are not tested on animals and are 
packaged in natural birch wood cases. In addition 
to lipsticks and lip balms, the company also 
makes mascaras, moisturizers, shavers and facial 
care products. 

CiCi Cosmetics out of Culver City, Calif., is 
also doing well in Ulta3 stores. CiCi Cosmetics 
has strong distribution in beauty supply stores, 
and at Marketplace it was introducing a new 

matte cream lipstick and matte lip liner 

pencil, both with unique benefits. The 

products are hypoallergenic and not 
tested on animals. 

Los Angeles-based Jordana 
Cosmetics has a beauty store 
heritage, and you could see it in 
its high tech displays for fast- 
turning items like lip liners, lip- 
sticks, lip glosses and mascaras. 

At price points averaging between 


$1 and $2, its cosmetics are perform- 
ing very well in chains like Duane 
Reade and Longs. 

Buyers were also busy at the BioCos- 
metics booth, checking out its new Black Opal 
color cosmetic line targeted to African-American 
women. The moderately priced line features a 
number of unique formulas including a matte- 
plus-moisture lipstick, vitamin-enriched lip pen- 
cils, triple-milled velvet blushers, and most im- 
portantly, since the brand franchise originated in 
skin care, a line of face makeups that include oil- 
free, lightweight liquid foundations, full coverage 
creme sticks and dual benefit creme-to-powder 
foundations for medium coverage. Because 
African-American skin tends to be oily, there are 
also four shades of an oil-absorbing powder. 

There were some single SKU products that 
looked promising, especially Ardell’s new Mani- 
cure Mate Brush-on Nail Glue, guaranteed not to 
spill or dry out. Los Angeles-based Ardell also 
owns the Woltra ethnic skin care brand, and it is 
introducing a line of face masks targeted to 
African-American women. The company is

Drug Store News, July 24, 1995

Putting some perspective 
on the future of OTCs 


With 1995 a little more 
than half gone and NACDS 
Marketplace behind us, it 
is time for some mid-year 
predictions. I predict that 
the following events and 
trends will take place dur- 
ing the next 12 months. 
‘When Marketplace con- 
— venes in San aren bent 
year, the show floor hours 
will be further expanded. As 
the number of exhibitors 
has grown, retailers find they don’t have 
enough time to meet with all the vendors they 
would like, let alone walk the floor looking for 
new products. One option would be to open the 
show floor for three full days, instead of the 
current three hours on Sunday, full days Mon- 
day and Tuesday and a half day on Wednesday. 
Three full days would only be a net increase of 
one hour over the current schedule, but it 
would be a more productive use of time. 
*Private-label sales of antacids will decline as 
Pepcid AC, Tagamet HB and a soon-to-be-avail- 
able (within six months) OTC version of Zantac 
draw users away from existing manufacturer and 
retailer brands. Private-label antacids account for 
11.5 percent of drug’s 41 percent share of the $900 
million antacids category. The impact of hot-sell- 
ing new branded items in antacids will recreate 
the situation that arose following the introduction 


HBC 


OTCs 


of Aleve more than a year ago. A substantial part 
of that product’s market share growth came at the 
expense of store brands. 

*-The Breathe Right nasal strip from CNS, a 
blockbuster item last year, will get even hotter 
this year as the product will soon be available in 
various sizes and in a new sports pack. Its success 
will attract private-label competitors, and a 
knock-off version of the patented Breathe Right 
will soon appear. 


Herbal products will be hot 


‘Herbal products and supplements will be hot 
items. Garlic and ginseng will continue to domi- 
nate sales, but newcomers such as gingko biloba, 
saw palmetto, feverfew and shark cartilage will 
grow quickly and expand their market shares. 

‘OTC department sales will continue to be at 
the mercy of the consumer press. Heavy publicity 
about Tagamet HB and an OTC Zantac will bene- 
fit the antacids category, but sales will occasional- 
ly suffer as negative reports surface about drug 
interactions and the growing number of Rx-to- 
OTC switches. 

‘Increasing numbers of managed care organi- 
zations will cover OTCs, creating a new prof- 
itability concern for chain drug retailers. Third- 
party payors will recognize that, in some cases, 
the use of an OTC will help a patient avoid the 
expense of a doctor’s visit and a prescription. As 
OTCs are added to third-party formularies, 
chains will face a new source of margin pressure.

Study cites Hispanics’ brand loyalty 


DALLAS — Hispanics in the 
Dallas/Fort Worth market 
overwhelmingly rely on 
Tylenol for headaches and 
Pepto Bismol for stomach 
problems, according to a re- 
cent market study by the Dal- 
las-based research firm of Rin- 
con & Associates. 

Nearly 55 percent of His- 
panics surveyed said they use 
Tylenol versus 21 percent for 
Advil, 1.7 percent for Aleve 
and 1.6 percent for Excedrin. 
Roughly 53 percent of those 
surveyed said they use Pepto 
Bismol, compared to 10 per- 
cent for Alka Seltzer, 3.3 per- 
cent for Mylanta and 2.5 per- 
cent for Maalox. 


The reason for the strong 
brand preference is that “those 
particular manufacturers have 
national efforts to target His- 
panics, so you would also ex- 
pect those brand preferences in 
other markets as well,” said 
Edward T. Rincon, president of 
Rincon & Associates. 

The study also examined the 
preferences of Hispanics in 
Dallas/Fort Worth, the na- 
tion’s eighth largest Hispanic 
market, when it comes to pre- 
scription medicines. Eckerd 
was the clear winner as a 
source for prescription drugs, 
mentioned by 63.5 percent of 
respondents as the pharmacy 
they used most often during 


the past three months. Kroger 
was a distant second, men- 
tioned by 4.6 percent of those 
surveyed. 

The study was conducted 
during April 1995 and in- 
volved telephone interviews 
with 600 Hispanics. Bilingual 
interviewers were used, and 
63 percent of the interviews 
were conducted in Spanish. 
There are approximately 
700,000 Hispanics in the Dal- 
las/Fort Worth area, roughly 
17 percent of the population. 

The study also examined 
media habits and brand pref- 
erences in other product cate- 


gories. For more information, 
call (214) 750-0102.

Bronchial inhalants come under fire after model's death 


PEMBROKE PINES, Fla. 
— Despite the excellent 
safety record of Primatene 
Mist, the recent death of 
budding supermodel Kris- 
ten Taylor hours after using 
one of the inhalers has cast 
doubt on the product’s domi- 
nance of the bronchial in- 
halants category. 

Primatene, from. the 
Whitehall Robbin’s division of 
American Home Products, 
had 1994 sales of roughly $52 
million, according to Informa- 
tion Resources Inc. The 30- 
year-old brand’s next closest 
competitor is Bronkaid Mist 
from Bayer Consumer Care 


with 1994 sales of $11 mil- 
lion. Drug’s market share is 
roughly 46 percent. 


Sales impact uncertain 


The full impact of Taylor’s 
death on Primatene sales 
won't be known for weeks. 

At press time, Taylor’s ex- 
act cause of death had not 
been determined. Initial re- 
ports attributed to Broward 
County Medical Examiner 
Dr. Joshua Perper were that 
use of Primatene Mist, which 
contains the active ingredient 
epinephrine, caused Taylor to 
have an irregular heartbeat. 
An official cause of death will 


not be known until blood toxi- 
cology tests are completed in 
late July, Perper said. 


Damage may be done 


Even if Primatene is ab- 
solved of responsibility in 
Taylor’s death, the brand’s 
equity may have already 
suffered damage, despite an 
enviable safety record. 

“For more than 30 years, 
Primatene Mist has played 
an important role for the mil- 
lions of consumers with mild 
asthma who have used the 
medication according to the 
label,” Whitehall Robins said 
in a prepared statement. 


Despite the product’s 
record of safe use, Taylor’s 
death is likely to rekindle 
calls from patient advocacy 
groups and health profes- 
sionals who believe epine- 
phrine-containing products 
should not be sold without a 
prescription. Opponents of 
OTC asthma remedies con- 
tend that the condition is dif- 
ficult for patients to self-di- 
agnose and therefore doctors 
need to be closely involved. 

The continued OTC avail- 
ability of epinephrine-con- 
taining OTCs was the subject 
of review last fall by the Food 
and Drug Administration’s 


Nonprescription Drugs Advi- 
sory Committee. Although 
concerned about the ability of 
consumers to self-medicate 
with OTCs, the group recom- 
mended the products contin- 
ue to be available because 
their low potency and short 
duration of action would not 
keep asthma patients from 
their regular doctor visits. 

“(The drug] has been used 
by consumers since the early 
1960s and has a safety record 
that is as good as other com- 
monly used OTC medicines,” 
according to the Nonprescrip- 
tion Drug Manufacturers As- 
sociation.

By Lisa I. Fried 


hen he lived on his 
own in Chicago, Joe 
Dickerson did most 
of his household 
shopping in a near- 
by Walgreens. 
“There was a food store a block or so 
away, explained the vice president 
and general manager of Wool- 
worth’s Drug Mart division. “But I 
went to Walgreens because it was 
easier to get in and out of.” 

Dickerson is not alone.

However, nearly one in two men 
shop in a drug store, according to a 
1994 Simmons Market Research 
Survey. And men are becoming in- 
creasingly concerned about their ap- 
pearance. Over a third of 540 men 
surveyed by Psychology Today ap- 
proved of using hair color to treat 
premature gray, and more said old- 
er men should color their hair. 
“Hair is a traditional signal of youth 
and power, an index of male virili-
