Survey: men a strong target 


Men also pay a lot of attention to 
their bodies. Thirty-eight percent 
of the men said that muscle mass 
was moderately important, and 10 
percent said it was extremely 
important. 

Some progressive drug chains are 
recognizing that men are indeed 
changing, and they are beginning to 
rethink their merchandising and 
marketing plans. 

“A couple gets up on Saturday 
and says, we’re going to the store,” 
said Andy Striefel, senior vice presi- 
dent-merchandising, Thrifty Pay- 
Less. “Where will they go? 


Drug stores are the overwhelming destination of choice for men for OTCs, at 64 percent, 
second only to prescriptions at 78 percent. 


nience and the ability to get in and 
out of a store quickly are the prima- 
ry reasons men shop in drug stores, 
according to an exclusive survey 
conducted for Drug Store News by 
America’s Research Group. 


Ignoring a key segment 


But if you're like most drug store 
executives, you rarely think about 
the men who shop your stores. “It’s 
not a critical mass, so it’s inefficient 
to spend against it in advertising,” 


said the senior vice president of 


merchandising at a national drug 
chain. This chain merchandises 
men’s toiletries next to tobacco-re- 
lated products. “It’s a logical adja- 
cency,’ the executive at the chain 
explained. After all, “we don’t want 
to push men away.” 

This is a common philosophy. The 
chain drug industry has traditional- 
ly ignored the men who shop its 
stores or taken a half-hearted at- 
tempt at reaching them. Most oper- 
ate on the philosophy that women 
read the ads, make the brand deci- 

sions and do the shopping. For ex- 

ample, in the Walgreens in Con- 
cord, Calif., the men’s toiletries 
section 1s loc ated directly across 
from the Cover Girl and Max Factor

Male shopping patterns changing 


One national chain that has nev- 
er advertised to men is now consid- 
ering creating promotions for the 
men who shop in its downtown 
stores during their lunch hour. “I’m 
sure there is more of an opportunity 
to reach men there,” said an execu- 
tive at the chain. 

To provide the industry with a 
better picture of the men in their 
stores, Drug Store News worked 
with America’s Research Group 
(ARG) to study male shopping 
habits. In total, ARG asked 416 men 
who had shopped in a drug store in 
the past three months to tell why 
they shop there, what they buy and 
what they like/dislike about drug 
stores. ARG also asked 584 women 
the same questions in the hopes of 
discovering different behavioral pat- 
terns among the genders. 

The information may surprise 
you.

about drug stores and shopping in 
general. Women like to browse 
drug stores much more than men 
do. Only 12 percent of men said 
they like to browse (compared with 
24 percent of women). Men (43 per- 
cent) are also more likely to find 
what they need and rush out of the 
stores than women (27 percent). 

Women are more sale-conscious 
(31 percent versus men’s 17 per- 
cent) and prefer to comparison shop 
more than men do (30 percent ver- 
sus men’s 15 percent), according to 
the survey. 

What do men buy in drug stores? 
We asked the men who made a pur- 
chase at a drug store within the past 
three months to tell us what they 
bought on their most recent trip. 

The majority went to pick up pre- 
scriptions (66 percent) and OTCs 
(52 percent). A quarter of the men 
bought a toiletries item. Twenty- 
two percent made a purchase in the 
greeting card and/or photo depart- 
ment. Twenty-one percent bought 
an oral hygiene product. 

When we asked the sample 
where they usually shop for vari- 
ous products, the majority cited 
drug stores as the choice for pre- 
scriptions (78 percent) and OTCs 
(64 percent). Drug stores are far 
more popular with men for vita- 
mins and nutritional supplements 
(44 percent) than mass merchants 
(29 percent) and supermarkets (18 
percent). 


Greeting cards a popular spot 


The greeting card department in 
a drug store is a popular place for 
men. Forty-one percent prefer to 
buy greeting cards in drug stores 
compared to mass merchants (34 
percent) and supermarkets (15 
percent.) 

Retailers with electronic greeting 
card kiosks in their stores are like- 
ly to draw even more men into the 
department, as they appreciate the 
individualized nature and persua- 
sive appeal of the machine. Thirty- 
five percent of CreataCard users 
are male, according to American 
Greetings.

men surveyed are more loyal to su-

stores (33 percent) and mass mer- 
chants (28 percent). Given men’s 
growing concern about their ap- 
pearance, the men’s toiletries sec-

Forty-three percent of men prefer 
to buy film/photo finishing in a drug 
store, but almost the same percent- 
age also shop for these items in mass 
merchants (41 percent). An equal 
number of men shop drug stores and 
supermarkets (36 percent each) for 
oral hygiene products, rather than 
mass merchants (26 percent). 

In general, most men plan their 
purchases in drug stores, but half 
buy snacks, beverages and other food 
items on impulse, which presents 
some major opportunities in terms of 
in-store merchandising. Given men’s 
preference to shop for toiletries in 
supermarkets, perhaps it might pay 
to put an endcap of shaving cream or 
related products near the conve- 
nience food section. 

The survey clearly shows that men 
have strong opinions about drug 
stores and do buy products in several 
categories. In a time when drug 
stores are losing more share to other 
retailers, drug chains could likely 
benefit by making their stores more 
appealing to men.

motions solely to women. 

Heightened media atten-

men didn’t use sun care pro-

chain is doing quite well 
with the Black Opal men’s 
skin care line and depart- 
ment store skin care lines 
targeted to sophisticated, 
professional men, he added. 

Andy Striefel, senior vice 
president of merchandising 
at Thrifty PayLess, believes 
that men are becoming 
more interested in skin 
care. He has approached 
mass skin care manufactur- 
ers about it. 

“I’ve told them there’s 
nothing for men,” Striefel 
said. “Men are buying Pleni- 
tude and women’s merchan- 
dise. We know it’s happen- 
ing—you can see it in the 
store. And in many cases, 
the woman is buying it for 
the husband.”

ucts available. Avon recent- 
ly launched Anew Perfor- 
mance For Men, designed to 
make shaving smoother.

Drug Store News, August 7, 1995 


Viewpoints 


ff DITORIAL 


Tune into America’s many cultures 


oday, there’s a renewed interest in their own heritage 
and culture on the part of African Americans. “On a va- 
riety of levels—in home furnishings, music, clothing, 
books and entertainment—Black consumers are clamoring 
for merchandise and information that reflects the Black expe- 
rience,” says Amy Hilliard-Jones, president and CEO of The 
Hilliard-Jones Marketing Group, a Chicago-based firm that 
develops “strategic multicultural marketing plans” for major 
corporations and entrepre- 


(such as Black magazines, African American radio stations 
and local Black newspapers), and where marketing pro- 
grams support ethnic events and community initiatives. 

“There has to be a corporate commitment to make this mar- 
ket a priority,” says Hilliard-Jones. “It involves promotion, ad- 
vertising, community events, and the building of goodwill at a 
grass roots level.” 

Goodwill is built at the corporate level, but it can be quickly 
undone at the store level. 


neurs. Hilliard-Jones has 
over 18 years of marketing 
and advertising experience, 
and her book on multicultur- 
al marketing, Reaching the 
Soul of America, is due out in 
early 96. 

What’s critical for chain 
drug retailers to understand 
is that “more and more peo- 
ple are considering the sensi- 
tivity of the retailer toward 
African Americans in the 
process of making purchasing 
decisions,” according to 
Hilhiard-Jones. 

Up to this point, most mass marketers have failed to create 
ongoing, comprehensive and integrated programs to reach 
out to ethnic customers, Hilliard-Jones observes, and they 
could be missing out on billions of dollars in potential sales. 
The African American market alone represents some $400 
billion in spending power, an increase of 33 percent since 
1990. Looking ahead, the Black American population will 
grow at a rate of 44 percent over the next 25 years, as com- 
pared to a 10.5 percent rate for the White population. 

For drug chains, says Hilliard-Jones, the most effective 
way to increase sales to ethnic consumers is with an inte- 
grated approach—where the advertising message reflects a 
genuine knowledge of and respect for the ethnic consumer’s 
culture, where the message is placed in targeted media 


Customer service is a critical 
component of your company’s 
communication with ethnic 
consumers. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 
i ee 


Chains must make a commit- 
ment to the training of store 
managers and associates be- 
cause customer service is a 
critical component of your 
company’s communication 
with ethnic consumers. 

With specialized products, 
such as ethnic hair care items 
(see story on page 12), cus- 
tomers expect store personnel 
to be able to answer ques- 
tions; if drug chains can’t pro- 
vide this service, consumers 
will go elsewhere, such as 
beauty supply or deparment stores, according to Hilliard- 
Jones. Equally important is having a broad selection of ethnic 
products consistently in stock in a well-maintained section. 

The opportunity to sell more products goes far beyond the 
“obvious” hair care and cosmetics sections. For example, 
Hilhiard-Jones cites herbal remedies and natural products for 
hair and skin care. “The trend to using natural products that 
is becoming part of the general market has always been a part 
of the African American culture and heritage,” she says. 

It’s not difficult for drug chains to appeal to important 
and growing ethnic population segments, as long as there 
is an ongoing, top-down commitment. “Building share in 
ethnic markets requires being there in ethnic markets— 
connecting with consumers at home, at retail and in their 
communities,” Hilliard-Jones advises. 


Canadian drug chains face a new day 


emember the “good old days?” Remember 

when there were few PPOs or PBMs or 

mail-order operators? Was there ever a 
time when pharmacists could charge $6, $9 
even $12 per script? This is the place in time 
that Canadian drug store retailers now find 
themselves. But that world is changing rapidly 
and we are definitely at a fork in the road. One 
path will lead to a U.S.-style marketplace 
where third-party administrators hold all the 
cards. This is already happening with new 
pharmaceutical benefit manager (PBM) en- 
trants just starting to cautiously test out the 
Canadian marketplace. The other path will 
lead to a new retail health care environment 
where the value that a pharmacist provides is 
clearly recognized and rewarded. Fortunately, there is still 
time for this latter scenario to unfold—if Canadian pharmacy 
operators can learn from the experience of the U.S. market 
over the last two decades. 

In many areas, Canadians have often looked across the 
border for innovations in retailing and other business initia- 
tives, but in the case of managed care, we look at the squeeze 
on retail pharmacy in the U.S. and shudder. 

The Canadian pharmacy industry is experiencing extensive 
upheaval and we are trying to define our role in managed 
care. This new role must preserve and enhance the role of 
pharmacies in the delivery of a top-quality health care system. 

In one sense you could say Canada has already achieved a 
healthy partnership for pharmacy, as all provincial govern- 
ments operate as pharmacy benefit managers and are the 
payers for approximately 50 percent of the prescriptions dis- 
pensed in the country. These governments have instituted for- 
mularies and have encouraged generic substitution and trial 
prescription programs. Provincial governments are probably 
some of the most sophisticated PBMs in existence and have 
been operating in this environment for 20 years. 

On the other hand, we now see companies such as FoxMeyer 
move into Canada to operate PBMs. As an industry, we are not 
experienced in dealing with these for-profit PBMs, who have a 
ra mandate and different ownership. 


GUEST COLUMN 


“The Canadian 
pharmacy industry 

is experiencing 
extensive upheaval.” 


_ Sherry Porter 


Sherry Porter is president 
and CEO of the Canadian As- 
sociation of Chain Drug Stores. 


A national pharmacy coalition was formed in 
Canada in June, representing all provincial pro- 
fessional associations and the Canadian Associa- 
tion of Chain Drug Stores. Its goal is to design, 
develop and promote the implementation of drug 
plan benefit management sirategies by pharma- 
cists. This is the first step in a very long process 
that will orient the pharmacy industry to plan 
for, accept and participate in the onset of a new 
and different managed care scenario in Canada. 

Another issue causing upheaval for retail 
stores with pharmacies in Canada relates to the 
sale of tobacco. In November 1993, the Ontario 
government introduced legislation that would re- 
move tobacco from those establishments that 
also had pharmacy dispensaries. After many 
months of lobbying by the chains and a large group of indepen- 
dent pharmacies, the legislation was passed and became law 
on Jan. 1, 1995. This was a case of pharmacy being completely 
blindsided by special interest groups. Pharmacists found them- 
selves in the very difficult professional situation of having to 
defend their right to sell a legal but controversial product. 

The pharmacy groups challenging the legislation felt this 
was a business issue and the battle was fought on that basis. 
Studies showed that for every dollar a customer spent on to- 
bacco, he/she spent an additional $.378 on other purchases. 
This clearly showed the loss of tobacco sales impacted not only 
the loss of margin contribution, but also a significant loss of 
traffic-building and sales. 

The first legal challenge based on constitutional grounds 
was rejected by the court of first instance, but since then, 
the case has been granted status with a higher court. This 
next round will be heard in the fall of 1995. 

Governments in other provinces have expressed strong in- 
terest in the Ontario case. If the case does not receive a favor- 
able ruling from the court of appeals, provinces across Canada 
would likely pass similar legislation. This social trend, spear- 
headed by the outcry of public interest groups, will undoubted- 
ly continue. Policy watchers in the U.S. should be particularly 
diligent in keeping abreast of the issue and involve them- 
selves in all consultations.

By Liz Parks 


the retail level, the ethnic 
products industry is becom- 
ing more price competitive 
every day as aggressive dis- 
counters like Wal-Mart, Sally’s 
Beauty Supply and independently 
owned beauty and barber supply 
stores continue to buy low, adver- 
tise low and sell low. 

“This industry is changing,” said 
Kent Humphreys, president of Ok- 
lahoma City-based Jack’s Service, a 
leading ethnic product distributor- 
ship, “and if retailers don’t under- 
stand the changes, they will miss a 
lot of opportunities.” 

“Kight years-ago, relaxer kits 
were selling for $8.99 and $9.99. 
Today, kits sell for $4.99, $5.99, at 
tops, $6.99,” one source said. “And 
as prices decline, margins decline. 
And it becomes a vicious cycle be- 
cause without profits, it’s harder 
for manufacturers to introduce 
new items, and without new items 
to drive sales, you can’t grow the 
category.” 


ee fight back against low prices 
and preserve what is left of 
shrinking margins, many chain 
drug retailers and some mass mer- 
chandisers like Target are offering 
their shoppers more value-added 
services. Those include broader as- 


kK! 


sortments, product mixes tailored to 
the neighborhood, improved in- 
stock service rates, and a greater 
range of products that appeal to 
African-American shoppers. 

With no new styling trend on the 
immediate horizon, 90 percent of 
the buyers are unwilling to guess 
when the ethnic beauty care catego- 
ry will turn around, but they do 
agree that when a store can get the 
right fix on its customer base, set 
up the right size department, stay 
in stock, carry the products in de- 
mand, be the first to have new 
iterns, then it’s still possible to grow 
sales. 

Right now, Minneapolis-based 
Target seems to be the best example 
and the one most often cited by cate- 
gory managers in the ethnic indus- 
try of a chain that has generated 
dramatic growth in ethnic beauty 
care, primarily because of its sophis- 
ticated micromarketing strategies. 

At Target, buyers create mer- 
chandise assortments that fit the 
demographics of different clusters of 
customers, organized by race, in- 
come, age, education and employ- 
ment status. Then the company tai- 
lors the mix for each store based on 
the types of customer clusters that 
each store services. 

Drug chains with point of sale 
scanning data available to them are 
moving in a similar direction. No one

hit by price competition 


has reached Target’s level of exper- 
tise yet, but chains like Walgreens, 
Eckerd, Osco, PayLess, CVS, Duane 
Reade and Rite Aid are trying. 

And, as one source pointed out, a 
chain does not have to institute a 
full blown micro marketing program 
to find new ways to satisfy its cus- 
tomers. In Alabama, Big B is plan- 
ning to add ethnic hair color lines 
like Dark & Lovely, Optimum Care 
and Revlon’s Fanciful to its general 
market hair color planogram. 

According to one source, several 
major chains will make a similar 
planogram change later this year, 
with the expectation, he said, “that 
total hair color sales will go up be- 
cause that’s where research tells 
them customers expect to find eth- 
nic hair color brands.” 


_ Gardner, vice president of 
arketing for Soft Sheen, which 
makes Optimum Care hair color, 
calls hair color “the chemical of the 
nineties. It isn’t relaxers or curlers 
that are driving sales these days,” 
she pointed out. “It’s hair color and 
that’s creating new opportunities. 
Until about a year ago, this was an 
under-performing category, but it’s 
hot now, and that’s partly because 
manufacturers are supporting hair 
color more vigorously and partly be- 
cause retailers are giving it a 
stronger presentation. 


“Women used to go to beauty and 
barber shops to buy color because 
that’s where they could find a selec- 
tion. Now chain drug stores are get- 
ting more of that business.” 

But a source who has familiar 
with the Osco/Sav-On stores in 
California pointed out that “signifi- 
cantly, ethnic skin care and ethnic 
shaving products always turn 
much faster in the general market 
sections. We’d always find the out- 
of-stocks in the skin care depart- 
ment and the shaving department, 
and, until we got the next ship- 
ment in, we’d go take the product 
off the shelf from the ethnic hair 
care planogram and put it wherev- 
er it was needed in the general 
market sets. 

“It’s always been obvious that 
women expect to find skin care 
products in the skin care depart- 
ment and men’s shaving products in 
the men’s toiletries department. Not 
in the hair care department.” 

A manager in one Los Angeles 
Sav-On store also reported that 
men’s shaving and women’s skin 
care sell out much faster in the gen- 
eral market planogram. “That’s 
where people expect to find these 
items,” he said.

tant, but it is particularly important

Drug Store News, August 7, 1995 


Skin and hair color drive ethnic category 


o far this year, ethnic 
GF skin care and hair col- 

oring products have 
been the hottest category 
segments within ethnic toi- 
letries. 

Buyers report that Black 
Opal is driving the growth 
in skin care while Optimum 
Care, Dark & Lovely, Dark 
& Natural and Revlon are 
driving the growth in hair 
color. 

The buyer for one major 
drug chain said he was sell- 
ing more relaxers and relax- 
er conditioning products 
than ever. “But the problem 
is,” he said, “is that I’m giv- 
ing them away. Everybody 
and their brother is promot- 
ing relaxers to build traffic.” 

According to distributors 
like Dan Medow, president 
of Detroit-based Standard 
Distributing; Mike O’Neil, 
president of Harris; and 
Jim Normandin, ethnic 
products merchandise man- 
ager for Hartford, Conn.- 
based Beauty Enterprises, 
the best selling relaxer 
brands are Optimum Care, 
Dark & Lovely, Dark & 
Natural, Soft & Beautiful 
and Just For Me, a chil- 
dren’s relaxer. 

In addition to skin care 
and hair coloring, there are 
also niche segments within 


ethnic hair care that are do-

Drug Store News, August 7, 1995 


23 


More and more retailers 
are developing upscale 
toiletries lines of their 
own, and the pendulum is 
shifting away from knock- 
off, generic products to 
high quality lines with 
unique formulations and 
packaging. 

mass marketer is con- 
sidering launching a skin 
care line for kids. 

And CBI Laboratories 
and OM Sciences are creating a 35-plus SKU 
line of bath, skin, sun and hair care products 
for a national drug chain. 

This upscale line, which the drug chain could 
launch in the fourth quarter, is being developed 
to build consumer loyalty and increase profits 
in the front end. 

Everything about the line has been carefully 
planned, from the scents (bath products scented 
with vanilla, mineral spa, wild berries and red 
apple) to the formulations (a five-step skin care 
system will be formulated with alpha hydroxy 
acids) to the price (20 percent below the leading 
national brand) to the merchandising (plans 
call for an outside vendor to develop customized 
displays). 

Marketing a unique line like this requires a 
much greater financial commitment than sim- 
ply creating a lookalike product, and this chain 
is now wrestling with that issue. But develop- 
ing a unique brand image for a new line can be 
almost as important as developing the line it- 
self, said Joe Busick, vice president of sales, de- 
signer store brands, CBI Laboratories. 

Chains need to develop an advertising and 
marketing strategy to spread the word to con- 


LISA |. FRIED 


New upscale lines need to 
integrate marketing, image 


HBC 


Toiletries 


sumers. “Just putting it on the shelf isn’t 
enough,” he said. 

Busick makes a valid point. In toiletries, 
the last thing consumers or drug stores need 
is another me-too product. Plus, with mass 
merchandisers grabbing up more market 
share in various toiletries categories, drug 
chains are smart to come up with unique 
store-branded lines. 

But as leading manufacturers know, sophisti- 
cated advertising and marketing programs can 
make or break a launch. If drug chains are go- 
ing to take on strong brands from national 
manufaciurers, they need to operate like them. 

But not too much like them. Procter & Gam- 
ble has recently initiated 13 trademark 
infringement suits against manufacturers 
of what it considered to be lookalike 
products/packaging. 

In 11 of the cases, the competing manufactur- 
er agreed to change the packaging, which prob- 

ably involved pulling the product off the shelf, 
going back to the drawing board and missing 
sales opportunities. 

Now Neoteric, which manufactures Alpha 
Hydrox, has followed P&Q’s lead by filing a suit 
against private-label manufacturer Cumber- 
land-Swan for trademark, trade dress and copy- 
right infringement, unfair competition and un- 
just enrichment. The suit centers on alpha- 
hydroxy acid-based products distributed 
through several of the leading drug chains. 

While national manufacturers understand 
the need for retailers to grow a private-label 
business, they’re also sending a loud message 
that they won't stand by idly while a drug chain 
or manufacturer tries unfairly to ride their 
coattails and, consequently, confuse the 
consumer. 


Neutrogena makes key exec changes 


LOS ANGELES — Change is in the air at John- 
son & Johnson’s Neutrogena division. The compa- 
ny has flattened out its top layer of management 
and is reorganizing the marketing department. 

In mid-July, Sheldon Zimbler, U.S. presi- 
dent, left the company, paving the way for 
president Jeff Nugent to assume total control 
of the division. Acting president Lloyd Cotsen 
announced he will retire Aug. 1, but he has 
agreed to remain on as a consultant. The 
moves prompted a restructuring 
of the marketing department

who spent 8 years at Lederle Consumer Prod- 
ucts, is the new vice president of sales. He re- 
places Michael Sullivan, who has a new post as 
director of the Eastern region. The company 
will not fill Zimbler’s, Kurtzman’s or Cotsen’s 
old posts.

split decision-making, but “op-

Let your store managers surprise you 


ob Tansley, recently promoted from assistant store 
manager to store manager of a Walgreens in West 
Hartford, Conn., is excited about the prospect of 
learning to speak Russian. After all, he explained, about 35 
percent of his customers are Russian immigrants; many of 
them have difficulty speaking and reading English. 
Just inside the entrance of this Walgreens—an established 
neighborhood strip mall store, not one of the bigger, atrium- 
lit, freestanding, drive- 


distinguish one chain from another in the automated, con- 
solidated, data-driven retail world of tomorrow. 

A store manager’s attitude, ethics, personal style, and 
enthusiasm (or lack of it) set the tone for the store as a 
business; the associates’ treatment of the customers will 
mirror the manager’s attitude toward those customers, as 
well as his or her treatment of the associates themselves. 

In my experience, most people have within them a great 
willingness to do whatever 


through-pharmacy proto- 
types—is a rack that holds a 
stack of handwritten, photo- 
copied flyers that translate 
the in-store specials into 
Russian. 

The flyers are neatly 
hand lettered by Tanya, 
one of the store’s two Russ- 
ian-speaking pharmacy _ 
techs. Tansley said he 
hopes to have the flyers 
typeset, once he finds a 
printer with the Russian 
alphabet. The new manager 
noted that this store does a lot of business in edibles, 
adding, “I’m looking for some Russian foods that might 
sell well here.” 


Store managers are captains on service front 


Beyond his interest in his Russian-speaking customers, 
though, what impressed me most about Tansley was his 
enthusiasm for his job and his pride in the store. He act- 
ed—almost—as if he owned it. And I think feelings of own- 
ership, pride and responsibility are qualities chains should 
treasure and foster in their store managers. 

After all, store managers are the captains on the front 
line of customer service—the quality that will ultimately 


Feelings of ownership, pride 
and responsibility are qualities 
chains should treasure 

and foster in their store 
managers. 


Marie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 


job they have to the best of 
their ability, and that’s a 
self-driven desire. But, this 
feeling can also be easily 
stamped out if an organiza- 
tion isn’t set up, first, to em- 
power people and, equally 
important, to recognize 
their achievements. 

I think you can find an 
example of an ideal manag- 
er in the movie Apollo 13. In 
it, the Ed Harris character, 
playing the head of Mission 
Control, continually defers 
to the recommendations of the respective experts working 
for him, even when—and this is wonderfully illustrated in 
the movie—those recommendations scare the daylights out 
of him. 

The head of Mission Control trusted his people, and the 
result—three astronauts rescued from certain death—is 
real-life proof that “normal” human beings, just like the 
ones in your company, can rise to challenges much greater 
than you would ever expect. If you give them that chance. 

Your store managers are the heads of Mission Control at 
your chain’s 25, 500, 1,000, or 2,000 satellites. They can 
serve your customers to a much greater extent than you 
would ever expect. If you give them that chance. 


Time to re-invent the pgatory system 


Editor’s Note: This column is based on a speech (aay COLUMN still fear—generics. In every deregulated industry, 


by Lewis A. Engman, former president of the Gener- guy 
ic Pharmaceutical Industry Association prior to his 
death on July 12, 1995. The speech, “The Generic 
Drug Marketplace: Competitive Strategies, Legal 
Challenges, and New Regulations,” was given to an 
audience at the The Food and Drug Law Institute 
on February 6, 1995, in Washington D.C. 


dam Smith once said that whenever trades 

people gather, their first topic of conversation 

is how to restrain competition and raise 
prices. However, he didn’t know of the generic 
pharmaceutical industry, which has been built on 
the idea of opening up competition and lowering 
prices. 

And we've had incredible success—not just in terms of 
balance sheets and income statements, but in terms of 
people served, prices reduced and the quality of medicine 
provided 

The pressing issue of the moment is how to make sure 
that the nation continues to enjoy the public service that 
this competitive marketplace provides. 

In my previous position as head of the Pharmaceutical 
Manufacturers Association, I worked with Senator Hatch 
and Representative Waxman. ironing out the details of 
the Waxman-Hatch Act. In return for restoring patent in- 
centives for developing new medicines lost. by the lengthy 
FDA approval process, Congress eliminated redundant 
testing of generic medicines. We all knew that the Act 
was going to increase competition in the pharmaceutical 
industry. 

No sane person could want to go back on that decision to- 
day.Consider this: if all prescriptions that could be filled 
with generic substitutes were filled with generic substi- 
tutes, patients across the nation could save almost $3 bil- 
lion a year out of their own pockets; private insurance pre- 
mium costs could fall by more than $6 billion; and the 
government could cut another $329 million from its vari- 
ous medicai cost-sharing programs. So in generic pharma- 
ceuticals, the Waxman-Hatch Act did exactly what it was 
supposed to do. 

Now, many of the brand companies feared— and some 


Lewis A. Engman 
Former president, 
Generic Pharma- 


ceutical Industry 
Association 


we've found a few old-line companies that have 
had fears of competition. Some once-prominent 
firms have faded. But the smart ones treated the 
new, open competitive environment as an opportu- 
nity, not a threat. 

That’s happening in our industry, too. Some 
brand-name companies, in an effort to be more com- 
petitive, are startiny or acquiring generic divisions 
of their own. Still, some branded companies are try- 
ing to turn back the clock to restrict the competitive 
benefits created by the Waxman-Hatch generic drug 
deregulation. 


Effective regulations must benefit public 


It is important to remember that government 
regulation itself can undermine the benefits of generic 
competition spawned by the deregulation of the Waxman- 
Hatch Act. The Food and Drug Administration has an im- 
portant role to play in setting standards for the safety, ef- 
ficacy and bioequivalence of medicines. And FDA 
regulation can be pro-competitive to the extent it assures 
the public that generic medicines are bioequivalent to 
their brand name counterparts. 

But regulatory proposals that impose new requirements 
under the guise of “harmonization” or “science,” without a 
showing of any benefit to the public to justify the added 
costs of such requirements, have the effect of undermining 
competition, and thus are no different from the efforts of 
some brand name companies to turn back the clock ana re- 
strict competition. 

Let me close with a personal statement. In the two 
decades since it was launched, the deregulation revolution 
that increased our competitiveness has prevailed over the 
status quo because it has done two things: lowered prices 
and raised the quality of goods for ali Americans.We must 
put the spotlight on reactionary attempts to turn back the 
clock and undermine the competitive benefits of the Wax- 
man-Hatch generic drug deregulation. 

We must stop perverse policies like rebates. We must 
join with the Food and Drug Administration, the Adminis- 
tration and Congress to re-invent the regulatory system 
in sensible ways.

Generics’ prospects at an all-time high 


Patent expirations, demand for more cost-effective treatments fuel growth 


By Ken Rankin 


year ago experts on 
the U.S. pharmaceuti- 
cal marketplace were 
writing another obitu- 
ary for the nation’s in- 
dependent generic 
drug manufacturers. 

After surviving the Food and 
Drug Administration’s drug ap- 
proval scandals of the 1980s, generic 
drug makers were facing what many 
Saw as an even more serious threat 
to their survival—an all-out inva- 
sion by their deep-pocket cousins in 
the brand-name drug industry. 
Many of the same research-orient- 
ed, brand-name pharmaceutical 
manufacturers who battled to dilute 
competition from lower-cost gener- 
ics for a generation were launching 
initiatives that would have the big 
pharmaceutical companies compet- 
ing in the generic business. 

The logic was simple: with man- 
aged care providers clamoring for 
more cost-effective treatment op- 
tions, and scores of big-money, 
brand-name pharmaceuticals about 
to lose patent protection, the gener- 
ic drug industry was poised on the 
brink of a major growth surge. 

During the past two years alone,

fuel generic

third-party payors and government 
agencies, as well as chain and indepen-

generic pharmaceutical market (retail and

reached $5.17 billion for the 12 months 
ending in March 1995. That represented a 
28 percent increase over the March 1994 


Generics drugs accounted for 39 percent 
of the total number of retail prescriptions 
filled in the United States in calendar-year 
1994, more than double the 19 percent —

of 1994 alone, generics represented 45

pharmaceutical industry analyst 
David Saks estimates that brand-

more than $9 billion were opened to 
generic competition. 

Other researchers report that 
patent expirations will continue to 
fuel generic industry growth for 
years to come. 

Over the next 12 months, for ex- 
ample, at least two dozen top sell- 
ers, including Abbot’s Hytrin 
(1993 U.S. sales $194 million), 
Sandoz’ Sandimmune ($198 mil- 
lion), and Stuart’s Diprivan ($128 
million), will lose patent exclusivi- 
ty and become targets for generic 
competition. 


$8 billion off patent by ’97 


An analysis by IMS America 
identified no less than 86 dozen 
brand-name pharmaceuticals with 
combined annual U.S. sales of $8 
billion that are scheduled to go off 
patent by the end of 1997. 

A separate analysis by Dillon, Reed 
& Co. projects that this year alone to- 
tal dollar sales of generics in retail 
and hospital pharmacies will jump 36 
percent to nearly $7.6 billion. 

Market analysts at Gemini Con- 
sulting, meanwhile, have all but de- 
clared unconditional generic victory 
in the battle with brand- 
name manufacturers for 
market share. Within a 
few years, they concluded, 
generics will capture 50 
percent of all U.S. pre- 
scription drug dollar sales, 
and a whopping 80 per- 
cent of unit sales. 

For their part, many 
brand-name drug makers 
seemed to have reached 
the same conclusion, and 
were ready to switch 
strategies. If they couldn’t 
beat out their generic 
brethren in the market- 
place, they’d join them 
through an ambitious new 
emphasis on mergers and 
acquisitions. 

During the past couple 
of years alone, Marion 
Merrell Dow moved to ac- 
quire the Rugby Darby 
Group, Ciba snatched up 
Geneva, AHP took over 
Elkins Sinn, and Hoescht 
struck a new strategic al- 
liance with Copley. 


‘Trojan Horse’ mergers 


The move that attract- 
ed the most attention, 
however, was industry gi- 
ant Merck’s decision to 
launch its own captive 
generic drug company, 
West Point Pharma—an 
organization that some 
predicted would soon 
dominate the U.S. generic 


market. 

But while Wall Street analysts 
were praising the pharmaceutical 
industry’s “Trojan Horse” strategy 
as brilliant, others were raising con- 
cerns that the absorption of generic 
producers by the brand-name seg- 
ment would create serious new im- 
pediments to competition. 

Federal Trade Commission an- 
titrusters launched a series of in- 
vestigations into acquisitions of 
generic drug firms, and industry 
critics charged that the real goal of 
these mergers is to reduce or even 
destroy price competition from the 
generic industry. 

As it turned out, however, the 
doomsday predictions of an immi- 
nent takeover of independent gener- 
ic drug manufacturers by brand- 
name producers proved to be 
premature, at best. 

After scaring the wits out of more 
than a few generic industry leaders, 
mighty Merck pulled in its horns 
and closed down its West Point 
Pharma operation last December. 

Shortly thereafter, Syntex’ Hamil- 
ton generic subsidiary announced 
that it was discontinuing operations 
also, and reports began circulating 
that other brand name-owned 
generic houses were in trouble. 

In commenting on these develop- 
ments at the Generic Pharmaceuti- 
cal Industry’s annual meeting earli- 
er this year, Dillon, Read analyst 
Jerry Treppel said, “The much bal- 


lyhooed entry of the brand-name 
drug companies into the generic 
drug marketplace has been a bust.” 
Although “the U.S. generic drug 
industry continues to be confronted 
with numerous challenges,” he said, 
“one of them emphatically is not the 
ability to compete...with the re- 
search-based drug industry.” 
Paraphrasing Julius Caesar, 
Treppel said, “For the brand drug 
companies it has clearly been a case 
of ‘They came, they saw, they left.’ ” 


The jury is still out 


GPIA chairman John Klein, how- 
ever, told Drug Store News that the 
jury is still out on the ability of 
brand-name pharmaceutical houses 
to make major inroads in the gener- 
ic drug industry. 

“The most successful of these 
mergers is the CIBA-Geneva 
arrangement,” but others haven’t 
worked out at all and “it’s still too 
early to evaluate th” success of 
brand-name alliances entered into 
by other companies such as Copley 
and Schein,” he said. 

Klein—who recently engineered 
the intramural merger of two of the 
generic industry’s top players, 
Zenith and I[VAX—does expect con- 
siderably more cross-pollination in 
the pharmaceutical marketplace. 

“Rather than a brand-name 
takeover of the generic drug mar- 
ket, I think we’re headed toward a

Some say the rebate rain should fall on everybody—but officials at the

will backfire on Medicaid and consumers. GPIA state affairs director Su-

Drug Store News: If brand-name drug manufacturers are asked to 
pay rebates to the Medicaid program, why shouldn’t generic companies 


Mora: Plain and simple—generic medicines lower health care costs. 
States are, however, on occasion tempted to try to squeak out an extra 
by placing rebates on the generic medicines. Un- 
fortunately, these efforts have exactly the opposite effect—they drive 
pharmaceutical prices up, not down. Rebates on generic medicines un- 
dermine generic competition, increase drug prices, and shift costs to pri- 


Drug Store News: Do you have any independent evidence to support 


Mora: In a study on rebates commissioned by GPIA in 1994, KPMG 
Peat Marwick’s Policy Economics Group concluded that “a generic rebate 
is both an inefficient and inequitable policy option for achieving sav- 
ings... The savings from use of generic drugs far outweigh the net savings

This fall, P & Gis mak- 
ing a serious move to 
build its color business, 
particularly its lip color 
business, with an inno- 
vative new formula 
they've named Contin- 
uous Color Self-Renew- 
ing Lipstick. 

And L’Oréal, which 
has built a reputation 
for marketing “star 
products,” is launching Colour Endure, a 
long-wearing lipstick which, like Revlon’s 
Color Stay, will not transfer off the lips. 

L’Oréal describes Colour Endure (SRP: 
$8.00) as “soothing, weightless lip colour 
that won’t fade, feather or bleed.” Its point 
of difference is that Colour Endure delivers 
comfort “without lessening staying power.” 

L’Oréal says it will spend $6.8 million in 
the first three months of the Colour Endure 
launch to support the brand on television 
and in print. The print ads promise that 
this lip colour “won't leave you. Just like 
true love, colour endures.” 

While the L’Oréal ads stand out for their 
playful juxtaposition of fidelity in love and 
color, Cover Girl ads encourage women to 
have some fun with their lips. 

To self-renew the new Cover Girl Contin- 
uous Color lipsticks, women have to do 
what Lauren Bacall did when she showed 
Humphrey Bogart how to whistle in “To 
Have and Have Not.” 

They have to put their lips together and not 
whistle, but press. That little pressure acti- 
vates the self-renewing process, releasing lit- 
tle color enhancers that have been stored on 
the lip’s surface in a sort of color “reservoir.” 

This is a formulation designed to deliver 
what P & G says are the three top needs of 
lipstick users: broad shade range, long-last- 
ing color and great feel. To get the word 
out, P & G says it will spend $10 million to 
support Continuous Color in year one. 

To encourage trial, P & G will send out 
promotional pre- -packs of Continuous Color 
featuring mini sizes priced at just $1.99. It 


LIZ PARKS 


Innovation the secret 
ingredient in star launches 


COSMETICS 


& Fragrances 


will do the first promotion in October and 
then again in May 1996. SRP for the Con- 
tinuous Color line is $4.25. 

If either of these two lipsticks work as well 
as they are supposed to, they could both wind 
up bringing more new users into the catego- 
ry. Women who never bother with lipstick or 
bother only infrequently may start using 
these lipsticks just because they feel so good. 

All the excitement in the lip color catego- 
ry has had a nice rub-off effect on other col- 
or segments. Face make-ups, which has had 
its own share of innovative launches, is up 
6 percent for the year to date, not a bad per- 
formance for a $777 million category. 

One of the fastest-growing segments in 
face makeup is the cream-to-powder 
brands, up 24 percent in dollar sales in 
1994 versus 1993 and up 28 percent in unit 
sales. Cover Girl was one of the first mass 
market brands to introduce a cream-to-pow- 
der formula with Ultimate Finish. Today, 
according to industry figures, cream-to- 
powder makeups account for 13 percent of 
all foundation sales. The category in mass 
barely existed just two years ago. 

Now L’Oréal is coming into the segment 
with Luminair, another “technology-driven 
formulation” that uses a new product ingre- 
dient called “aerosomes” that break during 
application to leave a soft, powdery finish 
that is never oily or greasy. 

L’Oréal uses nylon-12 in Luminaire to ab- 
sorb oil which, in turn, prevents unwanted 
oily breakthroughs. L’Oréal promises com- 
plete coverage with the first application, elim- 
inating the need for multiple layering. The 
formulation is also able to diffuse light, which 
helps minimize fine lines and wrinkles. There 
are eight shades with a $9.25 SRP. 

As part of its new global marketing strat- 
egy, L’Oréal launched Luminaire in France 
last year. In a year, it says, Luminaire has 
become the market leader. 

It has also become L’Oréal’s number-one 
line in the United Kingdom. L’Oréal will 
support the U.S. launch with a $1.2 million 
print campaign as well as with trial sam- 
ples that will retail for $1.99 SRP.

Warm weather saves category dampened by early rain on coasts 


By Lisa I. Fried 


unny weather in mid- 

Summer delivered fa- 

vorable sun care prod- 
uct sales to drug chains this 
season. But frequent rain on 
the East and West Coasts 
early in the summer hurt 
total sales, and now several 
manufacturers are predict- 
ing year-end sales in drug 
stores to be flat. 

Consumers continue to be 
concerned about the damage 
the sun has on their skin, 
and products with SPFs of 
15 or higher are delivering 
the most growth, according 
to retailers. Consequently 
several are scaling back or 
minimizing products with 
SPFs lower than 15. 

Products designed for 
sports and kids are also hot, 
and those segments contin- 
ue to grow with new product 
introductions. 

For the 24 weeks ending 
June 18, 1995, total sun 
care sales in drug stores 
dropped 6.1 percent to $95.5 
million, according to Infor- 
mation Resources Inc. Unit 
sales fell 6.4 percent to 16.1 
million. 


Volume replaces variety 


Several manufacturers 
said the unpredictability of 
sun care makes it a perfect 
category for category man- 
agement. “Retailers don’t 
have to carry the top 10 
[brands] to garnish sales,” 
said Rosanna McCollough, 
director of marketing for fa- 
cial care, Neutrogena. “If 
they devote space to the 
fastest selling ones, they can 
make it up in volume. A lot 
of retailers are getting a lot 
smarter and doing this.” 

With lower-priced lines 
showing strong sales growth,

Private label gains share 


Adding sun care products

heavy up on the number of

line to support them. “They 
want to get as much busi-

and racks.

Drug Store News, August 21, 1995 


27 


A competitive advantage 
health food retailers have 
long enjoyed when it came 
to the sale of nutritional 
products is their ability to 
respond to customer ques- 
tions. There’ are so many 
vitamins, minerals, herbs 
and assorted other chemi- 
— cal and natural “das grim 

to choose from. Without the 
help of a knowledgeable 

salesperson it can be hard 
for a consumer to select a product. 

This confusing category was made even more 
so by the Food and Drug Administration’s un- 
willingness to allow manufacturers to commu- 
nicate scientific-based product benefits. To do 
so would be considered labeling. And that 
meant the product was making drug claims. 
And that meant it would have to undergo clini- 
cal trials—a sizeable investment no manufac- 
turer was willing to undertake because most 
nutritional products were not patentable. 

This policy ensured these items didn’t grow 
much outside the realm of the health food 
stores, where retailers had the knowledgeable 
sales forces to deal with customers as opposed 
to mass retailers that needed the category to be 
more self-service. 

Things have changed considerably during the 
first half of this decade. At least some informa- 
tion about the uses and benefits of nutritional 
products has become mainstream, and chain 


Get a healthy education 
in nutritional products 


drug retailers have been able to expand their 
offerings. 

The category is becoming more self-service as 
people learn more, but that’s the tip of the ice- 
berg when it comes to the massive sales poten- 
tial these products have. And future growth of 
nutritional products will be aided by retailers 
working with suppliers on point-of-purchase ed- 
ucational materials that are now allowed as 
part of the Dietary Supplement Health and Ed- 
ucation Act of 1994. 

The easier availability of written information 
on nutritional products could be seen as a ma- 
jor blow to health food retailers’ key competi- 
tive advantage, knowledgeable service. But the 
nation’s leading nutritional products retailer, 
GNC, is already jumping into the self-service 
information game with attractive, sturdy 
binders mounted every four feet in some de- 
partments. These binders contain laminated 
pages that describe various substances and how 
they affect the structure and function of the 
body. 

For drug chains to gain a larger share of this 
fast growing category, they must offer the same 
kind of information within their nutritional 
products sections. And store associates should 
be able to answer at least basic questions as 
well. Otherwise, customers won’t buy those 
products with the funny sounding names; or 
they'll buy them where a full accounting of 
their benefits is available. Either way, the cate- 
gory would fall far short of its true potential in 
the drug store channel. 


PBM tests OTC substitutions 


YPRESS, Calif.—Treat- 
ing patients with OTC 
| drugs instead of costlier 
prescription products is the fo- 
cus of a pilot program being 
conducted by Prescription So- 
lutions, the pharmacy benefit 
management subsidiary of 
PacifiCare Health Systems. 
The objective of the program is 
to encourage doctors to switch 
patients to lower-cost, thera- 
peutically equivalent OTCs in 
appropriate circumstances. 
Scheduled for completion in 
October, the six-month test 
program will provide valuable 
decision-making data as man- 
aged care providers assess the 
changing OTC marketplace, 
Rx-to-OTC switches and 
whether these products belong 
on formularies. 


“Prescription drug market- 
ing has become so sophisticat- 
ed and widespread that pa- 
tients today are under the 
mistaken impression that for a 
medication to work it has to be 
a prescription,” said Jeff 
Herzfeld, Pharm. D., and vice 
president of marketing and 
business development at Pre- 
scription Solutions. “We be- 
lieve this program will help 
educate the consumer as to the 
therapeutic value of OTC med- 
ications. As an added bonus, it 
will also highlight the simple 
fact that you don’t have to pay 
prescription drug prices to get 
results.” 

Participants in the program 
include 29,000 patients served 
by two southern California 
clinics. 


According to Alex Gilderman, 
manager of clinical services, the 
program is not an effort to shift 
costs to patients. Since most 
health plans don’t cover the cost 
of OTC medications, those pa- 
tients who are encouraged to 
use an OTC instead of a pre- 
scription are given a coupon to 
redeem for a product or samples 
of the product to use so they 
have very little out-of-pocket ex- 
pense. 


Good response 


Thus far, the program has 
been favorably received by pa- 
tients and doctors, said Gilder- 
man, who added that many 
questions will still need to be 
answered before OTC coverage 
becomes commonplace among 
managed care organizations. 


Antacid market to digest new competition 


ith the debut of Tagamet 

HB in stores last week 

and Pepcid AC available 
now for more than two months, 
logic would seem to dictate hasty 
distribution of OTC Zantac. 
However, at press time, several 
chain drug buyers reported they 
had not been apprised of distrib- 
ution timetables or advertising 
plans for the OTC version of the 
world’s best-selling prescription 


An FDA advisory committee 
on July 13 recommended Zantac 


be available OTC. Even though 
widely expected final FDA ap- 
proval has not been granted, 
buyers said that technicality 
didn’t stop SmithKline Beecham 
or J&J/Merck from detailing 
chain accounts on their switch 
products the week following FDA 
advisory committee approvals. 
Pepcid AC was on store 
shelves five weeks after final 
FDA approval and Tagamet HB 
was available after seven weeks. 
There’s no word yet on when 
Zantac is likely to be available 


from Glaxo Wellcome. 

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly's Axid is 
another H2 product that could 
be the latest Rx-to-OTC switch. 
A joint meeting of FDA’s Non- 
prescription Drug and Gastroin- 
testinal Drug advisory commit- 
tees is scheduled for September 
29. A meeting agenda was not 
available at press time, but Axid 
could be a likely topic since the 
two advisory committees also 
met jointly to consider switch 
applications for Pepcid, Taga- 
met and Zantac.

Viewpoints 


Re-invent front end to bolster market share 


oday’s chain drug store evolved through the converg- 

ing of two different paths—the neighborhood pharma- 

cist who gradually carried more non- prescription 
products for the patient/customer’s convenience, and 
health-and-beauty-aids stores, which discovered that traf- 
fic and profits could be in- 


your business benefit if your message was more focused? 
One idea that comes to my mind is “the natural store,” a 
specialty format I visualize as “The Body Shop meets 
GNC.” This format could combine a full spectrum of natur- 
al products for both external and internal use, from vita- 
mins and nutritionals to 


creased when pharmacies 
were added. Could the time 
be coming for those two 
roads to diverge again? 

The current drug store for- 
mat evolved to serve one cus- 
tomer—the cash-paying, local- 
ly dwelling consumer. 
However , prescription drug 
decisions are increasingly be- 
ing made by third-party/man- 
aged care payors, and indus- 
try leaders are working 
diligently to create a viable fu- 
ture for retail pharmacies by 
providing a range of services that appeal to third parties as 
well as the consumer. 

While drug chains are also working to revive their non-phar- 
macy businesses in the face of market share losses to discoun- 
ters and supermarket combos (see story beginning on page 10), 
[ think they must be even more proactive than they have been 
in discovering as-yet-unforeseen possibilities for the “front end.” 

Will the spectrum of products that constitutes today’s 
drug store make sense if retail pharmacies become neigh- 
borhood health care centers, complete with booths for phar- 
macist counseling, nurse practitioners performing physical 
tests and other healthcare professionals and services being 
made available? And, at the same time, is there a future 
for some mix of the current front end in a store format sep- 
arate from the pharmacy? 

Drug chains today try to serve two masters, 
and convenience, which can lead to some “ 


health care 
strange bedfel- 


lows,” like an aisle of tobacco products and fatty, salty 
snacks across from asthma remedies and diet aids. Would 


Drug chains must be even 
more proactive than they 
have been in discovering 
as-yet-unforseen 
possibilities for the 

“front end.” 


Marie eriffin, Editor-in-chief 


shampoos and skin lotions 
to toothpaste and deodor- 
ants to fat-free snacks and 
natural sodas to cosmetics 
(which, full circle, could in- 
clude skin-protecting vita- 
mins and minerals). While 
developing store brands a 
la The Body Shop and GNC 
could be part of the strate- 
gy, a chain drug store oper- 
ator could leverage existing 
brand relationships and 
present a powerful format 
with a much broader and 
complete selection than the specialty stores currently do. 
And, most of the key drug store categories would fit this 
concept “naturally.” 

Another idea is the convenience department store, made up 
of a series of self-service kiosks. Based on scanning-based 
knowledge of each store’s customer shopping patterns, prod- 
ucts could be clustered logically—such as snack foods, OTC 
remedies, hair care, personal care, baby care, etc.—around a 
checkout to maximize speed and efficiency for the consumer. 


And, even though I am raising the question as to 
whether the pharmacy is a necessary component of the 


health and beauty care store of the future, I also know 
there are numerous ways to create a front end that’s a logi- 
cal and vital companion to the pharmacy. 

The pharmacy is not the only sector of the chain drug 
store that is seeing revolutionary change. And, as in phar- 
macy, you will only discover the real opportunities to sell 


health and beauty care products profitably in the future if 


you are willing to think out of the box today. 


Re-building the front end for the future 


Ss you review the financial reports of today’s 

successful drug chains, there’s no question 

about how critical the growth of the pharmacy 
business is to the success of the top chains. One could 
even put forth the belief for chains to put even more 
emphasis, energy and investment in maintaining the 
erowth of the prescription business, and more or less 
let the rest of the store go along for the ride. 

Not likely! The front-end is still a critical part of 
the chain drug store’s value equation to today’s con- 
sumer. But there’s no doubt a lot of confusion on 
where “up-front” can grow—and grow profitably. 

It is a part of the store’s business that needs to be 
constantly defined and re-defined both internally and 
to the customers. 


GUEST COLUMN 


Ken Banks, for- 


Berry, director of the Center for Retail Studies at 
Texas A&M University, in a recent essay for Arthur 
Andersen’s Retailing Issues Letter. One of today’s 
foremost experts on what it takes to be a successful 
retailer, Dr. Berry maintains that the stores with 4 
future for success share these four characteristics: 

1. They have a reason for being; 

2. They compete on value, not solely on price; 

3. They save customers time and energy; 

4. They are fun to shop. 

Applying these to the typical front end in to- 
day’s drug stores may hold the keys to developing 
successful strategies. Let’s take a closer look: 

Reason for being: Over the years, the front 
end has meant different things to different stores, 


It reminds me of several conversations that Ed meny of Eckerd from mini-discount stores (e.g., Longs, Thrifty 
Kelly (Eckerd senior vice president of merchandis- Drugs, is president PayLess} to simply expanded OTC and HBA cen- 
ing) and I had over the years, trying to come up ofFahligrenBenito _ ters in others.

any sense. If anything, simply calling it “the store” might quires on-going research. What were once great promotional 


have been as on target as we could get. 

After all, the pharmacy is truly a service and a health-care 
center, which puts it (rightfully) in a different class than retail 
in general. And if a “store” is a place that sells merchandise to 
customers who are willing to visit your establishment and 
give you some of their hard-earned cash for that merchandise, 
then “the store” probably is the best description. 

If you accept this premise, then talking about the demise 
of “The Store” is about as sound as saying that convention- 
al retailing as we know it is on the way out and will soon 
be replaced by some site on the information highway. That 
certainly is not the whole story. 

Actually, some stores are doomed for extinction—some 
aren't. Those “stores with a future” have some common 
characteristics, and I believe that the “front ends with a fu- 
ture” share these same attributes. 

These keys to future success are identified by Dr. Leonard 


categories and traffic-builders can now be purchased for a lot

discount or combo store at the other end of the center or across 
the street. 

It is the customer who should tell you where to focus 
your energies and shelf space. In countless focus groups 
over the years, I heard customers refer to “my drug store” 
as if it was one of their personal possessions. And in a way 
it is, especially, since many of them claim to visit the store 
one or more times every week. Reliable, convenient, easy, 
the drug store becomes part of the daily routine for many 
customers, and as that routine changes over the years, so 
must the store to maintain its reason for being.

is a key factor in a purchase decision—but it is not the only 
one. Price only puts the store on the playing field with its

Toiletries 


Future looking bright 
for sales of sunglasses 


Kudos to The Foster 
Grant Group. Seeking to 
become a valuable category 
management partner, the 
company has signed on 
with Information Re- 
sources to track sales data 
on its sunglasses lines. 
When the data becomes 
available in the coming 
months, IRI will be track- 
ing the sunglasses category 
for the first time. 

The move represents a “180-degree shift” in 
strategy for The Foster Grant Group from a fo- 
cus on distribution to a focus on growing sales, 
said Ken Shaw, 
sales for The Foster Grant Group. 

In the past year the parent company, Benson 
Eyewear, has effectively merged three separate 
sunglasses companies—International Eyewear 
and Accessories, Bonneau (which included the 
Foster Grant brand) and Optiray—into one com- 
pany, now called The Foster Grant Group. Each 
of the companies had a strong distribution base, 
and the newly consolidated company now holds a 
45 percent market share in food, drug and mass 


LISA |. FRIED 
RNID ET 


classes of trade, according to Shaw. (In terms of 


major drug chains, it currently sells Eckerd, 
CVS, Revco, Thrifty PayLess and Walgreens.) 

“There isn’t much wu: ntapped distribution there,” 
said Shaw. “We have to focus our energies on de- 
veloping and managing the category at a higher 
level in the markets we own. 1996 is the first op- 
portunity for The Foster Grant Group to market 
itself with the benefit of a full marketing cycle.” 

The company began tinkering with marketing 
this spring when it launched its first consumer 
advertising campaign in 25 years. The $2 million 
ad/promotional campaign, which ran exclusively 
in People, revived the successful “Who’s That Be- 
hind Those Foster Grants?” tagline. As a result, 
sales have more than doubled to $40 million, ac- 
cording to Shaw, and now the company is anxious 
to obtain regional and demographic sales data. 

The company has already started gathering 
POS data on its lines from some accounts and 
is consequently tailoring its product mix and 
price reductions accordingly. “We are really in- 
terested in increasing customer sales by more 
thoroughly managing the category,” he said. 
“When we do that, we are truly a category man- 
agement partner.” 

From January to May, sales of sunglasses 
rose 6 percent to $2.7 billion, according to the 
Sunglass Association of America. And despite a 
slow start this summer, sales for the rest of the 
year should be strong, report Foster Grant and 
other manufacturers. 

The growth areas of the category include frames 
made of metal, colored mirror lens treatments, 
sports frames and kids lines, report manufacturers. 


executive vice president of 


Sales of sunglasses were up 6 percent from January to 
May, and the outlook for the rest of this year looks 
bright, with the introduction of new lenses and frames. 


The number of SKUs of the old style ladies 
frames (fairly large, plastic gradient lenses) has 
shrunk, said Shaw. “They are not selling well. We 
are making room for the trend categories. Sun- 
glasses are worn for fun, fashion and protection.” 

These trends have prompted the company 
to develop several new shapes and lens treat- 
ments for 1996. It has refined its Revlon line 
with less bulky shapes and added a raised 
metal ‘R’ on the temples. It is also launching 
Blues, a line of frames with blue colored lens- 
es, which was inspired by an Italian design- 
er. It is also re-positioning its Car and Driver 
line with polarized, amber and yellow high- 
resolution lenses. 


Barbara Creations, which distributes the 
Ventura Eyewear and Hawaiian Topic sun- 
glass lines, is planning new frames with sim- 
ilar themes. On both of its lines, the compa- 
ny rolled out two shapes of clip on sunglasses 
to fit over smaller frames earlier this year. 
They have sold so well that the company just 
added two more shapes, according to Tibor 
Gross, vice president of Barbara Creations. 

The company also recently added several new 
sport styles (colored mirror lenses) on its 
Hawaiian Tropic line, created elaborate decora- 
tions on its Ventura Eyewear ladies glasses and 
introduced a line of polarized glasses (Ventura).

Drug Store News, September 4, 1995 


Nutritional 
supplements 


By Mike Troy 


h J being sol supplements are 
being sold everywhere these 
days. The category has 

moved well beyond the fad phase, 
and now, for many Americans, nu- 
tritional supplementation is an 
everyday part of life. Yet there re- 
mains untapped potential. 

As more non-users become cog- 
nizant of the health benefits of nutri- 
tional supplementation, future 
growth of the category would seem 
certain. Also boding well for future 
sales is the nation’s aging population; 
consumer research indicates that vit- 
amin and nutritional product usage 
increases as people grow older. 

Also fueling demand for products 
is the consumer press’ continuing 
fascination with all aspects of nutri- 
tional supplements and healthy liv- 
ing. New research findings on the 
health and quality of life benefits of 
various vitamins, herbs and other 
natural substances get wide play in 
newspapers and on radio and televi- 
sion. It is not uncommon, according 
to retailers and manufacturers, for 
a widely publicized story on a par- 
ticular nutritional product to create 
a run on stores that challenges the 
most sophisticated replenishment 
systems. 


Planograms and promotions 


Chain drug retailers, for the most 
part, have responded to the strong 
demand for vitamins and nutrition- 
als with expanded planograms and 
heavy promotion. The result: Drug 
store sales of vitamins totaled $962 
million during the 52-week period 
ended June 18, 1995, according to 
Information Resources Inc. (IRI). 
One year earlier, vitamin sales were 
$912 million during the 52-week pe- 
riod ended June 19, 1994. The year 
before that, they were $822 million, 
according to IRI sales figures. 

Drug stores are also holding firm 
with a 52.6 percent share of mass 
market sales. Compared to other 
OTC categories where the drug 
class of trade nas experienced some 
erosion, the vitamin category is 
holding its ground. 

Overall, the market for vitamins, 
minerals and supplements has 
grown at a compound rate of more 
than 9 percent over the past three 
years, increasing from $3.3 billion 
in 1991 to more than $4.6 billion in 
1994, according to figures cited in 
the 1994 annual report of General 
Nutrition Cos. (GNC).

“We are looking every day for new and exciting things 
from the vitamin companies.” 


—Ric Clarke, Revco 


“| would estimate that private label is doing about 
45 percent of our total vitamin business.” 


—Steve Hewes, Genovese 


“It is very important to be able to jump on a new item.” 


—Dennis Logsdon, CDMA 


“Our [vitamin and nutritional] 
sales are still up, about 10 percent 
this year,” said Revco D.S. division- 
al merchandise manager Ric 
Clarke. “There are obviously pres- 
sures to do better because once you 
get into those double-digit increas- 
es, you don’t want to go back. We 
are looking every day for new and 
exciting things from the vitamin 
companies.” 

When something does get hot or 
appears to have potential, Clarke 
said Revco will place the item on an 
endcap or a side wing. Two items 
Clarke will be watching closely are 
Sunsource’s new ginkgo biloba prod- 
uct and a new supplement getting a 
lot of press called melatonin. 

“Based on the marketing success 
Sunsource has had with other prod- 
ucts, they will be able to inform the 
public about this product and what 
it does, and we will be able to make 
some real quick incremental sales 
in the category,” Clarke said. 
“Something else I’ve been reading 
about lately is melatonin.” 

At Genovese Drug Stores, health 
and beauty care merchandise man- 
ager Steve Hewes said the chain is 
still enjoying high single-digit vita- 


min growth and strong private la- 
bel sales. 

“I would estimate that private la- 
bel is probably doing about 45 per- 
cent of our total vitamin business,” 
Hewes said. “Centrum and Thera- 
gran are still the two highest dollar 
volume brands, but they have suf- 
fered this year because the price 
point has increased to close to $10.” 

Other branded products achieving 
acceptable turns for Genovese in- 
clude the re-launched lines from 
Miles including Flintstones, One-A- 
Day and Bugs Bunny. 

“Locally, one brand that surprises 
a lot of people is Mead Johnson’s 
Poly-Vi-Sol and Tri-Vi-Sol, which 
people buy because there is a lack of 
fluoride in the water,” Hewes said. 

Genovese has grown sales by rely- 
ing on a heavy promotion schedule 
that Hewes said includes a vitamin 
or nutritional product that is “fea- 
tured in almost every print adver- 
tising vehicle.” 

Strong vitamin sales prompted 
the Chain Drug Marketing Associa- 
tion (CDMA) recently to add vita- 
mins to its new Quality Choice (QC) 
private label program. Dennis Logs- 
don, category manager for the QC 


program, said CDMA members 
have been very receptive to the pri- 
vate label offerings. The 82-SKU vi- 
tamin line became available in Au- 
gust. American Vitamin Company 
manufactures the line. 

“We decided to expand the QC 
program to include vitamins be- 
cause it is such a strong category 
for drug stores and also because 
there was a need among our mem- 
bership to offer their customers a 
value-priced vitamin alternative,” 
Logsdon said. 

In addition to a full line of vita- 
mins, there are also QC versions of 
leading brands such as Ginsana, 
Occuvite and Centrum, Logsdon 
said. He added that the program 
will be flexible in order to quickly 
add new items when they get hot. 

“It is very important to be able to 
jump on a new item,” Logsdon said. 

According to a buyer at a major 
chain, two challenges in the catego- 
ry are the ability to quickly stock 
hot new items and managing the re- 
plenishment of nutritional supple- 
ments when publicity about them 
creates surging demand. 

“There is always some medical 
study coming out that will drive one 
piece of the business forward,” the 
buyer said. “From a replenishment 
standpoint, you just have to keep 
your ear to the ground to stay on 
top of what the next trend will be. 
Most of the time suppliers know 
what is going to be hot.” 

The buyer added, “We are never 
going to compete with the GNCs of 
the world, but we need to capture 
more of the business than we have 
in the past.” 


Herbs get pumped 


Vitamins may comprise the bulk 
of sales in the broadly defined nu- 
tritional supplement category, but 
herbal products continue to be one 
of the category’s hottest segments. 
Drug and food store sales of herbals 
increased 34 percent to $124.5 mil- 
lion during the 12 months ended 
June 1995, according to Towne- 
Oller. Herbals now comprise nearly 
10 percent of sales in the $1.3 bil- 
lion vitamin and tonic marketplace 
tracked by Towne-Oller. Last year 
sales of herbals were $92.7 million 
and accounted for 7.6 percent of the 
category’s volume. 

Also worth noting is the increased 
popularity of herbs at health food 
outlets. GNC, for example, now de- 
rives 10 percent of its sales from

Splintered marketplace 


Vitamin and nutritional supplement 
manufacturers such as Lederle, Phar- 
mavite, Leiner, Miles and Nature’s Bounty 
are the chain drug industry's leading sup- 
pliers. However, because of the fragmented 
nature of the category, these five manufac 
turers account for only 40 percent of sales, 
according to the Towne-Oller figures. 

Lederle continues to be the leader of the 
pack with brands such as Centrum, Cen 
trum Silver, Centrum Jr. and the antiox1 
dant formula Protegra accounting for 12.3 
percent of vitamin sales in drug and food 
stores combined. Despite the popularity of 
the Centrum brand, e {forts LO capitalize On 
its equity with the launch of Centrum Sin 
gles met with lackluster results, according 
to retailers

the Whitehall Robins division of American 
Home Products (AHP). Lederle, which is a 
subsidiary of American Cyanamid, is now 
part of AHP since AHP acquired American 
Cyanamid last year. Added Dornbush, “We 
really don't get into the specifics of our pro 
motional plans, and we don't give out sales 
numbers

increased 1 percent during the past 12 
months.

Strategy for new items 


Sundown vitamins mar- 
keting director Andy Gray 
said the company approach- 
es new items cautiously but 
aggressively. For example, 
Sundown develops products 
in anticipation of consumer 
demand and then is able to 
quickly make them avail- 
able to retail accounts when 
mass media publicity cre- 
ates surging demand. “We 
don’t want to over inventory 
our accounts, Gray said. 
“We believe phyto-chemicals 
iS an opportunity, but the 
demand may not be there 
quite yet. We balance ag- 
gressiveness against our ex- 
pertise and understanding 
of what is happening in the 
marketplace.” 

Gray said Sundown cur- 
rently markets more than 
300 SKUs and believes 
there is room for growth. 
Household penetration 
rates can still expand, and 
the nation’s aging popula- 
tion bodes well for future 
demand.

Ginsana, Rejuvex, Garlique 
and now Ginkoba make 
Sunsource a leading player 
in the nutritional products 
category. Retailers are very

sive—$16 for the 42-count 
size—Amirault said Car- 
tilade can be source-tagged 
with either of the leading 
EAS technologies. 

Because most patients 
take shark cartilage for 
bone and joint conditions, 
Amirault said the optimum 
merchandising approach is 
to place the product in the 
natural products and anal- 
gesic planograms.

analgesic category, but we 
are not there yet,” Amirault 
said. “We are attempting to 
show buyers why it is appro- 
priate to put this food sup- 
plement next to those prod- 
ucts traditionally used for 
bone and joint conditions.”

gory s future is bright. The

ucts is expected to remain 
strong as the benefits of nu- 
tritional supplementation 
continue to make headlines. 
That bodes well for drug 
stores, the market share 
leader for these products.

Drug Store News, September 4, 1995 


G General Merchandise 


Kodak focuses on trade channels 
—and the future of imaging 


Technology is driving op- 
erational changes for all 
manufacturers, and East- 
man Kodak is no exception. 

Players in the photo in- 
dustry are riding hard on 
technology to reposition core 
product. It’s not just photog- 
raphy any more, it’s imag- 
ing, which has a wider and 
more futuristic application 
than the smaller world of 
prints and negatives. 

Like an echo of that change, a few months 
ago Eastman Kodak’s senior sales management 
reorganized along trade channel lines and 
moved, along with the consumer imaging divi- 
sion, to new offices in Atlanta. Meanwhile, 
manufacturing and consumer image/worldwide 
marketing remain on the Eastman Kodak cam- 
pus in Rochester, N.Y. 

Kodak’s Garry E. Briddon, general manager 
and vice president of the drug channel for con- 
sumer imaging, spoke with Drug Store News re- 
cently about how the structural changes came 
about—and he offered a snapshot of how Kodak 
is addressing the evolution. 


ALLENE SYMONS 


View from Atlanta 


Kodak’s June move to Atlanta signaled a new 
direction. Before the reorganization, the sales 
force was divided into zone offices, while na- 
tional accounts were serviced from Rochester. 

“The purpose of the reorganization into chan- 
nels was to provide the resources customers are 
asking for in order to move into areas like cate- 
sory management,” said Briddon. 

This is being handled through cross-function- 
al teams, with those teams sharing resources 
across different disciplines. 

A staff person will cover each aspect of the 
Kodak-retail account relationship from catego- 
ry management (including Nielsen and IRI 
analysis), through distribution and logistics, as 
well as electronic commerce through EDI and 
wire transfer of funds. 

“Most chains have identified front end store 
growth as critical to their long term success,” 
noted Briddon. “Photo is a key front end catego- 
ry, and it is getting a lot of emphasis from se- 
nior management in the drug channel.” 

“We are already seeing some results. We’ve 
begun active category work with several large 
chains and are assisting them with identifying 


Photo processing 
on aroll 


Thrifty PayLess just launched its “Rewards by 
the roll” promotion, a photo finishing-frequency 
program in which consumers earn points toward 
photo-related gifts ranging from photo T-shirts to 
photo buttons and photo watches. A brochure an- 
nouncing “Rewards by the roll” and featuring a 
$1.00-off coupon for color developing and printing 
was mailed to consumers and distributed in stores. 

The promotion was launched in conjunction 
with the current Thrifty Drugs and PayLess Drug 
Stores dual campaign offering advertised values 
at both chains in a single circular. The brochure 
also sports the new Thrifty PayLess slogan, “For 


values that are closer to home.” 


the opportunity gap that exists in the photo cat- 
egory.” If a chain has a photo category, it may 
think it is performing well. But the “opportuni- 
ty gap” becomes evident when that drug chain’s 
performance is contrasted with its competitors 
and with best-in-class examples. 

The gap—what causes those variables to hap- 
pen—is what Briddon’s group is helping several 
drug chains focus on. 


Click an image 


Kodak—in fact, the entire photo industry— 
faces the challenge of stimulating its current 
market and selling a new generation of video- 
oriented consumers on the fun, creativity and 
practicality of picture taking. 

The old term “photography” is on the way 
out, “imaging” is on the way in. Moreover, “We 
break out imaging into image taking, image 
making and image utilization, or how to add 
additional services,” explained Briddon. 

© Image taking: This includes film and cam- 
eras, or what has traditionally been called pho- 
tography. Kodak consumer marketing tries to 
stimulate picture taking through products like 
its one-time-use cameras, as well as film and 
camera launches and promotions. 

@ Image making: This aspect of imaging in- 
cludes minilabs, chemicals, paper, and services 
like new consumer mini color proof sheets. Ko- 
dak’s is called the Photo File Index System.. It 
makes reordering prints easier for the con- 
sumer than squinting at negatives. 

® Image utilization: This takes the image and 
adds utility. Examples include Kodak’s Copy- 
PrintStation as well as Fuji’s Pictrostat 300, 
and other opportunities like photo frames. For 
example, Kodak has a frame line from Inter- 
craft. Polaroid recently partnered with Boston- 


based Syratech Corp. to create a new line of 


photo frames. 

Image utilization like Kodak’s CopyPrintSta- 
tion provides immediate color (or black and 
white) prints of non-copyrighted materials in 
various sizes from either an original print or 
negatives (so it’s OK if you've lost the negative). 
The consumer can go from wallet to album size, 
up to a larger size for framing or vice versa. 

This type of service will take time to catch on, 
but as Briddon points out, once the retailer can 
get a customer to make “just one copy,” con- 
sumer education happens. That means another 
shopper has landed on the wide world of imag- 
ing and is ready to explore.

rewards just for 
taking pictures.
