New cameras sharpen chains’ photo focus 


By Allene Symons 


onsumers want to Cap- 

ture more memories in 

photos—especially 
those missed opportunities 
when someone says “I wish 
we had a camera.” 

Busy, stressed-out shop- 
pers are willing to shell out 
for easy, convenient cam- 
eras. And, increasingly, 
they want to snap moments 
that the basic family cam- 
era can't handle, like a child 
splashing in the pool or 15 
family members seated 
around a holiday dinner 
table. 

That’s why one-time use 
cameras are hot. They’re 
available almost wherever 
film is sold, affordable like a 
roll of film (ranging from $8 to 
$12), worry-free (no risk of 
theft or damage), and found in 
fun formats like waterproof, 
panoramic and telephoto. 

Most drug chains offer 
single-use cameras, along 


with an assortment of con- 
ventional cameras to satisfy 
consumers shopping for a 
point-and-shoot model in 
the $50-and-under range. 

What’s more, drug chains 
with beefed-up photo depart- 
ments and micro labs are 
finding that higher priced and 
feature-rich cameras over the 
$100 mark are also moving 
surprisingly well, according to 
reports by manufacturers and 
buyers at chains ranging from 
Genovese and Longs to 
Bartell and Eckerd. 


What’s the occasion? 


Another price-point sur- 
prise for drug chains is the 
growing popularity of one- 
time-use cameras sold for 
“occasions” in packs at prices 
around $40, like Kodak’s 
FunSaver Wedding Party 
pack. At first some buyers 
were reluctant to carry the 
packs because of the price 
point, and some still are, but 
after successful store tests

Drug chain needs 


One of the video issues 
for drug chains is how to 
consolidate video space and 
promote the product. Some 
chains like Big B and Rite 
Aid also emphasize in-and- 
out promotions of individ- 
ual titles. Chains may ad- 
just their video strategies 
as studios court the chain 
drug channel more aggres- 
sively. 

But for drug chains there 
are some hurdles when it 
comes to video promotions, 
which are geared more to 
food chains and mass mer- 
chants with large selections 
of video product.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. — 
Revco D.S. launched its holi-

S category management as complicated as some think? Or 

as simple and basic as others say? Moreover, how difficult 

is it to implement category management? And how long 
should it take? 

Conceptually, category management is a simple, basic busi- 
ness approach. Realistically, the practice of category manage- 
ment requires fundamental changes in everyday procedures, 
putting a new set of demands upon the retail organization, its 
systems and its people. It also requires a whole new way of 
dealing with manufacturer suppliers. 

The chain drug industry is in its infancy stages when it comes 
to category management implementation. However, others— 
primarily in the supermarket business—have paved the way. 


To help chains better | 
understand this leading- 
edge retailing process, 
Drug Store News turned 
to two of its leading ex- 
perts, two men who liter- 


ally “wrote the book” on 
category management: 
Brian Harris of The 
Partnering Group and 
Win Weber of Winston 
sais Stace Weber and Associates. Win Weber 
The special category management 
section starts on page 13.

Later, Ziegler explained to Drug Store News that the

“Although there’s no specific resolution on the table.” Ziegler 
added, “an association can start certain processes happening.” 

I then asked this year’s NACDS chairman, David Maher of 
American Stores, to explain his viewpoint. “Essentially, we 
must redefine the future marketplace and within that context. 
redefine the role of the pharmacist and of community pharma- 
cy,” he said. “It is my belief that this effort requires that the in- 
dustry come together—and not only community pharmacy and 
the pharmaceutical manufacturers, but academia as well.” 

To protect and foster the role of the community pharmacy as

“understands the issues and 
possible directions” from the 
vantage point of president 
and chief operating officer of 
$18-billion American Stores 
Co., parent of American 
Drug Stores. In June, Ameri- 
can Drug Stores announced 
that its year-old PBM, Rx- 
America, would be spun off 
to become a partnership be- 
tween American Drug and 
Geneva Pharmaceuticals. 
This marks the first vertical 
integration involving a chain 
(albeit through its separate PBM) and a generic manufacturer. 
(Geneva is a generic affiliate of Ciba Pharmaceuticals.) 

RxAmerica, like other chain-run PBMs, is competing 
against Medco, DPS and PCS, PBMs owned by manufacturers 
Merck, SmithKline Beecham and Eli Lilly, respectively. De- 
spite antitrust concerns voiced by NACDS and others, the 
Federal Trade Commission has allowed such mergers. So, like 
it or not, forming some sort of an alliance with a pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturer may become an accepted way of doing busi- 
ness in the future. In fact, I know that American Drug is not 
the only chain that has considered this avenue. 

The new realities of today’s health care marketplace demand 
that all segments of the industry think differently and operate 
differently. And I agree wholeheartedly with Ziegler and Ma- 
her that it is the role of NACDS to 1.) open doors for better 
communication and understanding among the various (and of- 
ten contentious) sectors of the industry, 2.) protect the role of 
the pharmacist as a valuable health care professional, and 3.) 
gather and disseminate realistic, actionable and unbiased in- 
formation that will enable all its members—large and small 
chains as well as associate-member manufacturers—to make 
intelligent, clear-eyed, decisions for their best possible futures. 


Why I believe in category management 


ment, Kevin Browett speaks from experience. Through- 
out 1994, Browett, then GMM at Kmart, began imple- 
menting category management within the $18 billion 
of hardlines merchandise, such as health and beauty 
care, sporting goods, candy, automotive, toys, table top, 
offices supplies, electronics, snacks and horticulture. 

In a later issue, Browett will detail the lessons he 
learned as he implemented category management 
at Kmart. But first, he shares his definition of cate- 
gory management and why he believes in the 
process.

strongly believe in the philosophy of category ME SUe haem Sion or “reason for being,” there can be no one sil- 
 RRERRRRRINRACRE 


management. 

One of the very first questions when discussing 
the subject is, “What is category management?” My 
definition is a very simple one. First, ignore the two 
words “category management.” Instead ask yourself, 
“What is the business I am in?” and “What does the 
customer want from my business?” You need to know 
what the customer wants and what you, as the retail- 
er, now have to deliver. 

To me, category management is no different than a basic 
business plan process. If we were to begin a business today, 
we would go through the following standard steps: 

1. Define what the business is. 

2. Define the mission statement of the business. 

3. Define who the customer is. 

4. Define what products the customers most want and 
why they want them. 

59. Confirm that the customers will continue to want 
these products and services into the future. 

6. Establish the process by which to deliver the products. 

7. Establish the process to source the products. 

8. Establish the process to distribute the products. 

9. Ultimately, sell the product to the customer. 


F. Kevin Browett 
is president of 
Browett and 
Associates, West 
Bloomfield, Mich. 


ver bullet for category management. 

Despite the challenges, I believe strongly in cat- 
egory management. Why? 

@ Today’s retail landscape mandates that execu- 
tives be able to manage across multiple disciplines 
and understand the total process and cost involved. 

@ The ability to understand customers’ wants and 
needs today, and as they evolve into the future, is an 
absolute necessity for this long-term planning process. 

e The days of trying to negotiate high/low cost and pric- 
ing is becoming antiquated. The complexity of business and 
the ability to manage at a finite level mandate what is the 
best end-to-end outcome in cost. What was a great cost ne- 
gotiation in the past may today be a bad decision when lo- 
gistics, cost of money, inventory flow, customer service and 
other components are taken into consideration. 

@ Last, but by no means least, the word “partnership” 
with the manufacturing base has been abused. The reality 
is that if both groups confront the true business issues and 
are willing to find “cost effective” ways to make it work 
both will benefit by better sales and long-term financial 
success. In most cases everyone is still looking for short- 
term results and quick fixes.

Beauty chain listens 
to what women want 


Freud, the father of psy- 
choanalysis, once threw 
up his hands in despair 
and, word has it. blurt- 
ed out something to the 
effect of “What do 
women want?” 

He might not have 


he’d had a chance to 
talk to the manage- 
ment at Ulta3. They 
seem to know what women want, at least 
when it comes to shopping, and they seem 
to have figured it out by inviting women to 
talk to them in focus groups. 

Ulta3’s management, though, has not 
only listened to women. They have reacted 
by transforming what they were told into 
brand new merchandising presentations for 
their stores. 

Their intention was, and is, to try to 
please women, particularly their target 
market of women in moderate to higher in- 
come households. These are women who 
have to spend a lot of time working hard to 
manage busy lives, active families and often 
their own careers. 

So what do such women want? Well, ac- 
cording to what Ulta3 was told, a little “es- 
cape” from the pressures of everyday life, a 
little indulgence, a little pampering. 

How could Ulta3 help women find their 
escape? Easy. Develop a prototype that pro- 
vides what Ulta3’s management calls 
“small indulgences” like one-stop shopping,

Rx-to-OTC switches 


face new challenges 


There was a time when 
new product launches and 
advertising campaigns cen- 
tered around a flimsy point 
of differentiation known as 
“new and improved.” 

In a few cases, when gen- 
uine innovation produced a 
legitimate benefit, such a 
claim may have been war- 
ranted. However, more of- 

ten than not, that wasn’t the 
case, and overuse of the ex- 
pression long ago rendered it meaningless. 

A similar situation is emerging in the OTC 
marketplace. Consumers are gaining access to 
more Rx-to-OTC switch products, and they are 
being bombarded with variations of the mes- 
sage, “now available without a prescription.” 
Even brands containing active ingredients that 
never required a prescription or haven’t re-

Viewpoints 


Industry ‘legends’ deserve recognition 


r us, Drug Store News’ Retail EXcellence (REX) Awards 
are an emotional high point because it’s our opportunity to 
help the industry honor its best. The REX retailer and 

wholesaler winners are chosen by manufacturers, and REX 
product, marketing, advertising and company awards are voted 
by the retailers, and this year, we at Drug Store News launched 
our own special recognition program, the Hall of Honors. For 
me, these awards were the most heartwarming of all. 

For their lifetime achieve- 


the self-service “revolution” in the 1950s and ’60s; an early 
adopter of retail technology, Walgreens computerized and 
automated its warehouses in the early ‘60s. 

At the precocious age of five, Irving Sapirstein (Stone) was 
stuffing postcards into envelopes in his family’s living room; 
by age 12, he was keeping the company’s books; after graduat- 
ing from high school, he became a full-time salesman for his 
father’s company, which was named American Greetings in 
1938 and went public in 


ments, we named to our Hall 
of Honors Charles R. Wal- 
green Jr., 89, who led Wal- 
greens from 1939 until 1971, 
and Irving I. Stone, 86, 
founder/chairman of Ameri- 
can Greetings. 

There are a number of 
interesting parallels in the 
careers of these two honorees, 
and of their companies. 

Both businesses were 
founded in the first decade of 
this century. Charles R. Wal- 
green Sr. studied pharmacy 
on his own and worked for a number of other druggists before 
purchasing his first store in Chicago for $6,000 in 1901. Jacob 
Sapirstein, Irving Stone’s father, started his business in 1906 
selling postcards from a horsedrawn wagon in Cleveland, Ohio. 

Both sons started in the business early and remain 
involved even in retirement. 

In 1925, at age 19, Charles R. Walgreen Jr. officially 
joined the then-65-store chain as a drug apprentice. After 
graduating from the Michigan College of Pharmacy in 
1928, he worked in various positions in the company before 
being named vice president at age 27. 

When his father died of cancer at age 66 in December 1939, 
Charles “Chuck” Walgreen Jr., age 33, was named president. 
After almost a quarter century in that post, C. R. Walgreen Jr. 
was named chairman in 1963, a title he held until he passed 
the baton to his son, Charles R. Walgreen III, in 1971. Since 
retiring, Chuck Walgreen has remained a consultant. 

Under C.R. Walgreen Jr.’s watch, Walgreens ventured 
across the border in 1946 by purchasing an interest in a 
Mexican chain (divested in 1984), and it entered Puerto 
Rico in 1960; it was one of the first chains to fully embrace 


This year, for the first time, we 
at Drug Store News launched 
our Own special recognition 
program, the Hall of Honors. 


Warie Griffin, Editor-in-chief 
A TN AMOI IEE HN EO IN AOS EA RARER ERC 


1952. 

After holding several posi- 
tions, Stone was named 
company president in 1960, 
then chairman and CEO in 
1978. Even though he 
turned over the title of CEO 
to Morry Weiss in 1987, 
Stone still serves as 
founder/chairman and 
chairman of the executive 
committee of American 
Greetings’ hoard of direc- 
tors. In fact, Stone still goes 
to the office every day, 
where he remains “the final word on every verse.” 

A last and most important link between Charles R. Wal- 
green Jr. and Irving I. Stone is the consistent growth, 
innovation and success of their respective companies. 

In the chain drug industry, Walgreens has been a consistent 
leader and innovator; in the past year alone, it passed such 
milestones as 2,000 stores and $10 billion in sales. For 20 years 
straight, it has increased its sales and earnings every quarter. 

Innovation is also a point of pride for American Greet- 
ings, which, among other things, was a pioneer in the 
installation and maintenance of card cabinets for retailers. 
Its Creative Department—of which Irving Stone was the 
first editor, writer, art director and manager—is now one of 
the largest art studios in the country. 

American Greetings boasts 89 years of consistent revenue 
growth and seven consecutive years of net income growth. 
Having passed the $1-billion mark in 1986, the company has 
already topped $1.8 billion and has its eye on $2 billion. 

For lifetimes of dedication, leadership and customer respon- 
siveness, we are proud to welcome Walgreen and Stone to our 


Hall of Honors.

the resurgence of the drug chain channel. 

Just a few hours earlier in a thought-provok- 
ing presentation by Britt Beemer, president of 
America’s Research Group, a room of attending

tion—consumers were shopping chain drug

their purchases in those outlets. This in the 


Carl Bellini, and the competitive intelligence of Jim 
Mastrian, this chain has virtually re-created itself. 
Revco and Arbor truly represent outstanding examples 
of chain drug stores that have survived fierce competi- 
tion to become more vital than ever before. 

Sharing the evening with them at REX were such 
outstanding performers as CVS, Eckerd Drug, Wal- 
greens and combo category management leader H. E. 
Butt. These chains, along with the likes of newly revi-

als like Big B, Genovese, Harco and K&B, underline 
the vitality of drug chain retailing today.

In fact, the survivors within the chain drug 
channel are looking mighty good, emerging 
stronger than ever after trial by fire; and the resiliency of our 
market has been tested and found more than equal to the task. 

This year’s REX Best Regional Chain, for example, Arbor 
Drug, hung in to outlast arch rival Perry Drug, to watch 
Kmart stumble in its own backyard, to see one-time deep 
discounting threat F&M fighting for survival and to stay 
the course against powerhouse Meijers. Under the skillful 
entrepreneurial talents of Gene Applebaum and superb 
execution by Max Ernst, Dennis Wozniak and an extremely 
able buying and merchandising team, Arbor, with record 
sales and earnings, is clearly “the little engine that could.” 

Revco, last year’s REX Comeback Chain of the Decade, 
and this year’s REX Large Chain of the Year award 
winner, epitomizes the spirit and resiliency of chain drug 
retailing. Through the management efforts of CEO D. 


traditional supermarkets under-performing in the core 

areas of pharmacy, cosmetics and health and beauty 
aids, manufacturers have become increasingly interested in 
the newly re-energized drug chain channel. 

Among those are many of this year’s Rex category cham- 
pions. These award-winning suppliers are prioritizing their 
relationships with those chain performers, willing and able 
to enter into what category management guru Win Weber 
refers to as “collaborative alliances.” 

If this year’s REX sent a message, it was that the chain 
drug industry has a bright future, a strong association to 
support it and a great publication, Drug Store News, to 
serve it. It’s been a rocky few years and problems still 
remain, but I think we’re going to have some fun in 96 and 
the years to come. 

Thanks to all the supplier and chain REX award winners 
for leading the way toward a new beginning.

Drug Store News, October 9, 1995

Pharmacy 


| WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE PERSPECTIVE 


New incentive program rules 
don’t solve ethical dilemmas 


To some pharmacy lead- 
ers, medication incen- 
tive programs represent 
a clear opportunity for 
pharmacists to secure 
their economic future 
and nail down a key 
position in the starting 
lineup of the health care 
team. 

To others, these 
“switch” programs are 
a minefield of ethical, 
moral and legal prob- 
lems for the profession. 
At the very best, they are a calculated 
attempt by commercial interests to induce 
pharmacists to engage in practices that 
they otherwise would not engage in. At 
worst, they represent outright bribes that 
enrich pharmacists at the expense of the 
public. 

To be sure, many of these incentive 
programs reward pharmacists for taking 
actions that may benefit patients through 
improved therapy or reduced costs. But 
that’s not their purpose. 

They are designed to help drug manufac- 
turers build market share and/or enable 
managed care networks to reduce their 
operating costs. If they also help patients, 
that’s fine—but it’s not essential. 

To help pharmacists pick their way 
through the ethical briar patch posed by 
these switch programs, the American Phar- 
maceutical Association released a new set 


of guidelines for participation in sponsored 
medication incentive programs. 

Among other things, the new APhA guides 
stress that such programs must protect the 
privacy rights of patients, and that both 
patients and pharmacists are entitled to full 
disclosure of all material facts before being 
asked to participate. 


No ethical guidelines 


But APhA’s guidelines fall short when it 
comes to offering pharmacists advice on 
whether participation in any particular 
switch program is ethically kosher. 

Although APhA says “the inherent 
program design must not cause any harm 
to the patient,” the guides contain no 
requirement that these incentives result in 
any benefit whatsoever to the patient. 

As long as the program rewards the 
pharmacist, it need offer no economic or 
therapeutic benefits to consumers in order 
to be ethically “acceptable” under APhA’s 
new standard. 

Pharmacists who follow these tissue- 
paper ethical standards should not expect 
to be immunized from criticism for partici- 
pating in incentive programs that are 
ultimately declared to be abusive. 

That’s clear enough from the following 
disclaimer tacked on to the end of the 
guidelines: “APhA does not assume any 
responsibility for the legality or propriety of 
any specific medication incentive programs 
that may be adopted which conform to the 
precepts of these guidelines.” 


13 


Pharmacists urge Congress 
not to end Medicaid rebates 


WASHINGTON, D.C. — 
Efforts by Senate Republi- 
cans to “sunset” OBRA ’90’s 
requirement for Medicaid re- 
bates from drug manufactur- 
ers could reduce the quality 
of care to the poor and rattle 
the “economic foundation” of 
retail pharmacy, drug store 
industry representatives 
warned Congress. 

In a joint letter to members 
of the Senate Finance and 
House Commerce Commit- 
tees, National Association of 
Chain Drug Stores (NACDS) 
president Ronald L. Ziegler 
and NARD executive vice 
president Charles M. West 
noted that the rebates which 
manufacturers pay in return 
for making their mu!ti-source 
drugs available to Medicaid 
patients have saved state pro- 
grams more than $5 billion. 

But under a plan approved 
by Senate Republicans in 
late September, the require- 
ment for these rebates would 
be cut from the law in three 
years—a change that would 
cost state Medicaid programs 
$6.9 billion, NACDS officials 
told Drug Store News. 

No similar rebate “sunset” 


provision was included in the 
Medicaid reform legislation 
passed by the House, and 
retail pharmacy leaders are 
hoping to have the Senate 
language stripped from the 
final version of the bill. 
“States cannot afford to 
lose this revenue as they 
attempt to provide quality 
health care services for low 
income and nursing home 
populations,” Ziegler and 
West said in their letter. 


Rebates contain costs 


At the same time, they 
argued that the rebate 
requirement assures that 
drug manufacturers con- 
tribute to Medicaid cost con- 
tainment, and that all pres- 
sure to lower program costs is 
not targeted at pharmacists. 

“Prior to enactment of the 
rebate program, state Medi- 
caid drug programs focused 
most of their cost manage- 
ment on reducing reim- 
bursement to community 
pharmacies,” NACDS and 
NARD said. “This approach 
did little to control overall 
program costs” because the 
“primary reason” for soaring 


Medicaid drug expenditures 
was the 88 percent jump in 


manufacturer drug prices 
from 1983 to 1993. 


Reimbursement cut? 


“Without the option of the 
rebate program, states once 
again might focus on reduc- 
ing pharmacy reimburse- 
ment to make up for the 
millions of dollars in rebates 
that they have been collect- 
ing from manufacturers,” 
the two groups said. 

Any additional cuts in 
Medicaid reimbursement to 
pharmacists “would further 
erode pharmacy’s already de- 
clining economic foundation,” 
Ziegler and West wrote. 

The drug store industry’s 
arguments are striking a re- 
ceptive chord among Con- 
gressmen from large states. 
Just last month members of 
both the New York and Texas 
Congressional delegations 
openly urged House Com- 
merce Committee Chairman 
Thomas Bliley (R-VA) to per- 
mit states to continue 


collecting such rebates even if 
Medicaid is converted to a 
“block grant” program.

section. Here are some 
innovative programs that 
drug chains are using to 
offer additional value to 
their hair color, bath and 
skin care customers. 

CVS and London Drugs 
have developed programs to 
build loyalty among hair 
color users. CVS’ frequent 
shopper program for hair color buyers offers 
customers who buy six units of hair color one box 
of hair color free. The chain is promoting the 
program on an information sheet given out at the 
register. 

London Drug has set up an 800 number 
manned by hair color experts to answer 
customers’ questions about products they pur- 
chase. This could be particularly valuable to 
first-time users who are unsure how to apply 
products and are concerned about damaging 
their hair. Callers to the hotline are asked to 
provide their name, address and product infor- 


LISA |. FRIED 


mation. Staff members follow up to see how the 
hair coloring experience worked out and later 
send them coupons for hair color. 

Given drug chains’ dominance in hair color— 
the channel garnered 51.8 percent of total 
sales last year—and the category’s solid 
growth, these chains are smart to create 
programs for this segment. 

In bath and skin care, the competition with 
other retailers is more challenging. But Wal- 
green and Del Laboratories have approached 
the challenge creatively. 

Last month, the chain created a vanilla-scented 
toiletries promotion in its circular. Customers 
who purchased $4 or more of Del’s vanilla-scented 
bath and skin products, lip balm and fragrances 
received a $1 off at the register. 

This type of effort is a win-win for both the 
retailer and the manufacturer. The program 
capitalizes on a popular scent, cross promotes 
two of Del’s brands—Naturistics and Natural 
Glow—and moves customers through different 
parts of the store. 

Given the popularity of natural scents, there 
are certainly possibilities for a promotion like 
this to include other brands as well. 


Allou seeks to buy bankrupt Russ Kalvin 


BRENTWOOD, N.Y. — 
Allou Health and Beauty Care 
Inc., distributor of health and 
beauty aids has offered $2.2 
million to buy Russ Kalvin 
Inc., a manufacturer of generic 
hair care products, which is in 
Chapter 11 bankruptcy. 

The asset-only deal is 
subject to approval by the 
federal bankruptcy court in 
Los Angeles. Russ Kalvin 
manufactures generic versions 
of leading hair care brands 
under the Russ Kalvin brand. 

For Allou, the acquisition 
would enable it to distribute 
several salon products at retail. 
It would also place the company 
in the manufacturing business 
for the first time. For Russ 
Kalvin, the deal would re-capi- 
talize the cash-strapped com- 
pany and enhance its marketing 
prowess. 


“Russ Kalvin has an excel- 
lent reputation for making 
generic salon products that 
are, in many cases, superior to 
salon products sold in salons,” 
said David Shamilzadeh, CFO, 
Allou Health & Beauty Care. 
“His combination of technology 
and quality and very high lev- 
el of service impressed me 
most about the operation.” 

“Not only are they buying our 
assets, they are re-capitalizing 
the company and putting money 
behind a marketing program,” 
said Kalvin, currently president 
of the 21-year-old company, who 
hopes to retain a post with the 
new company after a sale. (Such 
details have yet to be worked 
out. ) 

Should the court approve the 
deal, funds from the sale would 
be used by Russ Kalvin to pay 
off part of the $6.1 million it 


owes its major creditor, Foot 
Hill Capital Corp., a subsidiary 
of NorwestCorp. Russ Kalvin 
filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy 
in July after Foot Hill, its lender 
terminated its financing agree- 
ment with the company in June. 
The cash crunch slowed down 
shipping in the middle of an 
already difficult time for the 
business. In January 1994 the 
company’s Saugus headquarters 
suffered serious damage from 
the Northridge earthquake. 
Approximately $1 million worth 
of merchandise was destroyed, 
and the company had to shut 
down production for a month. 
The deal will likely affect 
the outcome of a trademark 
suit filed by Procter & Gamble 
against Russ Kalvin. That suit 
was put on hold pending the 
outcome of the company’s 
bankruptcy proceedings.

Body washes generate $200 million in sales... 


Chesebrough Pond’s 


nergizing. Revolution- 
iD ary. Explosive. Invigo- 

rating. No matter 
what term they use, retail- 
ers and manufacturers alike 
are pretty excited about the 
body wash category. 

They have good reason: 
Manufacturers report that 
this year-old category is 
enerating about 
| $200 million in 

sales, and with a 
host of new play- 
ers entering the 
fray, several pre- 
dict sales at least 
to double in two 
years. 

That prediction 
is based in reali- 
ty, assert several 
chain buyers. In 
fact “a doubling of 
sales may be con- 
servative,” said a 
' buyer at a nation- 
al chain. “If you 
take a look at 
Europe, body 
washes are the predominant 
method of washing.” 

Few manufacturers ever 
imagined that in one year 
liquid body cleansers would 
comprise a whopping 25 
percent of soap sales. The 
gains in body washes are 
hurting sales of liquid hand 
soap and contributing to flat 
sales in bar soap, say cate- 


gory watchers. 

While bar soap sales are 
flat, buyers are still pleased 
with overall soap perfor- 
mance. “Bar soap have 
always been a good leader 
item in the drug class of 
trade,” said a buyer who is 
merchandising body washes 
in the bar soap aisle. 
“People go down that aisle, 
and there is an opportunity 
to trade them up to a body 
wash.” 

As a result, some chains 
are cutting back facings of 
bar soap to add more body 
wash SKUs. Though with 
the growing number of body 
wash brands (at least 13 
were on the market at 
press-time) in the category, 
buyers can’t possibly fit all 
of them on the shelf. 

Some chains are carrying 
only those brands offered by 
bar soap manufacturers. 
Others are stocking the 
biggest sellers (Oil of Olay, 
Jergens, Dove and Caress 
comprise the top four). “If 
you have nine brands, you 
will cannibalize all the oth- 
ers,” said a buyer from a 
mid-sized chain, who is only 
carrying the best-selling 
brands. 

Still others are carrying 
several brands but display- 
ing them in different parts 
of the store. Revco is carry- 


ing seven brands: Oil of 
Olay, Dial, Jergens, Caress, 
Dove and Calgon brands are 
displayed next to commo- 
dity bath products. Across 
the aisle, the chain has 
several SKUs of Vaseline 
Intensive Care’s new body 
wash to the left of bar soap. 

To the right of the bar 
soap, the chain has a 
moisturizing body wash 
shelf talker over additional 
SKUs of Caress, Dove and 
Oil of Olay to call attention 
to the category. The shelf 
talker urges consumers to 
“experience skin that feels 
clean, moisturized, ever 
younger every day.” It also 
indicates that more body 
washes are located in the 
bath aisle. 

At the Genovese Drug 
Store on Manhattan’s Up- 
per East Side, Vaseline In- 
tensive Care, Jergens, Oil of 
Olay, Dial, Dove and Caress 
body washes are merchan- 
dised together within a 24- 
foot bath aisle that includes 
upscale bath brands, such 
as Sarah Michaels, Yardley, 
San Francisco Soap Co., 
Lissee and Naturistics. 
Calgon’s body wash is 
ae next to other Calgon 

ath products. 

The body washes “are 
doing wonderfully” and 
building more traffic in the 


bath department, said Su- 
san Carfagno, head cosmeti- 
cian for the store. “Once a 
few people are in the de- 
partment, others walk over 
to see what they’re looking 
at. Before you know it, there 
are six people in the aisle.” 
Indeed, the advent of 
body washes doesn’t appear 
to be cutting into sales of 
traditional bath products. 
For example, sales of

category in August, Chese-

showering habits. When

that this “skin-friendly” 
product would moisturize 
skin as it cleanses (36 per- 


cent), leave skin 
softer (21 percent)

mind, Chese- 
brough-Pond’s 
launched Vaseline 
Intensive Care

Wash, which is 
geared for women 
and families, with 
men as a secondary 
target. The product 
uses “silicon despo- 
sition technology” 
to deposit vitamins 


A and E, alpha 
hydroxy acid, es- 
sential fatty acids, glycerine 
and dimethicone on the sur- 
face of the skin during the 
wash process. Together these 
ingredients work to gently 
cleanse the skin and 
immediately relieve dry skin, 
according to the company. 
Another unique aspect of 
the product is the suction- 
cup/bracket device on the 
back of the bottle designed to 
enable the consumer to stick 
it right on the shower wall. 
The company, a leader in 
both the skin and bath cate- 
gories, is cross-promoting 
the body washes with its

Vaseline Intensive Care lo-

Drug Store News, October 9, 1995 


IVE Merchandise 


AG, Hallmark spearhead 
research for drug chains 


Greeting card companies 
have a big stake in drug 
chain survival. It’s not sur- 
prising that both American 
Greetings and Hallmark/Am- 
bassador are spending money 
on research and efforts to 
strengthen the front end of 
drug chains, even when it 
doesn’t have a direct hook to 
P\Gas avait hye their own products. 

mus =e Se Suppliers rightly 

conclude that if a chain 
grows front end traffic, then it grows the social 
expressions business. 

This is the flip side of today’s trend toward 
chain-specific customizing of promotions and mer- 
chandising: By sharing results of industry studies 
and sponsoring “think tanks,” vendors help 
strengthen the larger retail channel with the re- 
sult that, as they say, a rising tide lifts all ships. 

An example is the Retailer Research Council, 
established in April by the National Association 
of Chain Drug Stores (NACDS) and American 
Greetings with the goal of exploring critical is- 
sues facing the front end of drug stores. This is 
an action-minded group of nine charter mem- 
bers from chains around the country, ranging 
from K&B’s Lance Clark in the Southeast, to 
CVS’ Bob Fiorelli in the Northeast, to Snyder 
Drug’s Phil Perkins in the Upper Midwest and 
Dan Wilson of Longs on the West Coast. Other 
charter members include Steve Oliva of Hi- 
School Pharmacy, Mark Griffin of Lewis Drugs, 
Jim Harrison III of Harco and Nat Lipsyc of 
Medic Discount Drug. 

Last year, AG worked in concert with FMI 
and the food industry to conduct a study with 
the University of Chicago Graduate School of 
Business, in which executives from 38 super- 
market and 24 drug chains were interviewed 
about they grow their GM/HBC business. 

The result was a best practices survey called 
“How the ‘Best’ Grow their GM/HBC Business.” 
Findings point clearly to the shift from item- 
based buying to category-based marketing, with 
a focus on consumer demand and behavior. 

Among other findings: Nearly 50 percent of 
the drug stores surveyed say the best descrip- 
tion of their store image js convenience, primar- 
ily meaning that their store is close to their cus- 
tomers’ home or work. 

The top GM/HBC goal of half of the drug 
stores surveyed was growing/maintaining mar- 
ket share. Increasing gross profit dollars was 


the top goal for 25 percent. 

Some 65 percent of the drug stores use a high- 
low pricing strategy. On the local level, nearly 38 
percent of the drug stores can make store-level 
price changes instantly, and in 65 percent of the 
stores, the store manager can change prices in re- 
action to local competition. 

More than a year’s worth of historical scan- 
ner data is available to 57 percent of the drug 
stores; updates are available on a weekly basis 
for 50 percent. Only some 29 percent have ac- 
cess on demand. 

For a copy of the report, contact: Sara Eames, 
American Greetings Marketing/Public Rela- 
tions, (216) 252-4947. 


Seasonal consumers 


In a rather different approach, Hallmark/Am- 
bassador recently tackled a study of consumer 
preferences in seasonal purchasing and came up 
with discoveries about consumer needs. To pre- 
sent its findings, Hallmark/Ambassador spon- 
sored seminar on Consumer Trends-Seasonal Cel- 
ebrations at NACDS Marketplace in June. 

Some findings of the study, which included 
1,130 questionnaires and in-depth interviews 
with 37 drug store shoppers about how they 
shop seven major holidays, were—to jump to 
the bottom line—that retailers should market 
to the consumer, not the season. 

The study assessed consumer motivation, ac- 
tivities and purchases and concluded that con- 
sumers shop seasonally to satisfy four com- 
pelling needs, which are: 

@ Connecting traditions, celebrating family 
and tradition, often involving children, and in- 
cluding in many cases activities with religious 
meaning. 

e Appreciating others and expressing holiday 
cheer. 

® Creativity, self expression and originality 

e@ Fulfilling obligations, which includes con- 
cern with appearances and self-image and com- 
pensation for childhood disappointments. 

There are also multiple motivations involved 
in holiday celebrations. In addition, the study 
showed that 80 percent of consumers expressed 
a desire to relax during these holiday periods, 
so relaxation is a component in marketing to 
the seasonal shopper. 

For a copy of this study, which gives exam- 
ples based on Hallmark/Ambassador’s drive 
time marketing strategy, contact Mindi Ellis at 
(816) 274-5883.

Viewpoints 


Relationships require a tender touch 


You can't do it alone. That’s what the chain drug store in- 
dustry should have learned during the arduous, pressure- 
filled restructuring period of the past few years. 

For the most part, drug chains that survive today have 


more clout in terms of their financial strength and number 


of locations than they had five years ago. But along with 
clout comes power that must be wielded very carefully; you 
may now be in the position of making or breaking a prod- 
uct, a supplier or a category. 


which will directly undermine the supplier’s efforts to up- 
grade the category. 

At this critical juncture, the category could continue its 
slide into a commodity position, or it could be rejuvenated, 
presumably by this supplier, which has a leading position 
and is willing to invest in product development, marketing 
and merchandising. Besides the licenses, the supplier is 
bringing some genuinely original everyday display pieces, a 
program of seasonally ori- 


Despite all the verbiage 
given to the concept of 
“partnerships,” chains don’t 
always act as if they consid- 
er their suppliers to be long- 
term allies. Old habits die 
hard. The problem is that 
when it comes to the sensi-

way of undermining hard-

reputations.

A supplier is trying to bring a whole new level of fashion 
and promotional activity to what has been an everyday, ba- 
sic category for drug chains. While this category does have 
an element of fashion—specialty retailers have really 
jumped on it—that aspect has yet to be maximized at the 
mass level, which has continued to use the commodity ap-

1995 issue of Drug Store

mative. You both ask all 
the right questions. 


The lean toward catego- 
ry management is an is- 
sue to face everyone in the 
grocery and drug store 
field. | am not writing this 
as a Kroger manager. 
This is my personal view 
of a very informative, 
well-timed article. 

One issue still to be 
faced was touched lightly 
on: Will a supplier work 
well when his category 
does not correspond with 
our demographic needs? 
The old partnership is

Yet the biggest issue

Again your article has

ented freestanding displays, 
and some product introduc- 
tions that actually break 
new ground in the category. 

Actually, my opinion is 
that this supplier will be 
wildly successful in rejuve- 
nating the category—and 
that the drug chain will be 
sorry if it goes ahead with 
its direct-import plans. But 
that’s not my point. 

What bugs me is the 
chain’s mindset, which 
seems to be that once sup- 
pliers have set a category in motion—with great effort and 
investment, no doubt—it’s fine for the chain to develop a 
knockoff line, either through a private label or by direct im- 
porting. 

3y such actions, a chain says two things to a supplier: (1) 
“What the supplier has been doing wasn’t worth what I was 
paying, and (2) “Even though this category isn’t my core 
business, I know better.” 

There’s a place for both private-label and direct-import 
products in the drug store mix, of course, but they must be 
used strategically and in moderation. Too many categories 
with good potential have been eviscerated by retailers that 
decided to do it themselves or shift to another supplier with 
a better “deal” rather than work with the supplier who 
worked with them to build the business in the first place. 
Without retailers in their court, many innovative suppliers 
have neither the wherewithal nor the motivation to grow a 
business. 

Sure, a decision like the one to direct import one category 
of merchandise is a small one. But the big-picture issue is 
one of trust. If drug chains really want to develop partner- 
ships, they better make sure they develop trust first. Too 
many times, by their “little” actions, chains undermine the 
essense of what makes relationships work in the big pic- 
ture and the long term. 

Trust might not show up on a balance sheet, but it’s not 
“warm, fuzzy” stuff. In today’s retail environment. no one. 
no matter how smart or big—and that includes Wal-Mart 
with its sales of some $90 billion—can succeed alone. 

Keep that in mind every time you sit down with your sup- 
pliers. And every time you consider doing it without them.

But while prescription 
pharmaceuticals are becom- 
ing increasingly important 
to wholesalers (last year 
they accounted for nearly 82 
percent of total industry 
sales), the same is not true 
for over-the-counter drugs. 

In 1991 non-prescription 
drugs represented 11.5 per- 
cent of the average whole- 
saler’s total dollar sales. By 
last year OTCs dropped to 
only 9 percent and had de- 
clined for three straight 
years. 

Even more dramatic is 
the effect of consolidation on 
the U.S. wholesale drug 
industry. In 1980 no less 
than 139 full-service drug 
wholesalers were available 
to provide products and 
services to retail pharma- 
cies across the country. 

By 1993 the total had fall- 
en to 70, according to 
NWDA, and last year seven 
more wholesale druggists 
passed from the scene. 


Super wholesalers 


The end result of this con- 
solidation has been the cre- 
ation of a small group of 
super-wholesalers that dom- 
inate the industry and com- 
pete with several dozen 
smaller firms seeking to 
carve a niche in the market. 

Together, the six largest 
wholesale druggists account 
for over 80 percent of total 
industry dollar sales. Here’s 
how they stack up now: 

McKesson held on to its 
traditional slot as the na- 
tion’s largest drug wholesaler 
by posting a solid 8.9 percent 
sales gain to $10.6 billion for 
the 1994 calendar year. The 
San Francisco-based compa- 
ny now accounts for 21 
percent of all U.S. wholesale 
drug sales. 

Bergen Brunswig posted 
a 7.7 percent sales gain last 
year that brought the Los 
Angeles-based wholesaler’s 
total revenues to almost $9.4 
billion in calendar year 1994. 

No. 3 Cardinal Health 
racked up the largest dollar 
sales gain of any drug whole- 
saler during calendar year 
1994, as gross sales jumped 
33 percent from $5.2 billion 
to $6.9 billion. 

FoxMeyer had a tough 
year in 1994 as reflected in 
the company’s 3.5 percent 
sales decline from $5 billion 
to $4.8 billion. Officials at 
the Carrollton, Texas-based 
wholesaler say the company 
is now back on track, with 
sales rebounding to $5.2 bil- 
lion for the 1995 fiscal year. 

AmeriSource solidified 
its position as the nation’s 
fifth largest wholesale drug- 
gist on the strength of a i2 
percent sales increase to 
$4.3 billion last year.

Note that these charts represent only a portion of the category management 
presentation prepared by Gladson & Associates. 


basing your case on indisputable facts 


A major stomach remedy manufacturer asked us to perform a comprehensive 
brand performance analysis. They felt a particular mass retailer had allowed 
the category to deteriorate, but needed a thorough review first. 

We examined three years of category data, broken out by brand, form, 
size and flavor. This allowed us to view the category’s performance as a three- 
year movie, instead of a simple snapshot of recent activity. From this analysis, 
we found several things needing improvement. The category overall was in 
disarray: some products were inappropriately spaced and category blocks were 
unclear. Without needed changes, this category would continue to experience 
lost sales opportunities. 

The result was a convincing case for realigning the category, which was 
presented to—and accepted by— the retailer. 


How shiny are 
your shoes? 


When you go before a retailer, you 
need to put your best foot forward— 
and the bigger the retailer, the shinier 
the shoe. 

For a presentation, your best foot 
is carefully culled data; it’s what gives 
you credibility. The shoe is how well 
that data is presented. The top retail- 
ers expect polished, professional pre- 
sentations. It’s what they’re used to, 
so anything less suggests you aren’t 
taking them seriously enough. 

If you don’t have the resources to 
make this happen—both reviewing/ 
processing the data and presenting it 
clearly and professionally, then you 
need someone who does. 

This is where Gladson and Asso- 
ciates really gets down to business, be- 
cause for 25 years we’ve been distill- 
ing mounds of data down to those key 
points that will mean the most to our 
clients and the retailers. And we have 
the capability to make those points 
jump out and be noticed. 

We do it because that’s what it 
takes to keep our clients on top. 

It shows in our planograms, it 
shows in our diversity of services, and 


it shows at the retailer’s cash register.

Drug Store News, September 18, 1995

Antacids can still be 
H2 blockers’ Achilles heel 


H2 blockers Tagamet HB 
and Pepcid AC already 
command a combined mar- 
ket share of about 40 per- 
cent, and Zantac 75 and 
Axid aren't even on the 
market yet. However, all is 
not lost for antacids 
because they have a 
distinct product benefit 
that has not yet been com- 
municated to consumers. 
Onset of action is some- 


thing heartburn sufferers and chain drug 


retailers will be hearing a lot more about as 
antacid manufacturers leverage this product 
benefit and attempt to regain lost market 
share. 


Fast onset of action 


The phrase, onset of action, is medical termi- 
nology for how fast a drug starts working. 
Antacids such as Mylanta, Maalox, Tums and 
Rolaids provide relief by absorbing excess stom- 
ach acid, and they can begin working almost as 
soon as they hit the stomach. H2 blockers on 
the other hand take longer to relieve heartburn 
because they work systemically. They have to 
dissolve in the stomach and be absorbed before 
they can alleviate heartburn symptoms by 
inhibiting the production of stomach acid. Sure. 
H2 blockers provide long-lasting relief, but they 
cant document with clinical data that they 
relieve heartburn as quickly as antacids. 

Heartburn sufferers will have a choice to 
make. Opt for the quicker relief and frequent 
losing of antacids or the longer lasting and 

ore infrequent dosing available with H2 


blockers. My bet is serious heartburn sufferers 
ideally want both, but how quickly a product 


works will weigh heavy on the minds of 


consumers at the point of purchase. That’s good 
news for antacids since onset of action is really 
the only advantage they have over H2 blockers. 

Advertising for SmithKline Beecham’s Taga- 
met HB already stresses its dosing superiority. 
One dose of Tagamet HB reduces more acid 
than eight spoons of Mylanta, according to 
SmithKline Beecham ads. 

Johnson and Johnson could answer that ad 
soon with one of its own demonstrating Mylan- 
ta’s superior onset of action. At press time, a 
clinical study documenting such a claim was 
scheduled to be presented at a mid-October 
meeting of the American College of Gastroen- 
terology. 


Competing against themselves? 


How Johnson & Johnson uses the informa- 
tion will be interesting. J&J and other manu- 


facturers of H2 blockers also produce some of 


the leading antacid brands. The challenge they 
face is to demonstrate the benefits of their 
respective antacid products without undermin- 
ing their own H2 blocker. 

In the end the biggest beneficiaries will be 
chain drug retailers. When all four H2 blockers 
are available in early 1996, the category will go 
crazy with advertising and promotions and the 
digestive remedies buyer will be the envy of the 
buying staff. As for the category’s overall prof- 
itability, it will go the same phase as did anal- 
gesics when Aleve was introduced. The enor- 
mous amount of money spent on promoting new 
and existing brands will leave store brand 
antacids sitting on shelves to collect dust. 


Phar-Mor/Sundown pairing 
boosts vitamin sales 


SWITCHES 


ASHINGTON, D.C. — The new OTC 

ketoprofens from Bayer Consumer Care 

and Whitehall Robins are expected to set 
a new Rx-to-OTC switch record for time from 
FDA approval to arrival on store shelves. 

Both companies were notified of their Rx-to- 
OTC switch approvals Friday, Oct. 6, creating an 
unprecedented marketing situation as the two 
analgesic powerhouses seek a competitive ad- 
vantage. Bayer’s version of ketoprofen will be 
called Actron and director of medical affairs 
Steven Weisman said shortly after FDA ap- 
proval that “within weeks” the product would be 
available. “We are working quite aggressively to 
bring it to market as quickly as possible.” 

Whitehall Robin’s OTC version of ketoprofen 
will be called Orudis KT and at press time compa- 
ny officials declined to comment on its availability. 

Whenever the products hit store shelves, 
retailers can expect continued high levels of 
promotional activity, which haven’t subsided 
following the introduction of Aleve nearly 18 
months ago. Orudis KT and Actron are likely to be 
heavily supported. If there is a downside to all the 
switch activity, it is the impact on retailers’ private 
label sales. If the market reacts as it did to Aleve’s 
introduction, retailers can expect further 
weakening of private label analgesic sales. 


ASHINGTON, D.C. — Nicorette smok- 

ing cessation gum and the H2 Blocker 

AXID are headed for OTC shelves. The 
Food and Drug Administration’s Nonprescrip- 
tion Drugs Advisory Committee at a late 
September meeting favorably recommended both 
products be available without a prescription. 
Retailer availability hinges on final FDA 
approval and manufacturer marketing plans. 

Axid will be the fourth H2 blocker to enter the 
market, and it will be marketed by Whitehall 
Robins for the prevention of heartburn. Pepcid AC 
is also able to claim prevention along with treat- 
ment. Tagamet HB and Zantac 75 are indicated 
only for the treatment of heartburn. 

Nicorette will be marketed by SmithKline 
Beecham, and according to testimony at the FDA 
hearing, it will carry a hefty retail.
